paragraphs.text:
FROM DIOCLETIAN TO MICHAEL AND THEOPHYLACT HIS SON

Year of the world [?]. Year of the divine incarnation 27[?].
Diocletian, emperor of the Romans, year 1. Varahran, king of the Persians, year [?]. Gaius, bishop of Rome, year 7. Hymenaeus, bishop of Jerusalem, year [?]. Theonas, bishop of Alexandria, year [?]. Tyrannus, bishop of Antioch, year 2.

Year of the world 5780. Varahran, king of the Persians, year [?]. In this year Diocletian appointed Maximian Herculius as partner in his rule, in the fourth year of his own reign.

Year of the world 5781. Narses, king of the Persians, year [?].
Year of the world 5782. In this year Diocletian and Maximian Herculius razed to the ground Busiris and Coptos, cities in the Thebaid of Egypt, which had revolted from the Roman [rule] …

Year of the world 5785. In this year Diocletian and Maximian Herculius made Constantius and Maximian Galerius Caesars. Diocletian gave his own daughter in marriage to Galerius, and Maximian Herculius joined his own daughter Theodora to Constantius, even though each of them already had a wife; these they put away for the sake of their [kinship?] with the emperors …

Peter the hieromartyr, bishop of Alexandria, year 1. In this year Alexandria and Egypt, led into revolt by Achilleus, could not withstand the Roman assault, in which very many were killed, the [leaders] of the revolt paying the penalty …
Year of the world 5787. In this year Diocletian and Maximian Herculius stirred up a great and most terrible persecution against the Christians, and …

In this year, when a rebellion broke out in Gaul under Amandus and Aelianus, Maximian Herculius crossed over and put them down. But Crassus also revolted and seized Britain, while the Five Peoples seized Africa and Achilleus seized Egypt. Crassus held Britain for three years and was then killed by Asclepiodotus the prefect. In Gaul, against all expectation, Constantius Caesar's fortune turned right around. Within six hours of the same day he was seen first defeated and then victorious. The Alans had just overwhelmed Constantius' army and chased it right up to the walls. He himself was following last behind his fleeing army. The gates were shut and he could not get inside the wall, and the enemy were already reaching out their hands to seize him. But [the defenders] let down ropes from the wall and hauled him up. Once inside, he put fresh heart into the army, sallied out against the Alans and won a brilliant victory, in which six thousand fell. Maximian Herculius overcame the Five Peoples in Africa, and Diocletian put down Achilleus in Alexandria. With him was

also Constantine, the son of Constantius, who was still very young and distinguished himself in the wars. When Diocletian saw him, he was moved by envy and sought to kill him by treachery. But God wonderfully saved him and restored him to his father.

Year of the world 5789. Hormisdas, king of the Persians, …

Miltiades, bishop of Rome, year 1. Zabdas, bishop of Jerusalem, year [?]. Vitalius, bishop of Antioch, year 1. In this year Veturius, commander of the camp, began to drive the Christians out of the army, at first moderately, while from then on the [persecution] against all was smouldering …

In this year Diocletian sent Maximian Galerius against Narses, king of the Persians, who was at that time overrunning and plundering Syria. Galerius engaged him, lost the first battle near Callinicum and Carrhae, and fled. On his way back he met Diocletian riding in a carriage. Diocletian would not receive the Caesar in his own regalia, but made him run a long way ahead of the carriage. Later a large force was gathered, and Maximian Galerius Caesar was sent out again to the war against Narses. This time fortune was on his side, and he dared and achieved what no one else had. He pursued [Narses as far as inner Persia?], slaughtered his entire army, and captured his wives, children and sisters, along with everything Narses had brought with him, his stores of treasure, and the notables among the Persians. When he returned with all this, Diocletian, who was staying in Mesopotamia,

received him [splendidly?] and honoured him. Individually and all together, these men fought against many of the barbarians and achieved many successes. Elated by the good course of affairs, Diocletian demanded that the senators prostrate themselves before him, and would no longer be addressed in the earlier manner. He even adorned his footwear with gold, pearls and precious stones.

Constantine, the son of Constantius, was living in the East and in Palestine and held Christian beliefs. Galerius Maximian saw him advancing in understanding, in bodily strength and in his natural gift for learning. Divining that he would be the destroyer of his tyranny and of his beliefs, he planned to kill him by treachery. But by divine providence Constantine learned of the plot and, like David, found safety in flight and escaped to his own father, giving much thanks to Christ, who had saved him.

Year of the world 5794. In this year Galerius Maximian was won over by Theotecnus the sorcerer while he was sacrificing to demons and seeking oracles. Theotecnus slipped into the cave and gave him an oracle demanding a persecution of the Christians. He also fabricated 'Memoirs' of the Saviour and sent them everywhere as an insult, and ordered schoolmasters to teach them to the children, contriving to make our mystery a laughing-stock.

Year of the world 5795. Sapor, king of the Persians, …

In this year imperial decrees were issued ordering that the churches of Christ be razed to the ground and the divine books burned, and that priests and all Christians be handed over to torture and compelled to sacrifice to idols. This persecution was the most terrible of all, [producing] countless martyrs …

… Maximian Herculius [by agreement?] laid down the imperial power and took up the dress of private citizens. Diocletian lived as a private citizen at Salona in Dalmatia, his own city, and Herculius Maximian in Lycaonia [Lucania]. First, however, they celebrated a triumphal procession in Rome, in which the many carriages of Narses were paraded, along with his wives, children and sisters. After this they retired and lived on their own. In their place they had appointed Galerius Maximian to reign over the East and Constantius over the western regions. Constantius was content with a small part of the empire and was very gentle and good in character. He took no trouble to fill the treasury, but preferred his subjects to keep the wealth, and he was so restrained about acquiring money that he even put on public festivals and honoured many of his friends with banquets. He was greatly loved by the Gauls, who compared him with the harshness of Diocletian and the murderousness of Maximian Herculius, from whom they had been delivered through him. He died in Britain after reigning eleven years [?]. While still alive, in the sight of all the people, he [proclaimed?] as emperor in his place Constantine, his firstborn son, although his other sons were also living: Constantine's half-brothers on the father's side, namely Constantius and Hannibalianus, also called Dalmatius, who were born of Theodora, daugh-

ter of Herculius. Constantine was the son of Helena, Constantius' first wife. Constantius, their father, was a grandson of the emperor Claudius through his daughter, and Galerius was Diocletian's son-in-law through his daughter Valeria. Then Galerius Maximian came to Italy and appointed Caesars [?], putting Maximinus, his own son, over the East and Severus over Italy. The soldiers in Rome proclaimed Maxentius, the son of Maximian Herculius, emperor. At this Herculius was seized once more by a desire for the throne. He tried to strip his own son Maxentius of power, and he also tried to kill his son-in-law Constantius by treachery. In his attempt against his son he was driven off by the soldiers. In his attempt against his son-in-law he was denounced by his daughter [?], and was put to death, having fared badly. Eusebius of Caesarea says that Diocletian went mad, laid down the imperial power together with Herculius, and took up a private life; Herculius ended his life by hanging, while Diocletian wasted away, consumed by a long illness. Gelasius, bishop of the same Caesarea, says that they repented of their abdication, wanted to reign again, and were put to death by a common vote of the senate. With these men out of the way, and with the Christian-minded Constantius dead, the imperial power, as I said before, was held by Constantine Augustus and Maximian Galerius.

Year of the world 5797. Constantine [?], emperor of the Romans, year 1. Philogonius, bishop of Antioch, year 1. In this year the most divine and most Christian Constantine became emperor of the Romans in Gaul and Britain. At the same time four others were reigning alongside him: Maximian Gal-

erius, with two Caesars, Severus and Maximinus the son of Galerius, and Maxentius the son of Herculius, who had been proclaimed emperor in Rome by the soldiers. These men vied with one another in persecuting the Christians. Maxentius the tyrant, reigning lawlessly in Rome, committed every kind of terrible wrong: adultery with the wives of men in office, murders, robberies, and everything of that sort. In the East Maximinus was doing even worse, so that two very great evils had [divided?] East and West between them and were fanning the persecution against the Christians into flame. At that time the Romans also proclaimed Licinius Caesar, as a favour to Constantine. Licinius was Constantine's brother-in-law, married to his sister Constantia, and he falsely pretended to share our faith. Severus, evidently, had died. In the same year Peter, bishop of Alexandria, who was in prison, was beheaded by order of Maximian Galerius and his son Maximinus and died a glorious martyr. It was he who had excommunicated Arius, a deacon of his church. Arius later became the champion of a heretical sect and drew many away from true religion. Under these tyrants many others also won the martyr's crown for Christ. Among them were Phileas, bishop of Thmuis in Egypt; Peleus and Nilus, bishops in Egypt; Anthimus, bishop of Nicomedia; Tyrannion, bishop of Tyre; Silvanus, bishop of Emesa; and Silvanus, bishop of Gaza; Lucian, presbyter of Antioch; [?]

(55) Sozomen, Book I, chapter [?]: 'Arius, who was thought to be zealous for doctrine, at first sided with Meletius in his innovations. Then he left him and was ordained deacon by Peter, bishop of the Alexandrians, but was again expelled from the church by him. When Peter excommunicated Meletius' followers and would not accept their baptism, Arius criticised what was being done and refused to keep quiet.'
and again he was expelled from the church by him. When Peter excommunicated Meletius' followers and would not accept their baptism, he criticised what was being done and refused to keep quiet.

Paulinus, bishop of Antioch, year [?].

Year of the world 5802. In this year the most divine Constantine rose up for the [war] against the tyrants …

[Apparatus:] 'bishop'] 'presbyter' A. … [?] 'many' vulg. 'to taste' … 'his' A. 'the' added from A. 'restless' [?] g. 'the' omitted in A.

[?]. Maxentius the impious bridged the river that flows past the city of Rome with boats and drew up his army against the great Constantine. The great Constantine was afraid of Maxentius' sorceries, for Maxentius cut open infants to use them for divination. While Constantine was in great anguish, at the sixth hour of the day the precious cross appeared to him, formed of light and bearing the inscription: 'By this conquer.' And in a vision of the night the Lord stood beside him and said, 'Use what has been shown to you, and conquer.' Then he had a golden cross made, which survives to this day, and ordered that it be carried before him in the war. When battle was joined, Maxentius' forces were defeated and very many of them were killed. Maxentius fled with the rest, but the bridge was broken apart by divine power and he was drowned in the river, like Pharaoh of old [?], so that the [river?] was filled with horses and their riders, drowned together. The citizens of Rome, who had asked for him to come to their help [?], were set free from the tyranny of the wicked Maxentius. They garlanded the city and joyfully welcomed the victorious Constantine with the victory-bringing cross, acclaiming him as their saviour.

Year of the world 5805. In this year Constantine, whom God aided, having taken Rome, ordered before anything else that the relics of the holy martyrs be gathered and given holy burial. And

the Romans celebrated a victory festival for seven days, honouring the Lord and the life-giving cross and extolling Constantine the victor.

Year of the world 5805. In this year Maximinus, the son of Galerius, usurped the throne and claimed it for himself, and ended his life shamefully in Cilicia. His father Maximian Galerius heard that Maxentius, the son of Herculius, had been brought down at Rome by Constantine through the power of the cross. Puffed up with pride, he let loose the persecution against the Christians.

Year of the world 5806. In this year the most divine Constantine, together with Licinius Caesar and driven by zeal for God, marched against Maximian Galerius, who ruled the East. Galerius marched out against them
… in the East, not surviving him (Maximian) for long, he too met a most shameful death at the hands of Licinius, who had not yet gone mad at that time. Maximinus in [?]

with a vast host and engaged them, trusting in the oracles of demons and in sorcerous tricks. But since the life-giving cross [went before?] the great Constantine, the tyrant and his host were routed at the first onset. He [?] took off the imperial robe, put on a soldier's dress, slipped away with a few of his most loyal men, and fled from village to village. Then he gathered the priests of the idols and the soothsayers, who were [renowned?] for magic, together with his own prophets, and slaughtered them as deceivers.

Year of the world 5808. Macarius, bishop of Jerusalem, year 1. Eustathius, bishop of Antioch, year 1. In this year the most pious Constantine was about to take Galerius Maximian alive, but divine wrath overtook him first. [Flames?] kindled in the depths of his bowels and marrow, and the unbearable pain threw him face down on the ground, gasping for breath, until both his eyes burst out and left the impious man blind. His flesh, rotting from the immense burning in his bones, fell away, and so, rotted through, he gave up his God-fighting soul.

Year of the world 5809. In this year [Constantine] set apart a portion of Roman territory and assigned it to Licinius, who had fought as an ally of the divine Constantine and was deceitfully pretending to be a Christian. He proclaimed him emperor over it, after requiring him to agree that he would do nothing at all against the Christians. From then on, by the grace of God, the [persecution] of the tyrants against us ceased.
[Apparatus:] 'the law' read [?]. 'first the' vulg. 'imperial' omitted in a. 'by magic' vulg. 'this' [?]. 'from village' A; 'from village' (accusative) vulg.

and Crispus his son); second, that only Christians should serve in the army and govern provinces and command camps, and that those who persisted in idolatry should be punished with death; third, that the two weeks of Pascha should be kept free from work, the week before the Resurrection and the week after it. With things in this state, deep peace and calm held the whole world and the faithful were full of joy, while all the nations flocked daily to the faith of Christ, were baptised, and smashed their ancestral idols. He also decreed that the cubit that measures the rise of the river Nile in Egypt should be brought into the church, and not into the Serapeum, as had been the pagans' custom. Before he went completely mad, Licinius came to Antioch and put to death Theotecnus the sorcerer and his associates after many tortures.

Year of the world 5811. In this year Licinius began to stir up a persecution against the Christians. First he persecuted the Christians in the palace, forgetting the choices of the tyrants who had gone before him and his agreements with the great Constantine. Mad after women, he never stopped wronging and murdering Christians. The divine Constantine wrote ordering him to give up his madness, but he would not listen. He also had Basil, the bishop of Amaseia, and, as some say, the holy Forty Martyrs, and many others brought to their end through tortures.

Year of the world 5812. Alexander, bishop of Byzantium, year 1. In this year Arius, whose very name speaks of madness, made his heresy public in Alexandria against the

[Apparatus:] 'only' omitted in A; 'only' (adverb) h. omitted in A. 'the' omitted in a. vulg. 'divine'] 'great' a. 'was persuaded' A; 'persuaded' [?] a, but 'forty' omitted. 'Arius' A; 'the Arius' vulg. [?] NOTES.

Church and created a schism. The evil one worked with him, since he could not bear to see the Church at peace. There was also a most violent earthquake in Alexandria, so that many houses fell and many people died.

Year of the world 5813. In this year the great Constantine learned of the agitation stirred up by Arius and was deeply grieved. He wrote a joint letter to Alexander and Arius, advising them to put an end to this wicked agitation and to be at peace with one another. He also sent Hosius, bishop of Corduba, to Alexandria about Arius, and to the East to correct the easterners, who by old custom celebrated Pascha in a more Jewish manner. But he came back having achieved nothing on either count. In this year the great Constantine also made his son Constans Caesar and sent him to Gaul.

Year of the world 5814. In this year, as some say, Constantine the Great and his son Crispus were baptised in Rome by Sylvester, as the people of

elder Rome have the baptistery to this day as evidence that he was baptised by Sylvester in Rome after the tyrants had been destroyed. But those in the East say that he was baptised in Nicomedia, on the point of death, by Eusebius of Nicomedia the Arian, and that this was where he happened to fall asleep. They say he had kept putting off baptism in the hope of being baptised in the river Jordan. To me it seems truer that he was baptised by Sylvester in Rome. I think the decrees addressed to Miltiades that circulate under his name were forged by the Arians, who are eager to win credit for themselves from this, or who wish to disparage the pious emperor by showing that he was unbaptised. That is absurd and false. For if he was not baptised at the time of the council of Nicaea, then he could not have shared in the divine mysteries or joined in the assembly of the holy Fathers, which it is utterly absurd to say or even think. Other Arians and pagans slander the great Constantine as illegitimate; but they too are lying. His lineage was royal even before Diocletian. His father Constantius was a grandson of the emperor Claudius through his daughter, and by Helena, his first wife, he had the great Constantine. He also had other sons by Theodora, daughter of Maximian Herculius. Theodora was the sister of Maxentius, who ruled as tyrant in Rome and was killed by Constantine at the Milvian bridge, when Constantine also saw the sign of the cross in the sky. She was also the sister of Fausta, the wife of the great Constantine. Let no one be surprised that father and son married two sisters, for they did so as pagans, before their baptism. Their family lines are as set out below:

[Genealogical table, damaged:] Crispus, Constantine, … and Helena, wife of Julian the Apostate … Constantius, Constans [?] …

By Theodora, daughter of Herculius, he begets Constantius, father of Gallus and of Julian the Apostate; Dalmatius; [?] … the younger [?]; and in the margin: of Hannibalianus.

By Helena he begets Constantine, the great and God-beloved emperor, and him alone.

Constantine the Great begets Constantia, wife of the impious Licinius.

The great Constantine, by Fausta, daughter of Herculius, begets Crispus, Constantine, [?] Constantina [?], and Helena, wife of Julian the Apostate.

Year of the World 5815. In this year the pious Constantine saw that Licinius was pursuing the persecution with growing madness and plotting against his benefactor, so he took up arms against him by land and sea. A pitched war was fought in Bithynia, and Licinius was taken alive at Chrysopolis and handed over into Constantine's hands. Constantine, with his usual humanity, spared his life and sent him to Thessalonica to be kept under guard. Not long afterwards Licinius hired barbarians and was about to rebel, but the most gentle Constantine learned of it and ordered him to be beheaded with the sword. So the affairs of the Christian commonwealth at last enjoyed perfect calm through the power of the life-giving cross. The tyrants were out of the way, and Constantine, with God working alongside him, ruled the Roman empire alone. He appointed his own sons Caesars and lived in peace. The man was brilliant in every respect: in courage of soul, sharpness of mind, learning and eloquence, love of justice, readiness to do good, dignity of appearance, and courage and good fortune in war. He was great in wars against the barbarians, invincible in civil wars, and firm and unshaken in the faith. For this reason he won victory over all his enemies by prayer. This is also why he set up [crosses?] [?] in various places, in honour of God, for the conversion of the nations. In the same year Martinianus was killed after holding power as a usurper for three months. Licinianus, son of Licinius, was stripped of the rank of Caesar by Constantine. In the same year Narses, son of the king of the Persians [?] [Textual notes, partly illegible:] 'seeing' A, 'having seen' vulg.; 'by land' A, 'both by land' vulg.; [?] 'customary' from A; 'having learned' A; 'him' omitted in A; 'enjoyed' A, a variant spelling vulg.; 'co-worked by God' A, 'by the co-operation of God' vulg.; 'the' added from A; 'having appointed' A [?]; 'own' A, 'his household's' vulg.; 'the man [was] in all things' A, 'a man [in] all things' vulg.; 'fortune' A, 'good nature' others, 'good courage' vulg.; [?] added from A; formerly read 'he won'; 'Constantine' A [?], 'Constantius' vulg. [?] ... alone among the nations of the Parthians and Medes [?]. At that very time, campaigning against the enemies of the Christian faith, he won the victory by prayer. This is also why [?] in various places in honour of God [?]

of the king overran Mesopotamia and [captured?] the city of Amida [?]. Constantius the Caesar, Constantine's son, made war on him. After a minor setback he finally won the battle so decisively that he killed Narses himself. Year of the World 5816. In this year the twentieth anniversary of the reign of Constantine Augustus was celebrated. The holy, ecumenical First Council of the 318 Fathers also took place. Many of them were wonder-workers and equal to the angels, bearing in their bodies the marks of Christ from the earlier persecutions. Among them were Paphnutius, Spyridon, Macarius and James of Nisibis, wonder-workers who had raised the dead and performed many marvels. The holy council met at Nicaea in Bithynia and was presided over by Macarius of Jerusalem and Alexander of Alexandria, while Vitus and Vincent attended on behalf of the bishop of Rome. Since the church of Antioch was without a bishop, the council confirmed Eustathius, bishop of Beroea in Syria, as its bishop. Alexander of Byzantium did not attend the council because of his great age and bodily weakness, but presbyters took his place. Paul of Neocaesarea also attended, together with a great crowd of other holy men distinguished in life and in word. Eusebius Pamphili wrote great praises of them in the third book of his work on the emperor. The most Christian emperor supplied everything they needed. With the help of the holy and consubstantial Trinity, this holy and ecumenical council deposed Arius and those who thought as he did, namely Eusebius of Nicomedia and his party. The exception was Eusebius Pamphili, who for the time being accepted the term 'consubstantial'. The council sent them into exile. The all-praised emperor Constantine was present with the bishops and worked alongside them in everything that pleased God. He ordered others to be ordained in place of the deposed, and of the faith

the council issued a written exposition, which the orthodox now proclaim throughout the whole Church. While the impious Arius was present at the council and on trial, Eusebius of Nicomedia, Theognis, Maris, Narcissus, Theophantus and Patrophilus took his side. They composed a blasphemous statement of faith and submitted it to the council. When it was torn up, its authors changed sides and condemned Arius, except for Secundus of Ptolemais in Egypt and Theonas of Marmarica. These two were expelled with Arius and anathematized. The rest proclaimed the holy Creed of the faith, all of them signing it together with the most august emperor, and they acclaimed it. With that the assembly broke up. In this year Crispus, the emperor's son, fell asleep as a Christian, and work began on building Byzantium. The holy, ecumenical First Council met in the twelfth indiction, in the twentieth year of [Textual note:] 'Marmarica' A. [?] Goar's notes. [?] 'Byzantium began to be built': book 1, chapter 12: 'The emperor, having completed the public festival of his twentieth anniversary, at once applied himself to the building of churches. He did this in the other cities, and also in the city named after him, formerly called Byzantium, which he enlarged

of Constantine the Great, on 20 May. The council wrote an encyclical letter to Alexandria, Libya and the Pentapolis announcing the expulsion of Arius, Secundus and Theonas. The letter also gave a ruling on Meletius: he was to live privately and quietly in his own city, while those he had ordained were to be confirmed by a more mystical ordination. It also wrote about Easter: it was no longer to be kept with the Jews, but celebrated on Sunday instead, following the practice of Italy. The all-pious emperor likewise wrote letters everywhere commanding the same and confirming what the holy council had declared. He denounced Arius together with those who thought as he did and ordered that they be called Porphyrians, that their writings be burned, and that anyone who did not burn them be put to death. He also issued an imperial law that these things were to be done. Since the festival of the twentieth anniversary of his reign fell at that very time, he invited all the Fathers to a banquet, reclining at table [Textual notes:] 'and' A, 'indeed' vulg.; 'by him' A, 'under him' vulg.; 'denouncing' [fem. pl.] a. [?] ... of the council, as we find in the Acts [?], in the consulship of Paulinus and Julian, on 20 May. This was the 636th year from Alexander of Macedon [?] 'to be confirmed': [Latin] to be confirmed by ordination [?] ... 'appointed by ordination', by a holier ordination [?] ... 'to be received into communion on these terms, that they keep their honour and minister' [?]

with them, and he honoured them splendidly. He kissed the gouged-out eyes of Paphnutius and of other confessors like him, and the limbs maimed in the persecution, drawing a blessing from them. He urged all the bishops to keep the peace and to refrain from slandering their neighbours. The petitions some of them had handed in against one another he burned, swearing an oath that if he ever saw a bishop committing adultery he would gladly cover him with his own purple robe. He gave many gifts to all the churches and instructed the governors of the provinces to honour the priests, and he sent them all home rejoicing. Some Greek wise men in Byzantium reproached the emperor for doing wrong by changing religion against the customs of the Roman emperors. The emperor decided to send one of the philosophers to Bishop Alexander to debate with him. Alexander was a holy man but had no skill in argument. He said to the dialectician philosopher, who kept chattering, 'I command you in the name of Jesus Christ, the true God, to be silent and not to speak.' The moment he said this the man was struck dumb and became speechless. The emperor ordered Macarius, the bishop of Jerusalem, who was present at the council, to search on his return for the place of the holy Resurrection, the place of the Skull, Golgotha, and the life-giving wood. In the same year he crowned his God-minded mother Helena and granted her coinage, as befitted an empress. She had a vision bidding her go to Jerusalem and bring to light the divine places that the lawless had buried.

She asked her son Constantine to carry out what God had commanded her, and he obeyed. Moved by a divine prompting, the pious Constantine wanted to found a city bearing his own name on the plain before Ilium, above the tomb of Ajax, where the Greeks who campaigned against Troy are said to have had their naval station. But God commanded him in a dream to build the present Constantinople at Byzantium. He built it lavishly with splendid houses. He brought over the leading men from Rome, and selected others by family from other places, gave them large houses and settled them in the city. Then the Christ-loving emperor built the church of Holy Wisdom, the church of Holy Peace, the church of the Apostles, the church of St Mocius and the church of the Archangel at Anaplous. He ordered the idolatrous temples to be pulled down and churches to be built. At that time the temple of Asclepius at Aegae and the temple of Aphrodite at Aphaca were demolished, along with many others, and he gave their revenues to the churches. Then many nations came to baptism through the miracles performed by the captives taken in the time of the emperor Gallienus

[?] written: The emperor sent his praiseworthy and God-beloved mother Helena to Jerusalem, to Macarius of Jerusalem, with letters and an abundance of money, to search for the life-giving wood and to build up the holy places. The empress herself had asked to go, saying she had seen a divine vision bidding her go to Jerusalem and bring to light the holy places that the lawless had buried.

is, the great Constantine and his mother cut away two-thirds of the [temple?] [?] and set up the altar, because St Mocius had been put to death there. For this reason he also raised the church as his own [?]
This place, now called the Michaelion, lies on the [?] as one sails down from [?] towards [Constantinople?], at a distance from it for a sailor of about [?] stadia. The place now [?]

THEOPHANES [?] and Crispus his son; and second [?] Year of the World [?]. [?] In this year [?] against [?]. Year of the World 5811. In this year Licinius began to stir up a persecution against the Christians. First he [drove out?] the Christians in the palace, forgetting the fate of the tyrants before him and his agreements with the great Constantine. He did not stop raving after women, doing injustice and murdering Christians. The divine Constantine ordered him by letter to give up his madness, but he would not listen. He also had Basil, the bishop of Amasea, put to death under torture, and, according to some, the holy Forty Martyrs as well, and many others. Year of the World 5812. Year [?] of Alexander, second bishop of Byzantium. In this year in Alexandria Arius, whose name speaks of madness, [began to spread?] his heresy [Textual notes, partly illegible:] 'only' [pl.] omitted in A; 'only' [?]; 'of exultation' A; [?] A; 'the' omitted; [?] Sarapis [?] vulg.; 'divine'] 'great' a; 'was persuaded' A, 'persuaded' vulg.; [?] 'forty' [variant spelling]. [?] to be illustrated: [?] ... of the Greeks, that Sarapis was the one who made the Nile rise to water Egypt, because the cubit [measuring the flood] was carried into the temple of Sarapis. Constantine ordered the cubit of the Alexandrians to be moved to the church. [?] 'Ares, Ares, bane of mortals, blood-stained, stormer of walls.'

[?] through priests who had earlier been taken captive by the Goths, Celts and western Galatians who [overran?] the Romans. And now, under the victorious Constantine, a great many nations were enlightened and ran to Christ. The inner Indians came to believe in Christ when Meropius, a philosopher of Tyre, took his disciples Aedesius and Frumentius with him, entered their country to explore it, and taught them the word of God. Athanasius ordained Frumentius as their first bishop. Likewise the Iberians came to believe in his reign through a captive Christian woman, when they saw the miracles that took place and saw her heal their king of the darkness that had fallen over his eyes while he was hunting. Rufinus records this, having heard it from Bacurius himself, king of the Iberians. Likewise the Armenians came fully to the faith in his reign, receiving salvation through Tiridates their king and Gregory their bishop. At that time Dorotheus, bishop of Tyre, was also at his height. He had suffered much under Diocletian and endured exile and torture. He left a great many writings in Latin and Greek, since he was highly skilled in both languages, and his natural gifts made him a man of wide learning. He also wrote an exact account of the bishops of Byzantium and of many others. After returning from exile and attending the council, he went back to his own see and lived on until Julian the Apostate. That foul man raged against the Christians not openly but in secret, through his officials, and so the blessed Dorotheus went once more to the city of Odyssopolis. There he was seized by Julian's officials, endured many outrages, and in extreme old age died under torture for his confession of Christ, [being already one hundred and seven years old].
Year of the World 5817. In this year the Jews and the Persians saw Christianity flourishing in Persia and slandered to Sapor, king of the Persians,

Symeon, archbishop of Ctesiphon and Seleucia, as a friend of the emperor of the Romans and an informer on Persian affairs. A great persecution was stirred up in Persia, and a great many were crowned with martyrdom for Christ. Among them were Usthazades, Sapor's tutor, and Symeon the archbishop. Besides many others, a hundred clergy and bishops were martyred in a single day, along with countless multitudes. Of the notable people from the cities alone, they counted eighteen thousand martyrs put to death by the utterly godless Sapor with horrifying tortures foreign to nature. At that time Acepsimas the bishop, Aeithalas the presbyter and Tarbula, the sister of Archbishop Symeon, were also martyred, together with a great many other women. The most divine emperor Constantine wrote to Sapor urging him to spare the Christians, pleading with him to put an end to such cruelty. The letter is wonderfully and most divinely composed, but it did not persuade him. In the same year the divine Constantine sent the blessed Helena to Jerusalem with money to search for the Lord's life-giving cross. Macarius, the patriarch of Jerusalem, met the empress with due honour and searched with her for the longed-for life-giving wood, in quiet, with earnest prayers and fasting. After this, God soon revealed to Macarius the place where the temple and statue of the unclean demon Aphrodite stood. Using her imperial authority, the God-revering Helena quickly had it pulled down from its foundations by a crowd of workmen,
[?] cited: They slander Symeon, then archbishop of Seleucia and Ctesiphon, the royal cities of Persia, as a friend [of the Romans]. [?]

razing it and clearing away the earth [?] which Aelius Hadrian had built long ago. At once the holy tomb and the place of the Skull came to light, and near them, to the east, three buried crosses. Searching further, they also found the nails. Everyone was at a loss as to which was the Lord's cross, and the blessed Helena was deeply distressed. But Macarius, a bishop true to his name, resolved the question through faith. He brought each of the crosses in turn to a woman of high rank who had been given up for dead and was nearly gone, and so identified the Lord's cross. For as soon as it [?] touched the sick woman, she, who had been without breath or movement, sprang up at once by divine power, glorifying God with a loud voice. With fear and great joy the all-pious Helena took up the life-giving wood. Part of it, together with the nails, she brought to her son. The rest she placed in a silver casket and handed over to Bishop Macarius as a memorial for future generations. She also ordered churches to be built at the holy tomb and at the Skull, one in her son's name [?] where the life-giving wood was found, one in Bethlehem and one on the Mount of Olives. Then she returned to the all-praised Constantine. He received her with joy and placed the portion of the life-giving wood in a golden case, which he handed to the bishop for safekeeping. Some of the nails he had forged into his helmet and others worked into his horse's bridle, so that the word spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled: 'On that day what is on the horse's bridle shall be holy to the Lord Almighty.' The all-praised Constantine also wrote to Macarius, well named, to hurry on the building, and sent an official in charge of the work with plenty of money. He ordered the holy places to be built so finely that nothing in the whole world would match their beauty, and wrote to the governors of the province to assist the work eagerly out of public funds. The emperor celebrated joyfully and gave thanks to God, who had done such good things in the times

the patriarch of Jerusalem fell asleep in peace. He was succeeded on his throne by Maximus, a gentle and distinguished man who had endured many tortures for God in the persecution and had lost his right eye. At the same time the blessed Helena departed in the Lord at the age of eighty, after giving her son many instructions about devotion to Christ. She was buried in the church of the Holy Apostles in Constantinople, which her son Constantine had built as a burial place for Christian emperors. The blessed Helena was the first to be buried there, and she was honoured with splendid commemorations and all-night vigils. In Jerusalem the God-minded Helena used to serve the holy virgins at table herself, standing like a handmaid, and they continually called her blessed in holy commemorations. The emperor ordered Eusebius Pamphili to produce sacred books for the churches of Constantinople and gave him public funds for the purpose. Year of the World 5818. In this year Constantine the Great campaigned against the Germans, the Sarmatians and the Goths, and through the power of the precious cross won a mighty victory. He laid their lands waste and reduced them to utter servitude. In the same year he rebuilt Drepanum in honour of the martyr Lucian, who is buried there, [and gave it the] same name [as his mother] [?]

in the heroon of the holy and great Constantine, among the first [tombs], on the east side, lies his porphyry sarcophagus, in which he himself rests together with the divine Helena his mother. [?] mausoleum [?]

…he named it Helenopolis after his mother. Eusebius son of Pamphilus bears witness to the complete orthodoxy of the [creed? ] of the faith set forth at Nicaea by the Fathers. He did so in writing to his own fellow citizens, interpreting the words according to their meaning. Athanasius, in his letter to the Africans, testifies that [Eusebius] accepted the term homoousios. But Theodoret says that Eusebius son of Pamphilus shared the views of the Arians, Eusebius of Nicomedia and his circle. For this reason he joined in the deposition of the divine Eustathius of Antioch. Together with them he persuaded the emperor that Eustathius had been justly deposed, and arranged for him to be exiled to Illyricum. AM 5819. In this year the octagonal Church of the Lord began to be built in Antioch. AM 5820. In this year Constantine the pious crossed the Danube, built a stone bridge over it, and subdued the Scythians. AM 5821. Year 1 of Mark, bishop of Rome. In this year Constantine the pious, while building Constantinople, decreed that it should be styled New Rome, and ordered that it should have a senate. He also set up a porphyry column with a statue of himself on top, at the place where he had begun to build the city, on the western side of the gate that leads out toward Rome. He adorned the city by bringing to it, from every province and city, whatever work of beauty there was: statues, bronze and marble. AM 5822. Year 1 of Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria.

Notes: τὴν is omitted in r. [?] ὡς δεξαμένῳ [?]; εἰς δεξαμένῳ in the vulgate. ἑαυτοῦ is added from a. Ἀντ. τὸ in A; τὸ ἐν Ἀντ. in the vulgate. ἐπ’ αὐτῇ: ἐν αὐτῇ in the vulgate. τούτῳ τῷ ἔτει: τῷ αὐτῷ ἔτει in [?]. ἐν [?]. ἐπὶ τὸ δυτ.: ἐπὶ δὲ τὸ δ. in the vulgate. καὶ is omitted in A.

…[the pious ordered?] the overthrow of the idols and their temples, and they were destroyed in place after place. Their revenues were handed over to the churches of God. AM 5823. [Year 1] of Julius, bishop of Rome.

In this year the basilica in Nicomedia was burned down by fire from heaven. AM 5824. In this year, as the seventh indiction was about to begin, a famine struck the East. It took hold so severely that villages gathered together in great crowds in the territory of Antioch and of Cyprus and attacked one another. At first they plundered in raids, as if by night. In the end they broke into the granaries and storehouses in broad daylight, seized and carried off everything, and withdrew. A modius of grain came to cost four hundred pieces of silver. Constantine the Great granted the churches of each city an allowance of grain for the perpetual support of widows, orphans, hostels, the poor and the clergy. The church in Antioch received thirty-six [?] modii of grain. In the same year a most violent earthquake struck Cyprus. The city of Salamis collapsed and destroyed a large number of people. AM 5825. Year 1 of [?], bishop of Antioch. In this year Dalmatius was proclaimed Caesar. Calocaerus, who had made himself tyrant on the island of Cyprus,

could not withstand the Roman attack. He was defeated together with those responsible and put to death at Tarsus in Cilicia, burned alive by Dalmatius Caesar. In the same year Arius too was recalled from exile on the strength of what was in fact a feigned repentance. He was sent to Alexandria, but Athanasius would not receive him. AM 5826. In this year the thirtieth anniversary of Constantine, the most pious and victorious, was celebrated with great splendour. A star appeared at Antioch by day, in the eastern part of the sky, smoking heavily as if from a furnace, from the third hour until the fifth. Arius, with Eusebius of Nicomedia and those who shared his views, stirred up trouble. Through them they had submitted statements of orthodoxy to the emperor under oath, claiming that they were of one mind with the Fathers at Nicaea, but they were lying. The emperor was won over by them and grew angry with Atha[nasius… ?] …those deposed by Alexander, Euzoius being a deacon at the time. Having found a pretext, Eusebius and his associates fought against Athanasius as the champion of the true faith. AM 5827. Year 1 of Maximus, bishop of Jerusalem. In this year the emperor became angry with Athanasius because he would not receive Arius and Euzoius after their supposed conversion, which was feigned. Eusebius of Nicomedia and his party, together with the Melitians, found in this anger an instrument for their wickedness and began contriving their case against Athanasius. First they slandered his ordination, although Apollinaris the Syrian bore strong testimony to it. Second, there was the matter of the linen garment, which his enemies falsely accused the saint of imposing. Third, there was Philumenus, to whom they falsely said he had sent a large sum of gold for a plot against the emperor. The emperor summoned Athanasius, found that every charge was false, and sent him back to Alexandria with letters and great honour. In the same year the plot against Athanasius concerning Ischyras was contrived in the Mareotis. This Ischyras had passed himself off as a priest and went about [?]. When Athanasius learned of it, he put a stop to his audacity

through Macarius the presbyter. Ischyras fled and went to Eusebius of Nicomedia. He accused Athanasius of having broken sacred vessels from the altar during the celebration of the mysteries, and of having had sacred books burned through Macarius. They also falsely claimed that the saint had cut off the notorious hand of Arsenius and was using it for magic, so shameless were their slanders. When the emperor learned of the accusations against Athanasius, he first entrusted the inquiry to his own nephew Dalmatius at Antioch [?]. Later he transferred the trial to Caesarea, but Athanasius declined to go there because of Eusebius son of Pamphilus. He was then tried at Tyre by the adversaries of the truth. It was Eusebius of Nicomedia, I mean, who deceived the emperor, pretending that they wanted to see the holy places that had been built and to be present at their dedication. The emperor dismissed them with great honour and ordered that the accusations against Athanasius be settled, so that they could attend the dedication festival together with Athanasius. When they assembled at Tyre, Maximus of Jerusalem was also there, unaware of the plots against Athanasius. Athanasius entered the council of these ill-minded men and tore the slanders of his accusers apart like a spider's web. Exposed as liars, they went mad, threw everything into confusion, and shouted: "Away with the sorcerer who has muzzled us all!" Dalmatius the Caesar, the emperor's nephew, came with a body of soldiers and only just saved Athanasius, who was about to be killed by them. Then, by God's providence, Arsenius himself arrived at Tyre. When the fabrication about him had been exposed, the enemies turned to the slander concerning Ischyras. Because of the intolerable plots against him, Athanasius withdrew from Tyre. The Arian-minded then drew up a one-sided proceeding and deposed Athanasius in his absence. They entered into communion with Arius and Euzoius, sent them off to Alexandria, and so went up to the dedication with bloodied hands. The leader in all these evils was Eusebius of Nicomedia. But a true account holds that the great Athanasius, after fleeing from Tyre, went up to Jerusalem. There he offered prayers, anointed the houses of prayer with holy chrism and consecrated them

before the impious arrived. In this way he reached the emperor first and explained his whole case to him. The all-praiseworthy Constantine marvelled at the wickedness of his adversaries, honoured him with the highest marks of esteem, and sent him back to Alexandria with letters. After the return from the dedication, Eusebius of Nicomedia, a stranger to all piety, together with Theognis, Ursacius and Patrophilus, came to Byzantium. Saying nothing more of the earlier accusations against Athanasius, they put forward four false witnesses who held episcopal ordination. These men dared to say on oath: "We heard Athanasius threatening to stop the grain shipments that come from Egypt to Byzantium." In this way they roused the Christ-loving emperor to anger and got him to exile the great Athanasius to Trier in Gaul. With Athanasius in exile, Arius again threw Egypt into turmoil. When the emperor learned of it, he summoned Arius and asked whether he assented to the doctrines of Nicaea concerning the homoousios. Arius declared on oath that he did, practising deceit now as he always had. He had composed two documents, one in favour of the homoousios and the other against it. The second he had written himself, the first he had had written by someone else. And so, swearing that this was what he believed, he persuaded the emperor to order that he be received into the catholic Church. When the divine Alexander learned of this, he wept before God in the church called Irene. Quicker than words, divine justice overtook Arius. In a place worthy of the sins of his tongue it cut him off from life, both the present life and the life to come: his entrails poured out in the latrine at the very hour when he was about to enter the sacred precincts unworthily. These things happened in the thirty-first year of Constantine the Great, while the divine Alexander was bishop of Constantinople. It is not true, as Eusebius alone says, that Eusebius of Nicomedia already held the throne of Constantinople when he was contriving his schemes against Athanasius at the dedication. The total of the years also shows this to be false. Constantine reigned thirty-two years in all. After his first decade, in his thirteenth year, he came to Byzantium and found Metrophanes, Alexander's predecessor, as bishop. Alexander then held the see for twenty-three years. So from the beginning of the reign of Constantine the Great [?] to the falling asleep of Alexander there are thirty-seven years,

which Constantine did not live to see. Thus the total of the years shows that Eusebius did not hold the throne of Constantinople under Constantine. It is also shown by what was said above about Arius and Athanasius. Both the exile of Athanasius and the destruction of Arius happened after the thirtieth year of Constantine and after the dedication at Jerusalem, while the great Alexander was still alive. AM 5828. Year 1 of Euphronius, bishop of Antioch. In this year [?], a presbyter of Constantinople, became famous for his excellence. He had taken up the apostolic life and reached the height of virtue. So too did Zenobius the architect, who built the Martyrium in Jerusalem at Constantine's [command?]. In the same year many of the Assyrians living under the Persians were sold by the Saracens in Mesopotamia. The Persians declared war on the Romans. Constantine the pious came to the city of Nicomedia and drew up his forces against the Persians, but he fell ill and fell asleep in peace. Some Arian-minded writers say that he was then granted holy baptism by Eusebius of Nicomedia, who had been transferred to Constantinople. This is false, as has been demonstrated: he was baptized in Rome by Silvester, as we showed earlier. He lived sixty-five years in all and reigned thirty-one years and ten months. He wrote a will and left the empire to his three sons, Constantius, Constantine and Constans. He had used his rule piously and gently, and by God's providence he was the first to bear the title of Christian emperor. He conquered many barbarians, from Britain to Persia, and [?] tyrants, destroying his enemies by the sign of the precious cross.

He entrusted his will to an Arian presbyter whom his sister Constantia had maliciously brought in, with orders to give it to no one but Constantius, the emperor of the East. He also ordered that Athanasius return from exile. Constantius came from the East and laid his father's body to rest in the Church of the Apostles. The unholy Arian presbyter handed the will to Constantius and so gained great freedom of access in the palace. He even persuaded the empress herself to become an Arian, with Eusebius of Nicomedia and those of like mind as his collaborators. AM 5829. [Year 1] of Constantius [?], emperor of the Romans.

In this year Constantine the great and holy had gone to his rest, and his three sons ruled the Romans: Constantius the East, Constans the Gauls, and Constantine Italy. Constantius recalled Athanasius from exile and sent him back to Alexandria with letters of recommendation. The Alexandrians, and above all the clergy, received him with great joy. Eusebius son of Pamphilus, in the first book of his Against Marcellus and again in the third, strongly condemns those who dare to call the Son of God a creature. Socrates quotes these passages in defence of Eusebius, eager to show that he was not Arian-minded. But the truth shows him to have been unsteady in his reasoning, carried now one way and now another as the times changed. He died soon after Constantine the Great. He left Acacius as his disciple and successor on the throne of Caesarea. Acacius was a learned man and the author of [many?] writings, but he was closely attached to the Arians, evidently because he shared his teacher's views. In the same year Sapor, king of the Persians, invaded Mesopotamia intending to sack Nisibis. He besieged it for sixty-three days, but could not take it and withdrew.

James, bishop of Nisibis, who persevered in the [?] of godliness, easily accomplished by his prayers whatever he wished. He made the Persians fail in their hope of overthrowing Nisibis. They withdrew from the city at once, driven off by the spirit of his prayer. When they reached their own land they were paid the wages of their impiety in famine and plague, receiving back what they had done. Dalmatius the Caesar was killed by the soldiers immediately after the death of Constantine the Great. Constantius did not order the slaughter, but he did not prevent it. AM 5830. In this year, when the young Dalmatius was killed by the soldiers, Gallus and Julian were about to be killed along with him. They were the sons of Constantius, the brother of Constantine the Great. But illness saved Gallus, and infancy saved Julian, for he was eight years old. Constantius had earlier accepted the homoousios but later changed his mind. This came about through his own fickleness and through the deceit of the Arian presbyter, of [Eusebius?], the chief of the eunuchs, of Eusebius of Nicomedia, and of their associates. AM 5831. In this year Constantine, the son of Constantine the Great, attacked the territories of his own brother Constans. He joined battle and was killed by the soldiers, and Constans became sole ruler of all the western lands. Constantius, who reigned over the East, handed Gallus and Julian over to be educated on an estate called Macellum, near Caesarea in Cappadocia.
…to live in Cappadocia at Macellum. This is an imperial estate near Mount Argaeus, not far from the city of Caesarea, a magnificent…

These two brothers became readers, and they eagerly set about building a church for the holy martyr Mamas. But the earth would not accept the part that Julian had been allotted to build. He shaved his hair and pretended to practise monastic asceticism. Constantius and Constans passed a law that a Jew must not buy a slave; if he did, the slave was to be confiscated to the public treasury. If he dared to circumcise a slave, he was to be punished by the sword and his property confiscated. AM 5832. In this year Constantius built Amida and gave it strong walls. He also founded Constantia, formerly called Antoninopolis, and named it after himself. It lies seven hundred stades south of Amida. AM 5833. Year 1 of Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem. In this year a synod of one hundred and ninety bishops was held at Antioch, led by Eusebius of Nicomedia. They appointed Eusebius of Emesa bishop of Alexandria. When he was not accepted, although he was a Sabellian, Gre-

gory the Arian was sent instead, with a large army and a general named Syrianus, to drive Athanasius from the throne of Alexandria or even to kill him. Then Athanasius, clearly guided by God, went out with the chanters of the church and escaped the death that hung over him. As for Eusebius, whom the Alexandrians had not accepted, [?]. The same men changed the faith: they openly embraced Arianism, and after [his?] death [?] they wrote a different statement of faith that passed over the homoousios in silence. At that time they also held the dedication of the church of Antioch that Constantine the Great had built. In the same year Antioch was endangered by great earthquakes for three days. The church that was dedicated was domed and had taken six years to build. It was founded by Constantine the Great, and completed and dedicated by Constantius. AM 5834. In this year Constantius defeated the Assyrians and celebrated a triumph. Sapor, king of the Persians, added to his other crimes a persecution of the Christians under his rule. Constans, in the West, ravaged the Franks. A great earthquake struck Cyprus, and most of the city of Salamis collapsed. [AM 5835. … bishop of Constantino]ple: year 1 of Paul. In this year a great earthquake struck, and Neocaesarea in Pontus collapsed. Only the church, the bishop's residence, and the devout men who happened to be there were spared. The Romans joined battle with the Persians and killed many of them. In the same year Paul the Confessor was ordained bishop of Constantinople.

In this year a great earthquake struck and the island of Rhodes was laid in ruins. The Alexandrians killed Gregory, who had come against Athanasius like a brigand and held the throne of Alexandria for six years. George, an Arian and a monster from Cappadocia, was then ordained by the Arians. AM 5837. In this year Dyrrachium in Dalmatia was destroyed by an earthquake. Rome was shaken for three days and was in danger, and twelve cities of Campania were destroyed. Constantius came to Byzantium and drove Paul, bishop of Constantinople, from his throne. In his place he installed the most impious Eusebius of Nicomedia, that den of evils, like a brigand and against the law. AM 5838. [Year 1] of Liberius, bishop of Rome.

Year 1 of Eusebius of Nicomedia, bishop of Constantinople. In this year Constantius built the harbour at Seleucia in Syria, cutting a long way through a mountain, and he rebuilt the city. He also founded a city in Phoenicia, formerly called Antaradus, which he named Constantia. Sapor, king of the Persians, invaded Mesopotamia and besieged Nisibis for seventy-eight days, but again he withdrew in disgrace. In the same year there was an eclipse of the sun, so that stars appeared in the sky at the third hour of the day, on the sixth of the month of Daisios. Athanasius and Paul, and all who had been expelled for upholding the true doctrine, fled to Julius in Rome. Each of them told Julius about his own situation, and he restored each one to his own church with letters.

A.M. 5839. In this year Athanasius, Paul and those with them took courage from the letters of Julius, the pope of Rome, and reoccupied their own sees. But Constantius was staying at Antioch. When he learned that Julius had used letters to restore Paul and Athanasius to their own sees, he grew angry and ordered them driven from those sees. In the same year the sun again grew dim, at the second hour of the Lord's day.

A.M. 5840. In this year a great earthquake struck Berytus in Phoenicia and most of the city collapsed. As a result the mass of the pagans came into the church and promised to become Christians as we are. Then some of them broke away. As if stripping the Church of its forms, they went out, devised a place of prayer of their own and received the crowd into it. They imitated everything belonging to the Church and became to us what the heresy of the Samaritans is to the Jews, while still living as pagans.

A.M. [?]. In this year Shapur, king of the Persians, again besieged Nisibis and pressed it hard. He even brought a great number of elephants fit for battle, as well as hired kings and siege engines of every kind, and they threatened to wipe the city out from its foundations if the inhabitants would not give way. When the Nisibenes held out against the siege, he then decided to flood the city with the river that runs beside it. But the men defeated the enemy by their prayers, for they had God on their side. When the waters were about to undermine the walls and bring them down, one part of the wall did give way, and this happened by God's permission, as will be shown in what follows. For at once it came about that the city was saved, while the enemy were left swimming in the waters and many were destroyed by the water. Those who had suffered this [?] to enter through the fallen part of the wall,

and so they drew up the elephants in armour, made ready a [?] crowd and pressed the war more heavily, using every kind of engine. But the soldiers guarding the city won the victory from that point by the providence of God. They filled the gap with weapons of every kind and killed most of the elephants with onagers. Others fell into the [?] of the ditches, and others were struck and turned back. More than ten thousand of their heavy infantry died. On the rest a thunderbolt fell from heaven, and the dark clouds, violent rains and claps of thunder so terrified them all that most of them died of fear. Hemmed in on every side, the new Pharaoh, Shapur, was beaten by the waves of the [?]. Gazing [?] at the fallen part of the wall, he saw an angel standing on top of it, splendidly robed and holding the emperor Constantius by the hand. At once he was troubled and threatened the magi with death. When they learned the cause, they resolved to explain to the king that the power of the apparition was greater than their own. [Through this] he then recognized the cause of his danger and was seized with fear. He ordered the engines to be burned and everything prepared for the war to be broken up. Then he himself fled with his men to his homeland [?] earlier by a plague [?].

A.M. 5842. In this year Constantius Augustus, who was reigning alone, proclaimed his own cousin Gallus Caesar and made him partner in his rule. He renamed him Constantius and sent him to the East, to Antioch, since the Persians were still pressing hard.

A.M. 5845 [?]. In this year the Jews of Palestine revolted and killed many of the other peoples, both Greeks and Samaritans. They themselves were wiped out, families and all, by the Roman army, and their city of Diocaesarea was laid waste.

In the same year Liberius wrote to Constantius about the homoousion and about holy Athanasius. Constantius grew furious, sent men and exiled him [?]
