"becoming": "having become", other manuscripts. "the engines": "those of the foreigners", vulgate. "Diocaesarea": "therefore also Samaria", a, in the margin. "concerning": "on behalf of", A.

to Beroea in Thrace. This was arranged by Eusebius, the chief of the eunuchs, a man of Arian views. In his place Constantius had Felix ordained. Felix was a deacon of the same church who accepted the Council of Nicaea, yet senselessly remained in communion with the Arians. The people of Rome would not tolerate communion with him and held their own assemblies apart. At Constantius's command a council gathered at Milan, with three hundred western bishops but very few from the East. It broke up having achieved nothing, since the westerners again refused to accept the plots against holy Athanasius. When the Romans petitioned the emperor, he was forced to recall Liberius and restore him to his see. Felix left Rome and never came back.

A.M. 58[?]. Year [?] of [?], bishop of Rome. A.M. 584[?]. First year of Damasus, bishop of Rome.

A.M. 5846. In this year Gallus, also called Constantius, was Caesar and distinguished himself in war. But he could not handle his success and began to plot a usurpation. He killed Domitian, prefect of the East, and Magnus the quaestor, because they had informed Constantius of the plot. Constantius summoned him and ordered him put to death near the island of Thalamon. He kept Julian, Gallus's brother, under guard, but Eusebia, his wife, begged for Julian's release and sent him to Athens.

A.M. 5847. First year of Hilarion [?], bishop of Jerusalem. In this year Acacius of Caesarea and Patrophilus of [?], who were Arians, deposed Maximus of Jerusalem and brought in Cyril in his place, believing him to share their views. At this time, while Cyril was bishop of Je-

Cyril of Jerusalem was persecuted by the Arians. In his time [?] the Arians [?] Arsenius, Heraclius and Hilarius. He was recalled again under Gratian [?], and [took part] in the synod of the 150 [?] bishops at Constantinople. Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem.

rusalem, the sign of the life-giving cross appeared in the sky on the day of Pentecost. It was shining with light and stretched from Golgotha, where Christ was crucified, to the Mount of Olives, from which he was taken up. Around the sign there was a crown that looked like a rainbow. On the same day it was also seen by Constantius. A letter of Cyril about this to the emperor Constantius is in circulation, and in it he calls the emperor "most pious." For this reason some slander Cyril as a man of Arian views. They also say that he passed over the word homoousios in silence in the catecheses he composed for the benefit of the untaught crowds who came to divine baptism because of the miracle of the life-giving cross. But they are mistaken and in the wrong. He had good reason to call the emperor "most pious," since the emperor had been drawn into the heresy by the villainy of the Arians through simple-mindedness rather than conviction, and paganism had not yet been completely overthrown. He also had good reason to keep silent for the time being about the word homoousios. It troubled the many, and the opposition of the enemy made it frighten off those being baptized. Instead he made the meaning of the homoousion plain through words of equal force. This is what the blessed Cyril did: he expounded the creed of Nicaea word by word and proclaimed the Son true God from the Father, true God.

A.M. 5848. First year of Stephen, Arian bishop of Antioch.

A.M. 5849. In this year, after the death of Eusebius, who had ruled Constantinople impiously, Athanasius and Paul went again to Rome, to Julius the pope and to the emperor Constans, brother of Constantius. When Eusebius died, the people had restored Paul to the see of Constantinople. But the Arians ordained Macedonius against him, and civil war broke out as a result. When Constantius, who was staying at Antioch, learned of this, he ordered Hermogenes, a general who had been sent to Thrace, to deal with it on his way

and to expel Paul from the church. When Hermogenes tried to carry this out, the populace set his house on fire, killed Hermogenes himself and threw him into the sea. On learning this, the emperor rode from Antioch to the imperial city. He drove Paul from the see but did not install Macedonius for the time being. Then, in his anger over the murder of Hermogenes, he punished the city by cutting forty thousand loaves from its daily bread ration, out of the eighty thousand his father had granted. Then Paul, as already mentioned, went to Julius of Rome and came back to Constantinople with his letters. Constantius was again staying at Antioch. When he learned that Julius had restored Paul to the see, he grew angry and ordered Philip the prefect to drive Paul out and install Macedonius in the see in his place. The prefect was afraid of what had happened to Hermogenes because of Paul. So he summoned Paul to the bath by the Zeuxippus, let him down through a window and exiled him to Thessalonica, his native city. Then he took Macedonius in his own carriage and installed him over the Church like a tyrant, as brigands do. The orthodox resisted so fiercely that three thousand one hundred and fifty men were killed, and in this way the Arians gained control of the Church. Then Constantius also threatened Athanasius with death. In fear of this he fled again to Rome, and Paul followed close behind him from Thessalonica. They went to Constans and told him what had happened to them. Constans was grieved for the saints and wrote to his brother Constantius in distress, telling him either to give back their sees to Paul and Athanasius or face war, which he threatened to wage against him. He also urged him to have a council held at Serdica. Three hundred bishops from the West gathered there, along with thirty-six from the East. The easterners opposed the westerners and demanded that Athanasius and Paul first be expelled. But Hosius, bishop of Corduba, and Protogenes of Serdica would not allow the saints Athanasius and Paul to be excluded. Then the easterners went to Philippopolis and there shamelessly anathematized the homoousion. But the orthodox at Serdica confirmed the true definition of the faith of

Nicaea and anathematized the "unlike." They also restored their sees to Athanasius, to Paul, and to Marcellus of Ancyra, who confessed the homoousion and argued in his defence that his writings did not mean what his accusers claimed. In this way the Council of Serdica acted against the easterners who had broken away and confirmed the homoousion. Constantius then made a show of receiving Athanasius and Paul with honour and gave them back their sees. So Athanasius [went] to Alexandria and was received with great joy, [?] George the

Magnentius usurped power in Gaul and killed the pious Constans. Constantius Augustus was staying at Antioch, and when he learned of it [?] he sent men and exiled Paul from the city to Cucusus, where he was killed by the Arians. And then Macedonius seized the see. Constantius set out for Italy against Magnentius. The senate in Rome invested Nepotian [with the purple] and sent him against Magnentius. Nepotian fought Magnentius at Rome and was killed by him after reigning three months. Before the emperor could reach Rome, Constantina, also called Helena, the sister of Constantius, proclaimed Vetranio emperor. He was a man of high standing, and she set him up to fight against Magnentius. Constantius [came?] to Rome and received Vetranio with great honour, and together they made war on Magnentius around Mursa. Magnentius was defeated and fled to Italy. He was attacked many times by Constantius's soldiers, fought at Seleucus, was defeated and fled to Lugdunum. There he first slaughtered his own brother and his own mother, and afterwards killed himself. Decentius Caesar, his brother, hanged himself. Then Silvanus also usurped power in Gaul and was killed by Constantius's soldiers. Constantius came to Rome and entered with much
(59) For his twentieth anniversary Constantius Augustus entered Rome with great pomp and ceremony. His wife, the empress Eusebia, also entered with him, and they spent days

CHRONOGRAPHY [?]. pomp and ceremony, and was acclaimed above the emperors before him. His wife Eusebia also came with him, and he spent fourteen days in Rome. He went out to the Campus of the Tribunal and stood on a height, with the army and Vetranio present. There he addressed the people and tried to persuade them that the empire and its authority properly belonged to the one who had inherited it from emperors among his forebears. He also argued that it was better for the people and the commonwealth to have public affairs administered under one authority, and made other points along these lines. Then he stripped Vetranio, who had reigned ten months, of the purple, and at that same hour shared his table with him at a banquet. He sent him to Prusa in Bithynia with every honour, an escort of guards and many gifts. Vetranio was a Christian, and from then on he devoted himself to the church and gave much alms to the poor. He also honoured the priests until the day of his death. Constantius returned to Byzantium and, at the urging of his wife Eusebia, brought Julian, the brother of Gallus, out of custody. He made him Caesar and sent him to Gaul, giving him his own sister Helena, also called Constantia, in marriage. In the same year Julius the pope also fell asleep in Rome, and Liberius was ordained in his place, a man admirable in every way and orthodox. But the Arians so

turned the emperor against Athanasius that he decreed the death penalty for him. But even then the saint saved himself by flight.

A.M. 5850. First year of Macedonius, bishop of Constantinople. In this year a great earthquake struck Nicomedia around the third hour of the night. It overwhelmed the city and killed great numbers of people, and Cecropius, the bishop of the city, died with them.

A.M. 5851. First year of Leontius, bishop of Antioch. First year of Eudoxius, bishop of Constantinople, after Macedonius was expelled.

A.M. 5852. While Macedonius held the see of Constantinople like a tyrant, he moved the body of Constantine the Great from the Holy Apostles to Saint Acacius, claiming that the church was about to collapse. The people tried to stop him and there was a great slaughter, so that the well, the courtyard of the martyr's shrine and the surrounding streets were filled with blood. When Constantius learned of this, he was furious with Macedonius. He ordered him deposed and installed Eudoxius in his place, exchanging a great evil for a greater one. In this year the Persians captured the fortress called Bezabde. Constantius was staying at Antioch because of the Persian war when he heard that Julian, who had won renown in the wars in Gaul, had been proclaimed emperor by the army. He set out against Julian the usurper. When he reached Mopsucrenae, the first stopping place from Tarsus in Cilicia, he died on the third of the month Dios, having

bitterly condemned his own folly. He had been baptized [?] at Antioch by Euzoius the Arian, in the year of the world 5852, in the 11th cycle of 532 years [with the 12th beginning]. Once Julian became sole ruler, he shamelessly lived as a pagan. He washed off holy baptism with the blood of sacrifices and did everything by which demons are worshipped.

A.M. 5853. Julian, emperor of the Romans.

In this year Julian the Transgressor became emperor and ruled alone because of the great number of our sins. Elated by his victory over the barbarians, he took power for himself and put on the diadem, and before Constantius died he shamelessly turned to paganism. Constantius deeply repented of all this when he gave up his spirit: the murder of his kin, the innovations in the faith, and his proclamation of the Apostate. When Julian the Apostate became sole ruler by the judgements of God, all kinds of God-sent wrath fell on the land of the Romans. The lawless man wanted to show that Constantius had been unjust and inhumane, so he pretended to be just and recalled the bishops who were in exile. But he put to death Eusebius, the chief of the imperial eunuchs, on the claim that he was unjust. He also drove out the other eunuchs of the palace, because he had lost his wife, the sister whom Constantius had given him in marriage. Likewise he drove out the cooks, because his diet was frugal, and the barbers, because one was enough for many, as he said. From the public post he removed the camels, donkeys, oxen and mules and allowed only horses to serve. He did this out of his great avarice, to which he was a slave

as it is the first [?] form of idolatry. Then the pagans in the East were emboldened. In Alexandria they immediately dragged off George the bishop and killed him. They godlessly abused his remains, put them on a camel and paraded them through the city. Then they mixed his remains with the bones of dead animals, burned them and scattered the ashes. Then Athanasius, who had been hiding for a long time with a certain virgin, came out. He held a council in Alexandria, confirmed the doctrines of Nicaea and recovered his church. After George the Arians appointed Lucius for themselves and gathered in a private house. The pagans also crucified and slaughtered many other Christians. They dug up the remains of Patrophilus, bishop of Scythopolis, and scattered most of them, but they hung up the skull as an insult and mocked it. In Gaza and Ascalon they killed priests and consecrated virgins, cut open their bellies, filled them with barley and threw them to the pigs. In Phoenicia the people of Heliopolis killed Cyril the deacon and tasted his liver, because in the time of the blessed Constantine he had overthrown their idols. The man who cut open the deacon and tasted his liver suffered this: his tongue rotted and fell away, he lost his teeth and went blind, and he died in torment. Julian did many evils to the Christians at Caesarea in Cappadocia. He took away the city's rights and its name of Caesarea, and ordered it to be called Mazaca, as it was before, because the Christians there had done many evils to the pagans under Constantius and had razed the temple of Fortune. In Arethusa they committed terrible acts against the Christians, among them [?] Mark, the most holy monk, the

[Maris] of Chalcedon [hurled] many insults at Julian to his face while he was sacrificing in the temple of Fortune [?].

A.M. 5854. In this year the impious Julian passed a law that Christians should have no share in Greek learning. But Apollinarius did the Church much good. He used divine Scripture as his material and imitated the styles of the ancient writers. He also wrote a treatise against Julian, which he entitled On Truth. Julian ordered Athanasius the Great to be driven out of Alexandria, since the pagans had furiously stirred him up against him. As Athanasius went out [?], he told the Christians who were weeping for him to take heart. "Take heart," he said, "it is a little cloud, and it is passing." Julian also wrote to the people of Bostra telling them to expel Titus, their holy bishop, from the city. Then there was Dorotheus, the much-tried bishop of Tyre. He had written many ecclesiastical histories and was distinguished in letters, and he had become a confessor under Diocletian and again under Licinius, [?]. In the second year of the Transgressor, Julian's officials found him living privately in Odyssopolis and inflicted [?] tortures on him for his faith in Christ, though he was one hundred and seven years old. [The worthless Transgressor] imitated the good works of the Christians and ordered necessities to be supplied to strangers and the poor, deceiving the simpler folk. The impious man ordered Zeus, Ares, Hermes and the other demons to be painted alongside his portraits, and those who refused to venerate them to be punished as enemies of the emperor. When he distributed [?] to the army, he set out fire and incense beside it and forced the soldiers to burn incense. At Caesarea Philippi, which is now Paneas, the home town of the woman with the flow of blood, a statue stood in front of her [house] [?]: a statue of [our] Lord and God Jesus

…set up. The impious Julian ordered it taken down, and so it was: the pagans dragged the statue away, supposedly in mockery, and set up in its place a wooden image bearing Julian's name. The Christians took the statue and placed it in a church, but fire came down from heaven and burned up the Apostate's image. Under the base of the statue there grew a plant that was a remedy for every disease, and this was what moved the Apostate Julian to envy, so that he overthrew the Lord's statue. At Nicopolis in Palestine, formerly called Emmaus, there is a spring that heals every kind of ailment in both people and animals. For they say that our Lord and God Jesus Christ washed his feet in it after a journey, and the impious one ordered it to be filled in. At Hermopolis in the Thebaid there stands a persea tree. If anyone takes a leaf or twig from it, it is [?] against every human disease. They say that when the Lord fled into Egypt from Herod with the Theotokos and Joseph and came to that place, the tree bent down to the ground and worshipped him, and to this day it keeps the posture of worship. While Julian was staying in Antioch, he kept going up to Daphne and paying cult to the idol of Apollo, but he got no answer from the idol, as he had expected. He realized that the idol was silent because of the relics of the holy martyr Babylas laid up at Daphne, so he issued a decree that all the remains of the dead laid up there be moved, along with the martyr's. When this was done, the temple was suddenly burned by fire from heaven in the night. The idol was burned so completely that not a trace of it was left. It was said to have stood for [?] years. The temple was so ruined that those who came later saw its ashes and were amazed at this marvel of God's wonder-working. Julian was astounded at this. Suspecting that it had happened through a plot of the Christians, he proceeded to interrogate the priests who served there, and he subjected them to all kinds of

tortures, so that some of them even died. Yet all he heard from them was that it had not happened through the Christians or through any human plot. Fire had come down from heaven and set the temple and the statues alight, and some in the countryside had even seen the fire coming down that night. The emperor was enraged and, as though fighting against God, closed the Great Church and confiscated all the sacred vessels. Two counts, Felix and Julian, both apostates, were sent, and they said, “We thought there was some overseeing power that would stop us.” And Felix said, “See what sort of vessels the son of Mary is served with!” A little later Felix suddenly vomited blood from his mouth and ended his life in torment. On that same day Count Julian fell into a most grievous illness: his insides rotted and he brought up excrement through his mouth, and he died in torment. Year of the World 5855. In this year some of those enrolled in military service were drawn into apostasy, some by promises of gifts and ranks, others under compulsion from their own commanders. Theotecnus, a presbyter entrusted with a church in a suburb of Antioch, was led astray by a promise and went over to idolatry of his own accord. God punished him at once: he became worm-eaten and lost his sight, and he died chewing his own tongue. Heron, a bishop of the Thebaid, apostatized of his own accord in the city of Antioch, and God punished him at once as an example and a warning to many. A putrefying disease dissolved his limbs, and he lay cast out in the public square and breathed his last before the eyes of all. Others in these times distinguished themselves by confessing Christ. Valentinian, then tribune of the regiment called the numerus of the Cornuti, not only scorned his rank but was sent into exile. Afterwards God made him emperor

was proclaimed. Likewise Jovian unbuckled his belt, crying, “I am a Christian.” The army loved him, since he was a camp commander, and begged the emperor not to harm him. He too was proclaimed emperor after Julian. Artemius, the duke of the administration of Egypt, had shown great zeal against the idols in Alexandria in the time of Constantius, so his property was confiscated and he was beheaded. At Dorostolum in Thrace, Aemilianus, one of the soldiers, was martyred: Capitolinus handed him over to the fire. Many others in various places and in various ways distinguished themselves by confessing Christ. A certain Thalassius, notorious for his debauchery and profligacy, who even procured his own daughter for shameful acts, was honored by the emperor as a haruspex. He lived in Antioch near the palace. His house collapsed on him, and he alone perished, together with one eunuch, with whom he was found entangled. All his household, who were Christians, were saved, including his wife and those with her. A child of up to seven years was found there and saved, and when asked how he had been saved, he said he had been carried by an angel. The ill-named Julian, seeking to overturn the divine sentence, ordered the temple of the Jews to be rebuilt, and he put Alypius, a pagan zealous against Christ, in charge of the work. When he had dug out the hidden parts of the foundations, [?] a most violent wind blew up with a whirlwind and scattered the lime that had been prepared, two hundred thousand modii of it. When the Jews persisted with the work, fire came forth and burned them, and so they gave up their audacious attempt. The impious Julian also wrote a refutation of the divine Gospels, which the great Cyril of Alexandria brilliantly demolished in a special treatise. was a Tyrian by birth and had formerly been a wretched Christian. But after he was beaten by Christians in Caesarea of Palestine, he went over to paganism in anger, and then the dog dared to write against the truth. After these events the divine cross was seen in the sky, shining with light and encircled by a crown of light. It stretched from Golgotha to the holy Mount of Olives and was even brighter than in the time of Constantius. The sign of the cross also appeared of its own accord on the altar cloths, the books, and the other vestments of the churches, and on the clothing not only of Christians but also of Jews, and not only in Jerusalem but also in Antioch and other cities. Those Jews and pagans who shamelessly refused to believe found their own garments covered with crosses, and on some they were even black. Julian sent many people to oracles and prophetic shrines in various places, so that he might be seen to begin the war against the Persians with the demons' permission. Many different oracles were brought to him, but I will mention one. It runs as follows: “Now we gods have all set out to carry off the trophies of victory beside the Beast river, and I shall lead them, impetuous Ares, rouser of war.” Reassured by these oracles, he armed for war against the Persians, after fining the Christians large sums of money. While he was in Antioch, he was violently insulted by the Antiochenes over the price of goods. It was then that he composed the speech called the Antiochikos, supposedly in retaliation. A young man named Theodore, who had started the insults against him, he bitterly [?]. He did many great [evils] to the Christians and threatened to do more after the Persian war, and he ended his utterly foul life badly. For beyond the frontier, by divine justice, he was slain in this year, after reigning two years and nine months. He was struck down by God in the Persian [campaign] on the twenty-sixth of the month of January, in the sixth indiction,

at the age of thirty-one. While he was in Persia, in the month of Daisios, a sign occurred. In the house of a Christian countrywoman, a jar filled with water was changed in the evening into wine, bubbling like new must, and at that very hour she brought the full vessel to the village church. The presbyter of the place filled a small vessel from it and brought it to Bishop Abgar. At Carrhae a woman was found hanging by her hair, and in Antioch many human skulls were found. The Apostate had used them to take omens for the Persian war, and he had put seals and bolts on those places. Year of the World 5856. Of Jovian, emperor of the Romans, [year 1].

In this year Jovian, a chiliarch, a very gentle man and an orthodox Christian, was proclaimed emperor of the Romans by the whole army, the generals, and the high officials, in the same place in Persian territory where the Apostate had been slain. After a single engagement, the Romans and Persians agreed to proclaim peace, as though it came from God, and it was fixed for thirty years. Jovian had tried to decline the throne, saying he could not rule an army that had turned pagan under Julian, but they all cried with one voice that they were Christians. Jovian ceded the great city of Nisibis to the Persians to save the people who were left, and made peace. He sent out general laws on behalf of the churches to all the lands of the Romans, giving back to the catholic Church the standing and honor it had had under the blessed Constantine the Great. He recalled the bishops who were in exile, and he wrote to the holy Athanasius asking him to set out for him in writing the exact teaching of the blameless

He gave many gifts to those who confessed the homoousion and exempted them from taxes. Acacius of Caesarea, the most wicked Arian, met with other bishops at Antioch and drew up a document that was supposedly orthodox. In it he confessed the homoousion and the council at Nicaea, but out of fear of the pious emperor, not out of regard for God. The emperor Jovian entered Antioch in the month of Hyperberetaios. A child was born to a country gardener outside the city gate at the place called Tripylon. It was a girl, born in the seventh month, with two distinct heads, each fully formed, as though each head were separate from the neck. It was born dead in the month of Dios, that is, November. Jovian set out from Antioch for Constantinople. When he came to Ancyra in Galatia, he entered upon the consulship together with his son Varronian, whom he proclaimed nobilissimus without clothing him in the purple. In the same year Jovian, the most Christian, died at a place in Bithynia called Dadastana, having reigned nine months and fifteen days. Valentinian Augustus was then proclaimed emperor by the army, and he reigned eleven years. They chose him because he had won esteem as a Christian for his confession. He set out at once for Constantinople, and when he reached the imperial city, he proclaimed his own brother Valens partner in his reign. He assigned him the eastern regions and kept the western ones for himself. Year of the World 5857. Of Valentinian, emperor of the Romans, year 1.

In this year Valentinian Augustus proclaimed his son Gratian Augustus, having already proclaimed him partner in the reign and consul. As has been said, he had also proclaimed his brother Valens emperor, an ardent Arian who had been [baptized] [?] by Eudoxius. The orthodox approached Valentinian through Hypatius, bishop of Heraclea, asking for permission to meet in order to restore the doctrine of the homoousion. Valentinian answered them, “I am ranked among the laity, and it is not right for me to meddle in such matters. So you priests do as you see fit.” Then they met at Lampsacus and spent two months there. In the end they annulled what Eudoxius and Acacius had done at Constantinople and decreed that the faith of Seleucia should prevail. But the impious Valens overturned the decisions of Lampsacus and sent the bishops who had met there into exile. He handed the churches of Constantinople over to Eudoxius, who shared his views, and the orthodox had neither shepherd nor church. Year of the World 5858. In this year Liberius, bishop

of Rome, Athanasius of Alexandria, Meletius of Antioch, and Eusebius of Samosata had been recalled from exile by Jovian and were distinguished for right doctrine. So were Cyril of Jerusalem and other bishops who championed orthodoxy. Lucius led the Arians in Alexandria, and [?] in Antioch. The orthodox there were divided in two: Paulinus led one party and Meletius the other. Year of the World 5859. Of Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, year 1. Of Euzoius, bishop of Antioch, year 1. In this year Procopius rebelled at Constantinople in the month of September. He marched out to Nacolia and protected himself with a very large army, which frightened Valens, so that for a short time he let up his war against the churches. Then Procopius was betrayed by his own generals, Agilo and Gomarius. Valens tied Procopius by the legs to two trees that had been bent down close to each other and ordered them let go. The trees sprang violently upright and tore the usurper apart. He ordered the generals Agilo and Gomarius, who had betrayed him, to be sawn in two. The wretches suffered this for a loyalty they had shown to one who did not deserve it. At that time he also pulled down the walls of Chalcedon on account of Procopius. Once he had done away with Procopius, he moved against the truth again. He also forced Eleusius of Cyzicus to confess the heterousion. When Eleusius came to Cyzicus, he made his own transgression public, called himself unworthy of the [priesthood] [?], and urged that another bishop be chosen for Cyzicus. When the evil-minded Eudoxius learned of this, he appointed Eunomius bishop of Cyzicus in his place. At that time the emperor Valens was staying at
[…] has: that in the third year of his reign [?] he set out and campaigned against the Persians, and at that time Procopius also plotted a usurpation against [?]. [?]

Marcianopolis in Moesia. A great earthquake struck the whole earth by night in the tenth indiction. In Alexandria, ships moored at the shore were lifted high into the air, passed over the tall buildings and the [walls] [?], and were carried inside into courtyards and houses. When the sea withdrew, they were left on dry land. The people who were fleeing the city because of the earthquake saw the ships on dry land and went to plunder the cargo in them, and the water came back and covered them all. Other sailors reported that at that hour they were sailing in the middle of the Adriatic Sea when they were overtaken [?]. Suddenly, out in the open sea, the ship settled onto the seabed. A little later the water came back again, and so they sailed on. Year of the World 5860. In this year, while his wife Severa, the mother of Gratian, was still alive, Valentinian the Great unlawfully married Justina, whose beauty Severa herself had praised. By her he had children: Valentinian, known as the Younger, whom the army proclaimed emperor after his father's death, and three daughters, Justa, Grata, and Galla. Theodosius the Great took Galla as his second wife, and she bore him [Placidia] [?]. Arcadius and Honorius were Theodosius's sons by his first wife, Flaccilla. Valentinian also wrote a lawless law that anyone who wished to have two wives at once should not be prevented. The impious Valens had two daughters, Anastasia and Carosa. He built two baths named after them, as well as the aqueduct that to this day is called the Valentinian aqueduct. Some say that Domnica, Valens's wife, persuaded him to be such a fervent Arian. Others relate that he was baptized by Eudoxius after becoming emperor and swore an oath during the baptism itself that he held the views of Arius and would not accept the homoousion. And so both of these unholy men stirred up countless persecutions against the orthodox. They also sent to Liberius of Rome Eustathius the

These men gave Liberius a written statement in support of the homoousion, declaring that they rejected every heresy opposed to the council at Nicaea. Liberius received them and admitted them to communion, and he wrote to the bishops of the East testifying to their orthodoxy. Valens, campaigning against the Goths from Marcianopolis, spent the winter there. Year of the World 5861. Of Anianus, bishop of Antioch,

In this year a synod was held at Tyana. Among those present were Eusebius of Caesarea in Cappadocia, Gregory of Nazianzus, the father of Gregory the Theologian, Otreius of Melitene, and others. They rejoiced at Liberius's letters and sent word to all the orthodox bishops to come to Tarsus to confirm the right faith, but when Valens heard of it, he prevented it. Eudoxius again induced Valens to order the local governors to exile everyone who had been exiled under Constantius. Athanasius then left Alexandria of his own accord, because the people would not let the governor expel him. He hid for a long time in his family tomb, but later Valens, afraid that the Alexandrians would riot, wrote that Athanasius should return. Eunomius broke off communion with Eudoxius because Eudoxius would not be in communion with Aetius, Eunomius's teacher. The two of them were of one mind, but because everyone hated Aetius, Eudoxius turned away from him. He was not ashamed to turn openly away from his own doctrines as though they were impious. Eunomius had been secretary to the godless Aetius and had learned sophistical arguments from him, which he boasted about, though he was completely uninstructed in the divine Scriptures, as his seven volumes especially show. The people of Cyzicus drove Eunomius out as a heretic and blasphemer. He came and joined Eudoxius. He was a dreadful blasphemer who dared to say, “God knows nothing more about his own essence than we do.” More than [in] the pagan persecution befell the

…to the orthodox, under Valens and Eudoxius, the impious. At this time Eudoxius died, and the Arians put forward Demophilus as bishop, while the orthodox put forward a certain Evagrius. He was ordained by the holy Eustathius of Antioch, who was living secretly in Constantinople after returning from exile under Jovian; not finding him alive, he was hiding in the city [?]. Valens was staying at Marcianopolis when he heard of Evagrius' ordination. He exiled the holy Eustathius to Bizye, drove Evagrius out of the city, and handed the churches over to Demophilus.

Year 1 of Demophilus. In this year, when the impious Valens came to Nicomedia, the orthodox sent him an embassy of eighty men of priestly rank, led by Theodore, Urbanus and Menedemus. Valens ordered them all to be set on fire together with their ship, and they were all burned with the vessel, which stayed afloat as far as Dacibiza. A.M. 5863. In this year the abominable Valens gave the pagans leave to perform sacrifices and hold festivals. He likewise favoured and honoured the Jews. Only the orthodox, the members of the apostolic Church, did he persecute fiercely. A.M. [?]. In this year Valens entered Antioch in Syria and showed every kind of cruelty to the orthodox, killing many with the sword and drowning others in the river that flows past the city. When he reached Edessa he did even worse. He ordered Modestus the prefect to seize the crowd of the orthodox who were gathering in the church of St Thomas and slaughter them. But what happened with the woman who was eagerly dragging her child along to its death put Valens to shame, astounded the prefect and prevented the crime. Clearly God had arranged [Apparatus: τοῖς ὀρθοδόξοις omitted in a. δὲ added from A. προεβάλοντο] A: προέβαλον. ἀπέστειλαν] b: ἀνεστείλαντο. ὀγδοήκοντα (eighty)] A: πέντε (five).]

this. Valens exiled Eusebius of Samosata to Thrace. The saint was admired all the more on that occasion, because he left the city willingly and followed the men who were driving him out, although the people would not allow it. In his place the Arians put forward a certain Eunomius, a fiery Arian, with whom none of the people of Samosata would hold communion. Once, when he was bathing and urging the people to bathe with him, they would not bring themselves to bathe until they had emptied the water of the bath that Eunomius had entered and filled it with fresh water, saying it had been polluted by Eunomius. When he learned this he fled the city, implacably hated. After he withdrew, the Arians put forward a certain Lucius, an obvious wolf. Valens was likewise eager to hand over the churches in Cappadocia to the Arians. He seized on the opposition he had met from the great Basil, who was then a presbyter of the Great Church of Caesarea and was rousing Eusebius the bishop to zeal for orthodoxy, so that he would not yield to Valens' impiety. A.M. 5865. Year [?] of Artaxerxes, king of the Persians.

Year 1 of Peter, bishop of Alexandria. Year 1 of Meletius of Antioch, once again. In this year, while Valens was staying at Antioch, some men were discovered plotting against him, and a whole band of impious men was put to death, for they had worked out their conspiracy through divination and sacrifices. Athanasius, who had endured many contests and great toils, departed to the Lord after being bishop for forty-six years, forty of them spent in persecutions and in dangers for the sake of true religion. Peter succeeded him in the episcopate, but the Arians drove him out through a certain Magnus, treasurer of the imperial treasuries, and installed Lucius in his place. Then many orthodox men, and women who were virgins, were tortured in godless fashion, and many also died under torture. Peter fled to Damasus in Rome, as one who shared his faith. At that time he also wrote a letter describing the horrors the Arians had committed in Alexandria. In the same

year Basil became bishop of Caesarea, Eusebius having fallen asleep in piety. A.M. 5866. In this year Ambrose succeeded Auxentius as head of the Church of Milan, in the following way. The people were in uproar over the appointment of a bishop, and Ambrose, who was governor of the region, was sent by the emperor Valentinian, then residing there, to put a stop to the strife. He was still unbaptized, but deeply concerned for justice, and he boldly convicted even higher officials when they did wrong. The people ceased their quarrel and unanimously elected Ambrose bishop. When Valentinian heard this, he ordered that Ambrose be initiated and ordained bishop. In the sight of all he gave thanks to God, saying: "Thanks be to you, almighty Lord, our Saviour, for you have entrusted souls to this man, whom I made a ruler of bodies, and have shown my choices to be just." Meanwhile Lucius committed many evils in Alexandria together with the Arians. They sang songs of demons in the church of Theonas and brought in dancers. They stripped the virgins of their clothes, beat them furiously about the face [?], and led them naked through the city, abusing them licentiously. Some they even killed, and they would not give the bodies to their parents for burial, though the parents lamented bitterly. They also brought a debauched youth inside the sanctuary to commit obscenities at the altar. Since the whole West honoured the consubstantial Trinity, they petitioned Valentinian, held a synod in Illyricum and ratified the faith of Nicaea. Valentinian wrote an edict to the bishops in Asia, Phrygia and all the East, exhorting them to abide by what the synod had defined, and he took his brother Valens and his son Gratian as partners with him in the

edict. At that time Gregory the Theologian also took charge of the Church of Constantinople, at the urging of Basil, Meletius and the other champions of true religion. Had he not come in time and won the city back, it would have been entirely filled with the filth of Arius and Eunomius. They held all the churches except the oratory of Anastasia the martyr, and Demophilus was bishop of the Arians. In that period Gregory of Nyssa and Peter, the brothers of Basil, shone brightly, as did Optimus in Pisidia and Amphilochius in Iconium. Valens exiled Barses, bishop of Edessa, and Pelagius of Laodicea as champions of orthodoxy. Valentinian reproached his brother Valens for his heterodoxy. When Valens asked him for help against the Goths, he sent none, but said: "It is not right to aid a man who fights against God." A.M. 5867. In this year Valentinian the Great died at the age of eighty-four, after reigning eleven years. It happened in this way. The Sarmatians, a small and pitiable nation, had risen against him and been defeated, and they sent envoys asking for peace. Valentinian asked the envoys whether all the Sarmatians were as pitiable in body as they were, and they replied: "You have before you and see here the best of us all." At this he cried out violently: "Terrible things the Roman Empire must suffer, if, now that it has come down to Valentinian, Sarmatians such as these rise up against the Romans!" From the strain and the clapping of his hands a vein

burst, a great deal of blood poured out, and he died in a fortress in Gaul on the 17th of Dius, in the third indiction. His son Gratian was not there, and Valens was staying at Antioch, so the army present at the place where Valentinian the Great died proclaimed his four-year-old son Valentinian Augustus. His mother Justina was also present, in Pannonia. When Gratian learned of this, he kept his brother as co-emperor with himself, but he punished those who had proclaimed him in various ways, because it had been done against his will. Valens sent Trajan as general against the Goths, and he was shamefully defeated and came back. When Valens reproached him for cowardice, he answered: "It is not I who have been defeated, emperor, but you, for you are waging war against God and winning his favour for the barbarians." Valens put many people to death because of men suspected from divinations, on the basis of the letter, of being destined to reign. Among them was a certain Theodore, first

At the same time some of the Novatians in Phrygia began to celebrate Easter with the Jews. They met in the village of Pazus and laid down a rule to keep the Passover with the Jews. From them sprang the so-called Sabbatians, named after a certain Sabbatius. Later, too, Apollinaris the Syrian openly broke away from the Church at that time. Damasus of Rome and Peter of Alexandria were the first to denounce them. The impious Eunomius dared to perform baptism with a single immersion, saying that one must be baptized not into the Trinity but into the death of Christ, and he rebaptized those who had been baptized into the Trinity. Julian, also called Sabas, a holy ascetic, came to Antioch from Edessa and supported the orthodox who held to the homoousion, openly anathematizing the Arians. The divine Aphraates, with great boldness, refuted Valens' impiety to his face in Antioch. One of the eunuchs insolently reviled and threatened Aphraates. When he went off to prepare a bath for the emperor, he was struck in his mind, threw himself into the hot water and perished. Ephrem the Great also shone in asceticism and divine teaching. He poured out many ascetic discourses, and a great many doctrinal ones too, as if from a divine spring, and he gave some of his works to the Syrians to be sung to melody.

In this year the heresy of the Messalians, also called Euchites and Enthusiasts, sprang up. When they sing psalms they clash cymbals and rattle castanets, taking what is in David crudely and foolishly. Its heresiarchs were Dadoes, Sabbas and Adelphius, and some say Eustathius of Sebasteia as well. They were nobly opposed by Amphilochius of Iconium and Letoius of Melitene, and later also by Flavian of Antioch. Valens, having ravaged every Church, came from the East to Caesarea

raging against the divine Basil. What he did there the great Gregory also related in his funeral oration for Basil. At that time Galates, Valens' son, fell gravely ill and died, and his consort Domnica was also seriously ill. During the divine Basil's meeting with the emperor, Demosthenes, one of Valens' cooks, attacked him and committed a slight barbarism, and the teacher said to him: "Look, we have seen an illiterate Demosthenes too!" Valens, out of respect for Basil, gave many excellent estates to the maimed [?] in Basil's care. But seeing Basil's firmness and inflexibility, he decreed exile against him. When he tried to sign the document of exile he could not: three pens broke, and finally his hand was paralysed as well. A.M. 5869. In this year Mavia, queen of the Saracens, who had done the Romans much harm, asked for peace. She also asked that Moses, one of the ascetics in the desert, be given as bishop to the Christians among the Saracens. The emperor eagerly did so, but Moses refused to be ordained by Lucius the Arian and asked to be ordained by one of the orthodox [?] bishops in exile, and this was done. Once Mavia had received him, she made many of the Saracens Christians. They say that she herself was a Christian and a Roman by birth, who had been taken captive and pleased the king of the Saracens by her beauty, and so came to rule the kingdom. Sozomen relates much about this nation: where it came from, how it got its name, and that they are circumcised at thirteen. The Goths, under attack from the Huns, asked the emperor Valens for help through their bishop Ulfilas [?], a man of Arian views who had spent time in Constantius' day with Eudoxius and Acacius, the Arians. He taught the Goths to be Arians. The Goths were divided into two groups, one led by Athanaric and the other by Fritigern. Fritigern was defeated, received help from Valens and conquered Athanaric's forces. To please Valens, he taught the Goths to be Arians still more thoroughly.

In this year the Goths again [?] came out into Roman territory and devastated many provinces: Moesia, Thrace, Macedonia, Achaea and all of Greece, some twenty provinces. At this time armed men were seen in the air, formed in the clouds. And at Antioch a child was born that was perfect in its other parts but had one eye in the middle of its forehead, four hands and four feet, and a beard. Valens was staying in the city of Antioch, and when he learned about the Goths he came to Constantinople. The Byzantines mocked him as unmanly and afraid of war. Isaac, the holy monk, seized the bridle of Valens' horse as he was setting out to war for the last time and said to him: "Where are you going, emperor, waging war against God and having God for your adversary?" Angered, Valens had him put in custody and threatened him with death if he himself returned, as Ahab once threatened Micaiah. After he had left, some of his entourage confessed that divinations had been performed at his command about the venture that lay before him in the war. In that war Valens engaged the Goths, was defeated and fled with a few men into a cottage. The barbarians caught up with him, set fire to the house without knowing who was inside, and burned everyone in it. They say that the divine Isaac, in custody, perceived the stench of Valens burning, through a divine gift and the purity of his soul. He foretold his death to those who were with him before the messengers arrived from the war to report what had happened. After Valens' defeat and death by fire, the Goths, elated by their victory, plundered the suburbs of Constantinople savagely. But Mavia, queen of the Saracens, sent a Saracen army, and Domnica, Valens' wife, led out the people of the city, and together they drove off the barbarians. After these events, Gratian Augustus learned of them and came down into Pannonia as though to help. In Valens' place he invested Theodosius as Augustus, proclaimed him emperor and sent him to the war against the Goths. The Goths

In this year the emperor Gratian put forward Theodosius as his partner in the empire. Theodosius was a Spaniard from the West by birth, a man of noble family who had shown remarkable ability in war. He at once decisively defeated the barbarians in Thrace, and he was pious and orthodox. Gratian and Valentinian recalled the exiled bishops by law and expelled the Arians, with the cooperation of Damasus, pope of Rome. Then Peter, bishop of Alexandria, also returned, drove out Lucius and recovered his own throne. When he died, his brother Timothy was ordained in his place as bishop of the orthodox Church in Alexandria. In Antioch in Syria the orthodox had been split in two since the time of the divine Eustathius. Some had Paulinus as bishop, the others the holy Meletius, after Euzoius, the bishop of the Arians, was put forward. The emperors wrote a law in favour of the orthodox and sent it to the East through a certain Sapor, a general. When he reached Antioch, he found a quarrel: Paulinus was laying claim to the episcopate and Apollinaris was trying to seize the throne, while the holy Meletius stayed quietly out of the fight. Flavian, then a presbyter, opposed Paulinus, put Apollinaris to shame and urged the general Sapor to give the throne to Meletius. Sapor confirmed Meletius and departed. Then the great Meletius ordained Diodore bishop of Tarsus. Eusebius, bishop of Samosata, returned from exile and ordained many bishops in various cities. He came to Doliche to ordain Maris as bishop,

and as he was entering the city he was killed. An Arian woman threw a tile from a height onto the holy head of the saint, God permitting it by judgements known only to him. Of him Gregory the Theologian says: "I seek him who was slain among you yesterday [?], the old man like Abraham." At that time Gregory the Theologian was also teaching ever more boldly in Constantinople in the oratory of holy Anastasia, where they say marvellous miracles also take place through appearances of our all-holy Lady, the Theotokos. A.M. 5872. Year 1 of Timothy, bishop of Alexandria. A.M. 5873. Year 1 of Siricius, bishop of Rome. A.M. 5874. In this year the emperor Gratian was killed through the treachery of Andragathius, general of the usurper Maximus. Andragathius entered in a carriage pretending to be Gratian's wife, and when Gratian came to meet him unguarded, Andragathius killed him. After his death Valentinian held the Roman empire. At the same time Theodosius the Great fell ill in Thessalonica and was baptized by Acholius the bishop. He wrote a law in favour of the orthodox who held the homoousion and sent it to Constantinople. When he came to Constantinople, he told Demophilus that he must either renounce the error of Arius or leave the churches at once. Demophilus gathered the mass of the Arians and held services outside the city, with Lucius, the Arian bishop of Alexandria, alongside him. And so at last the divine Gregory, together with those whom he himself had enlightened in the orthodox faith, took over all the churches, which the Arians had held for a little more than forty years. A.M. 5875. Year [?] of Varanes [?], king of the Persians.

[?] four children [?], and they lived for two months and then died one after another, all four of them. A.M. 5876. In this year the great, holy and ecumenical Second Synod of the hundred and fifty orthodox bishops was assembled in Constantinople by Theodosius the Great, to confirm the doctrines of Nicaea. He also summoned thirty-six bishops of the Macedonian heresy, led by Eleusius. The holy hundred and fifty Fathers were led by Timothy of Alexandria, Meletius of Antioch, the most holy Cyril of Jerusalem and the divine Gregory of Constantinople. The Fathers urged the thirty-six bishops of Macedonius' persuasion to accept the doctrines of Nicaea, as they had done when they reached agreement with Liberius under Valens and submitted written statements. But the party of Silvanus, who had been sent to Rome, refused to assent to the truth. They departed, having made themselves a laughingstock to all, since they held one thing and agreed to another, and deceitfully produced Liberius' letters as testimony to their orthodoxy. The holy synod confirmed Gregory the Theologian in the episcopate of Constantinople and installed him on the throne against his will, because he had toiled greatly and freed the Church from the filth of the heresies. But that all-wise and most blessed man learned that some of the Egyptians resented this. He delivered his farewell oration and voluntarily withdrew from the throne of the imperial city. After he had taken his leave, the emperor and the synod chose Nectarius. He was a native of Tarsus who at that time held the office of praetor and was still unbaptized, but was dignified and devout in his way of life. The holy and ecumenical synod confirmed the homoousion,

The council also added to the creed the theology of the Holy Spirit. It issued canons as well, in which it granted the throne of Constantinople the privileges of New Rome. Gregory of Nyssa, Pelagius of Laodicea, Eulogius of Edessa and Amphilochius of Iconium shone at this council, together with the great Gregory and those already mentioned. The holy synod anathematized Arius, Eusebius of Nicomedia, Euzoius, Acacius, Theognis, Euphronius and the rest. It also condemned Macedonius the Pneumatomachian, along with Eudoxius, Aetius and Eunomius. After the synod had concluded in Constantinople, the great Meletius fell asleep in peace. His sacred body was carried to Antioch and laid near the tomb of the holy martyr Babylas. Flavian was then ordained bishop of Antioch while Paulinus was still alive, even though oaths had been given that Flavian would not accept ordination as bishop. So the Church of Antioch was again in turmoil, with some submitting to Paulinus and others to Flavian. At that time the emperor also brought the body of Paul the Confessor to Constantinople and laid it in the church that Macedonius had built while plotting against Paul. A.M. 5877. — Year 1 of [?], bishop of Constantinople. In this year Theodosius Augustus proclaimed his son Honorius, born to him by the most pious Placilla, nobilissimus and consul. He also prepared to make war on the usurper Maximus. While he was fighting Maximus in the western regions, a false rumour went out that Maximus had won, and the Arians rose up and set fire to the house of Nectarius, bishop of Constantinople. [?] A.M. 5878. — In this year in Antioch, at the gate called the Taurian, an addition was built to widen the bridge, and it was roofed over. A small basilica was also built in the Old City, near the great one. In Palestine, in the village of Emmaus, a child was born who was whole from the navel down but divided above. It had two chests and two heads, and each had its own senses. One would eat and drink while the other did not eat; one would sleep while the other

stayed awake. Sometimes they played with each other, and both would cry, and they would hit each other. They lived a little under two years. Then one died, and the other lived four more days before it too died. In the same year the emperor Theodosius set up the column of the Taurus. A.M. 5879. — In this year Timothy, bishop of Alexandria, died on the twenty-sixth of the month Epiphi, and Theophilus was ordained in his place. A.M. 5880. — Year 1 of Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria. In this year the pious emperor Theodosius defeated the usurper Maximus and put him to death on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August. He also put to death Andragathius, Maximus's general, for having treacherously murdered Gratian. A.M. 5881. — In this year Theodosius came to Rome with his son Honorius and installed him there as emperor on the fifth day before the Ides of June. Then he went back to Constantinople. A.M. 5882. — In this year Eugenius, formerly a grammarian, who was serving as an imperial secretary, made himself usurper and put on the imperial dress. With him was Arbogast, from Lesser Galatia. When Valentinian, the son of Valentinian the Great by Justina, heard of this, he hanged himself. Learning of this, Theodosius armed himself to march out and avenge him. Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, made a request to the emperor Theodosius and then purged the pagan temple in Alexandria and turned it into a church. The rites of the

pagans he exposed to public view: phalluses [?] and anything even more licentious and profane. The mass of the pagans, put to shame by this, committed many murders. When Theodosius learned of the murders they had committed, he declared the slain Christians blessed as martyrs. To the pagans he promised pardon if they converted to Christianity, and he ordered their temples to be demolished and the idols melted down and given for the needs of the poor. When the temple of Serapis in Alexandria was being pulled down, hieroglyphic letters were found in the shape of a cross. When pagans who had come to the faith saw it, they said that in the meaning of hieroglyphic writing the cross signified "life to come." A.M. 5885. — In this year Marcellus, bishop of Apamea in Syria, was moved by divine zeal and destroyed the pagan temples in Apamea. For this he was killed by the pagans. Nectarius of Constantinople abolished the office of the presbyter in charge of penance, because of the sin a certain deacon had committed in the church with a woman who was doing penance. In Rome and the whole West, however, the practice is carefully kept to this day, and a place is set apart for penitents. The emperor Theodosius wrote a law that no woman should advance to the rank of deaconess unless she was over sixty years old, in keeping with the Apostle. He exiled Eunomius, who was holding [?] and deceiving the people, and he died in [?]. In the same year Placilla, the wife of Theodosius, fell asleep. She was pious and loved the poor, and with her own hands she served the maimed and the sick. The people of Antioch smashed her statue and dragged it about, angry at the public taxes the emperor had imposed on them. He was furious with them out of his love for the most pious Placilla, and he would have destroyed them all if the bishop of Antioch [?] had not come and pleaded on behalf of the Antiochenes. John

Chrysostom, who was then a presbyter of Antioch and was present, delivered wonderful sermons to admonish those who had dared to act against the imperial statues. A.M. 5888. — In this year Theodosius marched against the usurper Eugenius and came down to Thessalonica with his army. When the army entered the city, the city was thrown into turmoil over the billeting of the soldiers and over a charioteer and the prefect's slave boy. The people insulted the emperor and murdered the prefect. The emperor held his patience for a short while and quieted the people. Then he ordered horse races to be held, and when the people and the factions had gathered to watch in the hippodrome, he ordered the army to shoot them with arrows. Fifteen thousand of the people died. When he came to Milan, Bishop Ambrose barred him from entering the church. It was then the feast of the Saviour's Nativity. When Rufinus the magister came to plead for him, Ambrose rebuked him severely. Then, at Ambrose's urging, Theodosius issued a law that those condemned to death or to confiscation of property should be given thirty days for their case to be reviewed. At that point Ambrose received him into the church, but only outside the sanctuary, not inside it as had been the custom before. Since then, to this day, the custom has rightly prevailed that emperors stand outside the sanctuary with the people. In the same year the Nile did not rise as usual, and the pagans rejoiced, saying the cause was that they had been forbidden to sacrifice to their gods. When the pious emperor learned of this he replied: "May it never be that a river that delights in sacrifices should flood the land." God accepted this and so blessed the rising of the river that everyone in Egypt was afraid the floodwater might swamp Alexandria itself. fought fiercely against Eugenius at the Alpine passes, captured him alive and put him to death. Arbogast escaped but took his own life. In the same year the relics of the prophets Habakkuk and Micah were found through divine guidance by Zebennus, bishop of Eleutheropolis in Palestine, after he received a revelation. They were found in two places in the territory around Eleutheropolis. When the emperor came to Rome, the bishops approached him, on the decision of Innocent of Rome, to complain against Flavian, bishop of Antioch. The most Christian emperor urged them toward peace and reunited them after seventeen years of division. He ordered bishops from the East to come to Rome, and among them came Acacius of Beroea as envoy [?]. Theodosius granted Rome many favours. He put an end to the outrages committed in the bakeries against strangers who fell into their hands and were shut up in the mills until old age. He likewise put an end to the abuse of adulterous women in the brothels, no longer allowing them to be shut up there and the act announced by a bell. A.M. 5886. — In this year, after the usurper Eugenius had been killed and affairs had been settled, the pious emperor Theodosius left Rome and set out for Constantinople. When he reached Milan he fell ill. He sent for his son Honorius, and when he saw him he felt

better. But after watching a horse race following his midday meal, he suddenly took a turn for the worse. Unable to go up to the races in the afternoon, he ordered his son to preside over them to the end. The following night he fell asleep in the Lord, at the age of sixty, having reigned sixteen years. He left his two sons as emperors: Arcadius, the elder, over the East, and Honorius over the West. Arcadius carried his body to Constantinople and buried it in the church of the Holy Apostles.

A.M. 5891. — In this year Anatolius, the most illustrious, was burned in Alexandria. The emperor Arcadius formed his own regiment in Constantinople, whose men he called the Arcadiani. A.M. 5892. — In this year Nectarius, bishop of Constantinople, fell asleep. Theophilus of Alexandria, who was present, tried hard to block the election of John Chrysostom. A certain Constantius, a count among Alaric's men, was entrusted with the girl Placidia. He carried her off, fled, and brought her to the emperor Honorius. The emperor welcomed Constantius and made him a senator. A short time later he gave him the girl in marriage and proclaimed him emperor. John, the great teacher, enlightened not only the church of Constantinople but also those of Thrace, Asia and Pontus, so that even before the holy synod of Chalcedon the bishop of Constantinople had authority over these churches. A certain Macedonian came over to the Church through the Father's teaching. He urged his wife to turn as well and take communion, and with difficulty he persuaded her. But she gave her maidservant some of the Macedonians' communion bread and told her to keep it with her. She then went up to Chrysostom and received communion from his holy hands, pretending to partake of it, but in the end she gave it to the maidservant. When she took the Macedonians' bread and raised it to her mouth, she found it had turned to stone. Shuddering, she came trembling to John's feet, confessed what she had dared to do, and sincerely joined the Church. The stone was laid up in the sacristy to be kept there. In the same year Arcadius set up the column of the Xerolophos and founded Arcadiopolis in Thrace. A.M. 5896. — In this year [?] John Chrysostom was great, shining in life, word and divine gifts, and exacting in every virtue. All the people loved him and were greatly edified by his teaching. But those who lived dissolutely turned against him, and they also joined in the war against him. In the course of these events came the affair of Eutropius the eunuch, and also the quarrel between Severian of Gabala and Serapion, John's archdeacon, the affair of the monks who fled from Egypt because of Theophilus, and the letters Theophilus sent to Epiphanius. Out of all these things, plots were laid against John, the servant of Christ. Epiphanius of Cyprus came to the Hebdomon and performed ordinations and held services against John's wishes. John overlooked this out of divine love and even urged Epiphanius to stay with him in the bishop's residence. But Epiphanius refused, because he had already been prejudiced by Theophilus's slanders against the blessed John. A.M. 5897. — In this year John Chrysostom preached a sermon against wicked women. His foes, the enemies of truth, used it to provoke Eudoxia, saying the sermon had been aimed at her. She told Arcadius that John had treated her terribly and arranged for Theophilus to be summoned, since he was an open enemy of John. Theophilus came to the Oak, the place now called Rufinianae, carried out the plot against John and drove him out of the city. When the people learned of this they rioted, refusing to let John be expelled. Meanwhile Eudoxia, swayed by the people's lamentations, pleaded with the emperor Arcadius, and sending the eunuch Brison she recalled John from Praenetus. But John would not enter the city before a public synod had been held, and he stayed in a suburb at Anaplous.

The people, however, shouted against the emperor and forced him to bring John back and reinstate him on his throne, so that Theophilus and his party took fright and fled the city. Then sixty bishops met and rightly annulled everything Theophilus and his party had done against the divine John. A.M. 5898. — In this year the empress Eudoxia had a silver statue of herself made and set it up at the place called Pittakia, near Saint Irene. The prefect of the city, a Manichaean with pagan sympathies, staged applause, choruses and dances in front of the statue and made such an uproar that he vexed the archbishop, not allowing him to celebrate the divine liturgy in peace; he often threw the chanters into confusion. The holy John attacked this in a sermon. The prefect then stirred Eudoxia up against John, claiming that John resented the honour paid to her statue. And so there was hatred against John once more, and anger once more. It was then that John preached the sermon that begins: "Again Herodias rages." At that the empress's enmity toward him was roused to the full, and again came deposition and exile. The people set fire to the church, and many put themselves in danger for John's sake. John was driven out of the city and exiled to Cucusus, and from there he was moved to Pityus. On the way, as he passed through Armenia and reached Comana, he died in the Lord. After his exile Arsacius was ordained; he was the brother of Nectarius, Chrysostom's predecessor. Innocent of Rome and Flavian of Antioch did not take part in John's expulsion. Instead they consoled the clergy of the city by letter and were indignant at the outrages. Epiphanius sailed away to Cyprus, God having apparently foretold his departure from this life. It is said that he foretold to John his death in exile, and John foretold to Epiphanius his death on board ship. Epiphanius said to those who saw him off: "I am in a hurry; I leave you the books, the city and the hypocrisy." In the same year Eudoxia died. Others even denounced themselves of their own accord, so as not to seem to deny Christ by their silence. AM 59[?]. In this year the emperor Honorius died in Rome on 15 August. The news was announced in Constantinople, and the city was closed for seven days. On his death a certain John, one of the imperial secretaries, seized the throne in Rome and sent an embassy to Theodosius asking to be recognised as emperor. Theodosius shut the envoys up in prison and sent the general Ardabur against him; but the usurper captured him and imprisoned him at Ravenna. When Theodosius learned of this, he sent Ardabur's son Aspar against him. Through the prayer of the God-loving emperor an angel of the Lord appeared in the form of a shepherd and guided Aspar and those with him, leading them through the lake that lies beside Ravenna. It was impassable, but God made it passable, as he did for the Israelites. Crossing over on dry ground, they found the gates of the city open, killed the usurper and freed Ardabur from his chains. After John had been killed, the emperor Theodosius made Valentinian, son of Constantius and Galla Placidia, Caesar and sent him to the West with his mother. He also sent with him Helion the patrician, who was to install him as emperor. And he reigned 31 years.

AM 5923. Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, year 1. In this year, after Sisinnius, bishop of Constantinople, had fallen asleep, Nestorius succeeded to the episcopate. He was a Germanician by birth. As soon as he ascended the throne, his false belief and his perverted mind in matters of doctrine were plain to see. He gave a homily on the faith to his syncellus and ordered him to preach it in church. It ran as follows: "Let no one call Mary Theotokos; for Mary was a human being, and it is impossible for God to be born of a human being." The first to seize on this statement was a certain Eusebius, an advocate in the imperial city of Constantinople, and as a result many of the Byzantines were troubled. Nestorius, eager to make his teaching prevail, spread the saying everywhere, calling the Lord a mere man. One Sunday, while Nestorius was presiding, Proclus was urged to preach, and delivered the Homily on the Theotokos, which begins: "A virginal festival today, brethren." From then on the impious Nestorius was hated by all for his arrogance and false belief. He also had a certain Anastasius, a priest from Antioch, whom he greatly favoured as a man who shared his views. This was a most reckless man, who blasphemed the ever-virgin Theotokos in church. Eusebius of Dorylaeum was the first to denounce him; and by acting in this way Nestorius stirred up much tumult and disturbance. In the same year also the fearful miracle of the holy

In this year Cyril, bishop of the Alexandrians, learned of Nestorius' blasphemies and wrote to him, exhorting and admonishing him to give up his perverted doctrines and hold fast to the orthodox faith. Nestorius wrote back with insults and blasphemies. Then Cyril wrote to the pope of Rome about Nestorius, and showed him the blasphemies that Nestorius had written to him. Then Celestine wrote to Nestorius, setting him a deadline of ten days to stop his blasphemy and repent; if he persisted in his false teaching, he would no longer be a priest in communion with the Church. Celestine and Cyril likewise wrote to John, archbishop of Antioch, and to Praylius of Jerusalem about Nestorius and his heresy. John wrote to Nestorius advising him to abandon the heresy, and reminded him of the Apostle's words: "God sent forth his Son, born of a woman." When Nestorius realised that the patriarchs would not consent to keep silent while the churches were in such turmoil, he got the emperor to write a sacra to Cyril full of reproaches. He thought he would strike him down by this, but instead he roused him all the more. For Cyril rose up and wrote to the emperor and to his sisters about the orthodox faith and Nestorius' false teaching, and at the same time asked for an ecumenical council to be held so that the case of Nestorius might be examined according to the canons. Then the emperor Theodosius wrote to all the bishops under his rule to come to Ephesus without any delay after Easter. He decreed that anyone not present at the council in Ephesus on the day of holy Pentecost would have no excuse before God or before us. …had not come, Nestorius got there first, full of arrogance. On the twentieth of June the synod convened, with Nestorius, Cyril and Juvenal presiding, Cyril holding the place of the bishop of Rome. While they were all discussing theology, Nestorius said with great arrogance: “I would not call a child of two or three months God. And so I am clean of your blood, and from now on I will not come back to you.” With these words he walked out, together with six bishops who shared his opinion. The next day Cyril's party met and sent three bishops to summon him, and he did not obey. In the same way he was summoned by the synod a second, a third and a fourth time, and he did not come. He even had the envoys insulted and dishonoured. Then the holy and ecumenical synod, after receiving back the bishops it had sent, insulted and dishonoured, pronounced sentence against him. It declared him stripped of every priestly rank and sent him notice of his deposition to his face. When this had been done, John, bishop of Antioch, arrived three days later with twenty-six bishops. When they learned that Nestorius had been deposed, they broke away from the holy synod, met in council with Nestorius, and deposed, as they supposed, Cyril and Memnon of Ephesus. Theodoret, thinking to attack [?], misinterpreted the Twelve Chapters and there spewed out the venom of Nestorius. But Cyril, now among the saints, rose up nobly and defended his Chapters. He interpreted them, uncovered the treasure of the Church's teaching contained in them, and made his own pious intent plain to all. John of Antioch was summoned by the holy synod three times and refused to come. He and those with him received sentence: they were cut off from all communion with the Church until they condemned themselves and confessed their error. The holy synod also decreed that what the Easterners had done lawlessly and uncanonically, in outrage against Cyril and Memnon, the most holy presidents of the Church, should have no force whatever. All this was reported to the emperor Theodosius, and bishops from both parties were ordered to go up to Constantinople. When they did, those of the holy synod prevailed with God's help. The deposition of Nestorius was confirmed, and Maximian was ordained bishop of Constantinople, being a pres-

(CHRONOGRAPHY.) -byter of that same church. The Easterners took Nestorius with them to the East. In the fourth year after Nestorius's deposition, John, bishop of Antioch, a man who feared God, saw that many of the leading men of Antioch were being corrupted by Nestorius. He wrote asking the emperor to expel him from the East. The emperor exiled Nestorius to Oasis, and sent orders to Cyril and John to unite without delay so as to rid the Church of all discord. John obeyed the order and wrote to Cyril, setting out his own faith. He accepted the confession of the Fathers at Nicaea and of the hundred and fifty at Constantinople, as well as what had been done at Ephesus. Cyril accepted it and wrote to John and the Easterners a letter that begins: “Let the heavens rejoice and the earth be glad.” Both agreed on the same confession, and the holy churches on either side were united in peace and concord. At that time Nonnus, the God-bearer, was shepherd of the Church of Edessa. It was he who dedicated to God the foremost of the mime actresses of Antioch, and presented her to Christ as holy Pelagia in place of Margarito the harlot. This saint, rejoicing at the concord of the saints, wrote words of admonition and teaching to Archbishop John, among them these: “Cleanse the Church, O man of God, of the Nestorian [?] and their wickedness.” As for the impious blasphemer Nestorius, divine justice overtook him in this life [?] with a rotting of all his limbs, and above all of his foul tongue. Stricken with this, he perished in death, forestalling his recall from Oasis to another

In this year Valentinian not only failed to recover Britain, Gaul and Spain, but also lost western Libya, the land of the people called Afri. It happened in this way. There were two generals, Aetius and Boniface, whom Theodosius had sent to Rome at Valentinian's request. When Boniface received command of western Libya, Aetius envied him and slandered him, claiming that he was plotting revolt and eager to seize Libya. He said this to Placidia, Valentinian's mother. Then he wrote to Boniface as follows: “If you are summoned, do not consent to come, for you have been slandered, and the emperors mean to get you into their hands by treachery.” Boniface received this and trusted Aetius as a true friend, and when he was summoned he did not come. The emperors then regarded Aetius as loyal. At that time Goths and many other very great nations were settled beyond the Danube in the northern regions. The four most notable of them are the Goths, the Visigoths, the Gepids and the Vandals. They differ in name only and in nothing else, and speak one language. All of them adhere to the false faith of Arius. In the time of Arcadius and Honorius they crossed the Danube and settled in Roman territory. The Gepids, from whom the Lombards and the Avars [?] later split off, settled the lands around Singidunum and Sirmium. The Visigoths sacked Rome under Alaric, then moved on into Gaul and took control there. The Goths first held Pannonia. Then, in the twelfth year of his reign, with the permission of Theodosius the Younger, they settled the lands of Thrace, spent fifty-eight years in Thrace, and took control of the western empire. The Vandals joined forces with the Alans and the Germans, those now
