Boniface, afraid of the Roman emperors, crossed from Libya to Spain and went to the Vandals. He found that Godigisel had died and that his sons Gunderic and Gaiseric were ruling in his place. He won them over and promised to divide western Libya into three parts: each of them would rule a third along with him, and together they would fight off any enemy whatever. On these terms the Vandals crossed the strait and settled Libya from the Ocean as far as Tripolis near Cyrene. The Visigoths, setting out from Gaul, took Spain as well. Some members of the Roman senate who were friends of Boniface informed Placidia of Aetius's false accusation. They also showed her Aetius's letter to Boniface, which Boniface had sent to them. Placidia was astonished. She did Aetius no harm, but sent Boniface a message urging him to return, backed with oaths. When Gunderic died, Gaiseric became sole ruler of the Vandals. Boniface accepted the assurance and campaigned against the Vandals, and a great army came to him from both Rome and Byzantium under the command of Aspar. Battle was joined with Gaiseric, and the Roman army was defeated. So Boniface went to Rome with Aspar and cleared away the suspicion by showing the truth. Africa came under the Vandals. It was then too that Marcian, a soldier serving under Aspar, was taken alive by Gaiseric; he later became emperor. A.M. 5952. — In this year the holy martyr Euphemia was translated in Alexandria on the sixth day before the Kalends of October. A.M. 5955. — In this year the Cantharus bath in Alexandria was completed. Some monks came to Constantinople and pestered the emperor about Theodore, the late bishop of Mopsuestia, accusing him after his death of being a heretic. The emperor allowed Proclus to write to the bishops of the East, telling them to hold an inquiry and, if the accusers were telling the truth, to anathematize Theodore. But John of Antioch and his synod wrote back to Proclus and to the emperor, testifying to Theodore's orthodoxy

In this year Charmosynus, the Augustal prefect in Alexandria, was struck on the temple in the hunting theatre and died on the first of the month Epiphi. A.M. 5936. — In this year the emperor Theodosius made Antiochus, the praepositus and patrician, who was also his [?], a priest. He also confiscated his house, because Antiochus was overbearing towards the emperors and showed contempt for him. For this reason he also passed a law that no eunuch should be raised to the rank of patrician. A.M. 5937. — In this year Cyrus, prefect of the city and of the praetor-

[Cy]rus of Panopolis, an epic poet, lived under the emperor Theodosius the Younger, who appointed him praetorian prefect and prefect of the city. He also became an ex-consul and a patrician. For Eudoxia, the wife of Theodosius, being empress and a lover of poetry, greatly admired Cyrus. But after she withdrew from the palace and was living in the East, at Jerusalem, Cyrus fell victim to a plot and became bishop of Cotyaeum in Phrygia. He lived on until the reign of the emperor Leo.

The people of Byzantium shouted about him in the hippodrome, while the emperor sat there listening: “Constantine built it, Cyrus renewed it.” The emperor was angry that they said this about him. On the pretext that Cyrus held pagan views, he removed him from office and confiscated his property. Cyrus took refuge in the church and became a cleric [?]. A.M. 5938. — In this year another John, called the Vandal, usurped power against Valentinian in Rome. Theodosius sent a force under the generals Aspar and Ardaburius. Battle was joined, John was defeated, and after receiving a pledge of safety he surrendered alive. They brought him to the emperor Theodosius and arranged for him to be granted honours. But Chrysaphius, a eunuch who wielded great influence in the palace, had him treacherously murdered. Before long, however, justice overtook Chrysaphius. In this year Chrysaphius the eunuch, who controlled both the palace and the emperor, was jealous of Flavian's ordination. The emperor was [?] and staying at Chalcedon, and Chrysaphius suggested to him that he tell the patriarch to send gifts of blessing for his ordination. The bishop sent back word that he had no money to send, “unless I use some of the sacred vessels.” From this arose no small ill feeling between them, without Pulcheria knowing of it. So much for events in Constantinople. In Alexandria, Dioscorus at the very outset plundered Cyril's relatives and seized their property. He deposed Cyril's nephew Athanasius, a presbyter, without cause, and confiscated everything he had. He did this in opposition to the orthodox faith of Cyril, being a heretic who had held the views of Origen from his tender years. He also bore a grudge against Flavian, because Flavian had given some small help to the relatives of the blessed Cyril. Chrysaphius was impious and could not bear to see the churches in concord. He set about throwing them into turmoil, and tried every means to drive Flavian out of the bishopric, because he wanted to put forward a certain Eutyches, an archimandrite who shared his views, as bishop. Since he had no power while Pulcheria controlled affairs, he first wormed his way into the confidence of Eudocia, who was inexperienced. He stirred her to jealousy against her own mother and suggested that she speak against her to the emperor, so that she might get the praepositus for herself; for Pulcheria needed the praepositus to administer affairs. The emperor, pestered by his wife, sent her this message: “Do not let this grieve you. It is not possible for you to have the praepositus, nor will I put a stop to my sister, who governs well, skilfully and piously.” Having failed in this, Chrysaphius turned to another scheme. He suggested to Eudocia that she press the emperor to allow the patriarch to ordain Pulcheria a deaconess, on the grounds that she had chosen virginity. Eudocia pressed him more and more and won over the emperor, who was easily swayed. When the emperor urged this on the blessed Flavian, he was deeply grieved, for he foresaw the scandals that would spring from it. He promised the emperor to do it, but wrote to Pulcheria asking her not to come into his presence, “so that I am not forced,” he said, “to do something that would grieve you.” She understood from his letter what was being planned. She sent the praepositus to Eudocia, withdrew to the Hebdomon and lived there in retirement. As a result the emperor and Eudocia were greatly vexed with Flavian, since he had given away the secret. While Pulcheria was in retirement and Eudocia was steering the empire, the following happened. A certain Paulinus, a magister,

was loved by Eudocia because he was very learned and very handsome, and she often met him in private. On the day of holy Theophany someone brought the emperor a large and wonderful apple. The emperor marvelled at it and sent it to Eudocia. She sent it to Paulinus, and two days later Paulinus sent it to the emperor. The emperor recognized it and hid it. Then he went and said to the Augusta: “My salvation, where is the apple I sent you?” She said: “By your salvation, I ate it.” Then, moved to anger, he ordered the apple to be brought, and Paulinus to be exiled to Cappadocia and put to death there. Eusebius the scholasticus, mentioned above, who had been the first to take issue with Nestorius, was promoted to the bishopric of Dorylaeum. Discussing the faith with Eutyches the archimandrite, he found that his views were not sound. He exhorted and urged him at length, trying to help him, but did not succeed. Then Eusebius reported the matter to Bishop Flavian. Flavian convened a synod of forty bishops and summoned Eutyches. He examined him in full accordance with the canons of the Church, found him to be a heretic and a deceiver, and deposed him. Chrysaphius, who shared Eutyches' views and controlled the palace, learned of this and became still more inflamed with anger against Flavian. He sent word to Dioscorus of Alexandria that he would help him achieve all his desires if Dioscorus would join him in accusing Flavian and Eusebius and fight for Eutyches. He also stirred up the Augusta Eudocia to this, reminding her of the grievances against Flavian over Pulcheria. Together the two of them prevailed on the emperor to decree that a second synod be convened at Ephesus. They gave Dioscorus the presidency of the synod and sent him a very large body of soldiers in support.

A.M. 5941. In this year, by order of the emperor Theodosius, the robber and lawless synod was assembled at Ephesus to judge the case of Flavian and Eutyches. It was run by the impious Dioscorus, on the urging of Chrysaphius the eunuch, surnamed Tzoumas, who had talked the fickle emperor into it. When everyone had gathered, Dioscorus took the chair. He would not allow any other notary to be present at the synod, but had only his own men write down the proceedings. When the inquiry began, Eutyches was required to state his own belief, and he answered: "I confess that our Lord was of two natures before the union, but after the union I confess one nature." Then Dioscorus said: "We too [?] with these..." [?] ...of Pope Leo saw Dioscorus's violence, and that he would not allow the pope's letter to Flavian to be read, nor the one to the synod, but that they were set aside, so they fled and went back to Rome. Dioscorus restored the priesthood to Eutyches, and promptly deposed Eusebius of Dorylaeum and Flavian of Constantinople. Even before the deposition, Flavian was driven out with shoves and kicks by Dioscorus's men, and on the third day he departed this life. On the following day the bishops were forced to sign by the violence of the soldiers and their swords. Domnus, bishop of Antioch, had signed under compulsion, but he came to his senses and stood up to Dioscorus and the officials. He cried out against what had been done [?] and asked to take back his signature. When Pope Leo learned of this, he went to the emperor Valentinian and the Augustae, and with tears asked them to write to the emperor Theodosius so that what had been done at Ephesus, against law and canon, might be set right. But Theodosius wrote back to his daughter Eudoxia as follows: "I want to inform your sweetness that Flavian was expelled from the churches by divine judgment, as the cause of many disturbances." Dioscorus also deposed Theodoret, Ibas, Andrew and

Domnus of Antioch, and all the eastern bishops. The emperor Theodosius was easily swayed and carried about by every wind. As a result he often signed papers without reading them. Among these, the most wise Pulcheria once slipped him an unread deed of gift that handed over his wife Eudocia into slavery. He signed it, and was rebuked by Pulcheria. In the same year Gaiseric grew powerful with the Vandal host. Calling himself [?] of land and sea, and having seized many islands subject to the Romans, he troubled Theodosius. So Theodosius sent eleven hundred transport ships with a Roman force under the generals Areobindus, Ansila, Inobindus, Arintheus and Germanus. When this force had anchored at Sicily, Gaiseric was alarmed and [sent envoys?] [?] to Theodosius about a treaty. A.M. 5942. Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, year 1. Maximus, bishop of Antioch, year 1. In this year Theodosius thought matters over and realized that he had been deceived by the villainy of Chrysaphius. He was grieved at the impiety done to Flavian and the injustice done to the other bishops [?]. Deeply angered, he first exiled Chrysaphius to an island. Then he turned fiercely on Eudocia and called her the cause of all the evils, since she had driven Pulcheria from the palace; at the same time he reproached her over the affair of Paulinus. In despair, she begged to be allowed to leave for Jerusalem. She took with her Severus the presbyter and John the deacon and went to Jerusalem. The emperor learned that these men [?] had frequently visited her in the city itself, were now with her in Jerusalem, and were receiving many gifts from her, so he sent men and had them beheaded. Then the emperor pleaded at length with the blessed Pulcheria and brought her back to the palace. She at once sent to Ephesus and had the remains of Saint Flavian brought back. She carried them with an armed escort along the Mese and buried them in the church of the Holy

Apostles. Then she built the [church?] [?] of the Chalkoprateia for the Theotokos; it had formerly been a synagogue of the Jews. Meanwhile, as we said before, the army was waiting in Sicily for the arrival of Gaiseric's envoys and for the emperor's orders. During this time Attila, the son of Mundiuch, a Scythian, had grown bold and arrogant. He got rid of [?] his elder brother and ruled alone over the kingdom of the Scythians, who are also called Huns. He overran Thrace, and it was chiefly because of him that Theodosius made a treaty with Gaiseric and brought the fleet back from Sicily. He sent Aspar with his forces, along with Areobindus and Argagisclus, against Attila. By then Attila had already overthrown Ratiaria, Naissus, Philippopolis, Arcadiopolis, Constantia and a great many other towns, and had amassed an enormous booty along with many captives. The generals were badly beaten in the battles, and Attila subdued every city and fortress as far as both seas, the Pontus and the sea that stretches past Callipolis and Sestos, except Adrianople and Heraclea, once called Perinthus. He even reached the fortress of Athyras itself. Theodosius was therefore forced to send envoys to Attila. He agreed to give him six thousand pounds for his withdrawal, and to pay him a yearly tribute of a thousand pounds as long as he kept the peace. Then, after the Roman army had returned from the war against Attila, Theodosius died a short while later, on the twentieth of the month of June, in the third indiction. Before anyone knew of the emperor's death, the blessed Pulcheria sent for Marcian, a man outstanding for his self-control and dignity, an old man of great ability, and said to

In this year the pious Marcian, having been declared emperor by divine choice, recalled all those in exile. The blessed Pulcheria handed over the universally hated eunuch Chrysaphius to Jordanes, the son of John. This John had usurped power in Rome, then gone over to Ardabur and Aspar and come to Byzantium, where he was granted honours; but he was treacherously killed by Chrysaphius. Jordanes took Chrysaphius and killed him. It is also worth recording from the beginning how God chose Marcian as emperor [?]. In earlier times, when the Persian war broke out, Marcian was a simple soldier and was marching with his own unit from Greece against the Persians. When he reached Lycia he fell ill and was left behind in the city of Sidyma. While spending time there he became attached to two brothers named Julius and Tatian. They took him into their own house and let him recover. When they went out hunting, they took him along with them. Tired out from their exertions, around midday they fell asleep. Tatian woke first and saw [?]... Having come [?], he attached himself to Ardabur and Aspar,

who were Arians. He spent fifteen years with them and became their domesticus. He went down with Aspar to Africa to fight against Gaiseric, and was taken prisoner in the war. Gaiseric shut up the captives in his own courtyard and watched them from the upper rooms. Around midday, looking down, he saw Marcian sleeping, and [an eagle?] [?] coming, spreading its wings and shading him. When Gaiseric saw this, he reckoned it to be a divine dispensation. He sent for the man, and on learning that he was Aspar's domesticus, he realized that he was destined to be raised to the throne. He did not want to kill him, reasoning that no one can hinder the will of God. But he demanded an oath from him that, if it pleased God for him to reign, he would never make war on the Vandals. So Marcian was released unharmed and came to Byzantium. A short time later Theodosius died, and Marcian was proclaimed emperor, as we said before. He was kind to all his subjects. Attila rose against Valentinian, the emperor of Rome, because Valentinian would not give him his own sister Honoria in marriage. He came as far as the city of Aurelia, where he engaged Aetius, the general of the Romans. He was defeated, lost most of his army by the river Liger, and returned in disgrace. Marcian remembered the kindness shown to him in Lycia. He sent for Tatian and Julius and proclaimed them his fathers. He made Tatian prefect of the City, and entrusted Julius with the government of the Libyans. The blessed Pulcheria built many other churches for Christ, above all the church of our all-praised Lady the Theotokos at Blachernae, at the beginning of the reign of the pious Marcian. Leo, the blessed pope of Rome, wrote to Marcian. He asked that what Dioscorus and [?] had dared to do at Ephesus against Saint Flavian be examined by an ecumenical synod, and the emperor ordered all the bishops to assemble. A.M. 5944. In this year the holy fourth synod took place at Chalcedon, in the month of October of the fifth indiction, one year and two months after Marcian's proclamation. All the bishops

assembled in the martyr-shrine of Saint Euphemia, together with the senate. The acts of the first indiction were examined, as well as the proceedings concerning Eutyches and the innovations made by Dioscorus at Ephesus. When Dioscorus was charged with these things, he pleaded ignorance of what had been done. But he could not escape the proof contained in the acts, and he was at a loss, and the truth was laid bare. Then, having no defence, he was put to shame. Those who had sat with him at the robber synod confronted him with the violence and coercion they had suffered at his hands. They asked the synod's pardon and were received back. One of them was Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem. Dioscorus, at a loss [and having no defence], no longer dared to appear before the synod. Then the synod, with the emperor Marcian also present together with the senate, pronounced sentence against Dioscorus and Eutyches and deposed them. [Where he also died.] The emperor exiled Dioscorus to Gangra. He praised the synod and said: "I give the greatest thanks to the Master and God of us all that, now that discord has been removed, we have all come together into one and the same confession." He showed kindness to the six hundred and thirty holy fathers and sent each of them home in peace. Proterius was ordained bishop of Alexandria in place of Dioscorus. A.M. 5945. Peroz, king of the Persians

Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, year 1. In this year the blessed and pious Pulcheria fell asleep in Christ. She had done many good works and had left all her property to the poor, and Marcian readily distributed it, though it was very great. She herself built many houses of prayer, poorhouses, hostels and guest-houses, among them the church of the holy martyr Laurence. When Dioscorus had been exiled and Proterius appointed, the partisans of Dioscorus and Eutyches started a very great riot and even threatened to stop the grain shipments. When Marcian
VARIANT READINGS. "τὰ παρ'": κατὰ A; καὶ τὰ b [?]. "αὐτῷ": omitted in [?]. "καὶ μὴ ἔχων ἀπολογίαν" [?].

learned of this, he ordered that the grain of Egypt be carried down the Nile not to Alexandria but to Pelusium, and shipped from there to the imperial city. The Alexandrians, now starving, asked Proterius to petition the emperor on their behalf, and so they put an end to their disorder. In this year the Baths of Diocletian in Alexandria were rebuilt, and Attila burned the [?]. In the same year a monk named Theodosius, a destructive man, hurried down to Jerusalem after the synod of Chalcedon. He learned that the Augusta Eudocia was inclined toward Dioscorus, whom the synod had deposed, and began to denounce the synod as having overturned the orthodox faith. He won over the Augusta and the monks, and by means of his own murderous crimes he seized the high-priestly throne in barbarous fashion. With the Augusta's men as his helpers, he ordained bishops city by city while the bishops were still at the synod. Severian, bishop of Scythopolis, would not submit to his false doctrine, so he led him out of the city and slaughtered him. He stirred up a persecution against those who would not communicate with him. Many he tortured, others he stripped of their property, and he set fire to the houses of others, so that people thought the city had been captured by barbarians. He also slaughtered Athanasius, a deacon of the Holy Anastasis, who had reproached him and exposed his impiety; he paraded his body through the city and threw it to the dogs. Domnus, archbishop of Antioch, fled into the desert, and so did Juvenal of Jerusalem. The destroyer Theodosius had held the throne of Jerusalem for twenty months when the emperor Marcian learned of it and ordered his arrest; but he fled to Mount Sinai. Once he and those he had ordained were out of the way, Juvenal recovered his throne. A.M. 5946. Basil, bishop of Antioch, year 1. In this year the emperor Valentinian in Rome grew suspicious of the power of Aetius, the patrician and general, and had him murdered, with the help of Heraclius, one of the eunuchs. Attila

was preparing to make war on Marcian, who would not consent to pay him the tribute that Theodosius had fixed. In the meantime he fell in love with a beautiful girl and celebrated his marriage to her. He became very drunk and was overcome [?] by sleep; blood gushed out in a flood through his nostrils and mouth, and he ended his life. His sons inherited his vast power, but quarrelled with one another and were destroyed. The Romans in the East, however, enjoyed complete peace, justice and gladness under Marcian's reign. Those years were truly golden because of the emperor's kindness, and calm was poured over all affairs. A.M. 5947. In this year Valentinian, the emperor of Rome, upheld the orthodox doctrines of the Church, but his own way of life was full of lawlessness. Although he was married to a most beautiful wife, Eudoxia, the daughter of the emperor Theodosius, he consorted with other women as if possessed by a demon. He also kept constant company with those who practise the magic arts. For this reason he was handed over to a most shameful death. Maximus, the grandson and namesake of the Maximus who usurped power under Theodosius the Great, was one of the patricians at Rome. He got inside the palace, slaughtered Valentinian, forced himself on Eudoxia and seized the throne. For by the very things through which a person sins, he is also punished. Eudoxia was outraged by this. She reckoned that no help would come to her from Byzantium, since her father Theodosius and Pulcheria were dead, so she summoned Gaiseric to Rome and begged to be rescued from Maximus's tyranny. When Gaiseric set sail for Rome with a great fleet, Maximus took fright and fled. His own companions killed him after he had reigned one year. Gaiseric met no resistance and entered Rome on the third day after Maximus was killed. He seized all the wealth and loaded the city's statues onto his ships. Among his plunder were church treasures of solid gold and set with jewels, and the Hebrew vessels that Titus Vespasian had brought to Rome after the capture of Jerusalem. Along with these he took the empress Eudoxia and her daughters and went back to Africa. He married Eudocia to his [?] son Huneric. As for Placidia, learning that she had a husband, the patrician Olybrius, he kept her under guard with her mother

Eudoxia. When the death of Maximus became known, Majorian reigned for two years. After him Avitus held the throne of Rome for two [years?] [?], and after him [?] for three years. After these there was no emperor; instead Ricimer, as general, managed affairs and wielded great power. In the same year Eudocia died in Jerusalem, having left much to the churches. A.M. 5948. Martyrius, bishop of Antioch, year 1. In this year Ravenna burned, and a few days later the patrician Remistus was killed at Classis. [?] days later Avitus was defeated by Ricimer and became [?] at the city of Placentia among the Gauls. A.M. 5949. In this year the emperor Marcian. Note: "τὸν Μαξ. θάν." A; "τοῦ Μ. θ." common text. "ἐδιῴκει" A, but cf. [?]

died on the day before the Kalends of [?], and Leo the Great became emperor. In the same year the Baths of Gratian in Alexandria were restored, as was the great basilica at the Stoicheion. Marcian was very devout and God-fearing. He went out on foot in the processions to the Campus and did many kindnesses to the needy. When the patriarch Anatolius saw this, he too stopped being carried in a litter in the processions, as was the custom, and walked instead. In this year Timothy the Cat used sorcery: he went around the monks' cells at night calling each of them by name. When a monk answered, he would say: "I am an angel, and I have been sent to tell everyone to break off communion with Proterius and with those of Chalcedon, and to appoint Timothy the Cat bishop of Alexandria." In the same year Eudoxia, the daughter of the emperor Theodosius and wife of Valentinian the [?], returned from Africa with one of her daughters, Placidia, the wife of Olybrius. Eudocia had been married to Gaiseric's son Huneric and did not return. A.M. 5950. Leo, emperor of the Romans

In this year Leo became emperor. He was a Thracian by birth and a tribune in rank, and he was crowned by the patriarch Anatolius in the month of February of the eleventh indiction. In the same year a terrible earthquake struck Antioch, and almost the whole city collapsed. A giraffe, a bull-stag and other wild beasts arrived in Alexandria. Along with them came Timothy, surnamed the Cat, who threw the city of the Alexandrians into turmoil. [?]

For he hired a crowd [?] of disorderly men, seized the throne of Alexandria by force, and although he himself had been deposed, he was ordained by two deposed men. From that point all the scandals sprang up in Alexandria. All the priests of the world had accepted the definition of the synod of Chalcedon, but this abominable man reviled it with a kind of unrestrained frenzy. He ordained bishops although he had never been ordained himself, and he performed baptisms although he was not a presbyter. The blessed Proterius became aware of the plot the Cat was preparing against him. He gave way before the wrath and took refuge in the venerable baptistery on the first day of Easter. But the forerunner of the Antichrist, respecting neither the holy day nor the sacred places, sent men who slaughtered the blameless high priest along with six others who were with him. They dragged his body with ropes, threw it out of the holy font and paraded it through the whole city, abusing it without mercy. In the end they burned it and scattered the ashes to the winds. In the same year the relics of Saint Anastasia were brought from Sirmium and laid in her church in the porticoes of Domninus. Timothy the Cat found some unpublished writings of Cyril the Great and falsified them in many places, as Peter, a presbyter of Alexandria, relates. A.M. 5951. Gennadius, bishop of Constantinople, year 1. Timothy the Cat held Alexandria like a robber for two years. In this year the emperor Leo, learning the

[?] of the Holy Anastasia [?] ... the holy Marcian built from his own wealth. When the saint wished to build it at the Psephia [?], where mosaic tesserae were also sold, he bought the site for two [?] because it was long, and because of the width [?] (for the house of prayer was small). There was a church of the Holy Anastasia with a wooden dome, and Basil [?] roofed it

[?] …the unjust death of Proterius and the lawless promotion of Aelurus, he sent Caesarius, cut out the tongues of [?] and exiled both of them as accomplices in the murder of Proterius. He did not proceed against the unholy Timothy, however, saying that judgment on him belonged to the bishops. In the same year Zeno was married to Ariadne, the daughter of Leo. Year of the World 5952. In this year the emperor sent letters to the bishops of every province. He asked them to write him their own opinion: first, whether they were satisfied with what had been defined at Chalcedon, and also what they had to say about the ordination of Aelurus. Among those he wrote to were Saint Symeon the Stylite, Bardas the monk and James the wonderworker, and he solemnly charged them to pass judgment on the disputed matters as men who would have to give account to the God of all. With one voice and one mind they confirmed that the synod at Chalcedon was holy, and they accepted the definition it had set forth. They also agreed in condemning Timothy as a murderer and a heretic. Gennadius too pressed the emperor to punish the outrages that had been committed, but Aspar the Arian worked against him. The pious emperor exiled Aelurus to Gangra, where his teacher Dioscorus had also once been. There too Aelurus began to hold schismatic assemblies and stir up disturbances, and when the emperor learned of this he moved him into exile at Cherson. Another Timothy, surnamed the White and also called Salophaciolus, was ordained bishop of Alexandria in his place. He was an orthodox and good man, loved by all.

[Year 1 of Timo]thy the White. In this year the most holy Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem, died, and Anastasius was ordained in his place. At the same time Symeon the great Stylite also fell asleep. He was the first of the Mandra, who had pioneered this form of virtue and had become a worker of signs.

Year of the World 595[?]. In this year a great fire broke out in Constantinople on the second of September, in the fifteenth indiction. It began at the dockyard and reached as far as the church of Saint [?] in the quarter of Amantius. Marcian the steward climbed onto the roof tiles of Hagia Anastasia holding the Gospel, and with prayers and tears he kept the building unharmed. Year of the World 5955. In this year Majorian was slain at Tortona by the patrician Ricimer, and [?] to the throne. Severus and Serpentius [?], on the Nones of July. In the same year a certain painter dared to paint the Saviour in the likeness of Zeus, and his hand withered. When he confessed, Gennadius healed him through prayer. Some of the historians say that the form with curly, sparse hair is more fitting for the Saviour. It is said that while this same Gennadius was praying at night inside the sanctuary, he saw an apparition of a demon. When he rebuked it, he heard it cry out that it would give way while he lived, but that after his death it would certainly gain control of the Church. Gennadius was afraid at this, and he earnestly entreated God about it. In the same year Studius built the church
…nine; and in the place itself, called the Mandra, [?] and forty; in a certain [?] ten, completing his contest; and on shorter pillars seven, and

of the Forerunner, and he installed monks from the monastery of the Akoimetoi in it. Gratissimus the praepositus built the church of Saint Cyriacus outside the Golden Gate and renounced the world there. Year of the World 5956. Of the bishops of Jerusalem, [?], year 1. In this year Emperor Leo made his son-in-law Zeno general of the whole East, and Basiliscus, the brother of the Augusta Verina, general of Thrace. When Zeno came to Antioch he found the holy Martyrius bishop there. Peter the Fuller, a presbyter of the church of the martyr Bassa at Chalcedon, was following Zeno. He persuaded Zeno to help him, hired some like-minded followers of Apollinarius, and stirred up countless disturbances against the faith and against Martyrius the bishop. He anathematized those who did not say that God was crucified, and he split the people of Antioch by adding to the Trisagion hymn the words 'who was crucified for us'. Among the Theopaschites this has remained in use from that time to this day. Martyrius went to Emperor Leo and, through the efforts of Gennadius, bishop of Constantinople, was received with great honour. When he returned to Antioch he found the people in revolt, with Zeno supporting them. So he resigned the episcopate in the church, saying: 'To an insubordinate clergy, a disobedient people and a defiled Church I bid farewell, keeping for myself the dignity of the priesthood.' Once he had withdrawn, Peter the Fuller leapt onto the throne of Antioch and at once ordained John, a man who had been deposed, as bishop of Apamea. When Gennadius learned of this he reported it all to the emperor, who ordered Peter the Fuller to be exiled. Hearing this, Peter escaped exile by flight, and by common vote a certain Julian was chosen as bishop of Antioch.

In the same year the remains of the prophet Elisha were translated at Alexandria, on the fifth day before the Ides of May, into the monastery of Paul the Leper. For he had healed a leper and made a man a leper, and so he was laid to rest in the Leper's monastery. Year of the World 5957. In this year the four-sided colonnade of Saint John in Alexandria was built, together with the sanctuary, and the public bath [?] was restored to the city. At this time also Daniel the Stylite, an admirable man, mounted his pillar at Anaplus. John the ex-consul, surnamed 'of Vincomalus', entreated the holy Bassianus and was enrolled with him as a monk. He always went in procession at the palace as one of the senators; then he would return to the monastery of Bassianus, as ex-consul [?], and at once [?] put on the monk's rough cloak and performed the service of the kitchen, the stable and similar tasks

In the same year Anthimus and Timocles, the composers of troparia, became known. In the same year, at the request of the senate of Rome, Emperor Leo sent Anthemius, the son-in-law of Marcian the former emperor, to Rome as emperor. He was a most Christian man who governed the empire piously. Year of the World 5958. In this year a sign appeared in the sky: a cloud shaped like a trumpet, seen every evening for forty days. Year of the World 5959. In this year [?] enrolled three thousand men as soldiers in Alexandria. The great cistern was built in the quarter of John, together with the two baths, Hygieia and Iasis, and the river was dug in

(52) 'The composers of troparia,' adds Theodore the Lector in Book 1, 'were divided into factions. All who rejoiced in the synod at Chalcedon gathered around Anthimus, for it was he who had arranged for the all-night vigils to be held. Those hostile to it attached themselves to Timocles.' Anthimus and Timocles

Year of the World 5961. Of the bishops of Antioch, Julian, year 1. In this year Emperor Leo fitted out a great fleet and sent it against Gaiseric, ruler of the Africans. After Marcian's death Gaiseric had done great harm in the lands under Roman rule, plundering, taking many captive and razing cities. Moved by zeal, the emperor gathered a hundred thousand ships from the whole eastern sea, filled them with soldiers and arms, and sent them against Gaiseric. They say he spent forty-five centenaria of gold on this fleet. As general and commander of the fleet he appointed Basiliscus, the brother of the Augusta Verina, who had already held the consulship and had often defeated the Scythians in Thrace. He was joined by no small force from the West, and he fought Gaiseric's fleet in many naval battles, sending [?] of its ships to the bottom; after that he could even have taken Carthage itself. But later he was lured by gifts and large sums of money from Gaiseric, and he gave way and was defeated

willingly, as [Priscus?] the Thracian has recorded. Some say that Aspar and Ardabur, who were Arians and for that reason could not come to the throne, made Leo emperor because he was their curator, expecting to run the empire themselves. When the emperor would not accept this, they tried to undermine what he was governing well, and they agreed to give the throne to Basiliscus if he betrayed the emperor's fleet and army to Gaiseric, who was an Arian and shared their beliefs. And they say it was for this reason that Basiliscus betrayed them. Then Gaiseric devised a stratagem. He filled some boats [?] with combustible material and came up at night while the Romans slept unguarded. With an offshore wind he launched the boats from the land against the Roman fleet, and they set many of the ships on fire. The rest fled the danger and returned to Sicily. Then at last Basiliscus's treachery was exposed, since he had lost [?] none of his army. In the same year Patricius, the son of Aspar, came to Alexandria with great pomp. Emperor Leo had made him Caesar in order to draw Aspar away from the Arian creed and make him well disposed to the emperor. At that time the Koreion bath was strengthened. Year of the World 5962. Of the bishops of Rome, Simplicius

In this year Emperor Leo sent Zeno, general of the East and his son-in-law, to Thrace on some military business, ordering that he be given an army from the local troops to support him. At Aspar's urging these troops very nearly killed Zeno, but he learned of the plot in advance and escaped by fleeing to Sardica, a city of Thrace. From then on Aspar was under suspicion with Emperor Leo. Year of the World 5963. In this year Emperor Leo sent
That when Marcian, who had been a good emperor, died rather early, Aspar on his own initiative arranged for Leo to become his successor

against Gaiseric Heraclius of Edessa, son of Florus the ex-consul, and Marsus the Isaurian, both energetic men, with an army from Egypt, the Thebaid and the desert. They fell on the Vandals unexpectedly and took Tripoli and many other cities of Libya, and they troubled Gaiseric more than Basiliscus's naval battle had. As a result Gaiseric arranged to send envoys to Emperor Leo to ask for peace, and he obtained it from Leo, who at that time needed Basiliscus, Heraclius and Marsus for the plot against Aspar. For Aspar, as I said before, had come under the emperor's suspicion and was surrounded by great power, and shortly afterwards he was treacherously killed by the emperor, together with his sons Ardabur and Patricius. The emperor had earlier made Patricius Caesar to win Aspar's goodwill. Year of the World 5964. Of the bishops of Constantinople, Acacius, year 1. In this year, after Aspar and his sons Ardabur and Patricius had been killed by Leo, Ostrys, Aspar's bodyguard, and Theoderic, son of Triarius and brother of Aspar's wife, attacked the city with a force to avenge the dead. Basiliscus, returning from Sicily, and Zeno, coming from Chalcedon, where he had been waiting for Aspar's murder, came to the city's aid in time and scattered the rebels; had they not done so, there would have been great turmoil in public affairs. Aspar's youngest son Ermenaric was smuggled away with Zeno's knowledge and escaped by being sent to Isauria. There he became the son-in-law of Zeno's illegitimate son, and after Leo's death he returned to Byzantium and lived prosperously to the end. In Italy Ricimer the general, whom I mentioned earlier and who was the son-in-law of Anthemius, then reigning piously in Rome, rose against his own father-in-law. War gripped the land, and the emperor's forces were so starved that they even resorted to hides and other unusual foods. Anthemius himself was killed in the seventh year of his reign. Then, because of the disturbances still going on in Rome, Leo sent Olybrius, the husband of

Placidia, to Rome and proclaimed him emperor. After the slaughter of Anthemius, Ricimer lived only three months and then died of disease, and Olybrius also passed away with him from a bodily illness. After their deaths Majorian succeeded to the throne, a vigorous man experienced in war. Finding the cities sacked by Gaiseric, he invaded [?] and took Liguria, and the Vandals came to fear him. But when he was about to crown himself with victory, he was seized in the meantime by dysentery and died. The general crossed [?] and escaped safely. While Gaiseric's people were occupied with these matters, the young Eudocia, granddaughter of Theodosius, who had spent sixteen years in Africa with her husband Huneric and had borne him a son, Hilderic, was aggrieved with her husband for being an Arian. She found an opportunity to flee and came to Jerusalem. There she venerated the holy places and embraced the tomb of her grandmother, and after spending a few days in the holy city she died in peace. She left all her possessions to the Holy Anastasis, and she entrusted Kourkos and his children to the archbishop of Jerusalem, since he had helped her and stood by her faithfully in escaping from her Arian husband Huneric. Year of the World 5965. In this year Emperor Leo crowned Leo, the son of Zeno and of his own daughter Ariadne, and so his grandson, and proclaimed him emperor. After the deaths of Olybrius, Ricimer and Majorian, Glycerius was proclaimed emperor of Italy, a man of some merit. After he had ruled for five months, Nepotianus [?] drove him from power and reigned himself for a short time, until a certain Orestes drove him out. Orestes's own son Romulus, surnamed Augustulus, succeeded him, and after ruling only two years, sole [Notes: αὐτῷ A; αὐτοῦ [?]. πολέμων A; πολέμου vulgate. Λιανὴν [?] A; εἰς τὴν ἐναλίαν [?]. ὤφθη; γέγονε [?]. Βοῦρκον A [?]. εἰς τὸ A; εἰς τῷ [?]. τούτῳ τῷ A; τῷ δ’ αὐτῷ vulgate. Ἀριάδνης [?]. ἔγγονον A; ἔγγονα vulgate. χρόνον οὐκ ὀλίγον A.]

ruler of the kingdom in Italy is established, 1,303 years after the reign of Romulus, who founded Rome. And it should be noted that the empire of the West, which flourished from the time of Romulus, came to an end once more with a Romulus after so many years. From then on Odoacer held power, a Goth by race but raised in Italy, who seized the government with a barbarian force. He took for himself the title of rex, appointed every office for the Romans according to their ancestral law, and held power for ten years. He lived in Ravenna, a city of Italy by the sea, prosperous and beautiful. Year of the World 5966. In this year dust fell from the sky. Clouds appeared, glowing like fire, so that everyone thought it was raining fire, and all trembled and made litanies. It lay a palm deep on the roof tiles. And everyone said that it had been fire, but had been extinguished and turned into dust by God's love for mankind

In the same year Emperor Leo fell ill in Byzantium and died, in the month of January of the twelfth indiction. He left as emperor Leo, the son of Zeno and Ariadne, still an infant, whom he had already designated. In February the boy crowned his own father Zeno in the kathisma of the hippodrome, with Verina and Ariadne assisting him. After the little Leo had reigned with his father Zeno for only ten months, he died of illness, and Zeno reigned alone for seventeen years and two months, counting the twenty months of Basiliscus's usurpation. Zeno handled the government badly. At the very start the Saracens [ravaged] Mesopotamia,

[Notes:] τῆς ἐν Ἰταλίᾳ βασιλείας A; ἐν Ἰταλίας βασιλείῃ vulgate. χειρωσαμένου A [?]; χειρωσάμενος vulgate. ὃς τοῦ ῥ[ηγός] A [?]. κατὰ τὸν πάτριον νόμον τοῦ γένους vulgate. τοσούτους A; τούτους vulgate. τὸ γένος A [?]; κατὰ τῶν πατρίων νόμων [?], κατὰ τὴν τῶν πατρίων νόμων [?]. εὐδαίμονα οὖσαν A [?]; εὐδαιμονοῦσαν [?]; εὐδαιμονοῦσαν οὖσαν [?]; εὐδαίμονα χώραν vulgate. μὲν Σαρακηνοὶ A; μὲν οἱ Σαρ[ακηνοὶ] vulgate.

[?] adds: 'This Leo was prompted by his own mother, the most illustrious Ariadne, so that when Zeno, the magister militum and patrician, his grandfather (read: father), did obeisance to him as emperor, he placed the imperial crown on the head of this Zeno. And Zeno of Kodisa, the Isaurian, reigned with his own grandson (read: son) for a short time. In the eleventh month of his consulship Leo the younger fell ill and died, in the month of Dios, which is November.' This Leo

Of the bishops of Antioch, Peter, year 1. In this year the little Leo, after reigning with his father Zeno for only ten months and going in procession as consul, died, and Zeno held the empire alone. Basiliscus, the brother of Verina, Zeno's mother-in-law, was staying at Heraclea in Thrace. With the help of Verina and some of the senate he rebelled against Zeno. Zeno was afraid of him and fled with his wife Ariadne and a good deal of money to Syria, to a strong fortress called Ouara. From there he moved with his wife Ariadne to Tessaide [?] for this reason: Illus and Trocundes were besieging him, out of goodwill, for the time being, toward Basiliscus. [?] Basiliscus was proclaimed emperor at the Campus. He made his son Marcus Caesar and crowned his wife Zenonis Augusta, and at once he took the field against the faith, with Zenonis above all urging him on. By an edict he recalled Timothy Aelurus, and also Peter the Fuller, who was hiding in the monastery of the Akoimetoi. All the other enemies of the holy synod at Chalcedon also spoke out boldly against the truth. Aelurus gathered the unruly Alexandrians living in Byzantium and came in procession from the palace to the church, riding on a donkey. When he reached the so-called Octagon he fell and broke his foot, and he turned back in disgrace. Basiliscus sent him to Alexandria with edicts against the synod, and Peter the Fuller to Antioch, and he strengthened both of them against the truth. Timothy Salophaciolus, bishop of Alexandria, learning that Timothy Aelurus had arrived, withdrew

to the monasteries of Canopus, where he had also lived the ascetic life. Aelurus ill-treated many, but he could not harm Timothy, because everyone loved him. As Aelurus entered Alexandria his partisans shouted that shameful cry: 'You have fed your enemies, papa!' And the unholy man answered: 'Yes, I really have fed them.' This impious man also anathematized the synod at Chalcedon. Julian, bishop of Antioch, died of grief at what was happening. Peter the Fuller seized the throne and went on to anathemas and disturbances, and as a result murders and robberies took place over the addition to the Trisagion. By a general edict Basiliscus rejected the synod at Chalcedon, and he ordered Acacius of Constantinople to do the same. But the whole city, with women and children, gathered together in the church against Basiliscus and prevented it. Acacius put on black and draped the throne and the altar in black. Daniel the great came down from his pillar out of godly zeal and joined Acacius and the people in their assembly for the time being. Peroz made war on the Hephthalite Huns, routed them and pursued them. But they fled through narrow places, little by little, into the mountains, withdrawing to the right and to the left. Then they came round behind the Persians and shut them in while they were off guard. Hemmed in, Peroz asked for peace. The king of the Hephthalites [said that he would] not grant it until Peroz fell down and did obeisance to him and gave him assurance on oath that he would never again campaign against the Hephthalites. Peroz, constrained by force, [did] this

…he was forced to do, and he returned in great disgrace. So, unable to bear the shame, he broke his oaths and marched against them again. A.M. 5968. — Of Timothy Aelurus, bishop of Alexandria, year 1. In this year the clergy and monks of Constantinople were fighting for the holy council at Chalcedon, and Acacius, afraid of the crowds, pretended to agree with them. So from the ambo he spoke out against Basiliscus and Zeno. When Basiliscus learned this, he was alarmed [?] by the fervour of the city's people and left the city, ordering the senate that no one should meet with Acacius, for the people were about to set the city on fire. But Daniel, the wonderful Stylite, took the monks and the zealous among the people and went out to Basiliscus, and spoke with him very boldly; but he would not receive them. In the same year Peroz again marched against the White Huns, called the Hephthalites, and perished with his whole army. They had dug a deep trench, laid reeds over it and heaped earth on top, and they stayed on the far side of it. They sent a few men out to meet the Persians. These men then turned to flight, crossed by the narrow paths, and escaped along with the rest. The Persians suspected no danger and pursued them headlong, and all of them together, with Peroz and his sons, fell into the pit and perished. When Peroz saw the disaster, he took from his right ear the pearl he wore, very white and large and beyond measure precious, and threw it away so that no one after him might wear it. For it was extraordinarily remarkable, such as no other king had ever had before. So Peroz perished with his whole army. Those who had not campaigned with Peroz chose as king Kavadh, the younger

son of Peroz. For two years the barbarians ruled the Persians and exacted [?] tribute from them. Kavadh ruled rather harshly and made a law that wives should be held in common, so the Persians deposed him, put him in chains and placed him in prison. They made Blases, also called Valash, the brother of Peroz, king, because Peroz had no other son. Kavadh's wife attended him in prison. The keeper of the prison began to desire the woman, since she was beautiful. Kavadh urged his wife to give herself to the man, in the hope that he might somehow be able to escape from the prison. When this was done, she went in to Kavadh without hindrance and [?] tended him. A friend of Kavadh named Seoses sent word to Kavadh through his wife that he had horses and men ready at a certain place. When night came, Kavadh persuaded his wife to give him her own clothes, put on his garments herself, and sit in the prison. So Kavadh came out of the prison, mounted the horse with Seoses, and reached the Hephthalite Huns. Their king gave him his daughter as wife, and then gave him a large army and sent it with him against the Persians. Seeing the woman dressed in Kavadh's clothes, the guards supposed for many days that Kavadh was in the prison. Kavadh invaded Persia with the Hunnic army and took control of the kingdom with no trouble. He blinded Blases, that is Valash, and kept him under guard, and he held the kingdom securely, for he was shrewd and energetic. After this he reigned eleven years. Of Anastasius, bishop of Jerusalem, year 1. In this year Illus and Trocundes were besieging Zeno. But Basiliscus was not keeping the promises he had made them, and the senate was weighed down by Basiliscus's rule because of the [?] of his ways and his folly. So Illus and Trocundes were reconciled with Zeno and wrote to him [?], and they took him and set out back toward the imperial city. On learning this, Basiliscus sent his nephew Harmatius, general of Thrace, against Zeno with his whole army and the people of Constantinople, having made him swear on holy baptism not to betray him. Harmatius met Zeno at Nicaea in Bithynia and so terrified him that Zeno very nearly turned

back with all his Isaurian auxiliaries. But Harmatius too was largely blinded, by Zeno's gifts and by the promise that he would succeed to the post of master of soldiers [?] and that his son Basiliscus would be made Caesar and sit enthroned beside Zeno. So he turned back against Basiliscus. Zeno reached the imperial city with Ariadne and was received by the people and the senate. Basiliscus came into the church, laid his imperial crown on the holy table, and took refuge in the baptistery with Zenonis, his heretical wife. When Zeno arrived he went to the church, and then entered the palace. He sent to the church and drove Basiliscus out, giving him his word that he would not behead him or his children. He sent him to Cucusus in Cappadocia and ordered that he be shut up in a tower with his wife and children and left to die of hunger; but some say he was put to death while being taken away. At once Zeno held a horse race and proclaimed Basiliscus, Harmatius's son, Caesar. As had been promised, the boy sat with the emperor in the imperial box and [?] the charioteers with the emperor. But Zeno reflected: “Harmatius did not keep faith with the emperor he swore to, and he will not keep faith with me either. If his son the Caesar grows to manhood, he will rise against me. I have done what I agreed with him: I made him master of soldiers and his son Caesar.” He ordered Harmatius put to death as a perjurer, and he was killed on the spiral staircase of the palace as he was going up to the hippodrome. His son the Caesar Zeno had ordained a reader, for Ariadne saved him as her cousin; afterwards he made an excellent bishop of Cyzicus. Zeno turned against Peter the Fuller because he had sided with Basiliscus. Peter was deposed by vote of the synod of the East. In his place John was appointed, who was thrown out after three months, and after him Stephen, a pious man, was appointed bishop of Antioch. Peter was being taken into exile at Pityus, but he tricked his escort and took refuge at St Theodore's in Euchaita. Meanwhile Timothy Aelurus died, and Peter Mongus was brought in to succeed him,

a wicked man and an enemy of the truth, who had already been deposed. He was ordained by a single bishop, who had himself also been deposed. Moved by divine zeal, the monks set upon him when he had held the see like a bandit for only thirty-six days, and they drove him out and restored Timothy Salophaciolus to the throne, as was fitting. A.M. 5970. — Of Timothy Salophaciolus, bishop of Alexandria, year 1. Of Stephen of Antioch, year 1. In this year there was a terrible earthquake in Constantinople on 25 September, in the first indiction. Many churches, houses and porticoes fell to the ground, and countless crowds of people were buried. The globe on the statue in the Forum fell too, and the statue of Theodosius the Great that stood on the column of the Taurus, and a considerable stretch of the inner walls. The earthquake went on for a long time, so that the city reeked. Stephen, who had been appointed to Antioch by common vote, was accused before Zeno of being a Nestorian by those who shared the views of Peter the Fuller. But at the emperor's order a synod of the East met at Laodicea, found him blameless and restored him to his throne. In the same year Theoderic son of Triarius, also called Strabo, nephew of the wife of the Aspar whom Leo had killed, rebelled against Zeno with a multitude of barbarians, having attached himself to Basiliscus and been made general by him. After Zeno's return he went out into Thrace, rose in revolt from there, and plundered the whole area around Byzantium as far as the mouth of the Pontus. Then, when he was about to be betrayed by his own men, he discovered the plot, came back, and killed those who had planned it. He himself died by falling on a spear that suddenly stood in front of his tent as he was mounting

With his brothers Romulus and Procopius fighting beside him, he drove all Zeno's men into the palace to shelter, and he very nearly took the palace. A.M. 5972. — In this year Illus the master of offices advised the emperor Zeno to expel his mother-in-law Verina from the city. By a trick he sent her to Chalcedon, and shortly afterwards to the fortress of Papurius, to live with Marcian and Leontia, her own daughter. She wrote to her daughter Ariadne, begging to be recalled from exile, and the empress pleaded with Zeno. He said to her, “Ask the patrician Illus about her.” She sent for him and pleaded with him in tears. But he would not be persuaded, and said, “You are trying to make another emperor against your husband.” Then Ariadne said angrily to the emperor, “Is it to be Illus in the palace, or me?” And the emperor said to her, “I want you. If you can do anything against Illus, do it.” She arranged for him to be murdered. She ordered Urbicius the chamberlain to induce someone to kill him. As Illus was going up the spiral staircase of the hippodrome, a scholarian named Spanicius, who had been given the task, brought his sword down on his head. But the master's guardsman had noticed him and caught

Bishop of Antioch: Stephen the second, who was thrown into the river Orontes. In this year Stephen, bishop of Antioch, fell asleep, and by order of the emperor Zeno they ordained another Stephen in his place. Out of goodwill toward the Fuller, the enemies of the faith slaughtered him with sharpened reeds in the baptistery of the holy martyr Barlaam and threw him into the river Orontes, arming their folly with rage. Because of this outrage against Stephen, Zeno ordered Acacius of Constantinople to ordain a bishop of Antioch, and he ordained Calandion. The Antiochenes, unaware of this, had also ordained John, called Codonatus, and Calandion transferred him to Tyre, the first see under Antioch. In the same year Timothy Salophaciolus also died in Alexandria, and there was ordained John

the Tabennesiote, a holy man and a champion of orthodox doctrine, who was a priest and steward of the church of Alexandria. The patrician Illus, with Leontius and the rest, came to the fortress of Papurius. He brought Verina Augusta out to Tarsus in Cilicia and had her crown the patrician Leontius emperor outside the city, at St Peter's. The lady Verina wrote an imperial letter to the Syrian Antiochenes telling them to receive Leontius as emperor. She also issued imperial letters to all the governors of the East, of Egypt and of Libya, telling them to receive Leontius as emperor and not to resist. A.M. 5974. — Of John the Tabennesiote, bishop of Alexandria, year 1. Of Calandion, bishop of Antioch, year 1. In this year the imperial letters of the lady Verina arrived and were read. Their content was as follows: “Verina Augusta to our governors and Christ-loving peoples, greeting. Know that the empire is ours, and that after the death of my husband Leo we appointed as emperor Trascalisseus [?], who was renamed Zeno, so that our subjects might be better governed [?]. But seeing the state going backwards because of his greed, we have thought it necessary to crown for you a Christian emperor adorned with piety and justice, who will save the affairs of the state and conduct its wars in peace. We have crowned Leontius the most pious emperor of the Romans, who will grant you all his care.” They accepted this and acclaimed Leontius emperor. A.M. 5975. — In this year Illus and Leontius released Longinus, Zeno's brother, and his mother from the fortress. Verina fell ill there and died, and some time later Ariadne brought her body back to Byzantium. A.M. 5976. — Of Felix, bishop of Rome…

In this year Leontius entered Antioch as emperor on 27 June, in the seventh indiction, and appointed Lilianus praetorian prefect. He went out and made war on the city of Chalcis [?]. Zeno sent John the Scythian against Illus and Leontius with a very large force by land and sea. A fierce battle broke out, and Illus and Leontius were defeated and fled to the fortress

of Papurius with Pamprepius the master of offices, who was said to be a sorcerer. Then John caught Trocundes, Illus's brother, as he was going off to gather barbarians, and beheaded him. Illus and Leontius, under siege, waited four years for him, deceived by Pamprepius the master, the sorcerer. So when they learned that Trocundes had been killed, they beheaded Pamprepius as a deceiver and threw him down from the wall.

In the same year the partisans of Peter Mongus, by money and trickery, persuaded Zeno to expel John the Tabennesiote, bishop of Alexandria, on the ground that he had been ordained against Zeno's wishes, and to bring Peter Mongus back to Alexandria from Euchaita. At this time too Zeno issued the Henoticon and sent it out everywhere. Some say it was dictated by Acacius of Constantinople. Before Peter Mongus returned to Alexandria, Zeno ordered him to enter into communion with Simplicius of Rome and with Acacius. So Acacius also wrote to the people of Alexandria telling them to receive Mongus and cast out John. When John heard that Peter was coming, the clergy and people begged him not to leave, since they were ready to die for him. But he foresaw what Peter would dare to do, and wisely and calmly he left. A.M. 5977. — Of Peter Mongus, bishop of Alexandria, year 1. In this year Theoderic son of Valamer was widely spoken of among barbarians and Romans as brave and prudent, and not without learning either. Once, while a hostage at Byzantium, he had studied with the best teachers. His father Valamer had led the Goths after the sons of Attila, in the reign of Leo. Zeno summoned Theoderic from Thrace to Byzantium, made him consul and commander of Thrace, and sent him with John the Scythian against Illus. After Illus and Leontius were shut up in the fortress of Papurius, he left John to besiege them and went to Zeno himself. Then he went out into Thrace, made camp, and advanced

on Byzantium. Restrained, they say, only by his regard for the city, he went back to Thrace, and at Zeno's urging he went down into Italy. He defeated Odoacer in a great battle and assumed the dignity of king at Ravenna. He also subdued very many other barbarians, and in particular brought the Vandals under his rule without even taking up arms against them, since Gaiseric had already died before Theoderic came to Rome. He ruled both Rome and the whole West. A.M. 5978. — Of Peter the Fuller, bishop of Antioch, year 1. In this year the bishops of the East wrote to Acacius reproaching him for receiving Mongus into communion. He paid them no heed and shamelessly compelled everyone to be in communion with Mongus. After the death of Simplicius, bishop of Rome, those of the imperial city and of the East appealed to Felix, pointing to Acacius as the cause of these evils. Among them John the Alexandrian also came to Rome and said the same. Felix held a synod in the church of Peter, chief of the apostles, and sent two bishops and a defensor to Constantinople, writing to Zeno and Acacius to expel Peter Mongus from the Church as a heretic. A.M. 5979. — In this year the envoys sent from Rome were seized at Abydus by decision of Zeno and Acacius. Their letters were taken from them and they were put under guard, and Zeno threatened to put them to death unless they entered into communion with Acacius and Peter Mongus. A.M. 5980. — In this year Illus and Leontius, after many battles and four years under siege in the fortress of Papurius, were captured through the treachery of the brother of Trocundes' wife, whom Zeno had sent to trick them. They were beheaded, and their heads were sent to Zeno, brought into the hippodrome on poles, and

from there set up across the water at Sycae as a trophy. On the advice of Acacius, Zeno was pressing the bishops of the East to subscribe to the Henoticon and to enter into communion with Peter Mongus. He also worked on the envoys of Felix of Rome and lured them with money, and he persuaded them to enter into communion with Acacius, contrary to their instructions. Yet the orthodox had delivered a protest to them three times: first by attaching it to ropes on a hook and hanging it on one of them in public [?]; second by slipping it into a book; and third by putting it in a basket of vegetables. When Felix learned what his envoys had done, he deposed them and wrote a sentence of deposition against Acacius. The man carrying it slipped past those at Abydus and reached the monastery of Dius. On the Lord's Day the monks of Dius handed the letter to Acacius in the sanctuary. Acacius's people killed some of the monks who had delivered it and imprisoned others to punish them. Acacius paid no heed to the deposition and struck the name of Felix from the diptychs. A.M. 5981. — Of Fravitta, bishop of Constantinople, three months. In this year Calandion, bishop of Antioch, brought the remains of Eustathius the Great from Philippi, where the saint had died in exile. The city of Antioch went out twelve miles to meet them with great honour. Those who had separated from the Church over the saint were reunited with it, a hundred years after his death. After Acacius died, Fravitta held the see for three months. He wrote to Felix that he was in communion with him and not with Peter Mongus; but to Mongus he wrote that he was in communion with him and had turned away from Felix of Rome. Felix … the same things to Mongus [?]

…[?] he received what had been sent by the Orthodox [?]; and when the apocrisiarii of Fravitas arrived with the synodical letters, Felix sent them away in disgrace. When Fravitas died, Euthymius, presbyter and keeper of the poorhouse of Neapolis, obtained the bishopric of Constantinople. At once, with his own hands, he erased the name of Mongus from the diptychs, and only then sat on the throne; and he entered the name of Felix of Rome. Year of the World 5982. Bishop of Constantinople Euthymius, year 1. Of Antioch, Palladius, year 1. In this year Peter Mongus died in Alexandria, and in his place Athanasius, surnamed Celites, was ordained. The emperor Zeno, now freed from the usurpers, expelled Calandion from the Church of the Antiochenes and exiled him to the Oasis, and installed Peter the Fuller. He also expelled Nestor, Romanus of Chalcedon, Eusebius of Samosata, Julian of Mopsuestia, Paul of Constantina, Manes of Himeria and Andrew of Theodosiopolis. The pretext was their goodwill toward the usurpers, but the truth was Zeno's Henoticon. Peter the Fuller entered Antioch and did much evil: anathemas against the council, expulsions of blameless bishops, unlawful replacements and ordinations, and the like. Earlier, "Christ the King, who was crucified for us" had been added to the Trisagion; Peter, on his return, removed "Christ the King." Xenaias, the servant of Satan, taught people not to accept the image of the Lord or those of the saints. He was a Persian by race and a slave by condition, who had run away from his own master, and in the time of Calandion he was stirring up the villages around Antioch

to abandon the faith, although he was unbaptized and called himself a cleric. Calandion drove him out. But Peter the Fuller ordained him bishop of Hierapolis and renamed him Philoxenus. When he later learned that he was unbaptized, he declared that ordination was enough for him in place of baptism. The most orthodox Euthymius drove from the church Anastasius the silentiarius, who later reigned so wickedly, as a heretic who shared the views of Eutyches. Seeing him gathering crowds, he overturned his chair in the church and threatened that, unless he stopped, he would shave his head and parade him before the crowds. He also appealed to Zeno and received authority against him. Zeno asked the most wise count Marinus (for he knew certain secret things and used to foretell things to him), "Who will reign after me?" He told him, "One of the silentiarii will succeed to both your empire and your wife." There was a patrician [?], a wise, pious, prudent and virtuous man. Zeno confiscated his house, threw him into prison, and ordered the excubitors guarding him to kill him. When this was done, the prefect Arcadius heard of it and reviled the emperor. Hearing this, the emperor ordered him to be slaughtered when he came into the palace. But the prefect learned of it, took refuge in the church, and was saved from a bitter death; the emperor confiscated his house. Year of the World 5983. Bishop of Alexandria Athanasius, year 1. In this year Felix accepted the synodical letters of Euthymius and was joined with him as an orthodox bishop. He left no son, only his brother Longinus, who had been consul twice and was leader of the whole senate, but was foolish, overbearing and dissolute. Longinus had many Isaurians in Byzantium, as well as Longinus the magister, who was his friend; trusting in these, he thought he would have the empire without effort. But when Ariadne, the senate and the whole army proclaimed Anastasius the silentiarius emperor, Longinus was disappointed in his hope. As he was coming to the throne, Anastasius was required by the patriarch Euthymius to give a written confession that he would not disturb anything in the Church or the faith, for Euthymius called him unworthy to reign over Christians. But when the empress Ariadne and the senate pressed him, he accepted his autograph statement that he received the dogmas of the council of Chalcedon as the definition of the faith. And so, having been crowned

King of the Persians Zamasphes, year 1. In this year, when Anastasius of Dyrrachium, called Dicorus, had become emperor, Longinus the brother of Zeno rebelled against him. Anastasius subdued him and sent him into exile in Egypt, at Alexandria, ordering that he be ordained a presbyter. He lived seven more years in Alexandria and then died. The emperor also suspected Longinus the magister and the Isaurians staying in the city, and removed Longinus from the office of magister. While Peter the Fuller was in Antioch [?], begging to return from exile to his own throne, the emperor recalled him from exile but would not allow him to go to Antioch, and had Palladius ordained in Antioch. Euthymius of Constantinople gathered the bishops then staying in the city and confirmed the holy council of Chalcedon. John the Tabennesiote, who was in Rome, heard that Anastasius had become emperor and came to Byzantium, hoping for a good return from him for the help he had given him in Alexandria. For John had taken him in when he came naked from a shipwreck

and had supported him so well that he made him forget his misfortune. But when Anastasius heard that he had arrived, with great ingratitude he ordered him to be exiled, refusing even to receive him. John, foreseeing this, fled to Rome

In this year the emperor Anastasius expelled the Isaurians in Constantinople because of their many outrages. Once outside, they plotted usurpation. Longinus the ex-magister gathered them, together with another force of barbarians and brigands, some 150,000 men. Trusting in the abundance of weapons and money that Zeno had deposited in Isauria, he came into the country of the Isaurians, for the emperor had allowed him to leave, though he suspected the attack. At once he rose in revolt and advanced as far as Phrygia and Cotyaeum, plundering many cities, though he did not lead the army himself. Its leaders were Lilingis, appointed governor of Isauria under Zeno, a most reckless man; Athenodorus, a very simple man and one of the senators; and Conon, bishop of Apamea, who had abandoned his throne and turned from priest into hoplite and general. Against them Anastasius set a Roman army led by John the Scythian, who had put down the usurpation of Illus and Leontius, and by John surnamed the Hunchback, both commanders of the Thracian army, and by Diogenes (these happened to be counts of the scholae) and certain other praiseworthy men. In a battle near Cotyaeum the general Lilingis was slaughtered. Most of the Isaurian army was almost destroyed and barely escaped to its own country. Had the Romans not been busy with the spoils, they would have won the war outright. But while they were caught up in this, the Isaurians seized a fortress on the heights of the Taurus and held out, fighting, into a third year, protected by the position of the towns and fortresses beyond the Taurus. Year of the World 5986. In this year Claudiopolis, which lies in a plain between the two Taurus ranges, was taken by Diogenes. The Isaurians could not bear this, and

came down from the Taurus and besieged Diogenes for a long time, so that his army was in danger of famine and destruction. But John the Hunchback crossed the passes of the Taurus, captured the guards, fell suddenly on the besiegers and destroyed their army, while Diogenes also came out against them. Then Conon the bishop was wounded and died shortly afterward, and this became the Romans' second and greatest victory. Year of the World 5987. Bishop of Jerusalem Martyrius, year 1. In the same year Zamasphes, son of Peroz king of the Persians, drove out Cavades and held the kingship of the Persians for four years [?]. In this year a certain Longinus, called the Selinuntian, who lived in Antioch of Isauria, which lies on a high mountain by the southern sea of the country, was supplying the Isaurians with provisions, bringing them in from everywhere by trading with many merchant ships. Longinus the magister and Athenodorus were living in that rough country. The emperor, wearied as the war dragged on, confided to bishop Euthymius that he wanted peace, and ordered him to assemble the bishops staying in the city, ostensibly to intercede on behalf of the Isaurians. But Euthymius disclosed the secret to John the patrician, father-in-law of Athenodorus, the leader of the usurpation. John ran and reported it to the emperor, and this stirred the emperor Anastasius to irreconcilable hatred against Euthymius. Thereafter he blamed Euthymius for the Isaurians' plots. Some who were plotting against Euthymius put a man up to striking him on the head with a sword in front of the martyr's shrine. Paul, the ekdikos of the Church, who was standing at his shoulder [?], took the blow on his own head and was in danger of his life; and he [?] killed the assailant with the so-called chain. Again, at the synaxis of the Hill [?], they lay in wait to kill Euthymius, but he escaped in lay dress and was saved. The emperor Anastasius took back his confession from Euthymius by force [?]. Year of the World 5988. King of the Persians Cavades

captured Longinus the ex-magister, Longinus the Selinuntian, Athenodorus and the rest of the usurpers. He beheaded them and sent their heads to Byzantium to the emperor Anastasius. Anastasius held a horse race and paraded the heads of the usurpers and the Isaurians sent to him in chains; then he hung the heads on stakes at Sycae and displayed them to everyone. He resettled the mass of the Isaurians in Thrace. He honored John the Scythian and the other John, the Hunchback, with the consulship and great distinction. To bishop Euthymius he sent word through Eusebius the magister: "Your prayers, great one, have covered your friends in soot." The emperor then assembled the bishops staying in the city and brought charges against Euthymius; to please the emperor they voted for his excommunication and deposition.
