In this year the people called Bulgars overran Illyricum and Thrace before anyone knew of them. Year of the World 5995. Salustius, bishop of Jerusalem, year 1. In this year Anastasius made a treaty with Arethas, who was known as the son of Thalabane and was the father of Badicharimus and Agarus. From then on all Palestine, Arabia and Phoenicia enjoyed great calm and peace. When an earthquake was about to strike Neocaesarea, a soldier on the road saw what looked like two soldiers heading for the city, and behind them another crying out: "Spare the house; the relics of Gregory are in it." When the earthquake came, most of the city collapsed, except for the church of Saint Gregory. Year of the World 5996. In this year Kavadh, king of the Persians, demanded money from Anastasius. Anastasius replied that if Kavadh wanted a loan he must draw up a written contract, but that he would give nothing on any other terms. So Kavadh broke the peace made earlier with Theodosius the Younger and invaded with a great host of Persians and foreign auxiliaries. He went first into Armenia and took Theodosiopolis, which was betrayed to him by Constantine, a man of senatorial rank who had commanded the Illyrian regiment. Then he came into Mesopotamia and besieged Amida, since there was not yet any Roman army of note in the region. Only Alypius had any forces, and few at that. He was a man praiseworthy in every way and a lover of philosophy, and he took every possible care over guarding the cities and the stores of provisions. He lived outside Constantina, which lies 57 [?] stades west of Nisibis, with Amida to the north. Some time passed, and there were a few skirmishes between Persians and Romans, in which the Romans were sometimes beaten and sometimes got the better of the barbarian nations. In the end someone betrayed Amida to the Persians. The barbarians had besieged it for more than three months, and it was betrayed by night from one of the towers, which was guarded by monks. The enemy used ladders,

and so they got inside the city. They plundered and sacked the whole of it and took a great deal of wealth. King Kavadh entered the city on an elephant on the third day after the betrayal. He left behind in the city not much wealth [?], but Glones as its guard, and returned to the city of Nisibis, while the Persian forces stayed between Amida and Constantia. Year of the World 5997. In this year the emperor Anastasius sent out an army of Goths, Bessi and other Thracian peoples, with great power. Its general and commander-in-chief was Areobindus, general of the East, the son of Dagalaiphus and a former ordinary consul. (His paternal grandfather was the Areobindus who won distinction against the Persians in the time of Theodosius the Younger. Areobindus was born to Dagalaiphus by Godisthea, the daughter of Ardabur, the son of Aspar, whom we mentioned earlier.) Many other generals were sent with Areobindus. The most distinguished were Patricius; Hypatius, the son of Secundinus and of the emperor Anastasius' sister; Pharasmanes, the father of Zuni [?], a Lazian by race; Romanus, mentioned above, who joined the army from Euphratesia; Justin, who later became emperor; Zemarchus; and some others. The army assembled at Edessa, a city of Osrhoene, and at Samosata, a city of Euphratesia. Hypatius, Patricius and their men busied themselves with freeing Amida from its Persian garrison. Meanwhile Areobindus, with the phylarchs Romanus and Asuades and some others, encamped as though to face Kavadh himself, who was then staying at Nisibis. He defeated the Persians in several battles, drove Kavadh away from Nisibis and forced him to retreat a long way from the country. In one engagement he also killed a very great Persian general. The Scythian who killed him brought his sword and bracelet to Areobindus, and they were sent to the emperor as a most remarkable token of victory. After the Roman generals had weakened the Persian army in this way, Kavadh made his preparations and sent out a very large army against the Romans. As a result Areobindus urged Hypatius, Patricius and their men to hurry from the area around Amida to his support. But they refused out of

envy, and Areobindus wanted to withdraw and leave for Byzantium. He would have done so, had not Appion the Egyptian, then prefect of the army, who was in charge of its expenses and the supervision of everything, persuaded him with difficulty to stay where he was. While the generals were quarrelling with one another, Kavadh came to Nisibis and learned of their discord. He was strong in numbers himself, and by splitting up his army in many directions he overran and ravaged practically the whole of Roman territory, as far as Syria itself. Meanwhile he sent many envoys to Areobindus about peace, saying that he would end the war for money. He overran the area around Edessa in particular, where Areobindus was. There, however, he did not fare well, and against all expectation he was beaten in battle by Areobindus. He also learned that Glones, his general and the guard of Amida, had been killed by a stratagem, so he went back by another road in a sorry state. He disregarded the hostages whom [?] … to Areobindus, and the peace talks; and contrary to the agreement they detained the excellent Alypius and Basil of Edessa. After his withdrawal into [?] his own territory, winter had already set in, so the Roman generals were dispersed among various towns of Euphratesia, Osrhoene, Mesopotamia, Syria and Armenia to spend the winter season. In the same year there was disorder between the two factions during a horse race, and many died on both sides. Among them was a son of the emperor Anastasius, whom he had by a concubine. Anastasius was deeply grieved, and he punished many and sent others into exile. Year of the World 5998. In this year the emperor sent out the magister Celer with a very large force. Celer took over almost the whole [?] army together with the general Theodotus, and to these two the emperor entrusted the conduct of the whole war. He urgently summoned Appion and Hypatius to Byzantium, since he thought they were not needed in the army because of their hostility towards the general Areobindus. He put the general Calliopius in charge of the army's expenses. Celer conducted the war excellently in various places, together with Areobindus, Patricius, Pharasmanes [?], Timostratus, Romanus and the rest. For the

man was eloquent and thoroughly educated, full of the grace of God, and brave. He was an Illyrian by race, from the same country as Anastasius. They overran much of the Persian land and many of its fortresses, which were destroyed, some by fire and others in other ways, so that Nisibis itself very nearly fell to the Romans. For plague too was raging among the Persians [?], and then a revolt broke out against them among the people called Cadusians and other nations. The Romans thus gained the upper hand over the Persians so completely that Kavadh sent the general Aspebedes to negotiate peace with the Romans in earnest. He was also to give Amida back to them in exchange for something quite small [?]. Despite countless toils, and although plagues had already overcome its guards [?], the Romans had not yet been able to wrest the city from the Persians, because of its position and its impregnable walls. The generals, however, saw that winter was coming on again, and they judged it better to buy the Roman army out of the winter of the region where the talks with Aspebedes were taking place, at the cost of a few talents. So they paid thirty [?] talents and got back Basil of Edessa, who was still a hostage among the Persians (for the excellent Alypius had fallen ill and died among them). They handed back the hostages they held, recovered Amida, and concluded the peace treaty, meeting on the border between Ammodios and the fortress of Mardes [?], and they confirmed it in writing. So ended the Persian war of Anastasius, in the fifteenth year of his reign. It lasted three years and did more damage to the Persian land than the earlier wars, and it came to an end at this point, the close of the fifteenth year of Anastasius' reign. When John, bishop of Alexandria, died, John of Nicaea was ordained in his place. In the same year Anastasius gave orders [?], and many of the bronze statues set up by Constantine the Great were melted down. From them he made a statue of himself, which he set up on the column of the Taurus. The statue of Theodosius the Great that had stood there before had fallen in an earthquake and been shattered. As a result the people rioted on a large scale. He did this also for needy temple-robbers

Year of the World 6003. In this year Anastasius decreed that a synod should be convened at Sidon. For Soterichus, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, had professed in writing at his ordination by Macedonius that he accepted the doctrines of the Council of Chalcedon as a definition of faith. Afterwards, however, he became its fiercest enemy. He went to the East and conferred with the impious Xenaias, and the two of them asked the emperor to hold a synod at Sidon to reject the holy Council of Chalcedon completely. The synod met and was quickly dissolved. For this purpose the emperor had sent Eutropius the tribune, who dissolved it and induced Flavian of Antioch and Elias of Jerusalem, with their bishops, to write to the emperor what he wanted to hear. Flavian wrote that he accepted only the three councils and Zeno's Henoticon, without mentioning the Council of Chalcedon. Elias of Jerusalem wrote that he rejected the Council of Chalcedon as well. Soterichus of Caesarea in Cappadocia and Xenaias reported to the emperor against Flavian and Elias, saying that they had joined forces because they did not want to declare themselves openly against the Council of Chalcedon. Anastasius was angered, and he prompted some monks to gather in Antioch under false pretenses and riot against Flavian, demanding that he anathematize the Council of Chalcedon, together with Diodore, Theodore, Ibas and Theodoret. Flavian lost his nerve and did so, anathematizing them in church together with the Council. In the same year the emperor also schemed against Macedonius. On a Sunday the schismatics, with hired crowds, were singing the Trisagion in the church of the Archangel in the palace and in the Great Church, and they added "who was crucified for us," so that the orthodox were forced to drive them out with blows. Through the schismatic monks and clergy, through Julian, once bishop in Caria [?] and later of Halicarnassus, and through the impious Severus, who was still a monk, the emperor waged open war on Macedonius, heaping

shameful public insults on him. The crowds gathered, with women and children and the abbots of the orthodox monks, and cried out: "It is a time for martyrdom; let us not abandon our Father!" They abused the emperor as a Manichaean, unworthy to rule. Frightened, he shut the gates of the palace and made ships ready for flight. He had sworn never to see Macedonius again, but now, in fear of the crowds, he begged to see him. As Macedonius came to him, the people declared to the abbots and monks: "We have our Father!"
