In this year the orthodox in Scythia, Moesia and the other regions urged Vitalian, son of Patriciolus the count of the federates, to rise against the impious Anastasius. He rose and destroyed many tens of thousands of the army fighting for Ana-

-stasius. He also seized a very large amount of gold sent for their pay, as well as weapons for the war, supplies, and everything else he could lay hands on. They say that in a single engagement he hurled down sixty-five thousand of the imperial army, together with their general Hypatius, son of Anastasius' cousin and of the patrician Secundinus. He took Hypatius alive and kept him under guard. The lawless emperor Anastasius and Timothy, the unholy bishop of Constantinople, inflicted many evils on the monks, laymen and clergy who stood for Macedonius and the council, and they even exiled many to the Oasis in the Thebaid. Timothy sent his synodical letters and the deposition of Macedonius to the bishops of each city for them to sign. The braver among them resisted both. The unstable signed both out of fear of the emperor. Those in between did not sign the deposition of Macedonius but only Timothy's synodical letters. That amounted to the same thing, even if it seemed different to them. Timothy wanted to insert the name of Severus in the diptychs and remove that of [?], but he was prevented by the people. For all the orthodox shunned communion with Severus, especially the monks. With a mob of peasants he punished many of them and killed them, and the sacrilegious man overturned the altars and melted down the sacred vessels of the orthodox. The most illustrious Juliana, who built the church of the Mother of God in the Honoratae, championed the council of Chalcedon vigorously. The emperor devised many ways to pervert her, but he could not persuade her to enter into communion with Timothy. Timothy himself went to her many times and did not persuade her either. The emperor also humiliated his nephew Pompeius with many troubles, along with Pompeius' wife, a modest woman devoted to good works, because they were zealous for the council and because they supplied Macedonius in exile with what he needed. Those whom Timothy sent to John Nikaiotes in Alexandria anathematized the holy council of Chalcedon from the ambo. When the abbot of the monastery of Dius died, Timothy came to install an abbot. The man about to be promoted said that he would not accept a blessing from a man who rejected the council of Chalcedon. Timothy said, "Anathema

to every man who does not accept the council of Chalcedon." Even so, the abbot did not consent to be appointed by him. John, Timothy's archdeacon, who was a Manichee, insulted Timothy and denounced him to the emperor. The emperor rebuked Timothy and found him bluntly denying it to his face and once again anathematizing those who accept the council of Chalcedon. The impious John of Alexandria prevented the Egyptians from going up to Jerusalem, so that at the feast of the Exaltation they would not be in communion with the council of Chalcedon. At that time terrible things were done by people possessed by demons in Jerusalem. A certain Anastasius, who wanted to become dux of Palestine, promised the emperor that if he did not persuade John, the bishop of Jerusalem after Elias, to enter into communion with Severus, he would pay three hundred pounds of gold. Once he had received the office, he came to Jerusalem, and when John would not comply he threw him into prison. Zacharias, an official of Palestine and a God-loving man, was moved by divine zeal and advised the bishop to promise the dux that he would do as he wished if he was restored to his throne. The dux released him and restored him. John then gathered the monasteries in the church of Saint Stephen, went up on the ambo, and anathematized Nestorius, Eutyches, Severus and Soterichus of Caesarea, proclaiming the four holy ecumenical councils. Hypatius, the emperor's nephew, was also present. He was not in communion with Severus at all. He now entered into communion with John and gave a hundred pounds of gold to the holy Theodosius, exarch of the monasteries, to distribute among the monks who were zealous for the orthodox faith and for the council of Chalcedon. The emperor ordered some of the officials to introduce the addition to the Trisagion from the ambo in the church of Saint Theodore of Sphorakios. The crowds were so indignant that they walked out on the day of the litany held in the Triconch to commemorate the dust. At that time Timothy also ordered all the churches by a written memorandum to say the Trisagion with the addition during the litanies. Many did so out of fear. But the monks came chanting a different psalm. When the people saw them, they cried out, "Welcome, the orthodox have come!" There was a great riot, many houses were burned and countless people were murdered. The mob shouted against Anastasius and demanded another emperor. Everyone acclaimed Vitalian as emperor, so that Anastasius fled and hid in a suburban estate near Blachernae. Even Ariadne herself reviled him as the cause of many evils for the Christians. When Alamoundaros, the

phylarch of the Saracens, was baptized, the impious Severus sent two bishops to pass on his corruption to him. By God's providence, however, the man was baptized by orthodox clergy who accepted the council. When Severus' bishops were trying to turn the phylarch away from the true doctrine, Alamoundaros refuted them wonderfully with the following stratagem. He said to them, "I received a letter today saying that Michael the archangel died today." When they said that this was impossible, the phylarch said to them, "Then how, according to you, was God alone, stripped of humanity, crucified, unless Christ was of two natures, if not even an angel dies?" So Severus' bishops withdrew in shame. Kavadh hamstrung some of the Christians in Persia, who afterwards walked about. Year of the World 6006. Hormisdas bishop of Rome

In this year Vitalian took control of all Thrace, Scythia and Moesia. With multitudes of Huns and Bulgars in his army, he took Anchialus and Odyssopolis, also captured Cyril, the general of Thrace, and came plundering as far as Byzantium. Sparing the city, he encamped at Sosthenion. Anastasius was in despair and sent some members of the senate to beg him to make peace. He swore together with the senate that he would also recall the exiled bishops to Heraclea in Thrace. Vitalian added further conditions. The chiefs of each schola were also to swear to this. Macedonius and Flavian, who had been unjustly expelled, were to recover their own thrones, and likewise all the other bishops. A council was then to be convened, which the bishop of Rome and all the bishops would attend, so that the outrages committed against the orthodox could be examined by common judgment. The emperor, the senate, and the other officials and the people swore to this and confirmed that it would be done. So peace was made, and Vitalian returned home. The patrician Secundianus, Anastasius' brother-in-law through his sister and the father of Hypatius, fell at Vitalian's feet with many tears, and Hypatius,

his own son, he received back alive from his chains in Moesia. Hormisdas, bishop of Rome, was pressed by Theoderic, who was doing Vitalian a favour. He therefore sent Ennodius the bishop and Vitalian the archdeacon for the holding of the council at Heraclea. About two hundred bishops also came from various places, but the lawless emperor and Timothy, bishop of Constantinople, made a mockery of them, and they went away with nothing accomplished. For the impious emperor broke the agreement and secretly told the pope of Rome not to come. He had sent Vitalian a sacra so that Vitalian would send it to Rome, to bring the pope to the council to be held at Heraclea. All the people and the senate openly reviled Anastasius as a perjurer. The lawless man shamelessly said that there was a law requiring an emperor to perjure himself and lie when necessary. Such were the words of that most lawless man with a Manichaean mind. Year of the World 6007. In this year Vitalian, indignant at Anastasius' perjury, inflicted many evils on the armies under Anastasius and on the rest of the state, killing, plundering and stripping people bare. Finally, as an insult, he sold each soldier for a single follis. Year of the World 6008. In this year the Huns called Sabirs crossed the Caspian Gates and overran Armenia, plundering Cappadocia, Galatia and Pontus, and very nearly took Euchaita. Because of this the holy Macedonius fled, and after great danger he reached safety at Gangra. When Anastasius learned of this, he gave harsh orders for him to be kept under guard there. They say he even sent a man to kill him. [?] He was buried in Gangra in the church of the holy martyr Callinicus, very close to the martyr's relics, and he performs many healings.

They say that as Macedonius lay dead, he sealed himself with the sign of the cross with his own hand. A certain Theodore, one of his companions, saw him in a dream saying to him, "Take this, go and read it to Anastasius, and say: 'I am departing to my fathers, whose faith I have kept. But I will not cease [?] to the Master until you come and we enter into judgment.'" In the same year in Alexandria a great many men, women and children were terribly struck by demons and all began barking together. In his sleep someone saw a fearsome figure who said that they were suffering this because of the anathemas against the council. In the same year the empress Ariadne also died. The monks of the desert, moved by divine zeal, drew up four protests. They sent two to the emperor, one to the governors of the province, and one to John, bishop of Jerusalem. In them they declared that they would neither depart from the holy council of Chalcedon nor enter into communion with the impious Severus, since they were ready to face death, and would even set fire to the holy places. The bishop of Thessalonica, out of fear of the emperor, entered into communion with Timothy of Constantinople. Then [?] forty bishops of Illyricum and Hellas came together. By a written confession they separated themselves from him as from their own metropolitan, and they sent to Rome and agreed in writing to be in communion with the bishop of Rome. The historian Theodore groundlessly calls the bishop of Thessalonica a patriarch, without knowing why. Year of the World 6009. In this year John Nikaiotes, the heretical bishop of Alexandria, died, and Dioscorus the Younger, nephew of Timothy

Aelurus, was put forward as bishop of Alexandria. He came to Byzantium to plead with the emperor on behalf of the Alexandrians over the murder of the son of Kalliopios the Augustalis. As he went in procession, he was publicly insulted by the orthodox, who thought he had come to attack the orthodox doctrines. He made his plea about the murder and left in haste. The cause of the murder was this. When Dioscorus was ordained, the crowds of country people walked out, saying, "Unless it is done as the canons of the holy apostles prescribe, he shall not sit as bishop." For it was the officials who had enthroned him. So Dioscorus went to Saint Mark's, and the clergy came and vested him a second time and ordained him again. Then he went to Saint John's and celebrated the synaxis. Theodosius, son of Kalliopios the Augustalis, and Acacius the general were there. The crowds became unruly and began to insult the Augustalis because he praised the emperor Anastasius. Given free rein, some of them rushed in, pulled the Augustalis' son down from his seat and killed him. The general Acacius killed as many as he could seize. When the emperor heard of it, he was angry with them, but Dioscorus pleaded with him and calmed him. Between India and Persia there is a fortress called Tzundadadar [?]. Kavadh learned that there was much money there and many precious stones, and he tried to take it. But demons haunting the place prevented its capture. He set in motion every device of his magi, and then of the Jews as well, and still failed in his aim. He was then persuaded that he could master it through the Christians' prayer to God, so he appealed about it to a Christian bishop, one of those in Persia. The bishop celebrated the synaxis, partook of the divine mysteries, and went to the place. He drove out the demons there and handed the fortress over to Kavadh without any trouble. Kavadh was astonished at this sign and honoured the bishop with the first seat, which until then the Manichees and Jews had occupied. He also gave freedom to anyone who wished to be baptized. Year of the World 6010. Dioscorus bishop of Alexandria, year 1. In this year the emperor Anastasius saw

in a vision a fearsome man holding a book. He opened it, found the emperor's name, and said to him, "See, because of your [?] I am erasing fourteen years," and he erased them. When he woke up, he summoned Amantius the praepositus and told him the vision. Amantius said, "I too saw something this night. As I stood beside Your Majesty, a huge pig came, seized my cloak, threw me to the ground and devoured me." The emperor summoned Proclus the dream interpreter and told him what they had seen. He said to them, "You will both die before long." When Timothy, bishop of Constantinople, died, John the Cappadocian, a presbyter and synkellos, was appointed bishop of Constantinople. He was ordained on the third day of Easter and put on the apostolic robe. The people rioted fiercely against John to make him anathematize Severus. In the same year, in the eleventh indiction, on 9 April, the impious emperor Anastasius died. He had reigned twenty-seven years and seven months, and it was the 234th year from Diocletian. The pious Justin became emperor in his place. He was an old and very experienced man, an Illyrian by birth, who had started out as a common soldier and risen as far as the senate. Some say that Anastasius was struck by a divine thunderbolt and died thunderstruck. Year of the World 6011. Justin emperor of the Romans

was proclaimed. He was a fiery zealot for the orthodox faith and distinguished in war. He had a wife named Lupicina, whom he crowned Augusta, and when she was crowned the demes called her Euphemia. After Anastasius' death, the Vitalian mentioned above became very close to Justin the Great. He received from him the rank of magister militum, came to Byzantium to hold the consulship and was proclaimed consul, and was also made count of the praesentales. He had such freedom of speech with the emperor that he even got an order for Severus to be expelled and put to death, for Vitalian was very orthodox. When Severus heard of it, he fled together with Julian, bishop of Halicarnassus. They went to Egypt and threw it into turmoil by stirring up the dispute about the corruptible and the incorruptible, at a time when Dioscorus was bishop of Alexandria. Bishops and clergy came from Rome with authority from Hormisdas, bishop of Rome, through Vitalian's efforts, while John the Cappadocian was still alive as bishop of Constantinople. They entered the holy council of Chalcedon in the diptychs alongside the other three sacred councils. With the impious Severus out of the way, Paul, the keeper of the hostel of Euboulos, was ordained bishop of Antioch. The emperor gave the city of Antioch a thousand pounds of gold. He also gave the other cities good order and put a stop to popular disturbances. The pious emperor Justin exiled Xenaias, also called Philoxenus, bishop of Hierapolis, a man with a Manichaean mind, and Peter of Apamea, together with all who shared in their corruption. He put to death Amantius the praepositus, Andrew the cubicularius, and Theocritus, Amantius' count, whom Amantius had wanted to make emperor, because they had plotted a usurpation. For the praepositus had given Justin money to hand out so that Theocritus would become emperor. But the army and the demes did not choose Theocritus as emperor and proclaimed Justin instead. These men took it badly and plotted a usurpation, and they were put to death. The emperor recalled all those whom Anastasius had unjustly exiled, including Appion the patrician, whom at Nicaea a presby-

[?] …whom they had ordained by force. The emperor, being a sensible man, made him prefect of the praetorium, and made Diogenianus general of the East. In the same year a terrifying comet appeared in the East, with a ray that shot downward. The astronomers called it a "bearded" star [and they were afraid]. A.M. 6012. — Of Paul, bishop of Antioch [?]

In this year Vitalian was treacherously murdered by the Byzantines. They were angry with him because he had killed many people during his revolt against Anastasius. When John the Cappadocian, bishop of Constantinople, died, Epiphanius, a presbyter and synkellos of the same church, was ordained on 25 February. Likewise, when Hormisdas of Rome fell asleep, John succeeded to the bishopric. In the same year the Blue faction ran riot, stirring up disturbances in all the cities

At that time the demes had control over the horse races. They held them whenever and however they wished, at their own expense, since they had houses, horses and stables, and also revenues for the races [?], which survive even to this day. The emperor was invited, but had no authority in the matter, and many seditious and outrageous things happened at race time. Some people attached themselves to the deme of the Blues, and others to the faction of the Greens [?]. At certain times civil wars were stirred up between the opposing factions, and the demesmen spat out shameless words against the imperial majesty, as various chronicles show. This happened, for example, under the emperor Justinian, under Anastasius, under Phocas the tyrant, and under others.

…the circus in Rome, which he called the hippodrome. He wished to break up the crowd of the people of Rome [?], because they were rioting and attacking him on account of his brother. He was the first to hold a horse race in the city of Rome, for the festival of the Sun and of the four elements subject to him, that is, earth, sea, fire and air. He reckoned that this was why the kings of the Persians fared so well in their wars, since they honoured the four elements. For in Rome they did not honour the four elements, not even with one [festival]. [?] Oenomaus, king of the land of Pisa, [?] in Europe [?]

…the circus in Rome, which he called the hippodrome. He wished to break up the crowd of the people of Rome [?], because they were rioting and attacking him on account of his brother. He was the first to hold a horse race in the city of Rome, for the festival of the Sun and of the four elements subject to him, that is, earth, sea, fire and air. He reckoned that this was why the kings of the Persians fared so well in their wars, since they honoured the four elements. For in Rome they did not honour the four elements, not even with a single festival. [?] Oenomaus, king of the land of Pisa, held contests in the western parts in the month of Dystros, on 25 March, in honour of the Sun, Titan [?]. In them, he says, earth and sea competed, that is, Demeter and Poseidon, the elements subject to the Sun. Lots were cast between King Oenomaus and the man who came to compete against him [?] [?]. When the lot called on Oenomaus to compete on behalf of Poseidon, he wore a blue garment, the colour of the waters, and his opponent wore the green garment, the colour of the earth. When the lot assigned Oenomaus the garment of the earth instead, he wore the green garment, and his opponent wore Poseidon's, the blue of the waters. The loser was put to death. A countless crowd came from every land and city to watch this annual royal contest. The citizens who lived in the coastal cities and the islands, and the sailors of the coastal villages,

in all the cities. It held power for five years. They slaughtered with swords the Greens they met, and also those hiding in their houses: they went up into the houses and killed them, and the authorities did not dare to punish the murders. This lasted [?] until the sixth year of the pious Justin. A.M. 6015 [?]. — Epiphanius, bishop of Constantinople, year 1. Timothy, bishop of Alexandria, year 1. In this year war broke out between the Romans and the Persians. Justin sent envoys and gifts to Zilgibis, king of the Huns, who agreed under his ancestral oaths to fight as an ally [?] against the king of the Persians. But Ka-

vadh also sent to him, and he made an agreement with him as well. When Justin learned this, he was greatly grieved. Zilgibis then set out to join the Persians with twenty thousand men to fight the Romans. Justin sent an embassy to Kavadh, king of the Persians, about peace. In a letter apparently about another matter, he also wrote to him about Zilgibis: that he had sworn oaths of alliance with the Romans, had received many gifts, and meant to betray the Persians. "We are brothers," he wrote, "and we ought to become friends, and not let these dogs make sport of us like this." Kavadh questioned Zilgibis privately: had he received gifts from the Romans, urging him to turn against the Persians? He said, "Yes." In his anger Kavadh killed him. He also sent a large force of Persians by night and destroyed Zilgibis's people, suspecting that they had come to him with treacherous intent. Those who managed to escape withdrew to their own land. Euphrasius of Antioch struck the Council of Chalcedon from the diptychs, along with the name of Hormisdas, pope of Rome. Afterwards, however, he took fright and proclaimed the four councils. Kavadh, king of the Persians, wanted to leave the emperor of the Romans as guardian of his house. He did not want his elder son to succeed, although Persian law called him to rule, nor the second, because his eye had been cut out. The father loved Chosroes, who had been born to him by the sister of Aspebedes. So he decided to make peace with the Romans, and proposed that Chosroes become the emperor's son. On these terms he sent envoys to Justin at Byzantium. The emperor summoned the senate to deliberate and refused to let this happen, for they called it a trick and a betrayal of the Romans. Proclus the quaestor, a wise and shrewd man, gave sound advice on this matter. A.M. 601[?]. — In this year Dyrrachium, a city of New Epirus in Illyricum, suffered from divine wrath. The emperor provided a great deal of money to restore the city. He also treated Corinth, the metropolis of Hellas, with great generosity in the same way. A.M. 6015. — Euphrasius, bishop of Antioch, year 1.

In this year Tzath, king of the Lazi, broke away from the kingdom of the Persians. Kavadh was reigning then and was fond of Tzath, so much so that he had appointed him king of the Lazi. Tzath came to Justin at Byzantium and begged the emperor to let him become a Christian and to proclaim him king of the Lazi. The emperor received him with joy, baptized him and proclaimed him his son. Tzath also married a Roman wife, Valeriana, granddaughter of Nomus, patrician and former curopalates. He took her with him to his own country after Justin had appointed him king of the Lazi. He wore a crown and a white royal chlamys with a gold tablion, on which the image of the emperor Justin was embroidered, and a white sticharion with gold embroidered ornaments, which also bore the emperor's image. His shoes were red and set with pearls in the Persian style, and his belt too was gold set with pearls. He received many gifts from the emperor and went home to his own land with joy. When Kavadh, king of the Persians, learned of this, he sent word to the emperor Justin: "Though there is friendship and peace between us, you act like an enemy, and you have taken over people who have been under the authority of the Persians from time immemorial." The emperor replied: "We have not taken over or enticed any of those subject to your kingdom. But Tzath came to our palace and fell at our feet, begging to be delivered from a foul and pagan doctrine, from impious sacrifices and from the error of demons, and to come to God, the Creator of all

things, and to become a Christian. We baptized him and sent him back to his own country." From then on there was enmity between the Romans and the Persians. In the same year the Homerites perpetrated the deeds against Saint Arethas and the people of the city of Negra. Elesbaas, king of the Ethiopians, then made war on the Homerites, and the Ethiopians won. A.M. 6016. — John, bishop of Rome [?]

In this year Theoderic, who ruled Rome and held Arian views, forced Pope John to go to Byzantium to the emperor Justin. He was to intercede for the Arians, so that they would not be compelled to abandon their heresy, since Theoderic was threatening to do the same to the orthodox in Italy. When John came to Byzantium, the patriarch Epiphanius invited him, but he would not accept until the bishop of Rome was seated above Epiphanius. John communicated with all the bishops, but not with Timothy of Alexandria. Kavadh, king of the Persians and son of Peroz, slew many myriads of Manichaeans in a single day, together with their bishop Indazar and the Persian senators who shared their beliefs. This is why. The Manichaeans had tutored his third son, called Phthasuarsan, whom his daughter Sambyke had borne to him, and won him over to their beliefs. They promised him: "Your father has grown old. If he dies, the archmagi will make one of your brothers king, so that their own doctrine may prevail. But by our prayers we can persuade your father to give up the kingdom and appoint you, so that the doctrine of the Manichaeans may prevail everywhere." He agreed to do this if he became king. When Kavadh learned of this, he ordered an assembly to be held, ostensibly, he said, to make his son Phthasuarsan king. He ordered all the Manichaeans, with their bishop and their wives and

children, to attend the assembly. Likewise he summoned the archmagus Glonazes and the magi, and the bishop of the Christians, Bazanes, whom Kavadh loved as an excellent physician. He called the Manichaeans forward and said, "I take pleasure in your doctrine, and while I am still alive I wish to give the kingdom to my son Phthasuarsan, since he shares your beliefs. So stand apart by yourselves to receive him." They took heart and boldly stood apart. Then Kavadh ordered the army to come in, and they cut them all down with swords, along with their bishop, before the eyes of the archmagus and of the bishop of the Christians. He sent decrees throughout all the land under his rule that any Manichaean found was to be killed and burned, their property brought into the royal treasuries, and their books burned. The pious emperor Justin took up the empire with great competence and courage. He sent decrees everywhere to the cities that all who caused disorder or committed murder were to be punished. He pacified the demes in Constantinople and made them greatly afraid. As soon as he became emperor he also crowned his wife Theodora as Augusta. He appointed the patrician Hypatius, son of Secundinus, general of the East, to guard the eastern regions against the Persians and the raids of the Saracens. He himself also carried out a great persecution of the Manichaeans and punished many of them. A.M. [?]. — In this year Anazarbus, metropolis of Second Cilicia, suffered a most terrible earthquake while Calliopius son of Irenaeus was its governor, and the whole city collapsed. Justin rebuilt it and called it Justinopolis. In the same year, by divine wrath, Edessa, a great and renowned city and metropolis of the province of Osrhoene, was flooded by the waters of its river. For the river Skirtos, flowing through the middle of it, [Apparatus [?]: "Boazanes" A …; 73 "his armies" A; 75 "the land under him" A, "his own land" vulg.; 76 "to be burned up" [?]; 78 [?] "great" [?]; "rebuilt" (ἀνήγειρεν) A, "raised" (ἤγειρεν) [?]; 80 "Justinopolis" A.]

passes through it and brings it much wealth and delight. At that time, however, it flooded like a sea, swept away the houses together with their inhabitants and drowned them. Among the survivors a story prevails that the same river had ravaged the city at other times too, but not like this. After the waters subsided, a stone tablet was found on the river bank. It was inscribed in hieroglyphic letters and read: "The river Skirtos, the Leaper, will leap evil leaps for the citizens." The emperor Justin provided a great deal of money to both cities for their restoration. In the same year a woman of giant stock appeared from Cilicia. She was a cubit taller than any full-grown man and very broad. She went around the cities and collected one follis from each workshop. A.M. 6018. — Chosroes, king of the Persians [?]

In this year, in the month of October of the 4th indiction, the first signs of God's wrath came upon the city of Antioch. A great fire broke out in the middle of the city from no visible cause, foretelling the threat from God that was to come. The fire started at the martyr's shrine of Saint Stephen and spread as far as the praetorium of the general. This was the beginning of sorrows. The fires went on for six months: many houses were burned and many people died. No one could tell where the fire was coming from, for five-storey buildings caught fire from their roof tiles. At the intercession of the patriarch Euphrasius the emperor gave the city two centenaria of gold. In the same year, on 20 May of the same indiction, at the seventh hour, while Olybrius was consul at Rome, Antioch the Great of Syria suffered an indescribable calamity from divine wrath. The wrath of God came upon it so heavily that almost the whole city collapsed and became a tomb for its inhabitants. Some were buried but still alive under the ground, and fire coming up out of the earth burned them. And
other fire came down from the air like sparks and burned up whoever it found, like lightning. The earth went on shaking for a whole year. A.M. 6019. — Felix, bishop of Rome [?]

In this year, while the earthquake continued, Euphrasius, bishop of Antioch, was buried by the earthquake and died. Every house and the churches collapsed, and the beauty of the city vanished. No such divine wrath has struck any other city in all generations. When the most pious emperor Justin learned of this, he was so deeply grieved that he took the diadem from his head and laid aside the purple, and he mourned in sackcloth for many days. Even when he went to church for the feast he would not wear the crown or the chlamys. He came plainly dressed in a purple mantle, weeping before the whole senate, and they all wept with him, wearing mourning. The emperor at once sent Carinus the count [?] with five centenaria for digging out the ruins, in the hope that he could save some people, and to rescue the buried property from thieves and plunderers. Then the emperor sent after him the patrician Phocas son of Craterus, the patrician Asterius and the prefect [?], wise men, and gave them a great deal of money to restore the city. On 4 April of the same 5th indiction, on the feast of Easter, the emperor Justin fell ill and, while still living, appointed his own nephew Justinian as emperor. He crowned him and reigned jointly with him for four months. In August of the same 5th indiction the most pious Justin died, leaving Justinian as emperor. After Euphrasius, bishop of Antioch, died, Ephraim of Amida, who was then count of the East, was ordained in his place. He [showed] divine zeal against the schismatics [?]. A.M. 6030 [?]. — Justinian, emperor of the Romans, year 1. John, bishop of Jerusalem, year 1. Ephraim, bishop of Antioch, year 1.

In this year, now ruling the empire alone, the great Justinian appointed the patrician Patricius the Armenian count of the East. He gave him money and ordered him to go and restore a city of Phoenicia Libanensis on the inner frontier, called Palmyra. He ordered the dux to reside there, and the holy places [?]… On 1 January of the same indiction the emperor held the consulship and gave out more money than any emperor

In the same year the king of the Persians made war on Tzath the Laz, because he had gone over to the Romans. So the emperor Justinian sent him military help and three generals, Belisarius, Cyricus and Peter. They fought and were defeated. The emperor was angry with the generals, because their envy of one another had cost them the victory. He replaced them and sent Peter, his notary, as general. Peter and the Lazi engaged the Persians, won, and killed many of them. In the same year the king of the Heruli, named Grepes, went over to the Romans. He came to Constantinople with his people and asked the emperor to let him become a Christian. The emperor baptized him at Theophany and stood as his sponsor at the font. His twelve senators and kinsmen were baptized with him. He went home to his own land with joy, having become the emperor's friend, and promised to fight as his ally wherever the emperor wished. The emperor appointed Tzittas general of Armenia, a warlike and

[Running head: Chronographia.] highly capable man. For Armenia had had no general, only duces and counts. A great number of Armenians served under him, since they knew the regions of Armenia. The emperor also gave him four numeri of troops from the East, and he became a great defence and help to the Romans. The emperor also gave him in marriage a sister of Theodora Augusta, named Comito. In the same year a barbarian woman of the Huns called Sabirs went over to the Romans. Her name was Boarex, and she was a widow with a hundred thousand Huns under her. She had ruled the Hunnic regions since she lost her husband Balach. Kavadh, king of the Persians, had persuaded two kings of another tribe of Huns, named Styrax and Glones, to fight on his side against the Romans. As they passed through her land on their way to Persian territory with twenty thousand men, Boarex captured them and cut down their men. She took one of their kings, called Styrax, prisoner and sent him in chains to the emperor at Constantinople. Glones she slew in battle. So she became an ally of the emperor Justinian and lived at peace with him. In this year the king of the Huns near Bosporus, named Gordas, also went over to the emperor. He became a Christian and was baptized, and the emperor received him. After giving him many gifts, the emperor sent him back to his own land to guard Roman interests and the city of Bosporus. That city got its name from paying the Romans oxen every year instead of money… [?] of Romans and tribunes, to guard the city against the Huns and to collect the dues of oxen. There was much trade in that city between Romans and Huns. When the king of the Huns who had become a Christian returned to his own land, he found his own brother and told him of the emperor's kindness and generosity, and that he had become a Christian. He took the idols that the Huns worshipped and melted them down, for they were of silver and electrum. The Huns were enraged, and

…having conspired with his brother, they went and slaughtered him, and they made his brother Muager king. Fearing that the Romans would seek vengeance for him, they came suddenly to the city of Bosporus and murdered the tribune Dalmatius and the soldiers. When the emperor heard this, he sent the ex-consul John, grandson of John the Scythian and son of the patrician Rufinus, with a large Scythian force. He campaigned against them, together with [?] by land from Odessopolis, and with Baduarius the general. When the Huns heard this, they fled and vanished. So there was peace in Bosporus, and the Romans held it without fear. The emperor Justinian took away all the churches of the heretics and gave them to the Orthodox, except those of the Exokionite Arians. The emperor also issued an edict concerning bishops, directors of orphanages, stewards and keepers of hostels: they were not to leave inheritances. What they had owned as property before their appointment they might dispose of. But from the hour of their appointment they were to have no licence to dispose of anything, and the holy house was to inherit all their possessions. The same emperor also completed the public bath at the Dagistheus, which the emperor Anastasius had begun to build, and he made the courtyard of the Basilica of Illus into a great cistern. Year of the World 6021. In this year Isaiah, bishop of Rhodes, and Alexander, bishop of Diospolis in Thrace, were deposed after they were found to be pederasts. The emperor punished them terribly: they were castrated and paraded through the city while a herald cried, "You who are bishops, do not outrage the honoured habit!" The emperor also issued severe laws against the licentious, and many were punished. There was great fear, and order was kept. The

emperor also renewed all the old laws, making them into a single book, which he called the New Ordinances. In them he does not allow a governor, in the places he governs, to buy an estate, build a house, or inherit from someone outside his family, unless that person is a relative of his. In the same year, on 29 November, at the third hour, on the fourth day of the week, in the seventh indiction, great Antioch again suffered the wrath of God, two years after its previous calamity. There was a great earthquake lasting an hour, and a terrible roar from heaven. Everything that had been built fell to the ground, the walls as well, and those old buildings that had not fallen in the first earthquake were brought down now. All the splendour of the city, both what came from the emperor's generosity and what the citizens had built at their own expense, collapsed. When the neighbouring [?] learned of this, they held processions of supplication with mourning. In this fall four thousand eight hundred and seventy people died. Those who survived fled to other cities, and lived in huts in the mountains. There was also a great and very severe winter. All who remained held processions of supplication barefoot, weeping and throwing themselves face down in the snow, crying, "Lord, have mercy." Then it was revealed in a vision to a God-fearing man that he should tell all the survivors to write above their doorways: "Christ is with us; stand fast." When this was done, the wrath of God stopped. Once again the emperor and the Augusta gave much money for the restoration and rebuilding of the city of Antioch, and he renamed it Theoupolis. On 11 March of the seventh indiction al-Mundhir, son of Zekike, the petty king of the Saracens, made a raid and plundered Syria Prima as far as the borders of Antioch, up to the place called Litargon and the estates of Skaphatha. He killed many people, and he burned the outskirts of Chalcedon, the estate of Sermion and the hunting country. When the Roman commanders heard of this, they marched out against him. But the Saracens and the Persians learned of it, took their booty and captives, and fled through the inner frontier zone. In April of the same seventh indiction a relief army sent by the emperor arrived, made up of infantry and of the so-called Lycocranitae from Phrygia, and

he appointed Belisarius general of the East, in succession to the patrician Hypatius [son of?] Secundinus. On 12 May the magister Hermogenes, a wise man, entered Antioch. He was an ambassador, sent by the emperor Justinian to the king of the Persians to discuss peace. In June the Samaritans and Jews in Palestine crowned a certain Julian as king. They took up arms against the Christians, and plundered, murdered and burned them. But God delivered them into the hands of Justinian, who destroyed them all and beheaded the usurper Julian. Chosroes, king of the Persians, received the magister Hermogenes, who came with gifts as an ambassador for peace. In July of the same seventh indiction Chosroes took the gifts but would not agree to make peace. He had been persuaded by Samaritans who had fled to him and offered to betray their country, all of Palestine, to him, claiming they had fifty thousand Jews and Samaritans as allies. Emboldened by them, Chosroes did not choose peace, because he wanted to use them to take Jerusalem as well, which held countless centenaria of gold and much [?silver]. He used the gold mines in the mountains of Armenia as a pretext: formerly they had paid nine talents each to the Romans and to the Persians, but now they paid the Romans alone. He also wrote to the emperor alleging certain other grievances. But the Samaritans' plot became known, and on their way back from Persia they were arrested at Ammodius. These were five notable Samaritans, from among their wealthy men. They were handed over to the general Belisarius, and under interrogation they confessed everything.

At the same time the dux of Palestine quarrelled with the phylarch of the Saracens who were subject to the Romans. The phylarch was afraid and withdrew into the inner frontier zone. When al-Mundhir learned of this, he made a raid, captured him and killed him. He took the phylarch's wives and children and went back. The duces of Phoenicia, Arabia and Mesopotamia and the phylarch learned of this and pursued him. When al-Mundhir heard this, he fled to the Indian regions, where no Roman had ever gone. They also seized his tents, and brought back many Saracen captives, men, women and children, along with all the Roman captives they found, and camels, sheep, oxen, a great deal of silk and clothing. They also burned four Persian forts [?] and returned with a great victory. Year of the World 6022. In this year, in the eighth indiction, the emperor Justinian began a great persecution against the pagans and every heresy, and [confiscated?] their property. Macedonius, the former referendarius, was also accused, as was Asclepiodotus, the former prefect, who out of fear [?] and died. And Pegasius of

Heliopolis and his children were interrogated in public [?]. [?], the patrician, son of Craterus, the quaestor Thomas and others were arrested, and there was great fear. The emperor decreed that pagans and heretics should not hold public office, but only Orthodox Christians, and he gave them three months to convert. In March of the same eighth indiction, at Antioch, Hermogenes, the former consul and magister, and Rufinus, the former general and patrician, set out as ambassadors to the Persian lands. When they reached Dara, they sent word to the king of the Persians asking him to receive them as well. While they were staying at Dara with Belisarius, the general of the East, and the other Roman commanders, they were encamped a short distance from the city. Meran, the chief general of the Persian king, was gathered at Nisibis with the king's son and the other generals of Persia and a great Persian force. In June of the eighth indiction he learned of this and attacked them, dividing his host into three divisions. When the Roman generals and the magister learned of this, they showed good generalship and charged the Persians. There was a great battle and a fearful clash. The Romans cut down the Persians and destroyed them, and they also took their [?standard]. Meran, the son of the Persian king and a few of the survivors fled to Nisibis, and the Romans won a great victory. When the Persian king learned of this, he allowed only the patrician Rufinus to come to him, together with count Alexander. They went to him in August. After much discussion they drew up the terms of a peace, and then departed in peace. Year of the World 6023 [?]. Bishop of Rome: Boniface

In this year, in September of the ninth indiction, a great and fearful star appeared in the west. It was a comet that sent its flashing rays upward, and people called it Lampadias. It went on shining for twenty days, and throughout the world there were popular uprisings and murders. At the end

of November the patrician Rufinus returned from his embassy to the Persians and came to the emperor Justinian, having drawn up the terms of a peace. When the emperor received him, he rejoiced greatly at the peace and ratified the agreed terms, and the affairs of both states enjoyed peace. Year of the World 6024 [?]. In this year, the fifth of Justinian's reign, in January of the tenth indiction, the so-called Nika rebellion broke out. The factions crowned Hypatius, a kinsman of the emperor Anastasius, as emperor. A large part of the city was burned: the Great Church, Saint Irene, the hostel of Samson, the Augusteum, the porch [?] of the Basilica, and the Chalke of the palace. There was great fear, and many of those found with Hypatius in the so-called Hippodrome died, thirty-five thousand, so they say. The Nika disorder came about in this way. When the factions had gone up into the Hippodrome, the Greens cried out the acclamations: "Because of Calopodius the cu-

[?]…-thokas [?]… Augusta [?]… proclaimed in the presence of the factions. Then a dispute arose between the Greens and the Blues over the places where they stood [?], and they began to riot against each other. [?]-okas sent some men and tried to stir up the riot among them. One of the men he sent insulted the demarch of the Greens and shoved him. The faction members could not bear this, and they cried out:

He adds [?]… the riot of the faction members that took place in Byzantium, whose name [?] came from the watchword of the factions. For they call it "Nika", because when the factions joined together they gave this to one another as a watchword by which to recognise each other. He adds the sedition [?]

-bicularius and spatharius." The Greens: "Many years, Justinian Augustus, may you conquer! I am wronged, O only good one, and I cannot bear it; God knows. I am afraid to name him, in case he prospers all the more and I am put in danger." The Mandator: "Who is he? I do not know." The Greens: "The man who oppresses me, thrice-august, is to be found in the shoemakers' quarter." The Mandator: "No one is wronging you." The Greens: "One man, and one alone, wrongs me. Mother of God, may he not lift up his head!" The Mandator: "Who that is, we do not know." The Greens: "You, and you alone, know, thrice-august, who is oppressing me today." The Mandator: "If there is anyone, we do not know of him." The Greens: "Calopodius the spatharius wrongs me, master of all." The Mandator: "Calopodius has nothing to do with it." The Greens: "Whoever he may be, he will share the fate of Judas. God will repay the man who wrongs me, and quickly." The Mandator: "You do not come to watch the games, but only to insult the officials." The Greens: "Whoever wrongs me will share the fate of Judas." The Mandator: "Be quiet, you Jews, Manichees and Samaritans!" The Greens: "You call us Jews and Samaritans? The Mother of God is with all of us!" The Mandator: "How long will you go on cursing yourselves?" The Greens: "If anyone does not say that our master believes rightly, let him be anathema, like Judas." The Mandator: "I tell you: be baptised into the one [God]." The Greens shouted over one another, crying: "As Antlas [?] commanded, be baptised into the one!" The Mandator: "Truly, if you do not keep quiet, I will have you beheaded." The Greens: "Everyone is eager to get hold of an office so as to be safe. Whatever we say in our distress, let your majesty not be angry, for the divine

bears with everyone. [The Greens:] We have a right to speak, emperor, and now we will name everything. Where the palace is, we do not know, thrice-august, nor how the state is run. I come into the city only once, when I am seated on a mule, and I wish I did not have to come even then, thrice-august." The Mandator: "Every free man may go wherever he wishes and appear in public without danger." The Greens: "I may feel sure of my freedom, yet I am not allowed to show myself. If a man is free but suspected of being a Green, he is certain to be punished in public." The Mandator: "Are you so ready to die that you will not even spare your own lives?" The Greens: "Let this colour be abolished, and justice has no place. Stop the murders, and let us be punished. Look, here is a gushing spring: punish as many as you like. Truly, human nature cannot bear both these things. Would that Sabbatius had never been born, so that he would not have had a son who is a murderer! This is the twenty-sixth murder, the one at Zeugma: in the morning the man was watching the games, and in the evening he was slaughtered, master of all." The Blues: "You alone, of the whole stadium, have the murderers." The Greens: "You slaughter, and then you leave town." The Blues: "You slaughter, and you stir up trouble. You alone of the stadium have the murderers." The Greens: "Lord Justinian, they provoke us, and no one kills them. Let anyone who wishes understand: who killed the woodseller at Zeugma, emperor?" The Mandator: "You killed him." The Greens: "Who killed the son of Epagathus, emperor?" The Mandator: "You killed him too, and you accuse [?] the Blues." The Greens: "Now, now! Lord, have mercy! Truth is being tyrannised. I would gladly argue against [?] those who say that affairs are governed by God. Where does this misfortune come from?" The Mandator:

"God cannot be tempted by evil." The Greens: "God cannot be tempted by evil? Then who is it who wrongs me? If there is a philosopher or a hermit here, let him explain the difference between the two." The Mandator: "Blasphemers and enemies of God, when will you be quiet?" The Greens: "If your majesty wishes, I will keep silent, though against my will, thrice-august. I know everything, everything, but I keep silent. Farewell, justice, you are no more! I will go over and become a Jew. Indeed, better to become a pagan than a Blue, God knows." The Blues: "What I hate I do not wish to see, and envy troubles me." The Greens: "Let the bones of the spectators be dug up!" Then they went down and left the emperor and the Blues watching the games. Immediately, at the instigation of certain [?] men, an occasion for popular disturbance arose in the following way. The prefect arrested three of the faction members who were causing disorder and hanged them on the gallows. One died at once, but the other two fell from the gallows. They were hanged again, and again they fell. When the crowd standing by saw them, they cried out, "Take them to the church!" Hearing this, the monks of Saint Conon seized them, put them in a boat and took them across to Saint Lawrence, because that church had the privilege that no one could be removed from it until he had obtained justice. When the prefect heard this, he sent soldiers to guard them. The factions learned of it and went to the praetorium, asking the prefect to withdraw the soldiers guarding Saint Lawrence. He gave them no answer. In their rage they set fire to the praetorium, and the porticoes burned from the arch of the Forum as far as the Chalke. They destroyed the silversmiths' shops and the whole quarter of Lausus by fire, and they ruthlessly slaughtered the soldiers who fell into their hands. They went into houses and plundered their contents. They set fire to the bronze-roofed entrance of the palace, the quarters of the Protectors, and the Ninth [?] of the Augusteum. Then the people went down to the harbour of Julian, called the harbour of Sophia,

to the house of Probus, looking for weapons and calling for another emperor for the city. They set fire to Probus's house, and it collapsed. They went on and burned the bath of Alexander and the great hostel of Samson, and the sick perished. They also burned the Great Church with both its colonnades, and the whole of it collapsed from its four walls [?]. The emperor was afraid, and he wanted to load the money onto a dromon and leave for Thrace, as far as Heraclea. He would leave the general Mundus to guard the palace, with his son and three thousand men, together with Constantiolus and the cubicularii. The factions dragged the dead and threw them into the sea; they had also killed many women. A rumour spread that the emperor had taken the Augusta and gone to Thrace, and so they proclaimed the patrician Hypatius emperor. He sat in the Hippodrome and was acclaimed by the factions, and he heard the insulting cries against the emperor Justinian. Two hundred young Greens also came from the Flavianae, armed and wearing breastplates, expecting to open the palace and bring Hypatius in. When the emperor heard what the people and Hypatius had dared to do, he went into the palace. He went up into the so-called Pulpita behind the Kathisma of the Hippodrome, to the dining hall with the bronze doors. With him were Mundus, Constantiolus, Belisarius and other senators, together with a force of armed soldiers, cubicularii and spatharii. Narses the cubicularius went out and secretly won over some of the Blue faction by handing out money. They began to cry, "Justinian Augustus, may you conquer! Lord, save Justinian the emperor and Theodora the Augusta!" Then the crowd split, and the two sides charged each other. Those from the palace came out with the same force, cut some of them off from the people, and charged into the Hippodrome. Narses went in by the gates, the son of Mundus through the Sphendone, and others

through the narrow passage of the Kathisma into the arena. They began to cut down the factions, some shooting arrows and others slaughtering, so that none of the citizens found in the Hippodrome, whether Blues or Greens, survived. Belisarius ran into the emperor's Kathisma with spatharii, seized Hypatius and brought him to the emperor, and they put him under guard. That day thirty-five thousand men died. After that no faction member ever appeared again, and that day there was quiet. On the next day Hypatius and his brother Pompeius were executed, and their bodies were thrown into the sea. Their houses were confiscated, and so were the houses of eighteen other patricians, illustres and consulars, as accomplices of Hypatius. There was great fear, the city grew quiet, and no races were held for a long time.

In the same year there was also a great shower of shooting stars from evening until dawn. Everyone was amazed and said that the stars were falling, and that they had never seen such a thing. Year of the World 6025 [?]. Bishop of Rome: John

In this year Theodora, the most pious Augusta, went to the hot springs of Pythia to take the waters. Four thousand people went with her: the patrician Menas, the prefect, the patrician Elias, count of the largitiones, other patricians, the cubicularii and satraps [?]. She gave many gifts to the churches and poorhouses and to the [?]

Year of the World 6026. In this year Priscus, the former consul and former imperial notary, incurred the anger of Theodora the empress. His property was confiscated, and by the emperor's command he was ordained deacon of Cyzicus. In the same year the Vandal wars took place, and Belisarius took Africa. For the

The Vandals, as was said under the earlier years, seized Spain in the reign of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius under Godigisclus their king, and crossing from there into Libya they took possession of it. When Godigisclus died, his sons Gontharis and Gizeric succeeded to his rule. When Gontharis departed from among men, Gizeric was proclaimed king of the Vandals. He took the city of Carthage and reigned thirty-nine years, and he also took Rome. When he died, his son Huneric succeeded to the kingdom. Huneric did great harm to the Christians in Libya and tried to force them to become Arians. He killed many, and cut out the tongues of others at the throat, yet afterwards by the grace of God these men spoke. Holding the Vandals in contempt, the Moors made war on them and did them much harm. After reigning eight years Huneric died, having lost Numidia and Mount Aurasium, which never again came under the Vandals. Gundamund, the son of Gento son of Gizeric, succeeded to the rule. He did even greater harm to the Christians, and died after reigning twelve years. He was succeeded by Thrasamund, a handsome, intelligent and generous man. He tried to force the Christians to change their ancestral faith, not by torture but by turning his back on those who refused. When his wife died childless, he made a very wise decision. He sent to Theoderic, king of the Goths, in Spain, and asked to take Theoderic's sister Amalafrida, who was a widow, in marriage. Theoderic gave him his sister as wife, together with two thousand picked Goths to serve as a bodyguard and five thousand other fighting men to attend them. Theoderic also gave his sister one of the promontories of Sicily, the one called Lilybaeum [?]. From that time Thrasamund was thought the strongest and most powerful of all who had reigned in Libya. He also became a friend of the emperor Anastasius, and he held the kingdom for twenty-seven years. When he died, Hilderic, son of Huneric son of Gizeric, became king. He was a gentle and good man, and was not harsh toward the Christians. In matters of war, however, he was very soft, and did not even want to hear of it. His nephew Hoamer, a man good at war, commanded the Vandals, and they called him Achilles. Hilderic had been a friend of Justinian before Justinian became emperor, in the time of Justin

his uncle, and Hilderic sent him many gifts and received gifts from him, strengthening their friendship. There was a kinsman of his from the family of Gizeric, named Gelimer, a clever and malicious man who knew how to stir up revolutions and lay hands on other people's property. He rose in rebellion against his own lord Hilderic, who had reigned seven years, seized him and threw him into prison with his wife Amalafrida. He killed all the Goths, and kept Hoamer and his brother Euagees in prison. Puffed up by his usurpation, he could not live within the established order. So he wrote to the emperor Justinian in his own defence, claiming that the kingdom lawfully belonged to him because Hilderic was not able to govern it. When Justinian learned this, he wrote back that he would not accept this usurpation. But Gelimer paid no attention to the letter. He blinded Hoamer, and shut Hilderic and Euagees up in stricter custody. When Justinian learned this, he made war on Libya. He brought the Persian war to an end, summoned Belisarius from the East, and took counsel about the matter. The senate was displeased. They recalled the fleet of the emperor Leo that had sailed against the Vandals under Basiliscus and been lost, how many soldiers had died and how much money had been spent. And they were afraid of how great the danger was, in case the emperor should choose them as general for this expedition. Then John the patrician came forward and said: "We, master, obey your commands and do not oppose them. But it is right for you to consider the length of the journey and the open seas. By land the distance is a journey of a hundred and forty days. Consider too how uncertain victory is, how painful defeat would be, and how useless regret would be afterwards." The emperor accepted his speech and set aside his eagerness for the war. But a certain bishop from the East roused the emperor again. He said that a dream had come to him from God, telling him to go to the emperor and ask him to rescue the Christians in Libya from the tyrants: "And I will help him and make him lord of Libya." When the emperor heard this, he could no longer hold back. He equipped the army and the ships, and prepared arms and provisions. He ordered Belisarius to be ready, since he would command in Libya. Pudentius at once rebelled and seized Tripo- [Variant readings: βασιλεύσαντος in A, βασιλεύσαντα in the common text; στρατείας ἐκλέξοιτο in A, στρατιᾶς ἐξελέξοιτο in the common text; ἀνόνητον in e, ἀνόητον in a, ἀνώνητον in the common text; σιτία in A, σιτεῖα in the common text.]

-lis [?], and wrote to Justinian asking him to send an army and take it over. In the same way Godas the Goth rebelled against his own lord Gelimer and took control of the island of Sardinia. He wrote to Justinian asking him to send an army and a general to take over the island, and Justinian sent Cyril with three hundred men to help him. But Gelimer sent his brother with a large fleet and a picked army of Vandals, took the island, and killed Godas. Belisarius took over the army, the fleet and the commanders: Solomon the general, Dorotheus of Armenia, Cyprian, Valerian, Martin, Althias, John, Marcellus and Cyril, whom I mentioned before, and many others of those who lived in Thrace. With them went a thousand Heruls, led by Pharas, and Massagetae mounted archers, led by Sinnion and Balas. There were five hundred ships, each holding up to fifty thousand medimni. There were thirty thousand sailors, Egyptians, Ionians and Cilicians. The single commander over the ships was Calonymus of Alexandria. There were also ninety dromons for naval battle. Over the whole force the emperor appointed Belisarius as sole commander. Belisarius came from Germania, which lies between the Thracians and the Illyrians. He took with him his wife Antonina. Gelimer had sent his brother Tzazon with a hundred and twenty ships and a picked army against Godas on the island of Sardinia. It was the seventh year of Justinian when Belisarius was sent to the island. Procopius the historian was with him. Setting out from the imperial city, they came to Abydos. Belisarius took care that the whole fleet should sail together and put in at the same place. When he reached Sicily, he sent Procopius the historian to Syracuse, so that he might find

(See Procopius: "They had long ships, ninety-two of them, fitted out as for a sea battle. They had a single bank of oars and were roofed over, so that the men rowing them would be as safe as possible from enemy missiles. People today call these ships dromons.")

some men who would guide him to Libya, so that he could land there suddenly and put the army ashore, since the men were afraid of the fight [?]. Belisarius set sail with the fleet and put in at the place called Caucana, two hundred stades from Syracuse. Procopius went into Syracuse and bought provisions from Amalasuntha, the wife of Theoderic and mother of Athalaric king of Italy, who were on friendly terms with Justinian. Unexpectedly he also met a man who had been his friend since childhood and knew the regions of Libya and the sea well. This man had arrived from Carthage three days before, and he assured Procopius that the Vandals had no worries at all and did not suspect that anyone was coming against them. In fact Gelimer was staying four days' journey from the sea. Procopius took this man to Belisarius at Caucana. When Belisarius learned this, he reached the coast of Libya on the third day and put in at a place called Caput Vada. They left the ships, built a palisade and dug a deep ditch, and set up camp in a single day. While the ditch was being dug, the earth sent up a great gush of water, though the place was waterless, and it met every need of the animals and the army. The next day the soldiers went off to plunder. The general punished them and said to them: "Using violence and living off other people's property is unjust at any time, and especially in times of danger. I brought you onto this land with only this one ground of confidence: that by justice and good deeds we might serve God and win the Libyans over to our side. But this lack of restraint of yours will turn things against us and will make the Libyans fight on the side of the Vandals. Obey what I say: buy your food and take it that way. Then you will not appear unjust, you will not turn the friendship of the Libyans into enmity, and you will serve God. Stop pouncing on other people's property, and reject a gain that is full of dangers." Belisarius sent troops against the city of Syllectus, and they took it without effort. They arrived by night and went in together with the peasants' wagons that were entering, and so they held it. When day came, they took the priest and the leading men of the city and sent them to the general. On the same day the official in charge of the public post deserted and handed over the public horses. The

veredarius who carried the royal dispatches was also captured. Belisarius set the army in order and marched on Carthage. He gave John the Armenian three hundred picked men and ordered him to keep always going on with them, but not to get far from the army. When he arrived at the city of Syllectus, he won the people over by kindness and gentle words. As a result they made the rest of the march as though in their own country: the inhabitants neither withdrew nor hid, but provided a market and served the soldiers in other ways too. They covered eighty stades each day all the way to Carthage. So they passed through the city of Leptis and Hadrumetum and came to the place called Grasse, three hundred and eight stades from Carthage. There was a palace of the Vandals there, very beautiful gardens, crystal-clear springs, and a boundless abundance of every kind of fruit. Each soldier pitched his hut among the fruit trees, and though the fruit was ripe and all of them enjoyed it, no one could see that there was any less of it. When Gelimer heard that the Romans had arrived, he wrote to his brother Ammatas in Carthage, telling him to kill Hilderic and all of Hilderic's kinsmen whom he held in prison, and to arm himself, the Vandals, and anyone else in the city fit to fight. Ammatas did as he was ordered. Belisarius instructed Archelaus the prefect and Calonymus the admiral to approach Carthage but not to attack it until he gave them the order. He himself came to Decimum, seventy stades from Carthage. Gelimer ordered his nephew Gibamund to go along the left side with two thousand men. Ammatas from Carthage, Gelimer from behind, and Gibamund from the regions on the left were to close in at the same point and encircle the enemy. Belisarius ordered John to go ahead, as I said before, and the Massagetae to march on the left of the army. But Ammatas did not arrive at the right time. He left the mass of the Vandals in Carthage and hurried to Decimum with only a few men, and these were not even in formation. He met John and came to blows with him, and was killed by John. Those with him turned and fled in disorder, and they threw into panic all who were coming from Carthage to Decimum, since they thought their pursuers were very numerous. John and his men slaughtered

THEOPHANES. So many were killed up to the gates of Carthage that onlookers thought it was the work of twenty thousand enemies. Gibamund and his two thousand ran into the Huns in the fighting, and all of them perished. Belisarius, who was at Decimum, learned nothing of this. He threw a palisade around a camp and fortified it, leaving his wife and the infantry there. He himself took the cavalry and the commanders and advanced toward Carthage. He found the fallen dead, Ammatas and the Vandals, and learned what had happened. Climbing a hill, he saw dust rising from the south and a great host of Vandal horsemen led by Gelimer, who knew of neither Gibamund's fate nor that of Ammatas. When they drew near each other, the Vandals got there first and seized the hill, and they struck fear into their opponents. The Romans turned and fled to a place seven stades from Decimum. But God wondrously changed the Vandals and made them cowardly. For if they had pursued at once, they would have utterly destroyed everyone with Belisarius, so great was the multitude of the Vandals, and they would easily have overpowered John as he returned from Carthage stripping the dead. Coming down from the hill, Gelimer found his brother dead. He gave himself up to lamenting, and so blunted the edge of his victory. Belisarius ordered the fugitives to halt, put everything in good order, and reproached them for their cowardice. When he learned that the enemy commanders had been killed and that John had won his victory, he advanced on Gelimer at a run and with courage. The barbarians were caught unprepared and turned to headlong flight. They lost many men and retreated toward Medeia [?], abandoning Carthage. When night fell, Belisarius, John and the Massagetae arrived at Decimum. When they learned everything that had happened, they rejoiced. The next day they all set out for Carthage, together with the infantry and Belisarius's wife. The Carthaginians opened their gates, lit lamps, and went out all together to meet Belisarius. The Vandals in the city took refuge in the churches. When the fleet arrived, the Carthaginians raised the chain in the harbour and let it in. Most of the fleet kept Belisarius's order and did not enter the harbour, but anchored outside. Calonymus, however, chose to disobey and went in. He plundered the ships and seized a great deal of money. He also broke into the workshops and houses near the harbour and took many people captive. Having taken Carthage without effort, Belisarius addressed the soldiers: "See what great good fortune

has come to us because we showed restraint toward the Libyans. Take care to preserve good order in Carthage. Let no one wrong anyone or snatch anything from him. These people have suffered many evils at the hands of the Vandals, a barbarian people, and our emperor has sent us to help them and grant them their freedom." With this exhortation he entered Carthage. He went up to the palace and sat on Gelimer's throne. The merchants of Carthage, and all who lived near the sea, came to him lamenting that they had been plundered by the fleet. Belisarius made Calonymus the admiral swear that he would bring back everything that had been seized and return it to its owners. But Calonymus kept some of it for himself and broke his oath, and before long he paid the penalty. He went out of his mind, chewed up his own tongue, and died. Belisarius feasted the army royally, and Gelimer's own servants served the food, poured the wine, and attended to everything else. The general took control of the city so peacefully that he did no violence to anyone, and no one in the marketplace even had to lock up his house. Instead the soldiers bought their food, ate, and made merry. He gave pledges of safety to the Vandals who had taken refuge in the churches and brought them out. He also saw to the walls of the city, which had earlier been neglected. People said that there was an old saying in Carthage that G would drive out B, and now it was fulfilled. For formerly Gizeric had driven out Boniface, and now Belisarius

Gelimer lavished large sums of money on the Libyan farmers and won them over to himself. He ordered them to kill any Romans who were going about the countryside. When the farmers did this, Belisarius learned of it and sent Diogenes, one of his guardsmen, to punish them. Diogenes and his men went into a house and went to sleep, expecting no hostile action. When Gelimer learned this, he picked three hundred men and sent them against him. They came and surrounded the house, but were afraid to go in at night. The Romans noticed them, and
