[?] παρετίθει τε καὶ in A, παρετίθετο καὶ in the common text. εἰς τὸ παλάτιον in A and e, ἐν [?]. οὐ μετὰ in A, καὶ [?]. οἰνοχόει in A and e. ἤσθιον in A, εἴσθιον in the common text. καταφυγόντας [?]. αἰκίσασθαι τοὺς γεωργοὺς in A [?], αἰτή- [?]

all of them got up, armed themselves and mounted their horses. There were twenty of them. They suddenly flung the doors open and, protecting themselves with their shields and defending themselves with their spears, routed their opponents. Gelimer, who was now in Numidia, gathered all the Vandals and as many of the Moors as were friendly to him, and prepared for war. He also sent a letter to his brother Tzazon in Sardinia, telling him what had happened. Tzazon at once set sail from Sardinia with all his men, reached the coast of Libya on the third day, and found Gelimer. They threw their arms around each other's necks, but said nothing to one another. Instead of saying "Greetings," they clung to each other and wept, and the army likewise lamented the disaster. Gelimer took both armies and advanced on Carthage, and tried to besiege it. He thought that those in Carthage would betray the city to him, and also those of the Roman soldiers who followed the teaching of Arius. He also sent to the leaders of the Huns and promised to give them many rewards if they would betray the Romans to him. Belisarius learned of this from deserters. He found that a certain Laurentius in Carthage was a traitor, and impaled him on a hill in front of the city. This threw those who were plotting betrayal into great fear, so that the Massagetae confessed what Gelimer had proposed to them. Belisarius won them all over to his friendship with conciliatory words and oaths. Then he at once ordered John the Armenian to take all the cavalry except five hundred and go out against the Vandals to skirmish with them. He himself followed the next day with the infantry and the five hundred horsemen. They found the Vandals encamped at Tricamarum, and both armies spent the night close to each other. A portent appeared in the Roman army: the tips of the spears blazed with a bright fire. The men were astonished when they saw it. At dawn both sides drew up their ranks and rushed into battle. John picked a few of the men around him, crossed the river, and attacked the Vandals. Tzazon charged and drove him back. The Vandals pursued him as far as the river. Then John took a large number of Belisarius's guardsmen and charged against Tzazon again with shouting and a great clatter. The battle became fierce, and Tzazon, Gelimer's brother, fell. Then the whole

…the Roman army crossed the river and advanced on the enemy. They routed them and chased them as far as their camp. Then they turned back and stripped the dead, especially those who wore gold, and withdrew to their own camp. Fifty Romans fell in this battle, and eight hundred Vandals. Belisarius arrived with the infantry in the late afternoon, toward evening. As fast as he could he set out with the whole army against the Vandal camp. When Gelimer learned that Belisarius was there with the infantry and the whole army, he mounted his horse without giving any orders. Terror-stricken, he fled headlong toward Numidia with a few of his kinsmen and servants. When the Vandals saw that he had fled and that the enemy was already in sight, men, women and children were thrown into confusion and began to wail. They cared nothing for their money or for their dearest ones as they lamented, and each fled wherever he could. The Romans came on and took the camp. They kept up the pursuit all night, killing every man they came across and making slaves of the women and children. They found more wealth there than had ever been gathered in one place. The Vandals had plundered the Roman empire and carried a great deal of wealth into Libya, and since the land itself was good and fruitful, they had also drawn large revenues from it. They had ruled Libya for ninety-five years and amassed riches, and on that day [?] all that wealth came back into Roman hands. In three months of war, from October to the end of December, Belisarius subdued the whole of Libya. He sent John the Armenian with two hundred picked men to pursue Gelimer and take him alive or dead. John overtook Gelimer and was about to capture him, but then the following happened. A certain Uliaris, one of Belisarius' guardsmen, was with John. Drunk with wine, he saw a bird sitting in a tree, drew his bow and shot at it. He missed the bird but hit John from behind in

the neck. John was mortally wounded and died, and he left great grief behind him for the emperor Justinian, for Belisarius, and for all the Romans and Carthaginians. So Gelimer escaped that day and went to the Moors. Belisarius [?] shut him up on Mount Papua, at the farthest edge of Numidia. He blockaded him there through the winter, and all the [necessities] ran out for him

(for the Moors have no bread, wine or oil, but eat spelt and barley uncooked, like brute beasts). In these straits Gelimer wrote to Pharas, whom Belisarius had left to guard him, asking to be sent a lyre, a single loaf of bread and a sponge. Pharas could not work out what this meant until the man who had brought the letter explained. Gelimer longed to see a loaf, he said, because he had not seen bread since he went up the mountain. He wanted a sponge because his eyes were inflamed from going unwashed, so that he could soothe them with it. And he wanted a lyre because he was a good player, so that he could lament and weep over his present misfortune on it. When Pharas heard this he was deeply grieved, and he mourned over human fortune. He did as the letter asked and sent Gelimer everything he needed. When the winter was over, Gelimer feared the Roman siege. He also pitied the children of his kinsmen, who had become infested with worms in their misery. His resolve weakened, and he wrote to [Pharas] asking for pledges of safety, so that he and those with him could come over to Belisarius. Pharas confirmed this with an oath, took them all and came to Carthage. Belisarius received him with great joy. Gelimer came in before Belisarius laughing. Some suspected that the extremity of his sufferings had driven him out of his natural wits and that he was deranged. His friends, however, thought the man shrewd. He had been a king of royal blood, with a strong army and great wealth, and had suddenly been forced to flee and endure hardship on Papua. Now he had come as a captive, and so, they reasoned, he judged human affairs worth nothing but loud laughter. Belisarius kept him, with all the Vandal leaders, not in disgrace, so that he could take him to the emperor Justinian at Byzantium. Belisarius at once sent Cyril with the head of Tzazon to the island of Sardinia, and to the island formerly called Cyrnus, and brought it under Roman rule. He sent another John to Caesarea in Mauretania, which lies thirty days' journey from Carthage, toward Gades and the setting sun. Yet another John, one of his shield-bearers, he sent to the strait at Gades and the other of the Pillars of Heracles, to hold the fort there which they call Septum. To the [?] … eating barley-meal no differently from the other animals [?]

islands near the mouth of the Ocean, Majorca and Minorca, he sent Apollinarius, a man brave in war. He also sent some of the Libyans and Vandals to Lilybaeum [?] and ordered them to take the fort. The Goths who were guarding it reported this to the mother of Athalaric. She wrote to Belisarius not to seize the fort by force until the emperor Justinian had learned of the matter and done as he saw fit. With that the Vandal war came to an end. But envy, as tends to happen in times of great good fortune, was brewing against Belisarius too. Some men slandered him to the emperor, saying that he was plotting to seize power. The emperor sent Solomon to sound out Belisarius' intentions: would he come to Byzantium with Gelimer and the Vandals, or would he stay where he was and send them on? For Belisarius knew who the officers were who had brought the charge of usurpation. Belisarius came to Byzantium and left Solomon as general of Libya. When Belisarius arrived at Byzantium with Gelimer and the Vandals, he was granted great honours, such as Roman generals had received in former times for their greatest victories. In the six hundred years that had passed, no one had come to such an honour except Titus and Trajan and other emperors who had led campaigns against a barbarian nation and conquered it. He displayed the spoils and the slaves taken in the war and led them in procession through the middle of the city, in what the Romans call a triumph. This was not done in the ancient manner, however: he went on foot from his own house to the Hippodrome. The spoils included everything that customarily serves the emperor's state [?]: golden thrones, carriages in which emperors' wives ride, a great deal of jewellery made of precious stones, golden drinking cups, and all the other things used at the emperor's banquets. There was also silver weighing many tens of thousands of talents, and royal treasures of every kind, which Gaiseric had taken when he plundered the palace at Rome. Among them were also the treasures of the Jews, which Titus son of Vespasian had brought to Rome after the capture of Jerusalem. The

captives in the triumph were Gelimer himself, wearing a purple robe over his shoulders, all his family, and those of the Vandals who were especially tall and handsome. When Gelimer entered the Hippodrome and saw the emperor seated on the tribune and the people standing on either side, he kept crying out the words: "Vanity of vanities, all is vanity." When he reached the emperor's tribune, they stripped off his purple robe and made him fall on his face and do obeisance to the emperor. The emperor and the Augusta gave the children and grandchildren of Hilderic, and all the members of the emperor Valentinian's family, generous [?] gifts of money. They allowed Gelimer large and pleasant estates in Galatia, where he could live with all his kinsmen. But the emperor did not [?] raise him to the rank of patrician, because he refused to give up the Arian belief. After the triumph Belisarius became consul, and the people of Byzantium received more largesse from his victory than ever before. While Solomon was governing Libya, the Moors went to war against the Libyans. The Moors are descended from the nations that Joshua son of Nun drove out of the land of the Phoenicians, who lived from Sidon as far as Egypt. They went to Egypt, but the Egyptians would not receive them, so they occupied Libya and settled there. In later times the Roman emperors conquered this land and named it Tingitana. At the Great Spring the Moors set up two pillars of white stone, engraved with Phoenician letters that read: "We are those who fled from the face of Joshua the robber, son of Nun." There were also other nations in Libya before them, natives of the land, whose king was Asclepeus [?], who they said was a son of the Earth. It was these who founded Carthage. Solomon took the troops from Carthage and marched against the Moors. He came to Byzacium, to the place called Mammes, where the Moors had pitched camp. They had made a circle of camels and placed their women and children inside it. As the Moors came out against him, he mounted his horse, led five hundred picked men, and ordered them to fall upon one
And after him, Antaeus their king, who wrestled with Heracles at Clipea, and who they said was a son of the Earth.

part of the circle and kill the camels. When they had slain about two hundred, they ran on into the middle of the circle, where the women were sitting. The barbarians were struck with terror and fled to the mountain in complete disorder. Ten thousand Moors were killed that day. All the women and their children were taken as slaves. The Romans took them, along with the camels and all the young [?], and entered Carthage celebrating the victory festival. The barbarians gathered again in full force, with their wives and children, leaving no one behind. They marched against the Romans and plundered the countryside of Byzacium. Solomon quickly set out with the whole army against them. When he reached Burgaon, where the enemy had encamped, he drew up the army for battle. The barbarians [?] stayed for a long time on the mountain of Burgaon and refused to come down to the plain. During the night Solomon sent Theodore with a thousand infantry and some of the standard-bearers. They were to climb the mountain behind the enemy in the dark, raise the standards on the heights at sunrise, and attack the enemy. He himself likewise went up at first light and attacked the enemy at the same moment. When the barbarians saw that they were caught between the Romans, they broke and fled, hurling themselves down the cliffs and dying. Sixty thousand Moors died in that battle. Of the Romans not a single man died, and none was even wounded: all of them won the victory unharmed. Most of the Moorish leaders went over to the Romans. The Romans took so many women and children that they sold a Moorish boy for the price of a sheep to anyone who wanted to buy. Then the old oracle of a woman [?] came true for the Moors, which said that their host would be destroyed by a beardless man. For Solomon had been a eunuch since childhood, having lost his genitals through some mishap [?]. He took all the booty and returned to Carthage. At this time a portent appeared in the sky. For the whole year the sun gave its light without rays, like the moon. For the most part it looked like the sun in eclipse, not shining clearly as it usually does. It was the

tenth year of Justinian's reign. At this time neither war nor pestilence ceased to afflict mankind. At the beginning of spring Justinian sent Belisarius to make Sicily tributary to the Romans. While he was wintering in Sicily and the feast of Easter arrived, the Romans in Libya mutinied against Solomon, in the following way. They had taken the wives of the Vandals who had been killed and held their lands as their own, and they refused to pay the emperor the taxes due on them. Solomon urged them not to rise against the emperor, but to pay him what was due [?]. Some of them, especially among the Goths, had gone over to the Arian belief. The priests of the Church excommunicated them and would not even baptize their children. So the mutiny broke out at the feast, and the soldiers plotted to kill Solomon in the church. They went out of the city, plundered its countryside and treated the Libyans as enemies. When Solomon heard this he was thrown into great alarm, and he tried with persuasive speeches to bring the army to end the mutiny. But they gathered together and shamelessly insulted Solomon and the officers. They went into the palace and voted Theodore the Cappadocian their general. Then, under arms, they killed everyone they met who was known to Solomon, whether Libyan or Roman. They plundered money, and went into houses and seized everything of value. Solomon took refuge in the palace church and stayed hidden. When night fell he left the palace with Procopius the historian and Martin. They boarded a ship and reached Belisarius at Syracuse in Sicily. Solomon had written to Theodore to look after Carthage and the emperor's affairs. The soldiers gathered on the plain of Bulla and chose Stotzas, Martin's guardsman, as their usurper. He was a spirited and energetic man, and they meant to drive out the emperor's officers under his leadership and take control of Libya. Stotzas came near Carthage and sent word ordering Theodore to hand the city over to him at once, so that they could remain unharmed. But the Carthaginians and Theodore declared that they were keeping the city for the emperor. When Stotzas heard this he began to besiege the city. Belisarius picked out a hundred men from his guardsmen and shield-bearers, took Solomon with him, and sailed to Carthage in a single ship, arriving about the time the lamps are lit. When day came and the usurper and the soldiers learned that Belisarius

had come, they fled shamefully and in utter disorder. Belisarius roused about two thousand of the army, pursued the fugitives, and overtook them at the city of Membresa. He saw that they had broken ranks and were moving about in disorder, so he too advanced against them. They broke and fled, and gathered together again when they reached Numidia. Few died in this battle, and most of these were Vandals, for Belisarius spared the Romans. He plundered their camp and found much money, and also the women on whose account the war had begun. When he had done this, Belisarius rode back to Carthage. Then someone came from Sicily and reported that a mutiny had broken out in the camp there and was about to overturn everything unless he arrived quickly. Belisarius settled affairs in Libya as best he could, handed Carthage over to Ildiger and Theodore, and went to Sicily. When Justinian heard this, he sent his nephew Germanus, a patrician, to Libya with a few men, together with Domnicus and Symmachus, men of wisdom. When Germanus reached Carthage he took a count of the soldiers. He read through the clerks' registers in which the soldiers' names were entered, and found that a third of the army was in Carthage and the other cities on the emperor's side, while all the rest had joined the usurper. For this reason he did not go out to fight, but attended to the army. He announced that the emperor had sent him to defend the soldiers who had been wronged and to punish those who had begun to wrong them. When the soldiers heard this, they came over to him little by little. Germanus received them with great kindness. He gave them pledges, treated them with honour, and paid their wages. When word of this spread and reached everyone, they renounced the usurper and came to Carthage. Stotzas, realizing by now that things were going badly, encouraged those who were left and marched on Carthage. Germanus armed the army and advanced against him. The army with him showed great eagerness and convinced the general of their loyalty to the emperor. When Stotzas' men saw this, they were overcome by cowardice and withdrew to Numidia. Germanus followed not long afterward with the whole army. When he overtook them, he found that many tens of thousands of Moorish barbarians had joined them, led by Iaudas and Or-

taias. They joined battle, and in the heat of the fighting one of the enemy killed Germanus' horse. Germanus fell to the ground and was in danger, but his guardsmen quickly shielded him, brought him a horse and set him on it. Then the [rebel] soldiers were routed, and in the confusion Stotzas managed to escape with a few men. Germanus urged on those around him and charged straight at the enemy camp, and he took it by force. There the soldiers plundered the money without any restraint and paid no heed to their general. Germanus was afraid that the enemy might join forces and attack him, so he stood there lamenting and calling on his men to keep good order. When the Moors saw the rout, they turned on the mutineers and pursued them along with the emperor's army. Stotzas had put his trust in the Moors. When he saw what they had done, he fled with a hundred men and went into inner Mauretania, and so the mutiny came to an end. The emperor recalled Germanus to Byzantium with Domnicus and Symmachus, and again entrusted the affairs of Libya to Solomon (this was the thirteenth year of Justinian's reign). He gave him other officers as well, among them Rufinus, Leontius and John son of Sisinnius. Solomon sailed to Carthage. He governed the people with moderation and kept Libya secure. He put the army in order, and if he found anyone in it under suspicion, he sent him away to Byzantium. Belisarius took Sicily, and Rome, which Vitiges held, and the cities around it. He brought Vitiges to Justinian at Byzantium, with his wife and children. The emperor sent Narses the chamberlain to Rome with a fleet to keep control of affairs there. Solomon, having governed Carthage and Libya well, marched against the Moors. First he sent his guardsman Gontharis, a man brave in war, with an army. Gontharis reached the river Abigas and encamped at Bagai, a deserted city. A battle was fought there. He was defeated and withdrew into his entrenchment, where the Moors blockaded him and pressed him hard. When Solomon drew near and learned this, he quickly

[?] The barbarians took fright and withdrew, and made camp at the foot of Mount Aurasius. Solomon engaged them and put them to flight. The Moors fled into the rough ground of the mountain and went off to the Mauretanians. Solomon plundered the plains in Mougade [?], burned all their land, carried off a great deal of grain, and returned to the fortress of Zerboule. Iaudas had taken refuge there with twenty thousand Moors. But Iaudas abandoned the fortress, climbed high up Mount Aurasius and stayed quiet there. Solomon besieged the fortress of Zerboule for three days, plundered everything in it, set a garrison there, and pressed on. He looked about for a way to reach the summit of the mountain, which was sheer and very hard to get through. But God made a way where there was none, in this manner. One of the optiones of the infantry, named Gentzon, whether driven by his own spirit or moved by something divine, went up against the enemy alone. Some of his fellow soldiers followed behind him, utterly astonished at what was happening. Three of the Moors who had been posted to guard the entrance saw the man and ran to meet him, thinking he was coming up against them. Because the place was so narrow they came at him one at a time, and he killed the first, and likewise the second along with the third. When those coming behind him saw this, they advanced on the enemy with a great uproar and commotion. When the Roman army heard and saw what had happened, they did not wait for the general or the trumpets or keep their ranks, but with a great din, urging one another on, they ran at the enemy camp. There Rufinus and Leontius performed deeds of valour worthy of note against the enemy. At once the barbarians fled wherever each of them could. Iaudas was wounded in the thigh by a javelin but escaped, and withdrew to Mauretania. The Romans sacked the enemy camp and no longer abandoned Mount Aurasius, but built forts and hold it under guard. There was a rock, extremely sheer, on which the Moors had built a tower and made it a strong refuge, secure and wholly impregnable. Here Iaudas happened to have stored his wealth and his women, and had appointed a single guard,

an old man, over the treasure. For he never suspected that the enemy would reach this tower, or be able to take it by force. But the Romans, searching through the rough ground of Aurasius, came there, and one of them, laughing, tried to climb up to the tower. The women jeered at him, together with the old man. But when the Roman, climbing with hands and feet, had got close, he drew his sword, leapt up, struck the old man on the neck and cut off his head. The soldiers, now emboldened and holding on to one another, climbed up to the tower, took the women and the treasure, which was great, and brought them to Solomon. Solomon threw walls around the cities in Libya. And since the Moors had withdrawn from Numidia in defeat, he made the region of Zabe, Mauretania and its metropolis Sitifis tributary to the Romans. For of the other Mauretania, Caesarea is the chief metropolis, and Belisarius had subdued it earlier. In this way all the Libyans became subjects of the Romans and enjoyed a secure peace. After four years of this peace, in the seventeenth year of Justinian, Cyrus and Sergius, the sons of Bacchus, Solomon's brother, were sent by the emperor to govern in Libya: Cyrus the Pentapolis and Sergius Tripolis. The Moors sent their elders to Sergius at the city of Leptis Magna, to bring him gifts and confirm the peace. Sergius, persuaded by Pudentius, a man of Tripolis, received the eighty most distinguished of the barbarians into the city, promising to do everything they asked, and confirmed the peace with oaths; but he drove the rest outside into the suburb. Then he invited them all to a meal and killed them. One of them escaped in secret and reported what had happened to his countrymen. When they heard it, they ran to their own camp, set out with all the others, and went against the Romans. Sergius, with Pudentius, met them, and when battle was joined Pudentius died after killing many, while Sergius, overcome with unspeakable fear, sailed to Carthage to his uncle Solomon. The Moors [?] abandoned all of Tripolis, and the barbarians plundered all the country there, enslaved a multitude of Romans, and went against the Pentapolis. [?]

When Cyrus learned of this, he fled and sailed down to Carthage. With no one opposing them, the barbarians took the city of Berenice and marched on Carthage; reaching Byzacium, they plundered most of the country there in raids. Antalas, who was hostile to Solomon because he had killed his brother, joined the barbarians and guided them against Carthage and Solomon. When Solomon heard this, he took the army and set out against them. Coming to the city of Theveste, six days' journey from Carthage, he made camp there. With him were Cyrus and Sergius and Solomon the younger, the sons of Bacchus. Seeing the multitude of the barbarians and [?], he sent to their leaders reproaching them that, though bound by treaty with the Romans, they had taken up arms against them, and saying that it was right to confirm the peace and secure it with oaths. The barbarians mocked what was said and replied: “Since Sergius swore on the Gospels and kept his oaths so well by killing the eighty, how are we to trust your oaths now?” When battle was joined the Romans were routed. Solomon's horse stumbled to its knees, and Solomon was killed, along with his bodyguards. Sergius, his nephew, was entrusted by the emperor with the government of Libya. But John son of Sisinniolus and the other commanders conceived such great hatred for Sergius that they would not even take up arms against the enemy. And the barbarians plundered everything without fear. Antalas wrote to the emperor Justinian: “All the Moors choose to be your servants and friends, but they could not endure the violent rule of Solomon and his nephews, and so they rebelled. Remove these men, and peace between the Romans and the Moors will be established.” The emperor refused to do this. Antalas and the Moorish army gathered again in Byzacium, and with them was Stotzas, who had a few soldiers and Vandals. The Libyans begged John son of Sisinniolus to raise an army and advance against the enemy together with Himerius, the commander of the units in Byzacium. He took the army and went against the enemy, ordering Himerius to lead the way. When they engaged, the Romans were defeated, and the barbarians captured Himerius alive along with his force; they put him under guard and handed the soldiers over to Stotzas, who agreed to campaign against the Romans. Through Himerius they took the city of Hadrumetum by a trick. Some of the Libyans fled to Sicily, others to other islands and

to Byzantium. The Moors and Stotzas plundered all Libya with complete impunity. The Libyans who came to Byzantium begged the emperor to send an army and an excellent general to Libya. The emperor [sent] Areobindus with a few soldiers, a man of noble birth and good judgement but quite without experience of warfare, and with him Athanasius and a few Armenians, commanded by Artabanes and John, the Arsacids. Yet he did not recall Sergius either, but ordered him to be general of Libya together with Areobindus: Sergius to wage the war against the barbarians in Numidia, and Areobindus to fight the Moors in Byzacium. On reaching Libya, Areobindus took half the army and sent John son of Constantiolus against Stotzas and the barbarians. When John saw the masses of the enemy, he was forced to engage them. He was bitterly hostile to Stotzas, so much so that each prayed to become the other's killer and to die that way. When the battle began, both rode out from their armies against each other. John drew his bow and hit Stotzas in the right groin, and he died a few days later. But the barbarians, attacking their enemies with great fury and being a countless multitude, killed John and all the Romans. They say John said: “Sweet is the death I die, now that my prayer against Stotzas has been fulfilled.” And Stotzas, on learning of John's death, died rejoicing. John the Armenian also died. When the emperor heard this he was deeply grieved, and he removed Sergius from his command and recalled him, entrusting the government of Libya to Areobindus alone. Two months later a certain Gontharis, commander of the units in Numidia, plotting treachery against Areobindus, secretly informed the Moors that they should march on Carthage. At once an enemy army from Numidia and Byzacium gathered in one place and hurried on Carthage. Cutzinas and Iaudas led the Numidians, and Antalas the men of Byzacium. With them too was John the usurper, with the mutineers, in place of Stotzas. When Areobindus learned this, trusting Gontharis as a friend, he handed the army over to him and sent him against the enemy with Artabanes and the Armenians. But

Gontharis sent his own cook, who was a Moor, to the barbarians, to tell Antalas that Gontharis wished to take him as a partner in the rule of Libya. Antalas heard the proposal gladly, but answered that such matters could not safely be managed through a cook. On hearing this Gontharis sent his bodyguard Ulitheus, as a trustworthy man, to Antalas, urging him to come near Carthage so that he might do away with Areobindus himself. Ulitheus met Antalas secretly, and they agreed that Antalas should rule Byzacium and receive half of Areobindus' wealth, together with fifteen hundred Roman soldiers, while Gontharis should take the royal dignity and power over Carthage. Having arranged this, Ulitheus returned to Gontharis. The barbarians advanced on Carthage in great haste. They seized Decimum and camped there, and the next day moved on Carthage. [?] Some of the Roman army fell on them unexpectedly and killed many of the Moors; Gontharis reproached and mocked these men as reckless and as putting Roman affairs in danger. Areobindus sent to Cutzinas and urged him to betray the Moors, and he agreed to do so; for the Moorish race is faithless both to others and to everyone. Areobindus confided this to Gontharis. Gontharis advised Areobindus not to trust Cutzinas, and sent Ulitheus to report it to Antalas. Gontharis was secretly planning to kill Areobindus, and persuaded him to leave Carthage and be present at the battle. But Areobindus, inexperienced in war and unable to put on his armour, kept delaying. And so the day wore on, and he put off the engagement until the next day and did nothing. Gontharis, suspecting that he was delaying on purpose because he had got wind of what was afoot, rebelled against him openly. Areobindus quickly left Carthage in flight and boarded a ship, and would have sailed for Byzantium had not a storm arisen and prevented him. He sent Athanasius to Carthage and summoned certain men, among them Artabanes, who strongly urged Areobindus not to lose heart, nor to be cowardly and afraid of Gontharis, but to go himself together with all his followers before any further harm was done. Gontharis slandered Areobindus to the soldiers as unmanly and cowardly and unwilling to give them their pay. Areobindus, with Artabanes and his followers, went through [the city] against Gontharis.

Fighting broke out on the battlements and at the other gates. Most of the soldiers did not know what Gontharis had been plotting, and gathered and armed themselves against him. But Areobindus, seeing men being killed, unused as he was to such a sight, could not bear his fear and fled; he took refuge with his wife and sister in the monastery by the sea, which Solomon had built and walled about as a secure fort. Then Artabanes too took to flight. Gontharis, having won by force, seized the palace. He summoned the bishop of the city and Athanasius and ordered them to give pledges to Areobindus and bring him to the palace, threatening that if he disobeyed he would besiege him and would no longer give him pledges for his safety. Areobindus received the pledges from Bishop Reparatus and came into Gontharis' presence, and lay prostrate on the ground, holding out to him as a suppliant the Gospels on which the priest had given him the pledges. Gontharis raised him up, swearing to him before everyone that he would do him no harm, but that the next day he would be sent to Byzantium with his wife and his property. He dismissed the bishop and took Areobindus and Athanasius to dine with him in the palace. He honoured Areobindus and placed him first on the couch. After dinner he told him to sleep in a bedchamber. Then he sent Ulitheus with some others and killed him, wailing and shrieking. He spared Athanasius because of his age. The next day he sent his head to Antalas, but he kept the money and gave him nothing in accordance with the agreement. When Antalas learned what had been done to Areobindus and reckoned up Gontharis' perjuries, he wished to go over to the emperor Justinian. Artabanes, having received pledges from Gontharis, went up to the palace with the Armenians and agreed to serve the usurper. But secretly he was planning to kill him. He confided the plan to his nephew Gregory and to his bodyguard Artasires, and Gregory said to him: “Now, Artabanes, it lies with you alone to match the glory of Belisarius. He received an army and great sums of money from the emperor, and commanders to accompany him, and a fleet such as no one had ever heard of, and with great toil made Libya tributary to the Romans. But now that Libya has rebelled and returned to its old state as at the beginning, it rests with you alone to bring it back to the emperor and save the situation. Consider your lineage: that you are an Arsacid by descent, and that being nobly born you ought always to act bravely and show many deeds of valour. For while you were still young, re-

-member that you killed Acacius, the Armenian governor, and Sittas, the Roman general, in battle, and campaigned alongside Chosroes the king of the Persians. Being such a man, do not stand by while the dominion of the Romans is held by a drunken dog. Artasires and I will serve you in whatever you command, as far as we are able.” Gontharis ordered Artabanes to lead the army and advance against Antalas and the Moors in Byzacium. With him were John, the leader of the mutineers, and Ulitheus the bodyguard; the Moors commanded by Cutzinas also followed him. Engaging Antalas and the barbarians, he routed them. But Artabanes, deliberately playing the coward, suddenly turned his standard and rode back to the camp. Ulitheus intended to kill him in the camp. Artabanes, however, said that he was afraid “that the barbarians might come out of the city of Hadrumetum to help the enemy and do us irreparable harm; rather Gontharis should come with the whole army, and so capture them all.” And he returned to Carthage and reported this to the usurper. The usurper, after consulting Pasiphilus, decided to arm the whole army and campaign with it himself, leaving only guards in the city. Every day Gontharis was putting many to death on suspicion. He went out of Carthage to a suburb where there were three couches from of old, on which he reclined with Artabanes and Athanasius and Peter, Solomon's bodyguard. Artabanes, thinking this a fitting moment for the murder of the usurper, confided the matter to Gregory and Artasires and some trusted bodyguards, and ordered the bodyguards to be inside with their swords; for it was the custom for bodyguards to stand behind commanders while they ate. He ordered them to set about the deed suddenly, when he himself gave them the moment by a nod, and told Artasires to begin the work first. He instructed Gregory to pick out many of the boldest Armenians and to be present at the palace, carrying only their swords, and to tell the plan to no one. As the drinking went on and Gontharis was soaked with wine, Artasires drew his sword and went at the usurper. One of the servants, seeing the naked sword, cried out, “What is this, my good man?” Gontharis turned his face and looked at him. Artasires struck him with the sword and cut off his right hand. As he leapt up, Artabanes drew a dagger and drove it into the usurper's side up to the hilt, and killed him on the spot. Then Artabanes

ordered Athanasius to take charge of the property in the palace, as he had in Areobindus' time. When the guards learned of Gontharis' death, they acclaimed Justinian as gloriously victorious emperor. Thereupon those loyal to the emperor burst into the houses of the mutineers and killed them. John fled with the Vandals into the church; Artabanes gave them pledges, brought them out, and sent them to Byzantium. The usurper's murder took place thirty-six days after the start of his usurpation, in the nineteenth year of Justinian. From this Artabanes won great fame among all men. Praejecta, Areobindus' wife, gave Artabanes great gifts. The emperor made him general of all Libya. Not long afterwards Artabanes asked to be released and came to the emperor at Byzantium, and the emperor appointed John, brother of Pappus, general of Libya. On reaching Libya, John campaigned against Antalas and the Moors in Byzacium, fought them and won a victory, killed many of the enemy, and recovered from them the standards the barbarians had taken from Solomon, which he sent to the emperor at Byzantium. The rest of the barbarians he drove out of Roman territory. Some time later the Leuathae came with a great army from the region around Tripolis into Byzacium and joined Antalas. John met them and was defeated, and after losing many men returned to Carthage. The barbarians came down as far as Carthage and plundered its countryside. Later John roused the soldiers' spirits, took Moors and others as allies, including those with Cutzinas, fought the enemy and routed them, and in a great pursuit killed a vast multitude. The rest fled to the furthest parts of Libya, and so affairs in Libya enjoyed a deep peace. Year of the World 6027 [?]. First year of John, bishop of Jerusalem. In this year Zamanarsus, the king of the Iberians, came to Constantinople to the most pious emperor Justinian with his wife and his nobles, asking him that he might be an ally of the Romans and a true friend. The emperor [welcomed] such a resolve
…having received him, he honoured him and his senators lavishly, and the Augusta likewise presented his wife with all kinds of pearl ornaments. And he sent them away in peace to their own [?]

In this year Pompeiopolis in Mysia suffered divine wrath. The earth was split open by the earthquake, and half the city was swallowed up together with its inhabitants. They were under the earth, and their voices could be heard crying out for mercy. The emperor did a great deal to have them dug out and rescued, and he rewarded those who searched for them generously. In the same year Justinian ordained that the hymn "Only-begotten Son and Word of God" be sung in the churches. He also built the clock of the Milion. AM 6029. — Bishop of Constantinople Anthimus, year 1. In this year, after Bishop Epiphanius died on 5 June in the fifteenth indiction, having been bishop for sixteen years and three months, Anthimus, the heretical bishop of Trebizond, was transferred to Constantinople. At that time Agapetus, bishop of Rome, came up to Constantinople and convened a synod against the impious Severus, Julian of Halicarnassus and the rest of the [?schismatics]. Among them Anthimus, bishop of Constantinople, was deposed as one who shared their views, and was expelled after being bishop for ten months. In his place Menas, a presbyter and warden of the hospice of Samson, was ordained by Agapetus, pope of Rome. And Agapetus [?] of Rome [?] in Byzantium

It is sung: "Only-begotten Son and Word of God, who are immortal, and who for our salvation deigned to become flesh of the holy Theotokos and ever-virgin Mary, and without change became man; who were crucified, [Christ our God,] trampling down death by death; who are one of the holy Trinity, glorified together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always, and unto
…fell asleep, and Silverius was ordained in his place, and lived one year. AM 6030. — Bishop of Rome Silverius

Of Constantinople, Menas, year 1. Of Alexandria, Gaianas, year 1. In this year, on 27 December in the first indiction, the first dedication of the Great Church took place. The procession set out from Saint Anastasia, with Menas the patriarch seated in the imperial carriage and the emperor walking in the procession with the people. From the day the most holy Great Church burned down to its dedication, then, there were five years, eleven months and ten days. AM 60[?]. — Bishop of Rome Vigilius, year 1. Of Alexandria, Theodosius, year 1. In this year the Bulgars set out, two kings with a multitude of Bulgars and a war band, against [?Scythia] and Moesia. Justin was general of Moesia at the time, and Baduarius of Scythia. These went out against the Bulgars and joined battle, and Justin the general was killed in the fighting. Constantine, son of Florentius, was appointed in his place. The Bulgars came as far as the regions of Thrace. Then Acum the Hun, general of Illyricum, whom the emperor had sponsored at his baptism, went out against them. They caught the Bulgars in the middle and cut them down, killing great numbers. They recovered all the plunder and won an overwhelming victory, killing their two kings as well. But as they were returning in triumph, other Bulgars met them and lassoed them as they fled: Constantine, Acum and Godilas. Godilas cut the lasso with his dagger and rode off, but Constantine and Acum were taken alive. The Bulgars released Constantine for a ransom of a thousand nomismata, and he came to Constantinople. Acum, however, they kept in their own country along with other captives. In the same year Chosroes, king of the Persians, took Antioch of Syria, the [?]

AM [?]. — In this year Mundus came over to the Romans. He was of the race of the Gepids, the son of Giesmus. After his father's death he went to Rhegas, his uncle on his mother's side, who was king of Sirmium. When Theoderic, king of Rome, learned of this, he sent for him, and Mundus was persuaded to go to him and stayed with him as his ally. After Theoderic's death he came to the Danube river and asked Emperor Justinian to let him be a subject of his empire. He came to Constantinople, and the emperor honoured him and his son lavishly and sent them away, having made him general of Illyricum. When he arrived in Illyricum, the Bulgars came out in great numbers, and he attacked them and destroyed them all. He sent some of their leaders from among the captives to Constantinople, together with many others, and they were paraded in the Hippodrome. There was deep peace in Thrace, because the Huns no longer dared to cross the Danube. The emperor sent the Bulgar captives to Armenia and Lazica, and they were enrolled in the regiments. AM 6055. — Bishop of Alexandria Paul, year 1. In this year, the fourteenth of Justinian, Chosroes, king of the Persians, made his fourth invasion of Roman territory. When he reached the country of the Commageni, he planned to march against Palestine and Jerusalem in order to plunder the treasures in Jerusalem, for he had heard that this was a good land with inhabitants rich in gold. The Romans had no intention of facing them in any way. Each of them occupied the strongholds as best he could, intending to guard them and save himself. When Justinian learned this, he sent Belisarius, who had just come back from the

West, to [?] again. Riding the horses of the public post, Belisarius reached Euphratesia with great speed. Justus, the emperor's [?nephew], had taken refuge in Hierapolis together with Bouzes, general of the East. When they heard that Belisarius had come, they wrote asking him to join them and guard Hierapolis. Belisarius rebuked them sharply, writing back that it was not right to guard a single city and leave the enemy free to march through Roman territory unopposed and ravage the cities of the empire. "For know well that to die with valour is better than to be saved without a fight. That would not be called safety, but rightly betrayal. Come instead with all speed to the place called Europus, where I will gather the whole army and, God willing, I hope to deal with the enemy." Hearing this, the commanders took heart. They left Justus with a few men to guard Hierapolis, and the rest went to Europus. When Chosroes learned that Belisarius and the whole Roman army were encamped at Europus, he was alarmed and decided to advance no further. He sent Abandanes, his secretary, a shrewd man, to Belisarius to spy out the general and the camp. The pretext was that he had come to complain that Emperor Justinian had not sent the envoys to Persia to settle the peace. When Belisarius learned that he was coming as an envoy, he himself picked out six thousand men, tall and handsome, and went out some distance from the camp as though to hunt. He ordered Diogenes, his bodyguard, and Adolius, an Armenian, to cross the river with a thousand horsemen, as though to test the crossing. When Belisarius knew that the envoy was close, he pitched his pavilion in a deserted place, to show that he had come there with no preparations at all. He arranged the soldiers so that on either side of the tent were Thracians and Illyrians, Goths and Heruli, and after them Vandals and Moors, spread over most of the plain. They did not stand in one place, but moved about in circles as if hunting, and seemed to pay the envoy of Chosroes only passing attention. They walked about with their tunics girded up and cheerful faces, carrying axes and spears. Chosroes, he said, because Justinian had not sent envoys to him about the peace as he had agreed, and had thus forced Chosroes to march against the Romans. Belisarius dismissed these words as nothing, saying that Chosroes was the cause of the war. If he wanted peace, he would not have come into Roman territory to seek it, but would have stayed in his own country and waited for the envoys. With these words he sent the envoy away. When the envoy reached Chosroes, he said that he had seen a general, Belisarius, exceedingly shrewd and brave, and soldiers whose like he had never seen: "I marvelled at their discipline," though they were drawn from many different nations. He advised Chosroes not to engage them in battle, for if he were defeated, the whole Persian kingdom might fall with him, since he was in Roman territory and had nowhere to flee. And to defeat Belisarius would be no great thing, for he would have beaten merely a Roman general. On this advice Chosroes at once resolved to return home. But he was afraid to cross the river, since the Romans held the crossing. With this in mind, he sent to Belisarius asking him to recall the men who had crossed the river and to grant him passage unhindered. Belisarius immediately sent envoys to him, commended him for withdrawing, and assured him that envoys from the emperor would come shortly to arrange the peace. Chosroes asked Belisarius to let him pass through Roman territory without danger, and Belisarius sent John of Edessa, a most distinguished man, to Chosroes as a hostage, so that he could pass through Roman territory safely. The Romans acclaimed Belisarius, for he had won greater renown by this deed than when he brought Gelimer as a captive, and Vitiges, the two kings, to Byzantium. It was truly worthy of report and praise: while the Romans were terrified and all hiding in their strongholds, and Chosroes with a great army was in the heart of the Roman empire, a single man came at full speed from Byzantium, encamped facing the king of the Persians, and Chosroes, unexpectedly outwitted by his wisdom, went back to his own country having achieved nothing. In the same year, when Timothy, bishop of Alexan-

dria, died, the impious Severus, the adulterous prelate of Antioch, and Julian of Halicarnassus, who had fled to Alexandria, fell out with each other over the corruptible and the incorruptible, as men estranged from the truth. One party put forward Theodosius as bishop of Alexandria, the other Gaianas. Gaianas held the see for a year, and Theodosius for two. Justinian had them brought to Byzantium and ordered them to live apart from each other. He appointed a certain Paul, who was thought to be orthodox, as bishop of Alexandria. But Paul commemorated the unholy Severus and was expelled from the see by the emperor's anger, and went and lived in Jerusalem. AM 6054. — In this year, in October of the fifth indiction, the great plague broke out in Byzantium. At the same time the feast of the Presentation of the Lord began to be celebrated in Byzantium on the second of February. And on 16 August of the same fifth indiction there was a great earthquake in Constantinople. Churches and houses collapsed, and the wall as well, especially near the Golden Gate. The spear held by the statue standing in the Forum of Saint Constantine also fell, and the right hand of the statue at the Xerolophos. Many died, and there was great fear. AM 6055. — Bishop of Alexandria Zoilus, year 1. In this year it came about that the king of the Axumites made war on the [?Indian] Jews, for the following reason.

The king of the Axumites [?] lies [?beyond] Egypt [?] and is a Judaizer. Roman merchants travel through the land of the Homerite to the Axumite and to the inner parts of India and Ethiopia. When the merchants entered the borders of the Homerite as usual, Damianus, the king [?], killed them and seized all their goods, saying that the Romans were mistreating the Jews in their country and killing them. As a result, trade between the inner Indians and the Axumite came to a stop. Adad, king of the Axumites, was indignant and sent word to the Homerite: "You have harmed my kingdom and inner India by preventing the Roman merchants from coming to us." They fell into great enmity and went to war with each other. As they were about to fight, Adad, king of the Axumites, made a vow, saying, "If I defeat the Homerite, I will become a Christian, for I am fighting on behalf of the Christians." By the working of God he won an overwhelming victory and took Damianus, their king, alive as a captive, along with their country and his palace. Then Adad, king of the Axumites, gave thanks to God and sent to Emperor Justinian to receive a bishop and clergy and to be taught how to become a Christian. Justinian was overjoyed at this and ordered that they be given whatever bishop they wanted. After careful enquiry, the envoys themselves chose a warden of the church of Saint John in Alexandria the Great, a pious man and a virgin, named John, sixty-two years old. They took him and went back to their own country, to Adad their king. And so they believed in Christ and were baptized, [?all] of them. AM 6038. — In this year, on 6 September, the first day of the seventh indiction, there was a great earthquake throughout the whole world, so that half of Cyzicus collapsed. In the same year the great bronze column near the palace, called the [?Augusteum], was completed, and the equestrian statue of Emperor Justinian was raised onto it. In the same year a wandering showman from the land of Italy, named Andrew, had with him a tawny, blind dog that performed tricks at his command. He would stand in the marketplace with a crowd standing around, and without the dog seeing, he would take the bystanders' rings,

gold, silver and iron, and lay them on the ground, covering them with earth. Then he would give the dog the order, and it would pick them up and give each person his own. In the same way it would hand back by name coins of various emperors mixed together. Moreover, with a crowd of men and women standing by, it would point out, when asked, the women who were pregnant, the fornicators, the adulterers, the misers and the generous, and it showed everything truly. So people said that it had a spirit of Python. AM 6057. — In this year the sea rose up against Thrace for four miles and covered it in the regions of Odessus, Dionysopolis and Aphrodisium, and many were drowned in the waters. Then by the command of God the same sea was returned to its own place. AM 6058. — Bishop of Jerusalem Peter, year 1. Bishop of Antioch Domnus, year 1. In this year there was a shortage of grain and wine and a very harsh winter. There was a great earthquake in Byzantium, and confusion over holy Easter.
The people kept Meatfare on 4 February, but the emperor ordered that meat be sold for another week. And all the butchers

…the state, and to secure the right ordering of spiritual things by means of bodily ones. Among other things, the ancients had been commanded to consecrate to God the tithes of their possessions. What they carried out in figure, we receive in a mystery. Accordingly the divine [?] of the apostles, knowing that [Christ came] not to destroy but to fulfil, and recognizing that something was lacking here, [?] … decreed that we should consecrate to God the tithes of the days of our life in each yearly cycle, so that by our zeal in these days and by more fervent repentance we might, with God's help, be able to heal the [?faults] of the soul committed through the whole year. We say that these days of fasting are the tenth of the year. Their seven weeks, leaving out the Saturdays and Sundays, make thirty-five days. Adding Great Saturday and half of the bright and radiant night, they come to thirty-six and a half days, exactly a tenth of the 365 days of the year. For the tenth of three hundred is thirty, of sixty six, and of five

…slaughtered and sold, but no one bought or ate. Easter was kept as the emperor had ordered, and the people found that they had fasted an extra week. AM 6059. — In this year Rome was taken by the Goths. Pope Vigilius came to Constantinople and was received by the emperor with great honour. He promised to bring about the union of the Catholic Church and to anathematize the Three Chapters. He was so honoured by the emperor that he grew arrogant and imposed on Menas of Constantinople four months of excommunication as a penance. Menas in turn imposed the same penance on him. The emperor, angered with Vigilius, [ordered] him to be arrested. Fearing the emperor's anger, Vigilius took refuge at the altar of Saint Sergius the martyr in the [?quarter] of Hormisdas. As he was being dragged from there,

Serges and Balichas. Another, [?Apollo] … when [?] the oracle [?] of the steps, when he carried out the slaughter in the Hippodrome. It was called the Harbour of Julian because the [?] who [?built] it was so called. [?]
