And at the urging of Theodora the Augusta, Vigilius received Menas, patriarch of Constantinople, on 24 June, at the Holy Apostles. In the same year, on 11 May, the Saturday of holy Pentecost, during the races held for the emperor's birthday, a fight broke out between the two factions. The emperor sent the excubitors and soldiers with drawn swords, and they killed many of them, and many were drowned as they fled. Others were slaughtered, and there was carnage [?]. AM 6040. — In this year there were continual earthquakes and heavy rains, and likewise in February a great earthquake, so that everyone despaired, was in great fear, went in procession and prayed to God to be delivered from the threats hanging over them. In the same year, in June of the eleventh indiction, the empress Theodora fell asleep, [?]

AM 60[?]. — In this year there was extremely terrifying thunder and lightning, so that many people were struck by the lightning in their sleep. On the day of Saint John there was very terrifying thunder and lightning, so that part of the plating of the column at the Xerolophos was stripped off, along with the carved head of the same column. In July there was a clash between the two factions, and the [?street] called that of Pardus was set on fire. Much was burned, from the Chalke as far as the place called Eleusia [?], and there were many murders. When a procession took place at the Hebdomon, the keepers of the wardrobe lost the emperor's crown, which was found eight months later. Every pearl and all the rest of its ornamentation was found intact.

THEOPHANES. [?]…linarius, year 1. In this year, in the month of October, while a horse race was being held, an ambassador of the Indians came to Constantinople bringing an elephant, and he entered the Hippodrome. In the month of January the name of Menas, patriarch of Constantinople, was moved down, and the name of Vigilius was read out first, placed ahead of it in the diptychs. In the month of March the elephant broke out of its stable at night; it struck many people and killed others. On 16 April, in the afternoon while a horse race was being held, the factions clashed with one another, and many died on both sides. They broke into workshops and plundered whatever they found. At that time John, surnamed [?], was prefect. On 28 July, a Tuesday, the dedication of the Holy Apostles took place, together with the deposition of the holy relics of Andrew, Luke and Timothy, the holy apostles. Bishop Menas went in procession with the holy relics. He sat in a golden imperial carriage set with jewels and held the three caskets of the holy apostles on his knees, and in this way he performed the

Year of the World 6045. In this year, in the month of April of the fourth [?] indiction, Narses the cubicularius was sent to Rome to make war on the Goths who had taken Rome. After Belisarius had taken it, they had risen up again, and the Goths had seized it. On 9 July there was a great and terrible earthquake throughout the whole land of Palestine, Arabia, Mesopotamia, Syria and Phoenicia. Tyre, Sidon, Berytus, Tripolis and Byblos suffered, and great multitudes of people died in them. At the city of Botrys a large part broke away from the mountain beside the sea, the one called Lithoprosopon. It was carried into the sea and formed a harbour, so that many very large ships could anchor in it. Before this the city had had no harbour. The emperor sent money to rebuild what had fallen in these cities. The sea also withdrew one mile out into the deep, and many ships were lost, and then by God's command it returned to its own bed. Year of the World 6046. In this year, in the month of September of the fifteenth indiction, the dedication of Saint Irene across the water in Sykai took place. The holy

relics went out from the Great Church with the two patriarchs, Menas of Constantinople and Apollinarius of Alexandria. Both sat in the imperial carriage holding the holy relics on their knees. They came to the ferry and crossed over, and the emperor met them. They opened this church of the holy martyr Irene. In the same year the harbour of the Hebdomon was dredged. At the same time Menas, bishop of Constantinople, died. In his place came Eutychius, the apocrisiarius of Amaseia, a monk of the monastery at Amaseia, who was made a presbyter on the same day, while the body of Menas still lay in state in the sanctuary. In the month of August news of victory came from Rome from Narses, the cubicularius and exarch of the Romans. He had joined battle with Totila, king of the Goths, and conquered him decisively. He took Rome and slew Totila, and he sent Totila's bloodstained garments with his jewelled cap to Constantinople, where they were thrown at the emperor's feet in the secretum. The year of Anthimus must also be assigned to the patriarch Menas, so that the sixteen years add up. Year of the World [?]. Eutychius, bishop of Constantinople, year 1. In this year the holy and ecumenical Fifth Council took place, against Origen the madman, Didymus the blind and Evagrius, and their pagan-minded drivel, and again against the [?] chapters. Vigilius of Rome did not sit with those who had assembled. He was set free after many people had interceded with the emperor, and he died in Illyricum on his way back to Rome.

[?] they killed the governor of that city in the Praetorium and plundered his property. His wife went up to the City and approached the emperor. He ordered Amantius the general to go down to Palestine and investigate the murder of Stephen. When Amantius found the culprits, he hanged some, beheaded others and mutilated others, and

in the eastern parts. In the month of December there was a mortality among people in various cities, especially among children. In the month of May, too, there was a shortage of bread in Byzantium. The people were in distress and cried out to the emperor, "Master, plenty for the city!" They also abused [?] the prefect at the birthday games, while ambassadors of the Persians were present in the Hippodrome. The emperor was angered and ordered Musonius the prefect to arrest those who had done this and punish them. It grieved the emperor that the factions had shouted against him in front of the Persian ambassador. There was abundance of wine, lard and every other kind of food, but a shortage of wheat and barley. On 13 July, a Thursday, there was lightning and frightful thunder, so that [?] were harmed, and heavy rain, so that after a long drought the earth was [?] saturated. Year of the World 6049. Pelagius, bishop of Rome,

In this year, in the month of December [?], on the commemoration of the Dust, Timothy, exarch of the monasteries and abbot of the monastery of Dalmatus, died. Anthimus, a recluse of the same monastery, succeeded him. A fire appeared in the sky in the shape of a spear, stretching from north to west. On 2 April [?] there was a frightful earthquake and [?]. Year of the World 6050. In this year, on [?] October, a Friday, in the sixth indiction, a great earthquake occurred [?] of the Sabbath. On 14 December there was another, very terrible earthquake, so that both walls of Constantinople fell, the Constantinian wall and the one built by Theodosius. At the Exaireton churches collapsed [?], as did those beyond the Hebdomon: Saint Samuel, the Holy Theotokos of Petala and Saint Vincent's. Many altars of churches and ciboria also fell [?].

The same thing happened in other cities as well. No one on earth in that generation remembered so great and terrible an earthquake. The earth went on shaking day and night [?] for ten days. For a short while people were contrite and held litanies, but once God had shown them mercy they turned to worse ways again. The emperor did not wear his crown for forty days. Even on the holy Nativity of Christ he went in procession to the church without it, and the customary banquets in the Nineteen Couches were stopped and their cost was given to the poor. At the same time a strange nation came to Byzantium, the people called Avars. The whole city ran together to look at them, since no one had ever seen such a nation. They wore their hair very long at the back, tied with ribbons and
[Of the temple of Saint Sophia?]: He made the ciborium and its columns of silver, and gilded them, and also the orb, the lilies and the cross of the ciborium.

braided. In the rest of their appearance they were like the other Huns. They had fled from their own country and come to the regions of Scythia and Moesia, and they sent envoys to Justinian asking to be received. In the month of February there was a mortality from the bubonic plague, especially among the young, so that the living were not enough to bury the dead. The mortality [?] lasted from February to July. Year of the World 6051. In this year, on 6 May, a Tuesday, at the fifth hour, the dome of the Great Church was being repaired, for it had been cracked by the earthquakes. While the Isaurians were at work, the eastern part of the apse [?] over the holy sanctuary fell and crushed the ciborium, the holy table and the ambo. The engineers were blamed: [?] to avoid the expense they had not built the centering, and they had cut into the piers that carry the dome, and for this reason it did not hold. Then the most pious emperor, seeing what had happened, raised other piers, which received the dome. So it was rebuilt, raised in height more than twenty feet above the original structure. In the same year Huns and Sclavenes rose against Thrace in great multitudes. They made war on it and killed and took captive many people. They also captured Sergius the general, son of Bacchus the priest, and Edermas the general [?] of Calopodius, the most glorious cubicularius and praepositus. Finding some places in the Anastasian Wall that had fallen in the earthquakes, they got in and took captives as far as Drypia, Nymphai and Chitukomi [?]. Everyone fled into the City with their belongings.

[?] When the emperor learned of this, he enrolled many citizens, and they sent them to the Long Wall. They joined battle there, and many of the Romans and scholarians died. Then the emperor gave orders, and the silver ciboria and silver altar tables were brought in from outside the City. The scholae, the protectors, the numeri and the senate guarded all the gates of the Theodosian Wall. When the emperor saw that the barbarians were staying, he ordered Belisarius the patrician to go out against them with others of the senate. Belisarius took every horse there was: the imperial horses, those of the Hippodrome, those of the charitable houses, and those of anyone who owned one. He armed the people and went out to Chitukomi [?]. There he made a fortified camp and began to capture some of the barbarians and kill them. He ordered trees to be cut down and dragged behind his army. The wind raised a great dust and carried it over the barbarians, who thought that the Romans were a great multitude and fled. They came to the area of Saint Stratonicus at the Dekaton. When they learned from their spies that the walls of Constantinople were guarded, they moved to the region of Tzurulon, Arcadiopolis and Saint Alexander of Zoupara [?], and stayed encamped there until holy Easter. After the feast of Easter the emperor went out, and [?] of the City with him, to Selymbria, to rebuild the Long Wall where the barbarians had got in. The emperor stayed there until the month of August, and likewise the barbarians roamed about outside the City until August. Then the emperor ordered double-prowed ships to be built, so as to go to the Danube and meet the barbarians as they crossed [?]. When the barbarians learned of this, they sent an envoy begging to be allowed to cross the Danube unharmed. The emperor sent Justin, his nephew and curopalates, and he brought them safely

In this year the emperor began to build the bridge over the river Sangarius. He diverted the river into another bed and built five mighty arches, and made it passable; before this the bridge had been of wood. Year of the World 6053. In this year, on 9 September, a Friday, in the ninth indiction, a rumour went round Constantinople that the emperor had died. He had come back from Thrace and was seeing no one. Then the factions suddenly seized the loaves from the bakeries and the public bakehouses, and by about the third hour no bread could be found anywhere in the City. There was also heavy rain that same day [?]. The workshops shut too, and word spread from the palace [?] that no one from the senate had seen the emperor, because he had a headache. From this people believed he had died. About the ninth hour the senate held a council and sent the prefect, who had lamps lit throughout the City as a sign that the emperor was well. In this way the City was calmed after the turmoil. After the emperor had recovered, Eugenius the ex-consul accused George, curator of the house of Marina, and Aetherius, curator of the house of Antiochus, of wanting to make Theodore, son of Peter the magister, emperor. Gerontius, the prefect of the City, was said to have agreed with them. The charge was investigated and not proved. The emperor was angered at Eugenius, and his house was confiscated, but he took refuge in the church and was saved. In the month of December there was a great fire at the harbour of Julian. Many houses and churches burned, from the beginning of the harbour as far as the house of Probus. A great [?] also struck Cilicia and Anazarbus, and there were earthquakes at Antioch the Great as well. The Orthodox and the Severans clashed with each other there, and many murders were committed. The emperor sent Zemarchus, count of the East, who [?] the rioters; he exiled many, confiscated their property and mutilated them. Year of the World [?]. In this year, in the month of October,

on the 12th, a Wednesday, in the tenth indiction, late in the evening a great fire broke out in the quarter of Caesarius and spread as far as the place called Omphakera. All the workshops and the porticoes as far as the Bous burned down. In the month of November, while a horse race was being held and before the emperor had come up, a riot broke out among the factions. The Greens attacked the Blues. The emperor learned of it and went up to the kathisma. When he saw the fighting, he ordered Marianus, count of the excubitors, together with the curator of the house of Caesarius, to go down and separate the factions. They went, but could not separate them. Many died on both sides, and many were wounded. The Blues got into the [?] of the Greens and shouted, "Burn here, burn there! No Green to be seen!" The Greens in turn shouted, "Ai, ai, everyone, everyone to the Mese!" They came into the neighbourhoods of the Blues, stoned whomever they found and shouted, "Burn, burn here! No Blue to be seen!" They kept breaking into the neighbourhoods until Sunday dawned and plundered people's property. The emperor ordered the Greens to be arrested, and they were punished with many tortures. The Blues took refuge in the church of the Theotokos at Blachernae. The Greens who had escaped took refuge in the church of the holy [?] at Chalcedon, but the prefect dragged them out and punished them. Their wives and mothers began crying out to the emperor in the churches, begging him to grant the Greens an indulgence. They were driven off with sticks, and the emperor was not reconciled with them until the Nativity of Christ. In the month of February the emperor ordered those of the seven scholae who were stationed at Nicomedia, Kios, Prousa, Cyzicus, Cotyaeum and Dorylaeum to leave and settle in Thrace, at Heraclea and the cities around it. In the month of March the scholae rose against their count over certain customary payments that they used to receive and that he had cut off, and they attacked him. Theodore Kondocheres, son of Peter the magister, happened to be there, and by using threatening words he managed to calm them. In the same [?] Baesipolis [?] was taken by the Huns. The emperor sent Marcellus the general, his own nephew, with a large army to recover the city and Persia [?]. In the month of April

Anastasiopolis in Thrace was also taken by the Huns [?]. On 3 May Zemarchus, curator of the house of [?], was accused of having said many terrible things against the emperor. His accusers were George, curator of the house of Marina, and John the ex-consul, relatives of the empress Theodora. Year of the World 6055. In this year, in the month of October, there was a riot of the factions at the Pittakia, and the emperor punished many. In the month of November there was a severe drought and a lack of water, so that many fights broke out at the fountains. In the month of August, too, the north wind blew and there was no south wind anywhere, and the ships could not come into the City. The patriarch even led out litanies [?] to Jerusalem, that is, to Saint Diomedes. In the same year, in the month of [?], news of victory came from Rome from Narses the patrician, reporting that he had taken two strong cities of the Goths, Verona and Brixia. On the 25th of the same month, a Saturday, in the evening, some men plotted to kill the emperor as he sat in the palace. They were Ablabius, of the Melistai [?], Marcellus the silversmith and Sergius, nephew of the curator Aetherius. Their plan was to rush in and kill him as he sat in the triclinium in the evening before dinner. They had men of their own working with them, Indians hidden in the Silentiarikion, in the Archangel and in the Harma, who were to create a disturbance when the attack took place. Ablabius had received fifty pounds of gold from Marcellus the silversmith to take part. But by God's good pleasure Ablabius confided in Eusebius the ex-consul, count of the foederati, and in John the [?] of Domentziolus, saying, "This evening we mean to attack the emperor." Eusebius informed the emperor and arrested them, and found them [?]

of the month the emperor held a silentium. He brought the most holy patriarch Eutychius to it as well and ordered their depositions to be read out. When Belisarius heard them, he was greatly distressed, and he fell under the emperor's displeasure. The emperor sent men and took away all of Belisarius's retainers, and confined him under guard in his own house. On 24 December the second dedication of the Great Church took place. The night vigil for this dedication was held at Saint Plato. From there Eutychius, patriarch of Constantinople, came out with the litany, with the emperor also present. The patriarch sat in the carriage wearing the apostolic habit and holding the holy Gospel, while all the people chanted, "Lift up your gates, O rulers." In the same month some parts of Africa were seized by the Moors, who had risen up against Africa in the following way. A man named Kutzinas, of that nation, an exarch of the Moors, used to receive a fixed sum of gold from whoever was ruler of Africa at the time. When he came to receive it, John, the ruler of Africa, killed him. The children of Kutzinas rose up to avenge their father's

blood. They rose against Africa and seized some parts of it, plundering. When the emperor learned of this, he sent Marcian, his nephew and a general, with an army to help Africa and pacify the Moors. The Moors went over to him, and Africa was at peace. In the month of April Procopius, prefect of the City, was replaced, and Andrew the ex-logothete took his place. Andrew was leaving the palace of the Chalke, seated in his carriage, on his way to the praetorium, when the Greens met him at the Lausus. They began to insult him and throw stones at him, and a great disorder broke out in the Mese between the two factions. They broke into the prisons, and the fighting went on from the tenth hour until evening. The emperor sent Justin, his nephew and curopalates, who drove them off. Again about the twelfth hour they joined battle, and they were arrested. They were paraded for many days, and those who had fought with swords had their thumbs cut off. On 19 July Belisarius the patrician was received back into favour and recovered all his dignities. Peter the magister also returned [?] from Persia, having made a peace treaty for sixty years concerning Lazica and the regions of the East. In the same month envoys came from Askel, king of the Hermichiones, a nation that lives beyond the barbarians, near the Ocean. In the month of August there was a lack of water, so that the public baths were closed and killings took place at the fountains. Year of the World 6056. In this year, in the month of October, in the twelfth indiction, the emperor Justinian went to fulfil a vow at the Myriangeloi, that is, at Germ[ia]

This Belisarius, the great general, who served as a general in the times of Justinian, [won] victories over all four quarters of the earth [?]. Later, blinded through envy (O fickle fortune!), he held a wooden cup at the Milion and cried, "[Give an obol] to Belisarius the general, [whom fortune exalted, but] envy blinds" [?]. Other chroniclers say that he was not blinded, but that as a punishment he was utterly disgraced, and that he later had his former glory restored.

…[?], a city of Galatia. In the month of November Arethas, the patrician and phylarch of the Saracens, came to Byzantium. He needed to put before the emperor which of his sons should hold his phylarchy after his death, and also to report what Ambrus [?], the son of Alamundarus, was doing in his territories. In the month of December a great fire broke out. The hostel of Samson was completely burned, along with the buildings in front of the Rufus, the courtyard near the Great Church called the Garsonostasion, the two monasteries near Saint Irene together with its courtyard, and part of its narthex. A.M. 6057. — In this year, in the month of March, in the indiction…

In the same year the emperor Justinian stirred up a doctrine about the corruptible and the incorruptible and sent out everywhere an edict foreign to true piety. But God forestalled him, and he died on 11 November of the following, fourteenth, indiction, having reigned 38 years, 6 months and 13 days. His nephew Justin the curopalates became his successor. In the same year the Theodosians and the Gaianites in Alexandria began to build meeting-houses. The Gaianites, acting on their own authority, ordained their archdeacon Elpidius as their bishop, and the emperor ordered him to be brought to him in chains. On the way, near Sigris [?], he died. The Theodosians, for their part, secretly by night ordained Do-

rotheus as their bishop. Then the Gaianites and the Theodosians came together and enthroned and ordained a common bishop for themselves, a certain John, a monk. But the Gaianites, thinking that the abba [?] had acted deceitfully, flayed off his beard together with the skin and flesh. A.M. 6058. — Of the emperor of the Romans Justin,

of the bishop of Jerusalem, year 1. In this year, on 14 November, in the fourteenth indiction, Justin the nephew of Justinian became emperor. He was crowned by the patriarch John, formerly a scholasticus. He was a Thracian by birth, magnanimous, capable in every way, and fond of building. He had a wife named Sophia, whom he also crowned Augusta. Being pious, he adorned the churches built by Justinian, namely the Great Church, the Apostles, and other churches and monasteries, bestowing on them treasures and every kind of revenue. He was thoroughly orthodox. He sent the abba Photinus, stepson of Belisarius the patrician, and gave him authority over every person and matter to bring peace to all the churches of Egypt and Alexandria. A.M. 6059. — In this year Aetherius and Addaeus, together with a physician, plotted against the emperor Justin. They were discovered and died by the sword. The emperor held a consulship and scattered so much money that many were made rich.

In the same year the abba Agathon, brother of Apollinarius the bishop of Alexandria, came to Alexandria and demanded accounts. He put under guard Eustochius, who was then a monk and steward of Alexandria, because of his stewardship. Eustochius escaped through the roof and came to Byzantium, at the time when Macarius had been driven from his church by a plot, and Eustochius was ordained bishop of Jerusalem in place of Macarius. A.M. 6060. — Of Eustochius bishop of Jerusalem, year 1. In this year the most pious Augusta Sophia summoned the bankers and the pledge-holders and ordered the debtors' bonds and the pledges to be brought to her. After examining them she took the pledges, paying [?] on behalf of the debtors, and returned the pledges to their owners. For this she was greatly praised by the whole city. Eustochius, having gone to Jerusalem, out of hatred for Apollinarius, Agathon and Macarius, expelled the monks of the New Lavra as Origenists. For this he was himself deposed, and Macarius was restored to his own throne. A.M. 6061. — Of the bishop of Jerusalem, Macarius again; of Alexandria, John; year 1. In this year, when a horse race was held and the factions were quarrelling with each other, the emperor sent mandates to each faction. To the Blues he said: “For you the emperor Justinian is dead.” To the Greens: “For you the emperor Justinian lives.” When the factions heard this they fell silent and quarrelled no more.

In the same year he began to build the palace of the Sophianae, named after his wife Sophia. The reason given was that his son Justus had been buried there before he became emperor, while he was still curopalates,
in the house of the Archangel [?]. He adorned it with various costly marbles. A.M. 6062. — Of the bishop of Rome Benedict,

In this year the emperor Justin began to build the second palace on his suburban estate, which he had owned before he became emperor. He did the same on the island of Prinkipos, which was also his estate, at the harbour, and he built the church of the Holy Anargyroi in the quarter of Dareios. He restored the public bath of Taurus and named it Sophianae after his wife Sophia. In the same year Anastasius the Great, bishop of Antioch, found fault with the copies of the synodical letters of John of Constantinople, who had ordained John of Alexandria. When that ordination had taken place, Anastasius was expelled from his own bishopric because of Justin's anger, and Gregory, monk and apocrisiarius of the monastery of the Byzantines, was ordained in his place. A.M. 6063. — Of Gregory bishop of Antioch, year 1. In this year Narses the cubicularius and protospatharius, the favourite of the emperor Justinian, against whom slanders were spread [?], built the House of Narses and the monastery of the Cathari. The emperor Justin heard that his nephew, whom he had as augustalis in Alexandria, was plotting against the emperor, and he sent and had him beheaded. A.M. 6064. — In this year Justin began to build the church of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul in the Orphanotropheion, and the church of the holy Apostles in the Trikonchos, which had burned down under the emperor Zeno. He also added the two apses, the northern and the southern, to the great church of the holy Theotokos of Blachernae, and made the church cross-shaped.

In this year the Romans and the Persians broke the peace, and the Persian war flared up again. The cause was that the Homerite Indians had sent an embassy to the Romans, and the emperor had sent Julian the magistrianus with a sacra to Arethas, king of the Ethiopians, by way of the river Nile from Alexandria and the Indian Sea. King Arethas received him with great joy, as he longed for the friendship of the emperor of the Romans. On his return Julian himself related that when the king received him, King Arethas was naked. Below his girdle, around his loins, he wore garments of linen and gold. Over his belly he wore slit garments [?] set with precious pearls. On his arms he had five bands [?] each, and gold bracelets on his wrists. On his head was a turban of linen and gold wound around, with four cords hanging from both knots, and around his neck a golden collar. He stood on top of four elephants, which stood with a yoke and four wheels, and above them was a sort of high carriage covered with gold plates, like the carriages of provincial governors. Standing on it he held a small gilded shield and two golden spears. His whole council stood about him under arms, singing songs to music. The Roman ambassador was brought in and made obeisance, and the king ordered him to rise and be brought to him. Receiving the emperor's sacra, he kissed the seal bearing the emperor's bust, and when he received the gifts he rejoiced greatly. On reading the letter he found that it asked him to arm himself against the king of the Persians and lay waste the Persian territory near him. It also asked that from then on he should no longer trade with the Persians, but carry on his commerce through the land of the Homerites, which he had subdued, and by way of the river Nile into Egypt, at Alexandria. At once King Arethas took the field before the eyes of the Roman ambassador and made war on the Persians, sending ahead the Saracens under his rule. He himself went into Persian territory and plundered all the land in those parts. Then King Arethas took the head of the ambassador

Julian in his hands and gave him kisses of peace, and sent him away with great attention and many gifts. Another cause also arose that troubled Chosroes. At that time the Huns, whom we usually call Turks, sent an embassy to Justin through the land of the Alans. Chosroes was alarmed at this and put forward as a pretext the revolt of the Armenians against him and their defection to Justin, and he demanded the refugees back. For the emperor of the Romans used to pay five hundred pounds of gold every year so that the Persians would guard the forts near that region, to keep the barbarian nations from invading and destroying both states, and so the forts were guarded at shared expense. But Justin broke the peace, saying that it was a disgrace for the Romans to pay tribute to the Persians. That is how this great war between the Persians and the Romans came about. Justin appointed Martinus, a patrician and his relative, general of the East and sent him against the Persians. A.M. 6065. — Of John bishop of Jerusalem, year 1. In this year, on 6 October, the emperor fell ill. He became angry with Baduarius, his own brother, and insulted him outrageously, ordering the cubicularii to beat him with their fists and throw him out of the silentium. Baduarius was count of the imperial stables. When Sophia learned of this she was grieved and reproached the emperor. He repented and went down to him in the stable, entering suddenly with the praepositus of the cubicularii. When Baduarius saw the emperor he fled from stall to stall in fear of him. The emperor cried out: “I adjure you by God, my brother, wait for me!” He ran and caught hold of him, embraced him and kissed him, saying: “I have wronged you, my brother. But accept me first as your brother and then as emperor. For I know that this happened through the working of the devil.”

Baduarius fell at his feet weeping and said: “Truly, master, you have the authority. But you humiliated your servant in the presence of the senate. Now, master, make your defence to these.” And he pointed to the horses. The emperor invited him to dine with him, and they were reconciled. At the same time a great battle took place between the Persians and the Romans near Sargathon, and the … won.

In this year the Avars came into the regions of the Danube. When the emperor learned of it he sent Tiberius, the count of the excubitors, against them. Tiberius engaged them but was defeated, having been taken by surprise, and he returned after losing many men. Hormisdas, the king of the Persians, appointed Artabanes general and sent him to cross the Euphrates and ravage the land of the Romans. He himself took his forces and came upon the Romans who were besieging Nisibis. When Martinus learned this, he abandoned Nisibis and withdrew to Roman territory. Artabanes came to the area around Antioch, laid waste the suburbs of the city, and advanced into Coele Syria. And so Artabanes, having taken a great many captives, returned to his own country. The emperor Justin, deeply distressed at what had happened, removed Martinus from his command and appointed Archelaus general. Artabanes took Dara and then went back. When Justin learned this he was stunned by the scale of the disaster and fell into an illness of derangement. He asked the Persian [?] for a truce, and the Persian agreed to make a truce for one year.

…the emperor adopted Tiberius, the count of the excubitors, proclaimed him Caesar, and had him sit beside him at the horse races and on festal days. For the emperor suffered in his feet [?] and was mostly confined to bed. A.M. 6068. — In this year Justin built the great aqueduct of Valens and supplied the city with an abundance of water. A.M. 6069. — In this year the emperor Justin took from the Hebrews their synagogue in the Chalkoprateia and made it into a church of our Lady, the all-holy Theotokos, next to the Great Church. In the same year, on 31 August, in the tenth indiction, John bishop of Constantinople died.

A.M. 6070. — Of Eutychius bishop of Constantinople, year 1. In this year, in the month of October, in the indiction [?], Eutychius regained the throne of Constantinople. The emperor fell ill, and when he had recovered a little from his sickness he summoned the archbishop, the senate, all the priests and the officials of state. Bringing forward the Caesar Tiberius in the presence of all, he proclaimed him emperor with these words: “Behold, God has favoured you. God has given you this dignity, not I. Honour it, so that you may be honoured by it. Honour your mother, who was once your mistress. You know that at first you were her servant, and now you are her son. Do not delight in blood. Have no share in murders. Do not repay evil for evil. Do not become like me in enmity, for I stumbled, being human. I became a sinner, and I have received what my sins deserved. But I will bring my case against those who did this to me before the judgement seat of Christ. Do not let this dignity puff you up, as it did me. Care for everyone as you care for yourself. Know who you were and who you are now. Do not be arrogant, and you will not sin. You know who I was, what I became, and what I am. All these are your children and your servants. You know that I preferred you to my own flesh and blood. In these men whom you see, you see the whole state. Look after your soldiers. Do not admit soldiers [?]. Let no one tell you that your predecessor lived this way. I say these things because I have learned from what I have suffered. Those who have

property, let them enjoy it; to those who have none, give.” When the patriarch had said a prayer and everyone had answered “Amen,” the Caesar fell at the emperor's feet, and the emperor said to him: “If you will, I am; if you will, I am not. God who made heaven and earth will put into your heart everything I have forgotten to tell you.” Having said these things, the emperor finished and dismissed the gathering. When the assembly had broken up, Tiberius distributed gifts to his subjects, and as much as at imperial proclamations

In this year, in the month of October, in the twelfth indiction, Tiberius became emperor. He was crowned by the patriarch Eutychius, as already mentioned. He too was a Thracian by birth. When he became emperor the factions cried out in the hippodrome: “Let us see, let us see the Augusta of the Romans!” He sent a mandate saying: “The one that stands opposite the public bath of Dagistheus, which is called a church, has the same name as the Augusta.” And the factions cried out: “Anastasia Augusta, may you conquer! Save, Lord, those whom you have ordained to reign!” When Sophia, Justin's wife, heard this, she was stricken to the soul. For she had wanted to marry Tiberius and remain Augusta, not knowing that he had a wife. Some said that even while Justin was alive she had been on intimate terms with him, and that she had persuaded Justin to make him Caesar. Tiberius sent for his wife Anastasia and brought her, together with the two daughters she had borne him, Charito and

[Note:] The Origins [of Constantinople]: “The so-called [bath] of Dagistheus. In former times the assembly of the two popular factions took place there, and there was a very large dining hall there, and whenever the demarchs wanted to hold the assembly there…”

[THEOPHANES' CHRONOGRAPHY?] Constantina. He crowned her Augusta and scattered lavish consular largesse. A.M. 6072. — Of Eulogius bishop of Alexandria, year 1. In this year the emperor Tiberius built the [?] at the harbour of Julian and named it after Sophia, the wife of Justin. He installed her there and gave her cubicularii to serve her, ordering that she be honoured as his mother. He also built a bath for her and provided everything for her care. He sent ambassadors to the king of the Persians, as was the custom, announcing his accession, but the king of the Persians would not accept peace. Then Tiberius gathered great forces, spent freely from the imperial treasuries, and raised many armies. He appointed a certain Justinian general of the East, who took the forces and came to Dara. The Persians also encamped near them, under the command of Mechosroes [?]. When the battle lines had been drawn up, they came to terms and made a truce with each other. Under its terms, for a period of four years neither Romans nor Persians would ravage the East, but the war in Armenia would go on. A.M. 6073. — In this year the king of the Persians took his forces and advanced into Armenia. When the Roman general heard that the king of the Persians meant to conduct the war in person, he lost heart, and fear came over the Roman army. So Justinian addressed the forces, put an end to their cowardice and roused their fighting spirit [?]. When battle was joined, the Persian archery was so heavy that it hid the rays of the sun, but the Romans
[Notes:] “under the command of Mechosroes” (with a variant spelling) A; “under Mechosroes” c Γ; “under the parts of Chosroes” in the common text. “for a period of three years” A,

turned aside the arrows with their shields and closed for hand-to-hand fighting. Because the Roman battle line was deep, the Persians could not withstand it. The mass of the Babylonians was routed, and great numbers were slain. The Romans captured the Persian baggage train and the royal tent, along with all the equipment, which was magnificent. They also seized the elephants and sent those splendid royal spoils to Tiberius. The king of the Persians could not bear the disgrace and laid down a law that no king of the Persians should ever again go out to war. The Roman army followed up the Persian disasters and advanced into the interior of Persia. They took many captives and much plunder in Persia, reaching as far as the middle of the Hyrcanian Sea. When winter came the Romans did not return home but wintered in Persia. In the same year Tiberius began to build the public bath of Blachernae, and he restored many churches, hostels and homes for the aged. He also ordered that he be styled “Tiberius Constantine” in contracts. A.M. 6074. — Of John bishop of Constantinople, year 1. In this year, on 6 April, in the fifteenth indiction, the patriarch Eutychius died, and six days later John the Faster, a deacon of the Great Church, was ordained. The emperor Tiberius bought slaves from foreign nations and formed an army in his own name, clothing and arming five thousand of them. He gave them as general Maurice, the count of the foederati, with Narses as his second in command, and sent them against the Persians. A great battle was fought, and the Romans won a decisive victory and took back from the Persians the cities and lands that the Persians had seized under Justinian and Justin. When Maurice returned to Constantinople he was received

[?] with great honour. Tiberius celebrated a triumph for Maurice's victories and made him his son-in-law, giving him his own daughter Constantina. In the same way he married his daughter Charito to Germanus the general, and made both men Caesars. On the 14th of August, in the 15th indiction, after eating early mulberries that were striking to look at but spoiled, he fell into a wasting sickness. When he was about to die, he summoned the patriarch John and the senate, together with the troops, to the tribunal. He was carried there in a litter, and since he could not speak, he had a reader announce to the people what would benefit the affairs of the Romans. He then proclaimed his own son-in-law Maurice emperor. Everyone acclaimed the emperor's decision and acclaimed Maurice as emperor. Tiberius went back and died in his own bed, having reigned 3 years, 10 months and 8 days. Year of the World 6075. Emperor of the Romans: Maurice [?]

In this year Maurice became emperor at the age of 43. Shortly afterwards he celebrated his wedding, after his father Paul had come to Byzantium. The groomsman was Maritis [?], the eunuch, who held high rank in the palace. In April there was a fire in the Forum, and gusts of wind fanned the flames and destroyed many houses. On the 10th of May there was a very great [earthquake?], and everyone fled to the churches, and the races for the emperor's birthday were not held. In the same month the Av-

[?] he received the bride and groom kindly. For it was not lawful to put crowns on them, because those being married were not private persons; the imperial dignity had already claimed this beforehand. [?] That bridal escort openly [?]

-ars sent envoys to the emperor Maurice. A short time before, they had captured Sirmium, a famous city of Europe, and now they demanded that another 20 thousand be added to the eighty thousand gold pieces they received every year from the Romans. The emperor, eager for peace, agreed to this. The Chagan also asked for an elephant, an animal from India, to be sent to him so that he could see it. The emperor sent him the largest one of all, and when the Chagan had seen it, he sent it back to the emperor. In the same way he asked for a golden couch to be sent to him. The emperor sent this too, but the Chagan scorned it and sent it back as well. Then he demanded that another 20 thousand be added to the 100. When the emperor refused, the Chagan went to war, destroyed the city of Singidunum, and took many other cities belonging to Illyricum. He also captured Anchialus and [threatened?] to destroy the Long Walls. The emperor sent Elpidius [?] and Comentiolus as envoys to the Chagan, and the barbarian agreed to keep the peace on the terms of the treaties. In the East the emperor made John Mystacon general of Armenia. John came to the river Nymphius, where it joins the Tigris, and [joined?] battle with the Kardarigas. (Kardarigas is not a personal name but a high rank among the Persians, held by the Persian general.) The Romans were getting the better of the barbarians, but Curs, the lieutenant-general, turned and fled out of envy and jealousy. When the rest of the Romans saw him, they turned and fled as well, and barely got back safely to their camp. In a second engagement the Romans were defeated, and many of them were killed. Year of the World 6076. In this year, on the 20th of December, in the 2nd indiction, the emperor was proclaimed consul and gave the city many treasures. He appointed Philippicus general of the East,

and made him his brother-in-law by giving him his own sister Gordia. Philippicus reached Persian territory and came near Nisibis. He made a sudden invasion of Persia and took many captives. When the Kardarigas, the Persian general, learned of this, he set an ambush, intending to waylay the Roman armies. But Philippicus brought the captives through safely, went down through the mountains into the land of the Medes, destroyed many villages of Media, and returned to Roman territory. Meanwhile the Chagan was scheming to break the peace by trickery. He armed the Sclavene peoples against Thrace, and they came as far as the Long Walls, taking much plunder. The emperor led the palace troops out of the city and ordered the demes to guard the Long Walls. He appointed Comentiolus general, equipped him, and sent him against the barbarians. Comentiolus fell on the barbarians unexpectedly, killed great numbers of them and drove them off. When he came to Adrianople, he met Ardagastus leading a host of Sclavenes with their captives. He attacked him, freed the captives and won a great victory. Year of the World 6077. In this year Philippicus took up the armies and set out for Persian territory. He overran Arzanene, took many captives, and struck fear into the Persian armies. But Philippicus fell ill and went to Martyropolis. He appointed his nephew to command the army and put Stephen in charge as commander of a regiment. The Kardarigas reached Martyropolis, burned all its suburbs, and went back. Philippicus, still ill, came to Constantinople, and the armies returned unharmed to their own quarters. In the same year a son was born to the emperor, and he named him Theodosius. Year of the World 6078. In this year Philippicus left the imperial city and encamped by the city of Amida. He gathered the soldiers and asked them whether they would go into battle willingly. The Romans swore oaths and convinced him that they would fight eagerly, so he went to Arzamon. When the Kardarigas learned of this, he dismissed the report with a laugh, thinking it was a dream. He called the magi and asked them who would win the victory. These servants of demons said that the gods would give the victory to the Persians. The Persians were overjoyed at these promises of the magi. At once they made fetters of wood and iron to put on the Romans. The general, for his part, ordered the Romans not to damage the farmers' work, so that God's justice, which hates wickedness, would not hand the victory over to the barbarians. The next day the general sent out two phylarchs of the Saracens, and they captured some Persians alive. From them the Romans learned what the enemy was doing: the prisoners said that the barbarians meant to attack the Romans on Sunday. So from dawn Philippicus drew up the Romans in three divisions and went out to meet them in battle. He himself took the image of the God-man, which the Romans honour as not made by human hands, and rode through the ranks, imparting divine power to the soldiers. Then, standing behind the battle line and holding this weapon, he sought God's favour with many tears, and God took the heavenly hosts as his allies. When battle was joined, Vitalius the taxiarch charged more boldly than anyone, broke through the Persian line and captured the baggage. The Romans began to busy themselves with the spoils. When Philippicus saw them, he was afraid that the others would also turn to plunder and forget their place in the line, and that the barbarians would wheel round and destroy them. So he put his own helmet on Theodore Ilibinus and sent him to strike with his sword those who were busy with the plunder. When they saw him, they thought he was Philippicus, left the spoils and went back into

battle. The fighting went on for many hours. Then the general gave the order to strike the Persians' horses with spears. When this was done, the Persian army turned and fled. The Romans won a great victory, killed many and stripped the dead. The next day the Kardarigas took up his forces and armed for battle again. A second battle was fought, and again the Romans were victorious and many Persians were killed. Two thousand Persians were taken alive and sent to Byzantium. The Kardarigas fled to Dara, but the Persians there sent him away with insults. Philippicus sent Heraclius, the father of the emperor Heraclius, who was his lieutenant-general, to reconnoitre the barbarians. He himself sent the men wounded in the battle to the [cities?] to be cared for. Then he took the army, invaded Babylonia, and laid siege to the fortress of Chlomaron. The Kardarigas raised a force of civilians with pack animals, and having collected this crowd he boasted that he would make camp. On a moonless night he came through difficult country to the rear of the Romans, though he had no intention at all of daring to attack them. But Philippicus was seized by a panic at the wrong moment, abandoned the fortress and fled for no good reason. When the Romans realized this, they also took to flight, and they fell into great dangers in country that was hard to get through, for the night was moonless. When the sun rose, they escaped their misfortune. When they caught up with the general, they abused him with the most shameful insults. The Persians thought the Romans' flight was a feint and did not dare to pursue them. Heraclius crossed the Tigris and set fire to all the important villages of the land of Media, and then returned to Philippicus with much plunder. Year of the World 6079. In this year the Chagan of the Avars broke the treaty and waged terrible war on Moesia and Scythia, destroying Ratiaria, Bononia, Aquis, Dorostolon, Zaldapa and Marcianopolis. The

[general Comentiolus?] went to Anchialus. He divided the army and separated the unfit from the best soldiers. He ordered the useless force, [forty?] thousand men, to guard the camp. Taking the picked men, who numbered six thousand, he gave two thousand to Castus and two to Martin, and took two thousand himself, and went against the barbarians. Castus came to Zaldapa and the Haemus, found the barbarians off their guard, and killed many of them. He took many captives and gave them to a bodyguard to keep safe. Martin came to the region around the city of Tomi. He came on the Chagan unexpectedly and killed so many of his forces that the Chagan had to save himself by flight. Martin, having won a glorious victory, went back to the general, to the place where Comentiolus had promised to wait for them. But Comentiolus, overcome by cowardice, had returned to Marcianopolis. Not finding him, they gathered their own troops and encamped at the passes of the Haemus. When Martin saw the Chagan crossing a river, he went back to the general. But Castus crossed the river, came up with the Avar vanguard and won the fight. Feeling no need of anyone's advice, he did not return to the general. The next day the Chagan seized the crossings and cut him off. His men were scattered, and each fled through the woods as best he could. Some were caught by the barbarians and gave away where Castus was hiding. When the barbarians captured him, they leapt and rejoiced. The Chagan marched through the south, advanced against Thrace and reached the Long Walls. Comentiolus had been hiding in the forests of the Haemus. Now he came out with Martin, and finding the Chagan quite unprepared, because the mass of the barbarians had spread out over Thrace, he moved against him at the first watch of the night. He would have won a great success then and there, if by some chance his attempt had not failed. A pack animal's load slipped, and a comrade of the animal's owner called out to him in their native language to straighten the load: 'Torna, torna, frater!' ('Turn, turn, brother!'). The mule's owner

did not hear the shout. But the troops heard it, and thinking the enemy were upon them, they turned and fled, shouting 'Torna, torna!' at the top of their voices. The Chagan was gripped by great fear and fled headlong. One could see Avars and Romans running away from each other, with no one pursuing. The Chagan then took his forces and laid siege to Appiaria again. He found Busas, the city's siege engineer [?], and tried to kill him. Busas begged them to spare his life and promised them a large sum of money if they did. So they tied him up and set him in front of the city, and he asked the inhabitants to ransom him, telling them how much he had fought for the city. But one of the citizens persuaded the people not to do it; rumour had it that Busas was sleeping with that man's wife. Since Busas had been treated with contempt, he promised the Chagan that he would hand over the city. He built a siege engine called a ram and took the city. Once the barbarians had learned this device, they captured very many other cities as well, and went home with many captives. When the people of Byzantium heard that Castus had been taken prisoner by the barbarians, they heaped abuse on Maurice and reviled him openly. At this time Heraclius, the father of Heraclius, attacked a Persian fortress and took it, and Theodore likewise took the fortress of Mazaron [?]. Both of them then came to Beiudes. The fortress was strong, but a soldier named Sapphires made stakes, drove them into the joints between the stones, and so climbed up. When he reached the top of the wall, a Persian pushed him off. Sapphires fell, and the Romans caught him on their shields. He dared the feat again and again was thrust off the stronghold; again the Romans caught him on their shields, and once more he set to the task. When he reached the top of the wall, he cut off the Persian's head. Then he [held up?] the head and filled the Romans with courage. Many followed the hero's example

and climbed the wall by the stakes, and the fortress was surrendered to the Romans. They killed some of the Persians and took the rest captive along with the baggage, and set the fortress on fire. Philippicus again set out for Byzantium, leaving Heraclius in command of the Romans. When he came to Tarsus and learned that the emperor had appointed Priscus general of the East and sent him out, he wrote to Heraclius, telling him to leave the army, go to Narses in Armenia, and give notice of Priscus's coming. The emperor had ordered Philippicus to cut a quarter of the soldiers' pay, for Maurice suffered from a love of gold. Philippicus was afraid this would give cause for a revolt, so he did not obey the emperor, because he was giving up his command. When Priscus reached Antioch, he ordered the soldiers to assemble at Monocarton. He also summoned Germanus, who had been entrusted with governing Edessa, together with the bishop, and set out with them for the camp, intending to celebrate Easter with them. The commanders of the army came to meet him with their banners two miles from the camp. Contrary to custom, Priscus did not dismount from his horse, nor did he use the usual greetings. This was the beginning of their hatred for him, for crowds resent insults to all of them alike. After the feast he arrogantly displayed the emperor's letters. The soldiers came thronging to the general's tent, some carrying swords, others stones, others clubs. Priscus was terrified, mounted his horse and escaped the danger by flight. They tore open his tent and plundered all his belongings. He reached Constantina, where physicians treated his wounds and the blows from the stones. He sent the bishop of the city to make excuses to the army, promising to persuade the emperor not to take away any of the allowances they usually received. But the army sent the bishop

away with insults. They proclaimed Germanus general against his will, raising him on a shield, overturned the emperor's statues and destroyed his images. They were about to proceed to open revolt and to surround the cities, had Germanus not prevented it with much exhortation and admonition. Priscus reported all this to the emperor. The emperor once again made Philippicus general of the East, and Priscus returned to Byzantium. But the army bound itself by oaths never to be ruled by Maurice. The barbarians revelled in the Romans' misfortunes. The emperor sent Aristobulus, the curator of the imperial estates, to the army to end the revolt with oaths and gifts and [?]. Once the revolt had been put down, a very great battle took place between the Persians and the Romans near Martyropolis. The Romans defeated the Persians by strength and generalship. The Persian general Maruzas was killed, and three thousand were taken alive, along with the commanders of the Persian regiments. Only a thousand men escaped, and they made their way back to Persia through many dangers. The Romans sent the emperor much of the Persian spoils, together with all the prisoners and their banners. Maurice built the Carian portico at Blachernae and had painters depict on it his own deeds from childhood up to his reign. He also completed the public bath there. Year of the World 6080. In this year, in September, in the 6th indiction, the Lombards made war on the Romans, and the Moorish peoples caused great disturbances in Africa. In Persia there is a prison called Lethe ('Oblivion'), in which the Persian king had shut up many people of various nations, together with the captives from the city of Dara. These men, giving themselves up for lost, rose against their guards, killed Manusas [?], took his sister and came to Byzantium. The emperor received them with great joy. Phi-

[?] he places this at the beginning of book 3, chapter 1: 'So when the winter season followed the war, the camp was broken up by the ever-moving, alternating change of the seasons. When spring came,' and so on. [?]

…the army barely accepted Philippicus as general. A battle was then fought between the Romans and the Persians at Martyropolis, and the Romans were defeated. The emperor again relieved Philippicus of the command and sent Comentiolus as general of the East. Comentiolus came to the neighbourhood of Nisibis, and he and the Persians clashed near Sisarbanon [?]. Heraclius, the father of Heraclius, distinguished himself in the battle and killed the Persian general. When their general was killed the Persians turned and fled, and the Romans pursued. They took a great deal of plunder from them, captured their baggage train as well, and sent many spoils to Byzantium. The emperor brightened the city with horse races and festivals and celebrated the victories with a triumph. Hormisdas appointed Bahram as general and sent him with large forces against Suania. Bahram fell on it unexpectedly, the Turks were defeated by the Persians, and Hormisdas grew so powerful that he even received a tribute of forty thousand pieces of gold from the Turks, though before this he had paid the same sum to the Turks. Bahram won great renown in this war and encamped on the river Araxes. When Maurice learned of this, he appointed Romanus as general and sent him with a force into Suania. Romanus reached Lazica and the river called the Phasis, and encamped facing Albania. When Bahram heard that the Roman army had arrived, he laughed at the matter. Still, he wanted to try his strength against a Roman battle line, for he had never fought the Romans. So he crossed the nearby river and advanced as if he meant to draw the Romans on into the interior of Persia. Romanus divided the Roman host. He left the untried men in the baggage camp, took ten thousand picked men and marched against the barbarians, and he ordered two thousand to go on ahead of the army. These met the Persian advance guard, routed it and destroyed it completely: as the Persians fled they came up against a cliff, and with their escape cut off they were all killed. The Romans advanced right up to the barbarians' palisade, and Bahram was dismayed at this. When Romanus heard of it he encouraged his army, and they drew up for battle on a plain in Albania. Bahram tried to win the battle by a stealthy attack, but his plan failed,

for Romanus was endowed with good judgement. When they engaged and many of the barbarians had been killed, the Romans won a very great victory. The barbarians were stripped of their spoils, and since they were denied burial they became food for wild beasts. When the Persian king heard of this he could not bear the disgrace. He sent Bahram a woman's clothing and removed him from his command. So Bahram rebelled and set out to seize power. He answered the insult with a letter to Hormisdas, which he headed: "Bahram sends this to Hormisdas, daughter of Chosroes." He assembled the armies and told them that Hormisdas was angry with them for being defeated by the Romans. He also showed them forged letters, supposedly from Hormisdas, ordering the soldiers' pay to be reduced. He reminded them of how harsh and utterly cruel Hormisdas was, how greedy and violent; how he delighted in murder and shunned peace; how he had thrown the nobles into chains, beheading some with the sword and drowning others in the Tigris; and how he forced the Persians into great wars so that they would be destroyed and never rise against him. With words like these Bahram won over the armies and kindled a great revolt against Hormisdas, and after binding Bahram by oaths they all resolved to depose Hormisdas. Hormisdas armed his cook Pherogan and sent him with a force against Bahram. Bahram told Pherogan and his troops that Persians must not take up arms against Persians, and he reminded them of Hormisdas' harshness, his injustice, his love of blood and slaughter, his faithlessness, his arrogance and his violence. Seeing that this was the truth, Pherogan's men went over to Bahram. They killed Pherogan, joined Bahram, and set out for Ctesiphon. Hormisdas was holding in chains Bindoes, a man of high rank. While affairs were in great turmoil, Bestam, the brother of Bindoes, burst into the prison and brought out his brother Bindoes. They gathered a crowd of peasants and townspeople, and at the third hour of the day they entered the palace. They found Hormisdas sitting in royal state on his throne and heaped insults on him. Bindoes seized Hormisdas, took the diadem from his head,

and had him put in prison, and he urged Chosroes to take possession of his father's throne. From the prison Hormisdas sent a messenger to the Persians asking to speak to them about what would benefit Persia. So on the next day the Persian senate assembled in the palace together with the people, and they brought Hormisdas in chains. Hormisdas reminded the Persians that they ought not to commit such offences against their kings. He recounted all the victories he had won since he began to reign and all the benefits he had conferred on the Persians: how he had made the Turks pay tribute to Persia and made the Romans long for peace, and how he had taken Martyropolis. He also related the great deeds of his forefathers. He asked them to reject Chosroes as king, calling him a lover of injustice, insatiable, bloodthirsty, arrogant, insolent and warlike. He had another son, he said, and he urged them to make that son king instead. Bindoes answered Hormisdas, laid his crimes before everyone and stirred them all up against him. They brought out Hormisdas' wife and son and cut them in two before Hormisdas' eyes [?]. Then they blinded Hormisdas and put him back in prison. For a time Chosroes treated his father kindly in prison and provided him with every comfort. But Hormisdas repaid him with insults and trampled on whatever the king sent him. In anger Chosroes ordered him to be beaten on the flanks with brutal clubs until he died. This grieved the Persians and turned them to hatred of Chosroes. Chosroes gathered forces, left the palace and marched against Bahram, and he came to the plain of the river Zab, where Bahram had his camp. Suspecting that some of his officers favoured Bahram, Chosroes had them killed. This threw the army into confusion, and Chosroes fled with a few men, while all the rest of his followers went over to Bahram. Chosroes did not know what to do. Some advised him to go to the Turks, others to the Romans. So Chosroes mounted his horse, let the reins go slack, and ordered everyone to follow wherever the horse went. The horse set off toward Roman territory, and he came to Circesium. From there he sent envoys to announce his arrival to the Romans. It happened that the patrician Probus was there. He received him and informed the emperor about him by letter. Bahram sent envoys to

the emperor asking him not to ally himself with Chosroes. But the emperor Maurice ordered the general Comentiolus to receive Chosroes at Hierapolis and to honour him with royal attentions. In the same year the emperor Maurice instituted a procession at Blachernae in memory of the holy Theotokos, at which encomia of our Lady were to be delivered, and he named it a festival. A.M. 6081. — Of Chosroes, king of the Persians, [?]

In this year the emperor Maurice adopted Chosroes, king of the Persians, as his son. He sent Domitian, bishop of Melitene, a kinsman of his, to him together with Narses, and entrusted Narses with the conduct of this war. Taking Chosroes and all the Roman forces, they invaded Persia. When Bahram learned of this, he took the forces he had and encamped at a place called Alexandriana. He meant to stop the armies coming from Armenia from joining Narses, for Maurice had ordered John Mystacon, the commander in Armenia, to take his armies and join Narses so that they could wage the war against Bahram together. During the night all the Roman forces united and drew up for battle against Bahram. Overcome by cowardice, Bahram encamped up against the mountain. A fearful battle was fought. Narses, scorning the Indian beasts, broke the barbarians' central phalanx. After this the rest of Bahram's phalanxes also gave way, and the usurper's army fled in a great rout. Narses pursued without letting up and slew the Persians. He took six thousand prisoners and brought them in chains to Chosroes, and Chosroes had them all killed with the spear. Those who were Turks he sent to the emperor at Byzantium. These Turks had the sign of the cross tattooed in black ink on their foreheads, and when they were asked…

…fearing assassination, he asked Maurice to let him keep a thousand Romans as a bodyguard. Maurice had great affection for the barbarian and granted his request. And so the war between the Romans and the Persians came to an end. A.M. 6082. — In this year, on 27 March, in the 8th [?] indiction, on the day of holy Easter, Theodosius, the son of the emperor Maurice, at the age of four and a half, was crowned by John, patriarch of Constantinople. In the same year the emperor Maurice completed the church of the Holy Forty, which Tiberius had begun to build. It stands on the Mese, at a place that was formerly said to be the praetorium. While deep peace settled on the East, [?] war surged over Europe. For this reason the emperor Maurice transferred the forces from the East to Thrace. A.M. 6085 [?]. — In this year, at the beginning of spring, when the regiments had reached Thrace, Maurice went out with them to see what the barbarians had laid waste. The Augusta, the patriarch and the senate begged the emperor not

to conduct the war in person but to entrust it to a general. He refused. As he set out on the campaign there was an eclipse of the sun. Gusts of extraordinary wind followed, a violent south wind. When he came to Rhegium he cheered the crowds of the poor with gifts of money. When the emperor went out hunting, an enormous wild boar charged at the Caesar. The horse was frightened by the sight and tried to throw the Caesar. It reared and plunged for a long time but could not throw the Caesar, and the boar went off unharmed. As he was making his way to Perinthus by sea, extraordinary winds and rain arose, the oarsmen [?] were helpless, and the emperor's vessel was driven along until it came safe, against all expectation, to the place called Daonium. That night a woman was giving birth and uttering pitiful cries. When morning came the emperor sent men to see what had happened. They saw that a child had been born without eyes or eyelids and with neither hands nor arms, and a fish's tail was attached to its hip. That same day the emperor's horse, the one that wore the golden trappings, suddenly fell and burst. The emperor took all these things as omens and was deeply grieved. On the next day the Romans seized three men, Sclavenes by race, who carried nothing of iron and had only lyres with them. The emperor asked them where they came from and where they lived. They said that they were Sclavenes by race and lived at the far end of the western Ocean. The Chagan had sent an embassy to them, they said, with gifts for their chiefs, so that they would join him in alliance against the Romans. Their chiefs had sent them to excuse themselves to the Chagan, saying that because of the length of the road they could not send him help. They said they had been on the road for eighteen months and so had fallen in with the Romans. They carried lyres because they did not know how to bear arms of any kind, since their country knew nothing of iron. The emperor marvelled at them, praised their stature and the size of their bodies, and sent them on to Heraclea. When he reached Anchialus and learned that envoys of the Persians and of the Franks had arrived in Byzantium, he returned to the palace.

A.M. 6084. — In this year the Chagan sought to add new terms to the treaty. The emperor would not accept the barbarian's proposals, so the Chagan took up war again. He besieged Singidunum and encamped near Sirmium. The emperor appointed Priscus general of Europe. Priscus made Salvianus his lieutenant and ordered him to go on ahead. They advanced against the barbarians, joined battle, and the Romans won. When the Chagan heard of this, he took his forces and marched to battle. Salvianus saw their numbers, was dismayed, and fell back to Priscus. Learning that the Romans had withdrawn, the Chagan went out to Anchialus, that is, to the church of St Alexander, and gave it over to the all-devouring fire. Then he moved on to Drizipera, built siege engines, and tried to sack the town. The people of Drizipera showed great boldness: they opened their gates and threatened to fight the barbarians, though they were in terrible fear. Then, at that very moment, divine powers came to their aid. At midday the barbarians thought they saw Roman forces marching out of the city and about to engage them. Dismayed, they fled headlong and came to Perinthus. Priscus could not bear even to look at the barbarians' numbers. He went into the fortress of Tzurulum and shut himself in securely, and the barbarian set about besieging Priscus. When Maurice heard this he did not know what to do, but by shrewd planning he outwitted that boundless force. With great gifts and promises he persuaded one of the Excubitors to fall into the barbarians' hands on purpose, and he gave him letters to Priscus that read as follows: "To the most glorious general Priscus. Do not fear this wicked venture of the barbarians, for it has come about for their destruction. Know that the Chagan will have to go back in great disgrace to the land the Romans granted him. Therefore let your glory hold out in Tzurulum and keep him occupied there,
