The Chagan seized the letters, read them, and was terrified. He made a treaty with Priscus, agreed to peace in return for a few paltry gifts, and went back to his own land in headlong flight. A.M. 6085. — Of Amos, bishop of Jerusalem, [?]

In this year the emperor Maurice sent Priscus with all the Roman forces to the river Ister to prevent the Sclavene nations from crossing it. When he came to Dorostolum, the Chagan learned of it and sent envoys to him, accusing the Romans of starting a war. Priscus replied, "I have not come to make war on the barbarians. The emperor sent me against the Sclavene nations." Priscus heard that Ardagastus had scattered the Sclavene hordes to go plundering. He crossed the Ister at midnight and fell on Ardagastus without warning. Ardagastus realized the danger, jumped onto a horse without a saddle, and barely escaped. The Romans killed great numbers of Sclavenes, ravaged the country around Ardagastus, and took many captives, and Priscus sent these to Byzantium in the charge of Tatimer. Tatimer travelled carelessly. He gave himself up to drink and luxury and neglected his duty. On the third day hordes of Sclavenes attacked him. He was seized by cowardice, fled, and reached Byzantium. But the Romans with him fought the Sclavenes stoutly, defeated the barbarians against all expectation, and brought the captives safely to the emperor at Byzantium. The emperor rejoiced and offered hymns of thanksgiving to God together with the whole city. Encouraged, Priscus advanced into the interior of the Sclavene country. A Gepid, a man of the Christian faith, deserted to the Romans and showed them the way in, and they overcame the barbarians. He also told them that Musocius, the king of the barbarians, was thirty miles away. Guided by the Gepid's treachery, Priscus crossed the river

and at midnight found Musocius sodden with drink, for he was celebrating a funeral feast for his own brother. Priscus took him alive and made a great slaughter among the barbarians. After taking many captives, the Romans gave themselves up to drink and luxury. The barbarians regrouped and attacked the victors, and their counterattack would have been more ruinous than the earlier victory had been glorious, had not Genzon come up with the Roman infantry and checked the barbarians' onslaught in a fierce battle. Priscus impaled the men who had been entrusted with the watch. At the same time Paul, the emperor's father, died in Constantinople and was buried in the imperial tombs. So too did Anastasia Augusta [?], Maurice's mother-in-law and the wife of the emperor Tiberius, and she was buried with her husband Tiberius. A.M. 6086. — In this year Priscus again reached the Ister, plundered the Sclavene nations, and sent many captives to the emperor. The emperor sent Tatimer to Priscus with orders that the Romans were to spend the winter season there. When the Romans learned this they objected that it was impossible, because of the barbarians' great numbers, because the country was hostile, and because of the unbearable cold. But Priscus persuaded them with convincing words to winter there and carry out the emperor's command. When the emperor Maurice heard this, he made Philippicus, his own brother-in-law and the general of the East, count of the Excubitors. He trusted him because he had given him his sister in marriage. Philippicus began to build at Chrysopolis the monastery of our all-holy Lady the Theotokos, with a palace in it intended to receive the emperor Maurice and his children. Inside it he made fishponds and gardens for the emperor's enjoyment. In Constantinople he built the house called Ta Philippikou. — Of [?] Cyriacus, year 1. Of Anastasius, bishop of Antioch, year [?]. — [Critical apparatus:] ἑώρταζεν] ἑόρταζεν vulg. — ἀντίδοσις A. — διεκώλυσε A; διέλυσε vulg. — αὐτῶν A.
[?] In this year Anastasius, patriarch of Antioch, returned to Antioch after the death of the patriarch Gregory, who had also succeeded…

In this year monstrous births took place in the suburbs of Byzantium: a child with four feet, and another with two heads. Those who write histories with care say that such things portend no good for the cities in which they are born. The emperor removed Priscus from his command and made his own brother Peter general of the Roman forces. But Priscus took up the forces and crossed the river before Peter arrived. When the Chagan heard that the Roman army had crossed, he was greatly astonished. He sent to Priscus asking to learn the reason, and demanding a share of the plunder as the price for letting them cross the river, for he was deeply vexed at the Romans' successes. So Priscus sent Theodore the physician, a man endowed with shrewdness and good sense, as his envoy to the Chagan on these matters. Theodore saw that the Chagan was full of pride and was giving his answers with a good deal of boasting (for he threatened that he was lord of all nations), and he calmed the barbarian's conceit with an old story. "Hear, Chagan," he said, "a profitable tale. Sesostris, king of the Egyptians, was renowned and exceedingly prosperous, brilliant in wealth and invincible in his forces, and he enslaved a great many mighty nations. Then he fell into arrogance. He had a chariot made, inlaid with gold and precious stones, and sat in it, and he put four of the kings he had conquered under the yoke to draw it. When this was done, on a certain notable occasion [?] one of the four kings kept turning his eyes backwards and watching the wheel as it rolled. Sesostris asked him why he kept his eyes fixed behind him, and he said: 'I marvel at the wheel, how unstable it is, moving now one way and now another, at one moment bringing low what is high, and at the next raising up what is low.' Sesostris, hearing the parable and wisely taking it to heart, decreed that kings should no longer draw the chariot." When the Chagan heard this he smiled and said that he would keep the peace, and that it was for Priscus to choose whether he wished to honour the Chagan with any of the

spoils. Priscus gave the captives to the Chagan in return for the crossing, and taking all the spoils he crossed the river without danger. The Chagan was greatly pleased to receive them, and Priscus came to Byzantium. Peter took over the command. AM 6088. In this year the emperor ordered Peter the general that the Romans should receive a third of their pay in gold, a third in arms, and the remaining third in clothing of every kind. When the Romans heard this they turned to mutiny. The general was afraid, and assured the camps that it was not true. He showed the army other letters, which ordered him to let those who had distinguished themselves and come safely through the dangers rest in the cities and be maintained in their old age at public expense, and to enrol the soldiers' sons in their own fathers' places. With this persuasion he calmed the troops, and they acclaimed the emperor. Peter reported all this to the emperor. Coming to Marcianopolis, he sent a thousand men on ahead. These came upon Sclavenes carrying off a great deal of Roman plunder and routed them. The barbarians slaughtered their captives, and having seized much booty they returned to Roman territory. In the same year the emperor built the round heliakon of the Magnaura, set up his own statue in the courtyard, and deposited the armoury there. AM 6089. In this year, while Peter the general was hunting, a wild boar met him and crushed his foot against a tree, and for a long time he lay ill in unbearable pain. The emperor heaped most shameful letters and unbearable reproaches on him, having heard that the Sclavenes were on the move near Byzantium. Peter forced himself and came to Novae. The notable soldiers of the city, together with the bishop, came out to meet the

general. When the general saw them, he admired their equipment and courage and ordered them to leave the town and join the Roman host. But the soldiers, who had been assigned to guard the city, refused to do it. The general was angered and sent Gentzon with a body of soldiers. When they learned of this they fled to the church, shut the doors of the sanctuary, and stayed inside. Out of reverence for the church Gentzon did nothing. Peter in his rage removed Gentzon from his command and sent a scribo to bring the bishop to him in disgrace. But the people of the city gathered with their whole households and drove the scribo out of the city in disgrace. They shut the city gates, acclaiming Maurice as emperor while heaping insults on the general, and so Peter withdrew from there in dishonour. He sent a thousand men ahead to reconnoitre, and they came upon Bulgars, a thousand in number. The Bulgars, trusting in the Chagan's peace, were marching without a care, and the Romans charged against them. The Bulgars sent seven men to urge them not to break the peace. When the advance guard heard this, they reported it to the general. The general said, "Not even if the emperor himself should come by will I spare them." Battle was joined, and the Romans were routed. The barbarians did not pursue them, for fear that in victory they might fall into danger. The general had the taxiarch of the advance guard severely flogged. When the Chagan learned of this, he sent envoys to Peter, blaming him for starting it and saying that the Romans had broken the peace without just cause. Peter used deceitful words and insisted that he had known nothing of the attack, but he would give back all the spoils twice over. And so the barbarians received the lost spoils in two portions and were content with the peace. Peter then marched against Peiragastus, the leader of the Sclavenes. The barbarians met them at the bank of the river and tried to prevent them from crossing. The Romans shot arrows at them from the ferry-boats and drove them back, and as they fled Peiragastus was struck in

the flank and died. The Romans crossed, seized a great many captives, and returned home. But their guides lost the way, and they fell into waterless country, and the army was in danger. Marching through the night, they came upon the river Helibacia. There was a thicket on the far bank of the river, and the barbarians hid in it and shot arrows at those who were drawing water. Great harm thus befell the Roman armies, and they turned to flight, beaten by the barbarians. When Maurice heard this, he removed Peter from his command and sent Priscus once again as general of Thrace. AM 6090. In this year Priscus the general went out into Thrace and counted his forces, and found that a great number of them had perished. Taking them [?] he came to the river Ister, to Novae. When the Chagan learned of this, he sent envoys to ask the reason for his coming. Priscus gave as his pretext that he had come to hunt. "It is not right," said the Chagan, "to hunt in someone else's territory." Priscus replied that the land was his own, and taunted the Chagan with his flight from the east. The barbarian demolished the wall of Singidunum and advanced into Roman territory. When Priscus learned this, he came to the island of [?], and taking dromons he went to the Chagan at Constantiola, wishing to speak with him. When the Chagan came to the river bank, Priscus conversed with him from the ship. The Chagan said to him, "What have you to do with my land, Priscus? Do you mean to take it out of my hands by falsehood? God will judge between me and Maurice the emperor. He will require at his hands the blood of the Roman army and of my army." Priscus said, "You will not take a single city from us." And the Chagan said, "In a little while you will see fifty Roman cities enslaved to barbarians." Priscus brought his ships along the river to Singidunum, sacked it, [?] the Bulgars from it, and began to rebuild the wall. The Chagan sent messengers to him, calling his falsely named gods to witness and blaming Priscus for what had happened. When winter came on, both sides

[?] brother of Maurice built the church of the holy Theotokos in the quarter of Arabindus, adorning it with marbles of many kinds. Likewise Cyriacus the patriarch also built, at the Diakonissa, the church of the holy

AM 6091. In this year the Chagan gathered his forces and advanced on Dalmatia. He captured Balbis [?] and sacked all the forty cities around it. When Priscus learned of this, he sent Goundouis to spy out what was happening. Goundouis overtook the barbarians as they made their way through rough country, and came upon two barbarians stupefied with wine, and he questioned them about the barbarians' movements. They said that the Chagan had handed the captives over to two thousand men-at-arms and sent them back home. When Goundouis learned this, he hid in a small ravine, and at dawn he fell upon their rear and killed them all at once. Then he took the captives and brought them to Priscus. When the Chagan learned of this failure, he returned to his own country, and Priscus went back home. AM 6092. In this year, in the third indiction, in the month of March, Priscus took up his forces and came to Singidunum. The Chagan gathered his forces, suddenly appeared in Moesia, and tried to take the city of Tomis. For this reason Priscus left Singidunum and drew near to him. When the feast of Easter came and the Romans were wasting away from hunger, the Chagan heard of it and told Priscus to send wagons to him so that he could send them provisions, that they might keep their feast with good cheer. So he filled four hundred wagons and sent them to them. Likewise Priscus sent the barbarian some Indian spices: pepper, Indian leaf, costus, cassia, and other sought-after things. The Chagan, who was staying at Thermion, was delighted to receive them. Until the feast was over, Romans and barbarians camped side by side, and there was no fear in either army. When the feast was

In this year the emperor Maurice, having adopted Chosroes king of the Persians as his son, sent to him Domitian, bishop of Melitene, his own kinsman, together with Narses, to whom he entrusted the conduct of the war. They took Chosroes and all the Roman forces and invaded Persia. When Bahram learned of this, he took up the forces he had with him and camped at a place called [?], hoping to prevent the armies coming from Armenia from joining Narses. For Maurice had ordered John Mystacon, the general of Armenia, to take up his armies and join Narses, so that together they might wage the war against Bahram. During the night all the Roman forces were united, and they drew up in battle order against Bahram. Bahram, gripped by cowardice, camped by the mountain. A fearful battle was fought, and Narses, scorning the Indian beasts, broke the centre of the barbarians' line. When this happened, Bahram's other divisions also gave way, and the usurper's army fled in great disorder. Narses pursued without check and slew the Persians. He took six thousand alive and brought them in chains to Chosroes, and Chosroes had them all killed with the spear. Those who happened to be Turks he sent to the emperor at Byzantium. The Turks had the sign of the cross tattooed in black ink on their foreheads, and when they were asked

over, the barbarians parted from the Romans. Maurice sent Comentiolus with an infantry force, ostensibly to support Priscus. When the Chagan learned this, he marched into Moesia against Comentiolus, [camping] thirty miles from him. Comentiolus, at a loss, sent a messenger to the Chagan. Some say that Maurice had suggested to Comentiolus that he betray the Roman army to the enemy because of their indiscipline. At midnight he ordered the army to arm, without revealing to the troops that he intended to give battle. Supposing that he had ordered them to bear arms for drill, they did not arm themselves as they should have. When day came and the barbarians arrived, a great uproar seized the army. Comentiolus threw the ranks into confusion and became the cause of their disorder. And so the Romans turned to flight. The barbarians, finding the army without a general, slaughtered them mercilessly. Comentiolus fled shamefully to Drizipera, but the townspeople pelted him with insults and stones and drove him out of the town. The barbarians came to Drizipera, sacked the city, and burned the church of Saint Alexander. Finding his tomb plated with silver, they impiously plundered it. They also desecrated the martyr's body, and after taking a great many captives in Thrace, they [went about] in a splendid throng exulting over the Romans [?]. When Comentiolus reached Byzantium, a very great turmoil and storm broke upon the city, so that in their fear the people wanted to abandon Europe and move across to Asia, to Chalcedon. The emperor took the Excubitors, gathered a body of armed men, and guarded the Long Walls. The demes guarded the city, and the senate urged the emperor to send an embassy to the Chagan. But God, avenging the martyr Alexander, sent a pestilence upon the barbarians. In a single day he killed seven sons of the Chagan by fever and plague-boils, together with great numbers of others, so that instead of the joy of victory, paeans and songs, the barbarian had laments and tears and inconsolable mourning. The senate begged the emperor to send an embassy to the barbarian at Drizipera, [someone] who with

gentle words would flatter the barbarian. The barbarian refused to accept the gifts, even though he was gripped by uncontrollable grief for his sons. He said to the envoys, "God will judge between me and Maurice the emperor, for it was he who broke the peace. But I will give the captives back to him for one nomisma a head." Maurice would not agree to pay. Again the Chagan asked for half a nomisma a head, and even so the emperor would not agree to pay, nor even four carats. The Chagan was enraged and killed them all, then went back home, imposing [a payment of] fifty thousand on the Romans in the treaty. And they agreed not to cross the Ister. From this much hatred was stirred up against the emperor Maurice, and people began to pelt him with abuse. Likewise the people in Thrace were stirred to revile the emperor. The army sent delegates to the emperor against Comentiolus, accusing him of treachery in the war. Among them was Phocas, who, while speaking with the emperor in the silentium, contradicted him so boorishly that one of the patricians struck him and pulled his beard. The emperor would not accept the charge against Comentiolus but dismissed them without result. And this too was how the plot against the emperor began. At this time in Egypt, when Menas the prefect was travelling with people on the river Nile at a place called the Delta, at sunrise creatures in human form appeared in the river, a man and a woman. The man was broad-chested and striking in appearance, fair-haired and grizzled. Down to the waist he bared his nature and showed himself naked to all, while the water covered the rest of his body. The prefect adjured him with oaths not to end the spectacle until everyone had had their fill of

this marvellous sight. The woman had breasts, a smooth face, and thick hair. Until about the ninth hour the people gazed at these creatures in wonder, and at the ninth hour they sank into the river. Menas wrote of this to the emperor Maurice. AM 6093. Isaac, bishop of Jerusalem: year 1. Anastasius, bishop of Antioch: year 1. In this year, on 26 March, in the fourth indiction, on the day of holy Easter, Sophia Augusta, the wife of Justin, together with Constantina, the wife of Maurice, had a priceless crown made and presented it to the emperor. When the emperor saw it, he went to the church and offered it to God, and hung it above the holy table on a triple chain of gold set with jewels. The Augustae were greatly grieved when they learned of this, and Constantina Augusta kept the feast at odds with the emperor. The emperor took no heed of the complaints of the armies in Thrace against Comentiolus, and that same Comentiolus took the infantry, came to the Ister, and joined Priscus at Singidunum, and the peace with the barbarians was broken. When it had been broken, they came to Viminacium, which is a large island in the Ister. When the Chagan heard this, he gathered his forces and advanced into Roman territory. He gave other forces to his four sons and posted them to guard the crossings of the Ister. The Romans built rafts, crossed the river, and joined battle with the Chagan's son, with Priscus in command, for Comentiolus had fallen ill and was staying on the island of Viminacium. The battle went on for many hours, and by sunset three hundred Romans had been killed, while four thousand of the barbarians perished. At dawn they again drew up the armies, began the battle once more, and again

killed eight thousand of the barbarians. Likewise on the third day the Romans drew up on the higher ground and advanced against the barbarians. They routed them, drove them into the waters of the lake, and drowned many of them, and among those drowned were also the Chagan's sons. And the Romans won a glorious victory. The Chagan gathered large forces and came against the Romans. Battle was joined, the Romans routed the barbarians, and this was the most notable of all the victories the Romans won. Priscus drew up four thousand men and ordered them to cross the river Tisza and reconnoitre the barbarians' encampments. The barbarians, knowing nothing of what had happened, were celebrating a feast and drinking together. The Romans fell on them by stealth and made a very great slaughter, for they killed thirty thousand Gepids and other barbarians. Then, taking a great many captives, they returned to Priscus. The Chagan again gathered his forces and came to the Ister. Battle was joined, the barbarians were defeated, and they were drowned in the streams of the river. Many Sclavenes perished with them as well. The Romans took alive three thousand two hundred Avars and two thousand other barbarians. The Chagan sent envoys to the emperor Maurice in an attempt to recover the prisoners. Maurice, not yet knowing of the Romans' glorious victory, wrote to Priscus to return only the barbarians to the Chagan. Comentiolus, having barely recovered from his illness, went out to Novae, looking for guides to lead him along the road of the emperor Trajan. An old man who knew the road said that it was difficult and impassable because of the heavy rains and because it was winter, and that it ran over high mountains covered in snow. Comentiolus did not heed the old man's words and set out along this road. An extraordinary cold and severe frost set in, and many of the Romans perished, along with most of the pack animals. He barely reached Philippopolis. The Romans wintered there, and Comentiolus went to Byzantium. In the same year a man clad in the monastic habit and renowned for his asceticism drew a sword and ran, blade in hand, from the Forum to the Chalke, [proclaiming] to all that the emperor … by murder

…foretold that he would die by the sword. In the same way Herodian also openly foretold to Maurice what would happen to him. Once, when the emperor was walking barefoot in a night procession with the whole city and was passing through the Karpianos quarter, some of the crowd rioted and threw stones at him. The emperor and his son Theodosius barely escaped, and he finished the prayer at Blachernae. The factions then found a man who looked like Maurice. They put a cloak on him, wove him a crown of garlic, sat him on an ass and paraded him around, chanting: "He found the heifer tender, and like the new cockerel he has mounted her, and he has made children like little sticks of wood [?]; and no one dares to speak, for he has muzzled them all. My saint, awesome and mighty, give it to him on the skull, so that he will not exalt himself, and I will bring you the great ox as a votive offering." The emperor arrested many of them and punished them. Year of the World 6094. In this year, in the month of November, in the fifth indiction, the emperor Maurice joined his son Theodosius in marriage to the daughter of the patrician Germanus, and Cyriacus, patriarch of Constantinople, crowned them. On 11 January Domitian, bishop of Melitene and a kinsman of the emperor, died. He was buried in the Holy Apostles by the patriarch Cyriacus and was honored by the whole senate [?]. The emperor made his own brother [?] Peter

general of Thrace once again and sent him out, for he had heard that the barbarian hordes had gathered near the Cataracts under their general Apsich. Peter sent an envoy to Apsich to discuss peace. But Apsich tried to take the Cataracts from the Romans, and the Chagan advanced on Constantia. The Romans withdrew to Thrace and reached Adrianople. When the emperor learned that the Chagan was marching against Byzantium, he wrote to Peter telling him to return to the Ister. He also sent Bonosus the scribo with ships to carry the army across. Peter sent his lieutenant general Guduin across the Ister, and they took a great many captives. When the Chagan learned of this, he sent Apsich with a large force to destroy the people of the "sailors" [?], since they were allies of the Romans. When this happened, a section of the barbarians went over to the Romans. Maurice came to his senses. He knew that nothing escapes God, who repays everyone according to their works, and he thought over the wrong he had done to the captives by not ransoming them. He judged it better to receive the punishment for his sins in this life rather than in the life to come. He wrote out petitions and sent them to all the patriarchal sees, to all the churches under his rule, to the monasteries in the desert and in Jerusalem, and to the lavras. With them he sent money, dry candles and incense, so that they would pray for him that he might be repaid here and not in the age to come.

He also had suspicions about his brother-in-law Philippicus, as though Philippicus were the one named by the letter [?]. Philippicus swore to the emperor again and again that he was faithful in his service and that he harbored no plot or deceit against him. While Maurice was praying to God for mercy on his soul, he saw a vision one [night] in his sleep. He was standing at the Bronze Gate of the palace, before the image of the Savior, with people standing beside him. A voice came from the image of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, saying: "Bring Maurice here!" The officers of justice seized him and set him beside the porphyry omphalion that is there. Then the divine voice said to him: "Where do you want me to repay you: here, or in the age to come?" When he heard this he said: "Master, lover of mankind, righteous judge, here rather than in the age to come." The divine voice then ordered that Maurice, his wife, his children and all his family be handed over to Phocas the soldier. Maurice woke up and called his chamberlain, and sent him to his brother-in-law Philippicus to bring him to the emperor at once. The chamberlain went and summoned him. Philippicus got up, called his wife and embraced her, saying: "Farewell, wife; you will not see me again." She cried out loudly to the chamberlain in tears: "I adjure you by God, what is the matter, that he is sending for him at this hour?" He swore that he did not know, and said: "The emperor got up suddenly from his sleep and sent me." Philippicus asked to receive communion, and then went off to the emperor. His wife Gordia lay on the ground, lamenting and weeping and praying to God. When Philippicus entered the imperial bedchamber, he threw himself at the emperor's feet. The emperor said to him: "Forgive me, for God's sake [?], for I have wronged you. From now on I am fully assured [?] about you." He ordered the chamberlain to leave, then rose and fell at Philippicus's feet, saying: "Forgive me, for I know for certain that you have done me no wrong. But tell me, whom do you know in our regiments, a soldier called Phocas?" Philippicus thought about it and said: "I know one, who was sent a short while ago as [?] [76] καί before εἰς added from A. [?] from the army, and he spoke against Your Majesty." The emperor asked: "What kind of man is he?" Philippicus said: "Young, reckless and cowardly." Then Maurice said: "If he is a coward, then he is a murderer." And he told Philippicus what had been revealed in the dream. That night a star appeared in the sky, the kind called a comet. The next day the magistrianus who had been sent to the holy fathers in the desert also arrived. He brought this answer from them: "God has accepted your repentance; he saves your soul and will number you with the saints together with your whole household. But you will fall from the throne with dishonor and in danger." When Maurice heard this he gave great glory to God. When autumn came, the emperor Maurice ordered Peter to have the army spend the winter there in the land of the Sclavinians. The Romans resisted and refused to do it, because their horses were worn out, because they were carrying a great deal of booty, and because hordes of barbarians had spread over the country, and they began to plot a mutiny. The general was angry with the army and put them to hard labor. Then rains and storms fell on the army, and severe cold. Peter made camp twenty miles from the road [?]. Maurice kept pressing Peter in letters to cross the Ister and draw the army's winter supplies from the land of the Sclavinians, so that he would not be forced to supply public rations to the Romans. The general summoned Guduin and said: "The emperor's commands weigh very heavily on me, ordering Romans to winter in a foreign land. To disobey is dangerous, and to obey is worse still. Avarice gives birth to nothing good; it is the mother of all evils. The emperor suffers from this disease, and so he is becoming the cause of the greatest evils for the Romans." He summoned the taxiarchs of the army and disclosed the emperor's plan to them. They told him that the army would not accept this. When the army heard it, they mutinied. The leading officers fled from them at once and came to the general. The masses gathered together and put forward as their leader
