Phocas the centurion. They raised him on a shield and acclaimed him exarch. When Peter heard this, he fled and reported everything to the emperor. The emperor heard this grim news and tried to hide it from the people. On the second day he even held horse races, to cover up the disaster. The Green faction shouted: "Constantine and Domentiolus, thrice-august lord of the Romans, are harassing your own faction, so that [?] may manage [?], for the sins we have. God, who created all things, will subdue every enemy and foe, both at home and abroad, and without bloodshed." The emperor declared to the factions: "Do not let the disorder and indiscipline of senseless soldiers trouble you at all." The Blues said: "God, who ordained that you should reign, will subdue to you everyone who makes war on your reign. And if it is a Roman who is ungrateful to you, he will subject him to you in servitude without bloodshed." The emperor armed them, calmed them with gentle words, and ordered them to guard the walls of the city together with the demarchs. The emperor's son was out hunting at Callicratia with his father-in-law Germanus, and the Romans sent letters to Theodosius asking that he should rule over them, or if not, that they might at least proclaim Germanus emperor, for they would no longer put up with being ruled by Maurice. When Maurice learned of this, he summoned his son to him. He ordered Comentiolus to guard [?]. He accused Germanus, together with his son Theodosius, of being responsible for the disasters. When Germanus tried to defend himself, Maurice said: "Germanus, there are two proofs behind my suspicion: the letters from the army to you, and the fact that

the army spared the herd of horses that graze for you in the suburbs. They plundered everything else, but they spared what is yours. Do not drag out your speech, Germanus; nothing [remains for you?] [?] but to die by the sword." Germanus fled for refuge to the church of the Mother of God at Kyrou. When the emperor learned this, he sent the eunuch Stephen to bring Germanus out of the church. Stephen tried to drag him out by force, but Germanus's guardsmen stood against him and pushed Stephen out. Then they took Germanus and fled with him to the Great Church. The emperor had his own son Theodosius beaten with rods, saying that it was through him that Germanus had escaped. He sent excubitors to bring Germanus out of the Great Church. At this a great uproar [?] broke out in the city. Germanus wanted to come out and give himself up, but the crowds would not allow it. Instead they insulted the emperor with gross abuse, shouting: "May whoever loves you have no skin, Maurice the Marcianist!" When those guarding the walls learned of this, they abandoned their watch. Then the Green faction burned down the house of Constantine, known as Lardys. At midnight Maurice took off the imperial robe and put on ordinary clothes. He boarded the dromons and fled with his wife, his children and Constantine. All night long the crowds hurled the most shameful abuse at the emperor and mocked him, and the patriarch Cyriacus as well. A great storm arose, and amid the gravest dangers he made it safely to St Autonomus. That same night he was struck by arthritic pains, the kind they call gout of the feet and gout of the hands. From there he sent his son Theodosius with Constantine to Chosroes, king of the Persians, to remind him of what Maurice had done for him and to ask him to repay that kindness to his son. Germanus sent to Sergius, the demarch of the Green faction, asking him to help him become emperor. He promised to favor the Green faction and to invest Sergius with high dignities. Sergius confided this to the more prominent members of the faction, but they would not accept it, saying:

"Germanus would never give up his partiality for the Blues." The Greens went out to Rhegium, honored the usurper Phocas with loud acclamations, and persuaded him to come to the Hebdomon. So Phocas sent Theodore the asecretis, and he read [a letter] to the people in the Great Church, saying that the patriarch, the factions and the senate should come to the Hebdomon. This was done, and when everyone had arrived at the Hebdomon, the patriarch Cyriacus required the usurper to make a profession of the orthodox faith and to promise to keep the Church free from disturbance. The usurper made a show of urging Germanus to take the throne. Germanus pretended he did not want it, and the factions acclaimed the usurper. So the evil was proclaimed. The usurper was made lord of the scepters, misfortune triumphed over prosperity, and the great calamities of the Romans began. The usurper was proclaimed in the church of St John the Baptist. He spent two days there, and on the third he entered the palace seated in an imperial carriage. On the fifth day he crowned his wife Leontia Augusta. On that same day the factions rioted against each other over disputes about seating places. The usurper sent his fellow rebel Alexander to calm the factions. Alexander laid hands on Cosmas, the demarch of the Blues, shoving and insulting him. The Blues were indignant and shouted: "Go away and learn the state of things: Maurice is not dead!" When the usurper heard these cries, he moved to murder Maurice. He sent soldiers and had them taken to the harbor of Eutropius at Chalcedon. First the emperor's five sons were killed before his eyes, so that he was punished even before his own death by the slaughter of his children. Maurice bore his misfortune like a philosopher. He called upon God who is over all, and he said again and again: "You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgments are upright."

So the children were put to death, while their father showed his virtue, as a kind of epitaph, in the very greatness of his misfortunes. For his nurse stole one of the imperial boys and handed over her own child to be slaughtered in his place, but Maurice would not allow it and demanded his own son back. They say that when this boy was killed, milk flowed out with his blood, so that everyone who saw it wept bitterly. In this way the emperor, who alone had risen above nature, departed this life. From that time on, misfortunes of every kind, and extraordinary ones, never ceased to strike the Roman empire. Chosroes, king of the Persians, broke the peace, the Avars laid Thrace waste, and both Roman armies were destroyed. When Heraclius became emperor, he held a careful review of the soldiery, and of the whole multitude who had served Maurice and then gone over to Phocas at the time of the usurpation he found no more than two men. So those who set up the usurper were wiped out under him. Year of the World 6095. Phocas, emperor of the Romans

In this year, in the month of November, in the sixth indiction, Phocas the usurper became emperor. As already told, he killed Maurice together with his five sons, and he ordered their heads to be displayed in the Campus of the Tribunal for many days. The people of the city went out and gazed at them until they began to stink. Maurice's brother Peter was also killed, along with many others. The story still prevails that his son Theodosius escaped and survived. Chosroes, king of the Persians, spread this rumor further, telling lies in different ways at different times. He claimed that he had Theodosius with him and was supposedly providing for him, so that he might take over the Roman empire. In fact he was craftily hoping to seize the Roman empire himself, as was proven in many ways, above all by his launching sudden wars and doing great damage to Roman territory. When Phocas sent Lilius to him as envoy, Chosroes seized him and put him in prison, so that he never returned to Roman territory. And he answered Phocas with insulting letters.

The usurper confined the empress Constantina, together with her three daughters, in a private house called the House of Leo. In the city of Alexandria a pious calligrapher was walking home from a night vigil. At midnight he saw the statues being pulled down from their pedestals and announcing in a loud voice that Maurice and his children were being killed, and everything else that was taking place in Byzantium. In the morning the man went and told this to the Augustalis, who ordered him to tell no one. The Augustalis noted down the day and waited to see what would happen. On the ninth day the messenger arrived with news of Maurice's murder. Then the Augustalis made public to the people the demons' prediction. Narses, who had become general of the Roman forces, rebelled against the usurper and took Edessa. Phocas wrote to the general Germanus to besiege Edessa. Narses wrote to Chosroes, king of the Persians, asking him to gather his forces and make war on the Romans. Phocas made his own brother Domentziolus magister, and Priscus count of the excubitors. Year of the World 6096. In this year, in the month of December, in the seventh indiction, Phocas went out in procession at the festivals and scattered a lavish consular largess. Chosroes, king of the Persians, gathered a large force and sent it against the Romans. When Germanus heard this he was afraid, but he was forced to start the war. Germanus was wounded in the battle, and his guardsmen got him safely to Constantina, while the Romans were defeated. On the eleventh day Germanus died. Phocas moved the troops from Europe to Asia and increased the tribute paid to the Chagan, thinking that the barbarian nation would then stay quiet. He divided these forces and sent some against the Persians, and the others, under Leontius, a eunuch and one of his magnates, to besiege Narses in Edessa. Chosroes gathered his forces and came to Dara. Narses left Edessa and fled to Hierapolis.

Chosroes, with the Romans, came to Arxamoun. Having built a rampart of elephants, he opened the war and won a great victory. He took many Romans alive, and these he beheaded. After this Chosroes went back to his own land and left the forces to Zongoes. When Phocas learned of this he raged against Leontius, had him brought to Byzantium in disgrace in iron fetters, and appointed his own nephew Domentziolus as general, whom he also made curopalates. AM 6097. In this year Chosroes sent Kardarigan and Rousmiazan, and he sacked many cities of the Romans. Domentziolus gave his word to Narses and persuaded him with many oaths that he would suffer no harm from Phocas, and sent him to Phocas. But Phocas did not keep this pledge and burned him alive. The Romans were therefore in great grief, because Narses had been a great terror to the Persians, so much so that Persian children trembled when they heard the name of Narses. AM 6098. Thomas, bishop of Constantinople, year 1. In this year Scholasticus, a eunuch and a distinguished man of the palace, took the lady Constantina and her three daughters in the middle of the night and fled with them to the Great Church. He did this on the advice of the patrician Germanus, who was reaching for the throne. A great riot then broke out in the city. The Greens gathered at the Kochlias and shouted abuse at Constantina, and Germanus sent the demarch of the Greens a talent of gold so that they would side with them. But the leading men of the faction would not accept it. The tyrant sent men to the church to drag the women away. The patriarch Cyriacus, however, stood up to the tyrant and would not allow the women to be dragged from the church by force. Once he had been assured by oaths from Phocas that he would not harm them, they were brought out of the holy precinct and shut up in a monastery. Phocas had Germanus tonsured, enrolled him among the clergy and kept him under guard in his own house. At that time Philippicus too cut off his hair and received priestly rank, and lived at Chrysopolis in the monastery he had built. In this year the Persians took Dara and all Mesopotamia

and Syria, and took a countless multitude of captives. When the patriarch Cyriacus died, Thomas, deacon and sacellarius of the same church, was ordained in his place on 11 October. AM 6099. Theodore, bishop of Alexandria, year 1. In this year the tyrant Phocas gave his daughter Domentzia in marriage to Priscus, patrician and count of the Excubitors. When the wedding had been held in the palace of Marina, he ordered horse races to be put on. The demarchs of the two factions set up laurel-crowned portraits of Priscus and Domentzia at the Tetrakionion alongside the imperial portraits. When the emperor saw this he was furious. He sent for the demarchs, Theophanes and Pamphilus, had them stood naked in the Stama, and ordered them beheaded. Through his protocursor he asked them on whose authority they had done this. They said that the painters had done it according to custom. The people and the crowds cried out, "Many years to our merciful lord!" The painters were asked why they had done it and said, "Since everyone was calling them the emperor's children, we did this on our own initiative." Priscus was gripped by fear and dreaded the emperor's anger. When the crowds cried out for mercy to be shown to the demarchs, Phocas pardoned them. But from then on Priscus bore a grudge and was not on good terms with Phocas. A woman named Petronia served the empress Constantina as a kind of go-between, carrying Constantina's replies to Germanus. As the rumour spread that Theodosius, the son of Maurice, was alive, both Constantina and Germanus placed high hopes in it. But the wicked Petronia disclosed all this to the tyrant. The tyrant handed Constantina over to the prefect Theopemptus to be tortured, and under torture she declared that the patri-

cian Romanus knew what had been said between them. He was arrested and confessed, and also said that others were his accomplices in the plot against the tyrant. Theodore, the prefect of the East, was arrested as well, and the tyrant had him flogged to death with ox-sinews. He cut off the hands and feet of Elpidius and gave him to the flames. He beheaded Romanus, and put Constantina and her three daughters to the sword at the harbour of Eutropius, where Maurice too had been killed. He killed Germanus and his daughter with the edge of the sword on the island of Prote. He did the same to John Tzitzas, who was also a patrician, to Theodosius, who held the rank of [?], to Andrew Scombrus, and to David, the chartophylax of the Hormisdas. At the same time the Persians crossed the Euphrates and took captives throughout Syria, Palestine and Phoenicia, wreaking great havoc on the Romans. AM 6100. In this year Priscus could no longer bear to watch the unjust murders and the rest of what Phocas was doing. He wrote to Heraclius, patrician and general of Africa, asking him to send his son Heraclius and Nicetas, the son of his lieutenant the patrician Gregoras, to come against the tyrant Phocas. He had heard that a revolt against Phocas was being planned in Africa, which was also why the ships from Africa did not sail at this time. Phocas killed the whole family of Maurice, Comentiolus the general of Thrace, and many others without mercy. At this time there was plague and famine of every kind. The Persians went out with Kardarigas and took Armenia and Cappadocia. They fought and routed the Roman armies, took Galatia and Paphlagonia, and came as far as Chalcedon, savaging people of every age without restraint. And while the Persians

were tyrannizing the Romans outside the city, Phocas was doing worse to them inside it, murdering and taking captives. AM 6101. Sergius, bishop of Constantinople, year 1. Zacharias, bishop of Jerusalem, year 8. John, bishop of Alexandria, year 8. In this year the Hebrews of Antioch rose in revolt against the Christians and slaughtered Anastasius, the great patriarch of Antioch, stuffing his genitals into his mouth. After this they dragged him into the middle of the city and killed him, along with many landowners, and burned them. Phocas made Bonosus count of the East and Kotton general and sent them against the Jews. They gathered troops and attacked them, killing many, mutilating others and driving them out of the city. Phocas put on horse races, and the Greens insulted him, saying, "You've been at the cup again! You've lost your mind again!" He gave orders to Constans, the prefect of the city, and he mutilated many of them and hung their limbs in the Sphendone. Others he beheaded, and still others he put in sacks and drowned in the sea. The Greens went and set fire to the praetorium, burning the secretum, the archives and the prisons. The prisoners came out and escaped. In his rage Phocas decreed that the Greens should no longer have any part in public life. Heraclius, the general of Africa, was being urged on by the senate, and he equipped his son Heraclius and sent him against the tyrant Phocas. His lieutenant Gregoras likewise sent his son Nicetas. They had agreed that whichever of the two arrived first and defeated the tyrant should reign. In the same year there was a very severe winter, so severe that the sea froze, and a great many fish were thrown up on shore. Then Phocas [ordered] Macrobius the scribon

[…] times. On the same praetorium: "The present praetorium was the house of a patrician widow named Marka. The prisons were stifling and dark and full of every kind of stench, and those shut up there could not bear it, so she gave her house for a fee to the emperor Phocas. Heraclius made it a prison, and

to be shot with arrows at the [?] and at the castellion of the Theodosians at the Hebdomon, hanging from the pole the recruits train on, until he died, since he had been privy to the plot. For Theodore, the prefect of Cappadocia, and Elpidius, the officer in charge of the armoury, together with various others, had plotted to kill Phocas at the horse races. Theodore, the praetorian prefect, gave a luncheon and began to reveal his purpose to them. As it happened, Anastasius, the count of the largesses, was also there. While the luncheon was going on and the plot was being laid out, Anastasius regretted being there. He did not say what was in his heart and kept silent. Elpidius pressed on: "Don't you want me, while he is sitting in his seat at the races, to [?] him, gouge out his eyes and so [?] him?" He also promised to give them weapons. Anastasius denounced the matter to Phocas, and Phocas ordered the prefect, Elpidius and the officials who knew of the plot to be questioned with the utmost rigour. Under questioning they confessed the details of the plot, including that they had wanted to make Theodore emperor. Phocas ordered Theodore, Elpidius, Anastasius and all who knew of the plot to be beheaded.

In this year, on 4 October, in the fourteenth indiction, Heraclius came from Africa. He brought ships fitted with towers, carrying reliquaries and icons of the Mother of God on their masts, as George of Pisidia also says, and a large army from Africa and Mauretania. Likewise Nicetas, the son of the patrician Gregoras, [came] from

[?] Alexandria and Pentapolis, with a large force of infantry. Heraclius was betrothed to Eudocia, the daughter of Rogas the African. At this time she was in Constantinople together with Epiphania, Heraclius' mother. [Phocas] seized them, both his mother and his betrothed Eudocia, and kept them under guard in the imperial monastery called the New Repentance. On reaching Abydos, Heraclius found Theodore, the count of Abydos, and by questioning him learned what was afoot in Constantinople. Phocas sent his brother Domentziolus the magister to guard the Long Walls. But when the magister learned that Heraclius had reached Abydos, he abandoned the walls and fled into Constantinople. At Abydos Heraclius received all those whom Phocas had exiled, and went on with them to Heraclea. Stephen, the metropolitan of Cyzicus, took a crown from the church of the holy Theotokos of Artake and brought it to Heraclius. On reaching Constantinople, Heraclius anchored in the harbour of [?]. Battle was joined, and by the grace of Christ he defeated the tyrant Phocas. The factions seized Phocas and killed him, burning him in the Bous. Heraclius entered the palace and was crowned by the patriarch Sergius in the chapel of St Stephen in the palace. On the same day his betrothed Eudocia was crowned Augusta. Both received the marriage crowns from the patriarch Sergius, so that on one and the same day he was proclaimed emperor and bridegroom. In the month of May the Persians campaigned against Syria. They took Apamea and Edessa and came as far as Antioch. The Romans met them in battle and were defeated, and the whole Roman army was destroyed, so that very few escaped. On 7 July, in the [?] indiction, Epiphania, the daughter of Eudocia, was born to the emperor, and on 15 August she was baptized at Blachernae by the patriarch Sergius. AM 6105 [?]. In this year the Persians took Caesarea in Cappadocia, and took many

tens of thousands captive there. When the emperor Heraclius came to the throne, he found the affairs of the Roman state in ruins. The barbarians had laid Europe waste, the Persians had overrun all of Asia and taken its cities captive, and they had destroyed the Roman army in battle. When he saw this he did not know what to do. He searched the army to see whether any survived of those who had campaigned with Phocas against Maurice and [shared] in his tyranny, and found only two in all the themes. In the same year, on 3 May, in the fifteenth indiction, Eudocia bore the emperor a son, Heraclius the younger, also called the New Constantine. On 14 August of the same fifteenth indiction Eudocia Augusta died. AM 6104. In this year, on 4 October, in the first indiction, Epiphania, the daughter of Heraclius, was crowned Augusta by the patriarch Sergius in the chapel of St Stephen in the palace. On 25 December of the same first indiction, Heraclius, the son of Heraclius and the New Constantine, was crowned by the patriarch Sergius. In the same year the Saracens campaigned against Syria. They ravaged a good many places and then went home. AM 6105. In this year the Persians took Damascus and carried off many people captive. The emperor Heraclius sent envoys to Chosroes asking him to stop shedding men's blood without mercy, and to set a tribute and accept payments instead. But Chosroes sent the envoys away with nothing and gave them no reply, for he hoped to seize the whole Roman empire. At the same time Heraclius married Martina and proclaimed her Augusta, having her crowned in the Augusteus; she was crowned by the patriarch Sergius. AM 6108 [?]. In this year the

Persians took the Jordan region, Palestine and the holy city by force. They killed many people there at the hands of the Jews: ninety thousand, as some say. For the Jews bought the Christians, each as far as his means allowed, and killed them. The Persians took Zacharias, the patriarch of Jerusalem, and the precious and life-giving Wood, along with many captives, and carried them off to Persia. In the same year Martina bore the emperor another Constantine, who was baptized at Blachernae by the patriarch Sergius. AM 6107. In this year the Persians took all of Egypt, Alexandria and Libya as far as Ethiopia. They took many captives and much booty and [?] money, and went home. They were not able to take Chalcedon, but they left a garrison to besiege it and withdrew. AM 6108. In this year the Persians campaigned against Chalcedon and took it by force. In the same year, on 1 January, in the fifth indiction, Constantine the younger, also called Heraclius, the son of Heraclius, became consul. He proclaimed as Caesar the little Constantine, his own brother, the son of Heraclius and Martina. AM 6109. In this year Heraclius again sent envoys to Chosroes in Persia asking for peace. Chosroes again sent them away, saying, "I will not spare you until you deny the Crucified, whom you call God, and worship the sun." AM [?]. In this year the Avars campaigned against Thrace. Heraclius sent to them asking for peace. When the Chagan agreed to make peace, the emperor went out beyond the Long Wall with the whole imperial guard and many great gifts and received the Chagan, having obtained pledges from him that they would make a peace treaty with one another. But that barbarian broke both the agreement and his oaths and suddenly, like a tyrant, advanced against the emperor.

The emperor was astounded at how unexpected this was and fled back to the city. The barbarian seized the imperial baggage and guard and as many people as he could catch. He went home after plundering many places in Thrace, which had been caught off guard because they had trusted in the hope of peace. AM 6111. George, bishop of Alexandria, year 1. In this year Heraclius sent envoys to the barbarian Chagan. He reproached him for the lawless things he had done and urged him to make peace, for he was planning a campaign against Persia and wanted to be at peace with the Chagan. Out of respect for the emperor's friendship, the Chagan professed to repent and promised to make peace. Terms were agreed, and the envoys returned in

In the same year the Persians took Ancyra in Galatia by force. AM 6112. In this year Chosroes made his yoke heavier on everyone, through bloodshed and taxation. Exalted by victory, he could no longer keep himself within bounds. Then Heraclius took up zeal for God. Having made peace with the Avars, as he believed, he moved the armies of Europe over to Asia, intending with God's help to march against Persia. AM 6113. In this year, on 4 April, in the tenth indiction, the emperor Heraclius celebrated the feast of Easter, and then at once, on the evening of Monday, set out against Persia. Being short of money, he took the funds of the pious foundations. He also took the polycandela and other liturgical vessels of the Great Church, and from them struck a great many nomismata and miliaresia. He left his own son to run affairs together with Sergius, the patriarch of Constantinople, and with the patrician Bonosus, a prudent man, intelligent and experienced in everything. He wrote to the Chagan of the Avars appealing to him to support the Roman cause, since he had made a pact of friendship with him, and he named him guardian of his son.

Setting out from the imperial city, he went by ship to the place called Pylae. From there he went on to the lands of the themes, where he gathered the armies and added new recruits to them. He began to drill them and taught them the business of war. He divided the army in two and ordered the halves to form battle lines and engage each other without bloodshed. He taught them the war cry, battle hymns, shouting and how to rouse themselves, so that when they found themselves in real wars they would not be taken aback, but would advance against the enemy with confidence, as if it were a game. The emperor took in his hands the image of the God-man that no hands had painted. The Word, who forms and shapes all things, produced it in an image as a likeness without painting, just as he produced a conception without seed. Trusting in this image painted by God, he began the contest. He pledged to the people that he would fight alongside them until death and would be joined with them as with his own children, for he wished to hold power not so much through fear as through love. He found the army sunk in great sloth and cowardice, in disorder and indiscipline, and scattered over many parts of the land, and he quickly gathered them all into one. All of them, as if with one voice, sang the praises of the emperor's might and courage. He encouraged them with these words: "You see, brothers and children, how the enemies of God have trampled our land, laid waste our cities and burned our altars. They have filled the tables of the bloodless sacrifices with murderous blood, and they defile with the most passionate pleasures the churches, which admit no passions." Then he again armed the people for military exercises and formed them into two armed lines: trumpets sounded, phalanxes of shields and armoured men stood ready. When the formations were firmly set, he ordered them to engage each other. Violent pushing and clashing broke out between them, and a semblance of war was staged. One could see a fearsome spectacle of slaughter without danger, onslaughts towards killing without blood, and the methods of war learned before the need arose, so that each man could take lessons from this harmless slaughter and be the safer for it. When he had armed them all in this way, he charged them to refrain from injustice and to hold fast to piety. On reaching the region of Armenia, [he sent] a host of horsemen ahead to fall secretly upon

[?] he intended to [?] the emperor. But the emperor's vanguard met them, brought their general to Heraclius as a prisoner, routed them and killed many. When winter came on, the emperor shut himself up in the region of Pontus, and the barbarians thought he would spend the winter there. But he slipped away from the Persians, turned back and invaded Persia. When the barbarians learned this, they lost heart at the unexpectedness of his invasion. Sarbaros, the Persian general, took his force and came into Cilicia, so that he could march into Roman territory and force the emperor to turn back. But he was afraid that the emperor would invade Persia through Armenia and throw it into turmoil, and he could not make up his mind what to do. Even so, he was forced to follow behind the Roman army, planning to take the battle by stealth and fall on them on a moonless night. But the moon was full that night, so his plan was foiled, and he reviled the moon, which they had once revered. The moon had happened to be full that very night by chance. After this Sarbaros [?] to attack the emperor and took to the mountains like gazelles, watching from the heights the skilful and wise generalship of the Romans. The emperor saw his cowardice and boldly made camp in [?] places, at complete ease, to provoke him to battle. The Persians would often come down from the mountain in secret and fight skirmishes, and the Romans won every one of them. The army grew more and more confident as they saw the emperor leaping out ahead in everything and fighting with great daring. Now a certain Persian, who had come over as a deserter a little earlier, was in the emperor's army. He ran off to the Persians, hoping that they would destroy the Roman army. But when he saw their cowardice, he came back to the emperor after ten days and gave him an exact account of the barbarians' timidity. Sarbaros could no longer bear staying on the mountain and was forced to rush into battle. He divided his army into three parts and came down suddenly as day was breaking, before the sun had risen, ready for battle. The emperor knew of it in advance. He likewise drew up the army in three phalanxes and led it out to battle. When the sun rose, the emperor was on the eastern side, and its rays blinded the Persians, who worshipped the sun as a god. The emperor had his troops pretend to turn in flight, and [Textual notes: 'region' (klēma) a; [?] 'Sarbaros' / 'the barbarian' in various copies; [?] 'skirmishes'; 'prevailed' in variant spellings; 'reported' f; 'Sobaros' in the common text; 'to rush' (ormisai) in the common text.]

the barbarians all broke their ranks, thinking that they were chasing them headlong. Then the Romans turned around, routed them bravely and killed many. They drove them as far as the mountain, forced them over cliffs and into impassable places, and crushed them all there. On the cliffs the Persians [?] like wild goats. The Romans also took many alive. They captured their camp too, and all their baggage. Then the Romans raised their hands to heaven and gave thanks to God, and they prayed fervently for the emperor who had led them so well. For men who had once not dared even to look at Persian dust now found the Persians' tents untouched and plundered them. Who would have hoped that the Persians, the hardest of all nations to fight, would ever turn their backs to the Romans? The emperor left the army with the general to spend the winter in Armenia and himself returned to Byzantium. In this year Muhammad appeared [?]; nine years; the thirteenth year of Heraclius' reign. A.M. [?]. In this year, on 15 March of the eleventh indiction, the emperor Heraclius set out from the imperial city and arrived in Armenia with all speed. Chosroes, king of the Persians, sent Sarbarazas with his army to invade the land of the Romans. Heraclius wrote to

Chosroes, telling him either to accept peace or he would himself invade Persia with his army. But Chosroes would not accept peace, nor did he take any notice of what was said [?], namely that Heraclius dared to approach Persia. On the twentieth of April the emperor invaded Persia. When Chosroes learned of this, he ordered Sarbarazas to come back. He gathered his armies from all over Persia, handed them over to Shahin, and ordered him to join them quickly with Sarbarazas and then march against the emperor. Heraclius called his army together and stirred them with words of encouragement, saying: "Men, my brothers, let us keep the fear of God in mind and fight to avenge the insult done to God. Let us stand bravely against enemies who have done many terrible things to Christians. Let us honour the sovereign power of the Romans, which has no master, and stand against enemies armed for impiety. Let us take up faith, the slayer of murderers. Let us bear in mind that we are inside the land of the Persians, and that flight carries great danger. Let us avenge the defilement of virgins, and let our hearts ache when we see the mutilated limbs of our soldiers. The danger is not without reward; it brings eternal glory. Let us stand like men, and the Lord God will fight on our side [?] and destroy our enemies." When the emperor had urged the people with these and other words, one man answered for them all: "You have opened our hearts, Master, by opening your mouth to exhort us. Your words have sharpened our swords and brought them to life. Your words have given us wings. We blush when we see you going ahead of us in battle, and we will follow you in all your commands." The emperor took the army and went straight into the interior of Persia, burning the countryside and the villages. Then a fearful wonder took place. At the summer solstice the air turned cool and dewy and refreshed the Roman army, so that they took heart and grew hopeful. Heraclius heard that Chosroes was in the city of Ganzak with forty thousand fighting men, and he set out against him. He sent some of his Saracens ahead, and they met Chosroes' outpost, killed some of them, put the rest in fetters and brought them with their commander to the emperor. When Chosroes learned of this, he abandoned the city and the army and fled. Heraclius pursued them and killed those he overtook, while the rest fled and scattered. The emperor took the city of Ganzak in the East, where there was the temple of Fire and the treasure of Croesus, king of the Lydians, and the deception of the coals [?]. The one who took these things made for Dastagerd

[?]. The emperor set out from Ganzak and took Thebarmais. He entered it and burned the temple of Fire, and when he had burned the whole city he went after Chosroes into the narrow country of the Medes. In that difficult terrain Chosroes kept moving from one place to another, and Heraclius, pursuing him, sacked many cities and districts. When winter came, he held a council about where to spend the winter with his people. Some said in Albania, others that they should attack Chosroes himself. The emperor ordered the people to purify themselves for three days. Then he opened the holy Gospels of God and found that they directed him to spend the winter in Albania. So he turned at once and set out for Albania. On the way, with a great number of Persian captives in his train, he suffered many attacks from the Persian armies, but with God's help he won victory over them all. A severe winter and bitter cold came down on him on the road, and he reached Albania with fifty thousand prisoners. Taking pity on them in his compassionate heart, he freed them from their bonds and gave them care and rest, so that they all prayed with tears that he would become the deliverer of Persia as well, and destroy Chosroes, the destroyer of the world. Second year of Muhammad [?]. A.M. 6113. In this year Chosroes, king of the Persians, appointed Sarablangas as general, a man swollen with great arrogance. He gave him an army of the troops called Chosroegetai and Perozitai and sent him to Albania against Heraclius. They invaded the borders of Albania but did not dare face the emperor in battle. Instead they seized the passes leading into Persia, intending to ambush him there. At the beginning of spring Heraclius set out from Albania. He made his way into Persia across open plains with plenty of food, covering a great distance by a long road

[?]. Sarablangas drove on by a narrow road, as a short cut, to get ahead of him in Persian territory. Heraclius encouraged the people, saying: "Let us recognize, brothers, that the Persian army, wandering around in impassable country, is wearing out its horses and exhausting its men. Let us hurry and march against Chosroes with all speed, so that we can fall on him unexpectedly and throw him into confusion." But the people would not agree to do this, especially the allies, the Lazi, the Abasgians and the Iberians. As a result they ran into misfortune. For Sarbarazas arrived with his people, whom Chosroes had armed with all his might and sent against Heraclius through Armenia. Sarablangas followed behind him and did not engage, waiting [?] for Sarbarazas so that they could fight the battle together. When the Romans learned that Sarbarazas was approaching, they lost their nerve. They fell at the emperor's feet and, with tears, repented of their wicked disobedience, realizing how wrong it is for a servant not to yield to his master's counsel. They said: "Give us your hand, Master, before they destroy us wretched men! For we [?] you in whatever you command." Then the emperor hurried to engage Sarablangas before he could join Sarbarazas' forces. He made many sallies against him by night and by day and filled him with fear. Then he left both of them behind and drove hard against Chosroes. But two of the Romans deserted to the Persians and persuaded them that the Romans were fleeing out of cowardice. Another rumour also reached them, that Shahin, a Persian general, was coming to their aid with another army. When they learned this, Sarbarazas and Sarablangas were eager to attack Heraclius before Shahin arrived, so as to win the glory of victory for themselves. Trusting the deserters, they marched against Heraclius, came close to him and made camp, intending to engage him at dawn. But Heraclius set out in the evening, and they marched through the whole night. When he was far away from them, he found a green plain and camped there. The barbarians thought they were fleeing out of cowardice and rode after them in disorder to catch them. But he turned to meet them and joined battle with them. He seized a wooded hill and massed his people on it, and with God's help he routed the Persians and chased them through

the ravines, killing a great number. While this fighting was going on, Shahin also arrived with his army. The emperor routed him too, killed many of his men and scattered the rest in flight. He also captured their baggage train. Sarbarazas joined Shahin and gathered the barbarians who had survived, and again they planned to march against Heraclius. The emperor drove on into the land of the Huns and its difficult country, through rough and impassable places. The barbarians followed behind them. The Lazi and the Abasgians lost their nerve, broke away from their alliance with the Romans and went back to their own country. Shahin was delighted at this and marched against Heraclius with the barbarians in a great rage. The emperor gathered his army, lifted their spirits with words and won them over with encouragement, saying: "Do not let their numbers alarm you, brothers. For if God wills, one will chase a thousand. So let us offer ourselves to God as a sacrifice for the salvation of our brothers. Let us win the martyrs' crown, so that the time to come may praise us and God may give us our reward." With these and many other words he put courage into the army. With a cheerful face he drew up his line for battle. The two sides stood a short distance apart and fought each other from morning until evening. When evening came, the emperor went on with his march. Again the barbarians rode after him. They changed their route, hoping to get ahead of him, but they blundered into marshy ground, lost their way and fell into great danger. The emperor crossed over and passed through the districts of Persarmenia. That country was held by the Persians, so many men flocked to Sarbarazas and his forces grew. When winter came, this host scattered to their own homes. When Heraclius learned of this, he planned to take the battle by stealth at night, while winter was pressing and the barbarian suspected nothing. He picked out strong horses and armed the bravest of the army in two divisions. He ordered one to go ahead against the barbarian, while he followed behind them with the other. They hurried through the night and reached the place called Salbanon at the ninth hour of the night. The Persians who were there learned of the attack, rose up and rushed against them. The Romans [killed] them all

except for one man, who brought word to the barbarian. The barbarian got up, mounted a horse naked and barefoot, and saved himself by fleeing. But the emperor caught his wives and the whole flower of Persia, officers, satraps and picked soldiers, who had climbed onto the roofs of the houses and were fighting from there, and he brought them down with fire. Some he killed, others he burned, others were taken in handcuffs [?]. Almost none of Sarbarazas' people escaped. They also took Sarbarazas' arms, his golden shield, sword and spear, his jewelled golden belt and his shoes. Taking all these, he marched against those who were scattered in the villages. When they learned that Sarbarazas had fled, they fled headlong. He pursued them, killed many and took prisoners, and the rest went back to Persia in disgrace. The emperor gathered his camp together and spent the winter in those parts in high spirits. A.M. 6116. In this year, on 1 March, the emperor Heraclius gathered his army and held a council about which road to take. For two roads lay before him, both narrow and hard going, one leading to Taranton, the other to the land of the Syrians. The road to Taranton was more advantageous, but it had no provisions of any kind. The road to the land of the Syrians, which crossed the Taurus, offered [?] and plenty of supplies. Everyone chose this one, even though it was steeper and deep in snow. They crossed it with great toil and in seven days reached the river Tigris. They crossed it and reached Martyropolis and Amida, and the army and the captives rested. From there the emperor was able to send letters to Byzantium, report everything that had happened to him, and fill the city with joy. The barbarian gathered his scattered people and came against him. The emperor picked out a select body of soldiers and sent them off to guard the passes leading to him. He himself hurried out by the eastern routes and went to face the barbarian head on. He crossed the river Nymphius and reached the Euphrates, where the bridge woven of ropes
[Textual notes:] 'made' (epoiēsato) A, b; 'procured' (eporisato) common text. 'These things' added from A. 'And' A; 'narrow and' common text. 'Constant march' [?] common text. 'Seven' [?]

and reins [?]. Sarbarazas untied the ropes of the bridge and drew the whole bridge across from one bank to the other. When the emperor arrived and found no way to cross by the bridge, he went along the bank and found a ford. Against all expectation he crossed it safely in the month of March. He reached Samosata, crossed the Taurus again and came to Germanicea, then passed Adana and came to the river Sarus. Sarbaros stretched the bridge back into its proper place, crossed the Euphrates unhindered and followed behind him. The emperor crossed the bridge over the Sarus, and finding rest there for the army and the animals, he camped there and let them rest. Sarbaros also arrived on the opposite side. When he found the bridge and its towers held by the Romans, he made camp. Many of the Romans rushed out across the bridge without orders, fell on the Persians and made a great slaughter of them. The emperor tried to stop them from rushing out in disorder, in case the enemy found a way to get onto the bridge and cross over with them. But the troops would not obey the emperor. Sarbaros laid an ambush and made a show of fleeing, and so drew many Romans, against the emperor's wishes, to cross in pursuit of him. Then he turned back, routed them, and killed all he caught outside the bridge, and they paid the penalty for their disobedience. The emperor saw that the barbarians had broken ranks in the pursuit and that many of the Romans posted at the towers were being killed by them, and he advanced against them. A gigantic man came out to meet the emperor and attacked him in the middle of the bridge. The emperor struck him down and threw him into the stream of the river. When he fell, the barbarians turned and fled. The bridge was so narrow that the barbarians threw themselves into the river, while others were cut down by swords. But the mass of the barbarians spread out along the banks of the river, shooting arrows and holding out, and would not let the Romans cross. The emperor crossed and bravely held out against the barbarians with a few of his companions, fighting beyond human strength, so that Sarbaros was astonished. He said to a certain Cosmas who was standing near him, a deserter from the Romans and a

renegade: "Do you see the Caesar [?], Cosmas, how boldly he stands in the battle, fighting alone against such a multitude, and how he shakes off the missiles like an anvil?" For he could be recognized by his true imperial boots. He took many blows, but [?] none. When they had fought this battle and evening had come, they drew apart from each other, and Sarbaros, afraid, withdrew during the night. The emperor gathered his people and set out for the city of Sebasteia. He crossed the river Halys and spent the whole winter in that region. Chosroes went mad with rage. He sent men and took all the treasures of the churches under Persian rule. He also forced the Christians to join the creed of Nestorius, in order to wound the emperor. [?] Leader of the Arabs: Muhammad [?], nine years. A.M. 6117. In this year Chosroes, king of the Persians, raised a new army, enlisting foreigners, citizens and household slaves, and choosing men from every nation. He handed this levy over to the general Shahin. He also took a further fifty thousand picked men from the phalanx of Sarbaros, joined them to it, and called them the Golden Spears. These he sent against the emperor. Sarbaros, with the rest of his army, he sent against Constantinople, so that, by making an agreement with the Huns of the West, whom they call Avars, and with the [?], the Slavs and the Gepids, they might march against the city and besiege it. When the emperor learned of this, he divided his army into three divisions. One he sent off to guard the city. The second he handed over to his own brother Theodore and ordered him to fight Shahin. The third he took himself and set out for Lazica. While he was staying there [?], he called the Turks from the East, whom they call Khazars, to his alliance. Shahin, with his newly levied troops, caught up with the emperor's brother Theodore and armed for battle. But God

…through the intercessions of the all-praised [Mother of God], God above all working with them. When battle was joined, hail came down on the barbarians against all expectation and struck many of them, while the Roman line enjoyed calm weather. The Romans routed the Persians and killed a great multitude. When Chosroes learned of this he was enraged with Sain. Sain fell ill from deep despondency and died. Chosroes ordered his body to be pickled in salt and brought to him, and he subjected the corpse to many outrages. Meanwhile the Khazars broke through the Caspian Gates and invaded Persia, entering the country of Adraigan with their general Ziebel, who was second in rank to the Khagan. Wherever they passed they took the Persians captive and gave the cities and villages over to fire. The emperor set out from Lazica and met them. When Ziebel saw him he ran forward, embraced him round the neck and did obeisance to him, while the Persians watched from the city of Tiflis. The whole people of the Turks fell face down on the ground, as if in a trance, and honoured the emperor with an honour unheard of among foreign peoples [?]. Their chiefs too climbed up on rocks and fell down in the same posture. Ziebel also presented his own son, a youth whose beard was just beginning, to the emperor, for he was charmed by the emperor's conversation and astonished at his appearance and his wisdom. Ziebel picked out forty thousand brave men and gave them to the emperor as allies, and he himself returned to his own country. The emperor took these men and advanced against Chosroes. Sarbaros, meanwhile, attacked Chalcedon, and the Avars came from Thrace, drew near the City and tried to take it. They moved many siege engines against it, and they brought dugout boats [?] from the Danube in a countless multitude past all numbering and filled the gulf of the Horn. For ten days they besieged the City by land and sea, but by the power and help of God and the intercessions of the immaculate Virgin Mother of God they were defeated. After losing great multitudes on land and sea, in deep disgrace they

turned back home. Sarbaros, at Chalcedon, [?] did not withdraw. Instead he wintered there, raiding and plundering the regions across the strait [?] and their cities. A.M. 6118. In this year, starting in the month of September, Heraclius invaded Persia with the Turks. This was unexpected because of the winter, and when Chosroes learned of it he was thrown into consternation. The Turks, however, seeing the winter and the constant raids of the Persians, could not bear to share the emperor's hardships. They began to slip away a few at a time, until they had all abandoned him and gone home. The emperor addressed his army, saying: “Know, brothers, that no one is willing to fight on our side except God alone and the Mother who bore him without seed, so that he may show his might and send down his help.” Chosroes gathered all his armies and appointed Rhazates, a most warlike and brave man, as their general, and sent him against Heraclius. The emperor kept burning the cities and villages of Persia and putting to the sword any Persians he caught. On the ninth of October, in the fifteenth indiction, he reached the district of Chamaetha and rested the army there for a week. Rhazates arrived at Ganzaka and fell in behind him. He followed the Romans, who consumed the provisions ahead of him, while he, coming behind like a hungry dog, was barely fed on their crumbs. Because he could find no supplies, many of his animals died. On the first of December the emperor reached a great river called the Zab. He crossed it and camped near the city of Nineveh. Rhazates, following him, also reached the ford. He went down three miles, found another ford and crossed. The emperor sent out Baanes the general with a few picked soldiers. Baanes came upon a Persian company, killed its commander and brought back his head and his solid-gold sword. He killed many others and brought back twenty-six alive, among whom

was Rhazates' sword-bearer. This man reported to the emperor that Rhazates meant to give him battle, since Chosroes had ordered him to do so, and that Chosroes had sent him three thousand armed men. These, however, had not yet arrived. When the emperor learned this he sent the baggage train on ahead. He followed behind it, looking for a place where he could fight before the three thousand joined the enemy. He found a plain well suited for battle, addressed the army and drew up his line. Rhazates came up too and drew up his forces in three divisions, and he advanced against the emperor. The battle was joined on the twelfth of December, a Saturday. The emperor dashed out ahead of everyone and met the commander of the Persians, and by the power of God and the help of the Mother of God he struck him down. The men who had dashed out with that commander were routed. The emperor then met another man and struck him down as well. A third attacked him, struck him on the lip with a spear and wounded him, but the emperor killed him too. Then the trumpets sounded and the two sides clashed. As the fighting grew fierce, the emperor's horse, called Phallas [?] or Dorkon, was wounded by the foot soldiers and took a lance thrust in the thigh. It also took many sword blows on its face, but it was wearing armour of sinew [?], so it was not hurt and the blows had no effect. Rhazates fell in the battle, together with the three tourmarchs of the Persians, nearly all their officers and the greater part of their army. Fifty Romans were slain. A good many were wounded, but only ten of these died. The battle was fought from early morning until the eleventh hour. The Romans took twenty-eight Persian banners, not counting those that were broken. They stripped the dead and took their breastplates, their helmets and all their weapons. The two armies stayed two bowshots apart, for neither side had been routed. During the night the Roman troops watered and fed [?] their horses. The Persian cavalry stood until the seventh hour

of the night over the bodies of the dead Persians. At the eighth hour of the night they moved off and returned to their camp. They took it with them, went away and camped at the foot of a rugged mountain, gripped by fear. The Romans took many solid-gold swords, gold-worked belts and pearls, and Rhazates' shield, which was solid gold with a hundred and twenty plates. They also took his solid-gold breastplate, and they brought back his tunic together with his head, his bracelets and his solid-gold saddle. Barsamouses, the ruler of the Iberians who had come under the Persians and the Romans [?], was taken alive. Not once in the whole day did the battle come to a halt. So the Romans won, but this happened through the help of God alone.

The emperor gave the army fresh heart and marched against Chosroes, hoping to frighten him into sending for Sarbaros from Byzantium, that is, from Chalcedon. On the twenty-first of December the emperor learned that Rhazates' army, having escaped from the battle, had joined the three thousand sent by Chosroes and was following behind him. Having reached Nineveh and crossed the great river Zab, [the emperor] [?] Chosroes. George marched forty-eight miles through the night and seized the four bridges of the Lesser Zab. He found Persians in the forts and took them alive. On the twenty-third of December the emperor reached the bridges, crossed them and camped at the houses of Yesdem. There he rested the army and the horses, and he celebrated the feast of Christ's Nativity in that place. When Chosroes learned that the Romans had seized the bridges of the Lesser Zab, he sent word to the Persian army that had been with Rhazates, telling them to make all haste, get ahead of the emperor and come to him. They hurried, crossed the Lesser Zab at other places, got ahead of the emperor and marched in front of him. The emperor reached another palace of Chosroes, called Rhousa, and this too he

destroyed. He suspected that the enemy would give battle at the bridge over the river Torna. But when they saw him coming they abandoned the bridge and fled. The emperor crossed unhindered and came to another palace, called Beklal. Chosroes had also built a hippodrome there, and the emperor destroyed this as well. Some of the Armenians serving with the Persians came to the emperor and said: “Chosroes is camped with the elephants and his own army five miles beyond the palace called Dastagerd, at a place called Barasroth. He has ordered the army to gather there to fight you. For there is a river there that is hard to cross, with a narrow bridge, many narrow passages between the buildings, and [?] foul streams.” After taking counsel with his officers and the army, the emperor stayed in the palace of Beklal. For in one enclosure there he found three [hundred?] fattened ostriches, in another about five hundred fattened gazelles, and in another a hundred fattened wild asses, and he gave them all to the army as a gift. They celebrated the first of January there. They also found sheep, pigs and cattle beyond number, and the whole army rested, enjoying themselves and glorifying God. They seized the herdsmen, and from them he learned exactly what had happened: on the twenty-third of December Chosroes heard that the emperor had crossed the bridge over the Torna, and at once he left the palace at Dastagerd. [The emperor] took another road and went to another palace, called Bebdarch. They destroyed this too and set it on fire, and they gave thanks to God, who had done such wonders through the intercessions of the Mother of God. For who would have expected Chosroes to flee before the emperor of the Romans from the palaces at Dastagerd and go to Ctesiphon? For twenty-four years he had not been able to bear the sight of Ctesiphon, and his royal residence had been at Dastagerd. The Roman troops found

in the palace of Dastagerd three hundred [?] Roman standards, which he had captured at various times. They also found stores of goods left behind: a great deal of aloes, including large logs of aloe weighing ten and eight [?] pounds, a great deal of silk, pepper, linen shirts far beyond measure, sugar, ginger [?] and many other goods. Some found uncoined silver, garments of pure silk, pile [?] carpets and needlework rugs in great quantity and of great beauty. Because these were too heavy, they burned them all. They also burned all of Chosroes' pavilions and the tents [?] he used to pitch when he camped in the field, and many of his statues. In these palaces he also found ostriches, gazelles, wild asses, peacocks and pheasants in countless numbers, and huge lions and tigers kept alive for his hunting. Many of the captives fled to the emperor, people of Edessa and of Alexandria and a great multitude from other cities. The emperor also celebrated the feast of Lights at Dastagerd, cheering and refreshing both the army and the horses. Meanwhile he was destroying Chosroes' palaces, buildings of the highest value, wonderful and astonishing, which he razed to the ground, so that Chosroes might learn what pain the Romans had suffered when he laid waste their cities and burned them. Many of the palace attendants were also captured. When they were asked when he had left Dastagerd, they said: “Nine days before you arrived, he heard that you were coming and secretly broke through the city wall near the palace. In this way, held up by others [?], he went out through the gardens, he, his wife and his children, so that there would be no uproar in the city. Neither the armies nor the officials knew about him until he had gone five miles. Only then did he send word for them to follow him to Ctesiphon.” And the man who could not manage five miles a day covered twenty-five in his flight. His wives and children, who had never laid eyes on one another, now fled in a jumbled crowd, shoving one another aside. When night overtook him, Chosroes went to lodge in the house of a lowly farmer, barely squeezing through its door. When Heraclius saw that door afterwards, he marvelled. Three days later Chosroes reached Ctesiphon. So it was that the man who had received an oracle from sorcerers and astrologers twenty-four years earlier, when he was besieging Daras in the days of Phocas, emperor of the Romans, that he would perish whenever he went to Ctesiphon, and who could not bear to travel even a single mile from Dastagerd in that direction, now went there as a fugitive. He did not dare to stay even there. He crossed the pontoon bridge over the river Tigris to the city on the other side, which we call Seleucia and the Persians call Gouedeser. He deposited all his money there and settled there with his wife Sirem and three other women, who were his daughters [?]. The rest of his wives and his many children he sent forty miles further east, to a strong place. Some of the Persians slandered Sarbaros to Chosroes, saying that he favoured the Romans and spoke against him. So Chosroes sent his sword-bearer with an order to Kardarigas, Sarbarazas' fellow general at Chalcedon. In it he wrote that Kardarigas was to kill Sarbarazas, then take the Persian army and hurry to Persia to support him. The man carrying the letter was seized by the Romans in Galatia. His captors slipped past the Persians, brought him to Byzantium and handed him over to the emperor's son. When the emperor learned the truth from the messenger, he at once sent for Sarbarazas. Sarbarazas came and stood before the emperor. The emperor handed him the letter to Kardarigas and showed him the messenger. He read the letter, and once he was convinced it was true he immediately changed sides and made a treaty with the emperor's son and the patriarch. He then forged Chosroes' letter, adding to it the names of forty other satraps, officers, commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds who were to be killed along with himself. He skilfully affixed the seal, assembled the commanders and Kardarigas himself, read out the letter and said to Kardarigas: “Do you agree to do this?” The officers were filled with rage. They renounced Chosroes and made peace terms with the emperor, and after taking counsel together they decided to withdraw from Chalcedon and go home without doing any damage.

Heraclius wrote to Chosroes: “I am in pursuit, yet I am running toward peace. I do not burn Persia willingly; you force me to do it. So let us throw down our weapons even now and embrace peace. Let us put out the fire before it consumes everything.” Chosroes would not accept this, and the hatred of the Persian people against him grew greatly. He conscripted all the men of his officials and all the servants of his own household and of his wives. He armed them all and sent them off to join the army of Rhazates and take up position at the river Arba, twelve miles from Ctesiphon. He ordered them to cut the bridge [and the pontoon bridge] as soon as the emperor had crossed the river. On the seventh of January the emperor set out from Dastagerd. After marching for three days he camped twelve miles from the river Arba, where the Persian camp was. They also had two hundred elephants there. The emperor sent George, the tourmarch of the Armeniacs, to go as far as the river and find out whether the Arba could be forded. George found that they had cut the bridges and that the Arba had no ford, and he returned to the emperor. The emperor then moved off and came to Siazouros, and all through the month of February he went about burning the countryside and the cities. In the month of March he came to a village called Barzan and spent seven days there. He sent Mezezios the general out on a raid, and Goundabounas came over to him. This man was a commander of a thousand in Sarbaros' army, and he came with five others, three counts and two officers. Mezezios brought them to the emperor. Goundabounas reported important news to the emperor. “When Chosroes fled from Dastagerd and went to Ctesiphon and Seleucia,” he said, “he fell ill with dysentery and wanted to crown his son Merdasas, whom Sirem had borne him. He crossed back over the river, taking with him Merdasas, Sirem and her other son Saliar, but he left his firstborn son Siroes, Siroes' brothers and his own wives on the other side of the river. When Siroes learned that he meant to crown Merdasas, he was alarmed, and he sent his foster-brother to me with the message: ‘Come across the river so that I can meet you.’ I was afraid to cross because of Chosroes, so I sent him word: ‘Write to me through your foster-brother whatever you want.’ And Siroes wrote to me: ‘You know how the state

of the Persians has been ruined by that wicked man Chosroes. He wants to crown Merdasas and has slighted me, his firstborn. If you speak to the army and persuade them to accept me, I will raise their pay, I will make peace with the emperor of the Romans, and we will be able to live well. So work hard with your men to make me king. I will promote [?] and support all of you, and you above all.’ I sent him word through his foster-brother: ‘If I can, I will persuade the army and do my utmost.’ I then persuaded twenty-two counts and brought them over to my view, along with other officers and many soldiers. I reported this to Siroes, and he sent me word that on the twenty-third of March I was to take the younger guardsmen and meet him at the pontoon bridge over the river Tigris, so that we could bring him to the army and march against Chosroes. With Siroes are the two sons of Sarbarazas, the son of Esdem, many other sons of officers and the son of Aram, all picked men. If they manage to kill Chosroes, well and good. But if they fail, they will all desert with Siroes to the emperor. He has sent me to you, my lord, for he knows that the emperor of the Romans once saved Chosroes and has since suffered many wrongs at his hands, and that because of that man's [?] the emperor can trust me.” The emperor Heraclius sent him back to Siroes with instructions to open the prisons, bring out the Romans held in them, give them weapons, and so move against Chosroes. Siroes obeyed the emperor. He brought out the prisoners [?] and attacked his father Chosroes, the parricide. Chosroes tried to flee but could not, and he was seized. They treated him with contempt, bound his arms tightly behind his back with iron fetters, hung iron weights on his feet and neck, and took him into the house of darkness, which he himself had built new and fortified as a treasury. There they starved him, giving him a meagre ration of bread and water. For Siroes said: “Let him eat the gold he gathered for nothing, [?].” He sent the satraps to insult him and spit on him. He brought in Merdasas, the son Chosroes had wanted to crown, and slaughtered him before his father's eyes. He killed all his other children before his eyes too, and he sent all his enemies to insult him [and beat him] and spit on him. For five days

…when they had done this, Siroes ordered him to be shot down with arrows, and so, little by little and in torment, he gave up his wicked soul. Then Siroes wrote to Heraclius with the good news that the vile Chosroes had been killed. He made a lasting peace with him and handed back to him all the Christians held in prisons, and all the captives throughout Persia, together with the patriarch Zacharias and the precious and life-giving wood of the Cross that Sarbarazas had taken from Jerusalem when he captured the city. Leader of the Arabs, Muhammad, 9 years. A.M. 6119 [?]. — King of the Persians, Siroes, year [?]. In this year, after peace had been made between the Persians and the Romans, the emperor sent his brother Theodore with letters and with men of Siroes, king of the Persians. They were to send the Persians in Edessa, Palestine, Jerusalem and the other Roman cities back to Persia in peace, so that they could pass through Roman territory unharmed. The emperor had made war on Persia for six years, and in the seventh he made peace and returned to Constantinople with great joy. In this he fulfilled a kind of mystical figure. For God created the whole of creation in six days and called the seventh the day of rest. In the same way the emperor carried out many labours over six years, and in the seventh year he returned to the city in peace and joy and rested. When the people of the city learned that he was coming, they were all seized by an irrepressible longing and went out to Hieria to meet him, with the patriarch and his son, the emperor Constantine. They carried olive branches and lamps and acclaimed him with joy and tears. His son came forward and fell at his feet, and they embraced each other, and both of them wet the ground with their tears. When the people saw this, they all gave thanks…

In this year, at the beginning of spring, the emperor set out from the imperial city and travelled to Jerusalem, bringing the precious and life-giving wood of the Cross so that he could give thanks to God. When he arrived at Tiberias, the Christians brought charges against a man named Benjamin, saying that he was mistreating them. He was a very wealthy man [?], and he received the emperor and his army as guests. The emperor condemned him, saying, “For what reason do you mistreat the Christians?” He answered, “Because they are enemies of my faith,” for he was a Jew. The emperor admonished him and won him over, and baptized him in the house of Eustathius of Neapolis, a Christian who had also received the emperor as a guest. On entering Jerusalem, the emperor restored Zacharias the patriarch, and the precious and [?]
[After relating these things, he adds:] Not long afterwards Heraclius also went to Byzantium, where the people received him with great acclamation and surpassing glory. [A little later:]

wood to its proper place. He gave many thanks to God and drove the Hebrews out of the holy city, ordering that they should not be allowed to come within three miles of it. When he reached Edessa, he gave the church back to the Orthodox; the Nestorians had held it since the time of Chosroes. When he came to Hierapolis, he heard that Siroes, king of the Persians, had died, and that Adeser his son had taken over the Persian kingdom. Adeser held power for seven months. Then Sarbarazas rose against him, struck him down, and reigned over the Persians for two months. The Persians killed him and made Borane, the daughter of Chosroes, their sovereign, and she held the Persian kingdom for seven months. She was succeeded by Hormisdas, who was driven out by the Saracens, and from that time to this day the Persian kingdom has been under the Arabs. Leader of the Arabs, Muhammad, 9 years. A.M. 6121 [?]. — King of the Persians, Hormisdas. In this year, while the emperor Heraclius was in Hierapolis, Athanasius, the patriarch of the Jacobites, came to him. He was a clever man and a villain, with the villainy that is innate in the Syrians. He opened discussions with the emperor about the faith, and Heraclius promised to make him patriarch of Antioch if he would accept the Council of Chalcedon. Athanasius pretended to accept the council and confessed the two natures united in Christ. He then asked the emperor about the energy and

the wills: how ought these to be spoken of in Christ, as twofold or as single? The emperor, baffled by these unfamiliar terms, wrote to Sergius, the patriarch of Constantinople. He also summoned Cyrus, the bishop of Phasis, and when he questioned him, he found that Cyrus agreed with Sergius on the one will and the one energy. For Sergius was of Syrian birth and had Jacobite parents, and he confessed one natural will and one energy in Christ and wrote that this was so. The emperor followed the advice of both of them, and found that Athanasius too agreed with them. Athanasius knew that wherever one energy is spoken of, one nature is also recognized. Persuaded on this point, the emperor wrote to John, the pope of Rome, setting out the view of the two of them. But the pope did not accept their heresy. When George of Alexandria died, Cyrus was sent as bishop to Alexandria. He joined with Theodore, the bishop of Pharan, and brought about that watered-down union, in which they too wrote of one natural energy in Christ. As a result of these events, the Council of Chalcedon and the catholic Church fell into great disgrace. For the Jacobites and the Theodosians boasted, saying, “It is not we who have entered into communion with Chalcedon. Rather, Chalcedon has entered into communion with us, since through the one energy it has confessed one nature of Christ.” Meanwhile Sophronius was ordained bishop of Jerusalem. He gathered the bishops under his authority and anathematized the Monothelete doctrine, and he sent synodical letters to Sergius of Constantinople and to John of Rome. When Heraclius heard this, he was ashamed. He did not wish [?] to undo his own decisions, but on the other hand he could not bear the reproach. Then, thinking he was doing something great, he issued the so-called Edict, which laid down that neither one energy nor two should be confessed in Christ. When the followers of Severus read it, they mocked the catholic Church in taverns and bathhouses, saying, “The Chalcedonians used to think like Nestorius. Then they came to their senses and returned to the truth, uniting with us through the one energy into the one [?] nature. But now they have condemned what was right, and they have lost both, since they confess neither one nor two in Christ.” After the death of Sergius, Pyrrhus succeeded to the throne of Constantinople, and he impiously upheld the doctrines decreed by Sergius and Cyrus. When Heraclius died and his son Constantine became emperor, Pyrrhus, together with Martina, killed him with poison.
