and Heraclonas, the son of Martina, became emperor. But the senate and the city expelled Pyrrhus as an impious man, together with Martina and her son. Constans, the son of Constantine, became emperor, and Paul was ordained bishop of Constantinople; he too was a heretic. John, the bishop of Rome, assembled a synod of bishops and anathematized the heresy of the Monothelites. In the same way various bishops in Africa, Byzacium, Numidia and Mauretania assembled and anathematized the Monophysites. When John of Rome fell asleep, Theodore was ordained pope in his place. Pyrrhus went to Africa, where he met the most holy Maximus, revered for his monastic achievements, and the godly hierarchs of that region. They refuted him, won him over, and sent him to Pope Theodore in Rome. He submitted a statement of orthodox faith to the pope and was received by him. But he left Rome, went to Ravenna, and returned like a dog to his own vomit. When Pope Theodore learned this, he called together the whole body of the Church and went to the tomb of Peter, chief of the apostles. There he asked for the divine chalice, let some drops of the life-giving blood of Christ fall into the ink, and with his own hand wrote [?] the deposition of Pyrrhus and of those in communion with him. When Pyrrhus reached Constantinople and Paul had died, the reckless heterodox installed Pyrrhus on the throne of Constantinople again. After Pope Theodore died, the most holy Martin was ordained in Rome. Maximus also arrived in Rome from Africa and fired Pope Martin with zeal, and they assembled a synod of 150 bishops. They anathematized Sergius and Pyrrhus, Cyrus and Paul, and they clearly set forth the two wills and energies of Christ our God. They proclaimed this in the ninth year of the reign of Constans, the grandson of Heraclius, in the eighth indiction. When Constans learned of it, he was filled with rage. He had the holy Martin and Maximus brought to Constantinople, tortured them, and sent them into exile in the regions of Cherson; and many

of the orthodox [?] bishops he also punished. After [?] … and striking us, the people of Christ. Then for the first time came the defeat of the Roman army, the one at [?]. I mean also Yarmuk and the lawless bloodshed there. After that came the captures of Palestine, of Caesarea and of Jerusalem, then the destruction of Egypt, and after that, one after another, the captivity of the inland regions, of the islands and of all Romania. In Phoenicia the Roman army and fleet were utterly lost, and all the Christian peoples and places were laid waste. This did not stop until the persecutor of the Church was miserably killed in Sicily, in the bath of Daphne. A.M. [?]. — In this year Muhammad, the leader and false prophet of the Saracens, died, after appointing Abu Bakr his kinsman [?], and everyone was afraid. At the beginning of his appearance the deluded Hebrews thought he was the Christ they were expecting. As a result some of their leading men came to him, accepted his religion, and abandoned that of Moses, who saw God. Ten men did this, and they stayed with him until his murder. But when they saw him eating camel meat, they realized that he was not the one they had thought. They did not know what to do, and the wretches were afraid to abandon his religion. So they taught him lawless things against us Christians, and they stayed with him. I consider it necessary to give an account of his ancestry. He was descended from a single, very widespread tribe, from Ishmael, son of

Abraham. Nizarus, a descendant of Ishmael, is named as the father of them all. He had two sons, Moudaros and Rabias. Moudaros had Kourasos, Kaisos, Themimes, Asados and others who are unknown. All of these lived in the Midianite desert and raised livestock there, living in tents. There are also others further inland who are not of their tribe but of Joktan: the so-called Amanites, that is, the Himyarites. Some of them traded using their camels. The Muhammad mentioned above was poor and an orphan, and he decided to go to a rich woman named Khadija, who was a relative of his, as a hired man to drive camels and trade in Egypt and Palestine. Little by little he grew bolder and won over the woman, who was a widow, and he took her as his wife and came to own her camels and her property. When he came to Palestine, he spent time with Jews and Christians and sought certain scriptural teachings from them. He suffered from epilepsy. When his wife noticed this, she was deeply distressed, since she was of noble birth and was now joined to such a man, who was not only poor but epileptic. He tried to soothe her by saying, “I see a vision of an angel called Gabriel, and because I cannot bear the sight of him, I faint and fall.” She had a monk as a friend who lived there in exile because of his false belief. She told him everything, including the name of the angel. He wanted to reassure her, and said to her, “He has told the truth, for this angel is sent to all the prophets.” She was the first to accept the word of the false monk. She believed him and announced to other women of her tribe that Muhammad was a prophet. And so it spread from women to men, first to Abu Bakr, whom he also left as his successor. In the end his heresy prevailed over the regions of Ethribos through war; earlier it had been practised secretly for

…a certain Arian monk, falsely so called, bearing witness for him out of greed for shameful gain. And so the woman was deceived, and she announced to other women of her tribe that he was a prophet, and went on [?] … [?] (Latin, damaged: “…was confirming false testimony to Muhammad…”) [?]

[?] (35), and through war [?] ten years, and openly nine. He taught his followers that anyone who kills an enemy, or is killed by an enemy, enters paradise. He said that paradise consisted of bodily eating, drinking and intercourse with women. In it there was a river of wine, honey and milk, and there were women, not like those here but of another kind, and intercourse there lasted a long time and its pleasure was continuous. He taught other things too, full of debauchery and folly. They were also to sympathize with one another and help those who were wronged… In that same year, in the fourth indiction, on 7 November, a son, David, was born to Heraclius in the East. On the same day Heraclius was also born, the son of Heraclius the Younger, who was also called Constantine, the son of Heraclius the Great. He was baptized at Blachernae by Sergius the patriarch in the fifth indiction, on 3 November. A.M. 6125. — Leader of the Arabs, Abu Bakr

Bishop of Jerusalem, Modestus, year [?]. In this year the Persians rose up against one another and fought among themselves. At the same time the king of the Indians sent Heraclius congratulatory gifts [?] for his victory over the Persians: a large quantity of pearls and precious stones. Muhammad had died earlier. He had appointed four emirs to make war on the Christians of Arab race. They came opposite a village called Mouchea [?], where Theodore the vicar was stationed, intending to fall upon the Arabs on the day of their idolatrous sacrifice [?]. The vicar learned of this from a certain Qurayshite named Koutabas, [?]

[?] the soldiers of the desert garrisons. He learned from the Saracen the exact day and hour at which they meant to attack, and he himself fell upon them at the place called [?]. He killed three emirs and most of their troops. But one emir got away, Khalid, whom they call the Sword of God. Some of the neighbouring Arabs used to receive small payments from the emperors for guarding the approaches to the desert. At that time a certain eunuch came to distribute the soldiers' pay. When the Arabs came as usual to receive their pay, the eunuch drove them away, saying, “The master can barely pay his soldiers; how much less these dogs!” Aggrieved, the Arabs went off to their fellow tribesmen, and it was they who guided them to the region of Gaza, a very rich land, which lies at the approach to the desert near Mount Sinai. A.M. [?]. — King of the Persians, Hormisdas

In this year Abu Bakr sent four generals. As I said before, they were guided by the Arabs, and they came and took Hera and the whole region of Gaza, which lies at the approach to the desert near Mount Sinai. Sergius only just managed to come from Caesarea in Palestine with a few soldiers. He joined battle, and was the first to be killed, together with his soldiers, who numbered three hundred. The Arabs took many captives and much booty and returned after a brilliant victory. At that time there was an earthquake in Palestine. A sign appeared in the sky to the south, the so-called beam, foretelling the dominion of the Arabs. It remained for thirty days, stretching from south to north, and it was shaped like a sword. A.M. 6125. — Bishop of Jerusalem, Sophronius, year 1. Bishop of Alexandria, Cyrus, year 1. In this year Abu Bakr died, after being emir for two and a half years, and Umar took over the rule. He took the city of Bostra with

In this year the Saracens, an immense multitude, marched against Arabia towards the region of Damascus. When Baanes learned of this, he sent to the imperial sakellarios, asking him to come quickly with his army to help, because there were so many Arabs. The sakellarios joined Baanes. They set out from Edessa and met the Arabs. Battle was joined on the first day, which was a Tuesday, 23 July, and the sakellarios's troops were defeated. Then Baanes' troops rebelled, proclaimed Baanes emperor, and renounced Heraclius. At that the sakellarios's troops withdrew, and the Saracens, seizing their chance, joined battle. A south wind blew against the Romans, and they could not face the enemy because of the dust, so they were defeated. They threw themselves into the narrow passes of the river Hieromyax and perished there utterly. The two generals had forty thousand men between them. After their brilliant victory the Saracens came to Damascus and took it, along with the regions of Phoenicia, and they settled there. They also campaigned against Egypt. Cyrus was accused before the emperor of having given the gold of Egypt to the Saracens. In his anger the emperor sent for him and had him recalled. Manuel, a certain Ar-

CHRONOGRAPHY. …menian by race, [?] as augustalis. When the time was up, the Saracen tax-collectors arrived to receive the gold. But Manuel sent them away empty-handed, saying, “I am not the unarmed Cyrus, to pay you tribute. I am armed.” As soon as they had left, the Saracens armed themselves against Egypt. They joined battle with Manuel and drove him off, and he escaped to Alexandria with a few men. Then the Saracens imposed tribute. When Heraclius heard what had happened, he sent Cyrus to persuade them to withdraw from Egypt on the terms of the former agreement. Cyrus went to the Saracen camp and defended himself, saying that he was not to blame for the breach, and asking whether they would be willing to confirm the earlier agreement with oaths. The Saracens were not persuaded. They said to the bishop, “Can you swallow this enormous column?” He said, “That is not possible.” They said, “Nor is it possible any longer for us to withdraw from Egypt.” A.M. [?]. — King of the Persians, Hormisdas

In this year Umar marched against Palestine. He besieged the holy city for two years and took it on terms. Sophronius, the high priest of Jerusalem, obtained a treaty of the greatest security for the whole of Palestine. Umar entered the holy city dressed in filthy garments of camel hair. Displaying a satanic hypocrisy, he asked to see the temple of the Jews that Solomon had built, so as to make it a place of worship for his own blasphemy. When Sophronius saw him, he said, “Truly this is the abomination of desolation spoken of by Daniel the prophet, standing in the holy place.” And with many tears the champion of piety lamented over the Christian people. While Umar was there, the patriarch urged him to accept a linen cloth and a garment from him to wear. He would not agree to put them on. With great difficulty Sophronius persuaded him to wear them until his own clothes had been washed. Then Umar gave them back to Sophronius and put on his own again. Meanwhile Sophronius died. He had adorned the church of Jerusalem by word and deed, and had fought against the false doctrine of Heraclius and of the Monothelites who sided with him, Sergius and Pyrrhus. In the same year Umar sent Iyad to Syria, and they brought the whole of Syria under the Saracens.

A.M. 6128. In this year John, surnamed Kateas, the governor of Osroene, came to Iad at Chalcedon and agreed to give him 100,000 nomismata each year, so that he would not cross the Euphrates, either in peace or in war, for as long as he paid that sum of gold. On these terms John returned to Edessa, and after collecting the annual tribute he sent it to Iad. When Heraclius heard of this, he judged John guilty of having done it without the emperor's knowledge. He summoned him and condemned him to exile, and in his place he sent a general named Ptolemy. A.M. 6129. In this year the Arabs took Antioch. Umar sent Muawiya as general and emir of all the land under the Saracens, from Egypt to the Euphrates. King of the Persians Hormisdas, years [?]. A.M. 6130. Bishop of Constantinople Pyrrhus, year 1. In this year Iad marched across the Euphrates with his whole army and occupied Edessa. The Edessenes opened their gates and received terms for their countryside, for the general and for the Romans with him. The Arabs then went on to Constantia. They besieged it, took it by storm and killed three hundred Romans. From there they went up to Daras, took it by storm as well and killed many there. In this way Iad took the whole of Mesopotamia. A.M. 6151. In this year the Saracens marched against Persia and joined battle with the Persians. They won decisively and subjugated all of them. Hormisdas, the king of the Persians, fled to the inner Persians, to the royal residences. The Saracens captured Hormisdas's daughters along with all the royal baggage and brought them to Umar. At this same time Umar ordered a census of the whole inhabited world under his rule. The census covered people, livestock and

A.M. 6152. In this year the emperor Heraclius died of dropsy in the month of March, in the 14th indiction, after reigning 30 years and 10 months. His son Constantine reigned after him for four months, and then died, poisoned by his stepmother Martina and the patriarch Pyrrhus. Heraklonas, Martina's son, then reigned together with his mother Martina. A.M. 6153. Emperor of the Romans Heraklonas, six months. Bishop of Constantinople Paul, year 1. In this year Muawiya took Caesarea in Palestine after a siege of seven years, and he killed 7,000 Romans there. At the same time the senate deposed Heraklonas, together with his mother Martina and Valentinus [?]. They cut out Martina's tongue and cut off Heraklonas's nose, and after exiling them they raised Constans to the throne. He was the son of Constantine and the grandson of Heraclius, and he held power for 27 years. Pyrrhus was expelled from his see, and in the month of October, in the 15th indiction, Paul, a presbyter and steward, was ordained patriarch of Constantinople; he held the see for 12 years. A.M. 6154. Emperor of the Romans Constans [year 1]. In this year Constans, now emperor, said to the senate: "My father Constantine, who begot me, reigned for a considerable time together with his own father, my grandfather Heraclius, while Heraclius was alive. After Heraclius died, however, he reigned only very briefly, for the envy of Martina, his stepmother, cut short his excellent hopes and removed him from life. She did this for the sake of Heraklonas, whom she bore unlawfully to Heraclius. Your vote, with God's help, justly cast her and her child out of the imperial office, for your surpassing majesty saw clearly that the empire of the Romans must not appear utterly lawless. Therefore I call upon you to be counsellors

and guides for the common welfare of my subjects." With these words he dismissed the senate, after honouring them generously with gifts. A.M. 6155. In this year Umar began to build the temple in Jerusalem. The building would not stand, but kept collapsing. When he asked the reason, the Jews told him, "Unless you take down the cross that stands on top of the Mount of Olives, the building will not stand." On this account the cross was removed from there, and so their building held firm. For this same reason the haters of Christ took down many crosses. A.M. 6156. Bishop of Alexandria Peter [year 1].

In this year the patrician Valentinus [?], [?] of Constans, rebelled. The emperor sent men who killed him, and he won the people back to goodwill toward himself. There was also an eclipse of the sun in the month of Dios, on the fifth day of the month, the sixth day of the week, at the ninth hour. A.M. 6157. In this year Umar, the leader of the Saracens, was murdered in the month of Dios, on the 5th day, by a Persian renegade. Finding him at prayer, the man stabbed him, driving his sword into his belly, and so took his life. Umar had been emir for 12 years. After him came Uthman, his kinsman, the son of Affan. A.M. 6158. Leader of the Arabs Uthman [year 1].

In this year Gregory, the patrician of Africa, rebelled together with the Africans. A.M. 6159. In this year a violent wind arose over the land. It uprooted many plants, tore up huge trees by the roots and threw down many column shafts. In the same

year the Saracens marched against Africa. They engaged the usurper Gregory, put him to flight and killed those who were with him. Then they agreed on tribute with the Africans and returned home. A.M. 6140. In this year Muawiya mounted an expedition by sea against Cyprus. He had 1,700 vessels, and he took Constantia along with the whole island and ravaged it. When he heard that Kakorizos the cubicularius was coming against him with a very large Roman force, he sailed away to a point opposite Arados. There he anchored his fleet and tried to take Kastellon, the small town on the island, using every kind of siege engine. When this achieved nothing, he sent a bishop named Thomarichos to the townspeople. The bishop was to frighten them into giving up the town, accepting terms and leaving the island. But when the bishop went in to them, they kept him inside and did not yield to Muawiya. Since the siege of Arados had proved fruitless, Muawiya returned to Damascus, because winter

A.M. 6141. In this year Muawiya marched against Arados with a powerful array and took it on terms, which allowed the inhabitants to settle wherever they wished. He burned the town, tore down its walls and left the island uninhabited, as it remains to this day. In the same year Pope Martin held a synod in Rome against the Monothelites. A.M. 6142. In this year [?] the camp commander marched against Isauria with the Arabs. He killed many, took captives and returned with five thousand prisoners. The emperor Constans sent a man named Procopius to Muawiya to ask for peace. Peace was made for two years, and Muawiya took Gregory, the son of Theodore, as a hostage, in

A.M. 6143. In this year Pasagnathes, the patrician of the Armenians, rebelled against the emperor. He made a treaty with Muawiya and gave him his own son as well. When the emperor heard of this, he came as far as Caesarea in Cappadocia. Then, despairing of Armenia, he returned home. A.M. 6144. In this year Gregory, the broth-

A.M. 6185. In this year Pasagnathes, the patrician of the Armenians, rebelled against the emperor. He made a treaty with Muawiya and [gave] him his own son as well. When the emperor heard of this, he came as far as Caesarea in Cappadocia. Then, [despairing] of Armenia, he returned home. A.M. 6[?]. In this year Gregory, the broth- [Apparatus:] [?] "and ships" A; "and also ships" vulg. [?] A; γενομένου vulg. ⁵ "in Damascus" A. ⁷ "to this day" [?]. Similarly on p. 294, concerning Busur: "And took captive-"

-er of Heraclius died at Heliopolis. His body was embalmed with myrrh and brought to Constantinople. In the same year dust came down from the sky, and great fear fell upon people. Bishop of Constantinople Paul

Paul died, and Pyrrhus was restored once more, for 4 [?] months and 23 days. A.M. 6145. In this year Muawiya captured Rhodes and pulled down the Colossus of Rhodes, 1,360 years after it had been set up. A Jewish merchant from Edessa bought it and loaded its bronze onto nine hundred camels. In the same year Habib, the Arab general, marched against Armenia. He met Maurianus, the Roman general, and chased him as far as the Caucasus mountains, then plundered the land. A.M. 6146. In this year Muawiya went on campaign and ordered a great fitting-out of ships, so that his fleet could sail against Constantinople. The whole of this fitting-out was taking place at Tripolis in Phoenicia. Two Christ-loving brothers who lived in Tripolis, the sons of the Trumpeter, saw this. Stung by zeal for God, they rushed to the city prison, which held a great number of Roman prisoners. They broke open the gates and freed the prisoners. Then they rushed at the emir of the city and killed him along with those with him. They burned all the equipment and sailed away to Roman territory. Even so, Muawiya did not abandon his preparations. He himself marched against Caesarea in Cappadocia, and he appointed Aboulabar commander of the fleet. Aboulabar came to the place called Phoenix in Lycia, where the emperor Constans was with the Roman fleet, and fought a sea battle with him. On the night before the emperor was to fight, he saw himself in a dream in Thessalonica. When he woke up, he told the vision to a dream-

interpreter, who said: "O emperor, I wish you had not slept and had not seen this dream. Your being in Thessalonica is interpreted as [?]: the victory is turning to your enemy." The emperor paid no attention to this, and he drew up the Roman fleet in battle order for a sea fight. When the two sides engaged, the Romans were defeated, and the sea was mixed with Roman blood. The emperor had dressed another man in his own clothes. The aforementioned son of the Trumpeter leapt into the imperial ship, snatched up the emperor, transferred him to another ship and saved him against all expectation. He himself, that most valiant man, took his stand on the imperial ship and killed many, giving himself up to death for the emperor. The enemy surrounded him and pinned him in their midst, thinking he was the emperor. After he had killed many, he too was killed by the enemy, together with the man wearing the imperial clothes. The emperor, routed in this way, was saved, and he abandoned everyone and sailed away to Constantinople.

A.M. 6147. In this year Uthman, the general of the Saracens, was murdered by the people of Yathrib, after being emir for 10 years. Strife then broke out among them. Those in the desert wanted Ali, the cousin of [?] and the son-in-law of Muhammad. Those in Syria and Egypt wanted Muawiya, who also prevailed and held power.

Leader of the Arabs Muawiya, 29 years. A.M. [?]. In this year Muawiya marched against Ali. Both armies gathered near Barsilissos [?], at Kaisaron [?] close to the Euphrates. Muawiya's men gained the upper hand and seized the water. Ali's men, suffering from thirst, began to desert. Muawiya did not want to fight, and he won the victory without effort. A.M. [?]. In this year the emperor marched against Sclavinia, took

many captives and subjugated it. In the same year St Maximus and his disciples went through their ordeal for their struggle on behalf of the orthodox faith against the Monothelites. Constans could not bring them over to his false belief, so he cut out the saint's divinely wise and most learned tongue, together with his right hand. He did this because Maximus, together with his disciples the Anastasii, had written a great deal against Constans's impiety. These men wrote it all down word for word, as lovers of learning know. A.M. 6150. In this year an agreement was reached between the Romans and the Arabs, after Muawiya sent an embassy because of the rebellion. Under it the Arabs were to pay the Romans a thousand nomismata, a horse and a slave every day. At this time there was also a great earthquake, with buildings collapsing, in both Palestine and Syria, in the month of Daisios, in the 2nd indiction. In the same year Marti-

[?] -n, the most holy pope of Rome, was exiled. He had struggled nobly for the truth, and he became a confessor and died in the regions of the East. A.M. 6151. In this year Constans killed his own brother Theodosius. While the Arabs were at Siffin, Ali, [ruler] of Persia, was murdered. Muawiya now ruled alone, living like a king in Damascus and storing his treasures of money there. A.M. 6152. In this year a heresy arose among the Arabs, those called the Kharijites. Muawiya subdued them. He humbled the Arabs in Persia and exalted those in Syria. He called the latter Shamites and the former Iraqites. He raised the pay of the Shamites to as much as two hundred nomismata, and cut the pay of the Iraqites to as little as thirty nomismata. A.M. 6153. In this year the emperor left Constantinople and moved to Syracuse in Sicily, intending to transfer the seat of empire to Rome. He sent for his wife and his three sons, Constantine, Heraclius and Tiberius, but the Byzantines would not let them go. A.M. 6154. In this year the Arabs marched against Roman territory, took many captives and laid waste many places. A.M. 6155. In this year part of Sicily was taken captive, and the captives were settled in Damascus of their own free will. A.M. 6156. In this year there was an error concerning the fasts. Abdurrahman, the son of Khalid, marched against Roman territory, wintered there and ravaged many lands. The Slavs defected to him, and five thousand of them went down with him to Syria. [Apparatus:] "did not let go" A; "did not dissolve" vulg. "more"

They settled in the region of Apamea, in the village of Skeuokobolos. A.M. 6157. Bishop of Constantinople Thomas, year 1. In this year Busur marched against Roman territory. Thomarichos, the bishop of Apamea, died, and the bishop of Emesa was burned. A.M. 6158. In this year Busur again marched against Roman territory and ravaged the region of Hexapolis, and Fadalas wintered there. A.M. 6159. In this year Saborios, the general of the Armeniacs, who was of Persian descent, rebelled against the emperor Constans. He sent the commander Sergius to Muawiya, promising to bring Roman territory under Muawiya's rule if Muawiya would join him against the emperor. When Constantine, the emperor's son, learned of this, he too sent Andrew the cubicularius to Muawiya with gifts, so that Muawiya would not cooperate with the rebel. When Andrew reached Damascus, he found that Sergius had arrived before him. Muawiya pretended to be on the emperor's side. Sergius was sitting with Muawiya, and when Andrew came in, Sergius saw him and rose. Muawiya rebuked Sergius: "You were afraid!" Sergius excused himself, saying that he had done it out of habit. Muawiya turned and said to Andrew, "What do you want?" Andrew said, "For you to give help against the rebel." Muawiya said, "You are both my enemies, and I give my help to whichever of you offers me more." Andrew said to him, "Have no doubt, emir: a little from an emperor is better for you than a great deal from a rebel. Still, do as you please." After saying this, Andrew fell silent. Muawiya said, "I will think about it," and ordered both of them to leave. Muawiya then called Sergius aside privately and said to him, "Do not bow to Andrew any more, for you will gain nothing by it." The next day Sergius arrived first and was sitting with Muawiya. When Andrew came in, Sergius did not rise as he had the day before. Andrew looked around and insulted Sergius harshly, and he threatened him: "If I live, I will show you who I am." Sergius said, "I do not rise for you, because you are not a man, nor a woman either." Muawiya stopped them both and said to Andrew, "Agree to give as much as Sergius is giving." "And how much is that?" said Andrew. Muawiya

said, "Hand over the revenue of the public taxes to the Arabs." Andrew said, "Bah, Muawiya! You are advising us to give away the body and keep the shadow. Make whatever agreement you like with Sergius, for I will not do this. We pass you by and take refuge in God, who is more able than you to defend the Romans, and we place our hopes in him." With these words he said to Muawiya, "Farewell," and left Damascus for Melitene. He went that way because the usurper was in that region, through which Sergius would have to travel. When Andrew reached Arabissos, he met the guard of the pass, who had not gone over to the usurper. He ordered him to watch for Sergius on his way back and to bring him to Andrew. Andrew himself went on to Amnesia [?] to wait for Sergius, and he reported what had happened to the emperor. Sergius, meanwhile, settled with Muawiya whatever terms they saw fit, and he took Fadalas, the Arab general, with a barbarian force to fight alongside Saborios. Sergius went on ahead of Fadalas, and as he was joyfully making his way to Saborios, he fell into Andrew's ambush in the passes. They seized him and brought him to Andrew in chains. When Sergius saw Andrew, he threw himself at his feet and begged him to spare him. Andrew said to him, "Are you not Sergius, who boasted of his genitals in front of Muawiya and called me effeminate? Look, from now on your genitals will be no use to you; they will be your death." After saying this, he ordered his genitals to be cut off, and he hanged him on a gibbet. When Constantine heard that Fadalas had arrived to help Saborios, he sent the patrician Nicephorus with a Roman force to oppose Saborios. Saborios was at Hadrianopolis, and when he learned that Nicephorus was coming against him, he began training himself for war. One day, as was his habit, he rode out of the city on horseback. When he came near the city gate, he struck his horse with the whip. The horse bolted and smashed Saborios's head against the gate, and so he died a miserable death. In this way God granted the victory to the emperor. When Fadalas came to Hexapolis and learned all that had happened, he was at a loss. He sent to Muawiya to ask for help, because the

Romans had become united again. Muawiya sent him his son Yazid, equipped with a great host of barbarians. The two of them came as far as Chalcedon and took many captives. They also took Amorium in Phrygia, leaving five thousand armed men there to guard it, and then went back to Syria. When winter came, the emperor sent that same Andrew the cubicularius. There was deep snow, and Andrew arrived at night. He climbed the wall by means of a wooden ladder, and his men got into Amorium. They killed all the Arabs, all five thousand of them, and not a single one was left alive. In the same winter there was a flood at Edessa, and many people died. A sign also appeared in the sky. A.M. 6160. Bishop of Constantinople John, year 1. In this year the emperor Constans was murdered at Syracuse in Sicily, in a bath called Daphne. The reason was this. After he killed his brother Theodosius, the Byzantines hated him. They hated him above all because he had brought Martin, the most holy pope of Rome, to Constantinople in disgrace and exiled him to the region of Cherson. He had also cut out the tongue and cut off the hand of Maximus, the most wise confessor, and condemned many of the orthodox to tortures, exile and confiscation of property because they would not accept his heresy. He had sent the two Anastasii, disciples of Maximus the confessor and martyr, into exile and torture. For these reasons he was violently hated by everyone. Out of fear he decided to move the seat of empire to Rome. This is why he wanted to bring the empress and his three sons to him as well, and he would have done so, had not Andrew the cubicularius and Theodore of Koloneia blocked his plan. He spent six years in Sicily. When he went into the bath, a certain Andrew, the son of Troilus, went in with him to attend him. As the emperor began to wash with Gallic soap, Andrew picked up the bucket, struck the emperor on the top of his head with it and immediately ran away. When the emperor stayed a long time in the bath, the men outside burst in and found him dead. After burying him, they forced an Armenian named Mizizios to become emperor, for he was very handsome and fine-looking. When Constantine heard of his father's death, he set out with a very large fle-

[?] reaches Sicily, and after capturing Mizizios he puts him to death together with the murderer of his own father. Having settled the affairs of the West, he set out for Constantinople, and he reigns over the Romans with Tiberius and Heraclius, his own brothers. [While the emperor Constans was in Sicily, Mizizios rose against him with others in the bath, and they killed him. The emperor took vengeance on Mizizios and those with him who had dared this, and beheaded them. He did the same to Justinian the patrician, the father of Germanus who later became patriarch; and Germanus, who was rather sturdy, he castrated.] Year of the World 6161. Year 1 of Constantine, emperor of the Romans. In this year Constantine reigned with his brothers. The Saracens campaigned against Africa and took eighty thousand captives, as they say. The men of the Anatolic theme came to Chrysopolis, saying, "We believe in the Trinity; let us crown the three." Constantine was troubled, because he alone had been crowned while his brothers held no rank. He sent Theodore, the patrician of Koloneia, who praised them and turned them back, and he took their leaders, as though they were to go up into the city, deliberate with the senate, and have their wish carried out. But the emperor at once hanged them across the water at Sykai. When the rest saw this they were put to shame and went home in grief. The emperor slit his brothers' noses. Year of the World 6162. In this year there was a great winter, and many men and beasts perished. Fadalas wintered at Cyzicus. Year of the World 6163. In this year [?] campaigned, took many captives, and returned. Year of the World 6164. In this year a rainbow appeared in the sky in the month of March, that is Dystros, and all flesh shuddered, so that everyone said it was the end of the world. At this time the deniers of Christ fitted out a great fleet, sailed along the coast of Cilicia and wintered there: Muhammad son of Abdallah at Smyrna, and Kaisos in Cilicia and Lycia. And there was a plague in Egypt. He also sent [?] the emir with yet another fleet to

their aid, as a most able man and bold in battle. When the aforementioned Constantine learned of this movement of the God-fighters against Constantinople, he too built large biremes carrying cauldrons of fire, and dromons fitted with siphons, and ordered them to lie at anchor in the Proklianesian harbor of Caesarius. Year of the World 6165. In this year the aforementioned fleet of the God-fighters set sail and anchored in the Thracian parts, from the western promontory of the Hebdomon, that is, the so-called Magnaura, as far as the eastern cape called Kyklobion. Every day a battle was fought from morning until evening, from the outwork of the Golden Gate as far as Kyklobion, with each side thrusting and being thrust back. They kept this up from April until September. Then they turned back and went to Cyzicus, took it, and wintered there. In spring they set out again and likewise joined battle with the Christians by sea. They kept this up for seven years, and, put to shame by the help of God and of the Mother of God, having lost a multitude of fighting men and suffered very heavy wounds, they returned in great grief. As this fleet, sunk by God, was departing,

it was caught by a winter storm and a violent gale in the region of Syllaion, and was utterly shattered and destroyed. Sufyan the son of Auf, the second brother [?], joined battle with Florus, Petronas and Cyprian, who had a Roman force, and thirty thousand Arabs are killed. Then Kallinikos, an architect from Heliopolis in Syria, who had fled to the Romans, prepared sea fire, set the ships of the Arabs alight and burned them with their crews. Thus the Romans returned in victory, and the sea fire [?]

Year of the World 6166. Year 1 of Constantine, bishop of Constantinople. In this year Abdallah son of Kais and Fadalas wintered in Crete. Year of the World 6167. In this year a sign appeared in the sky on a Saturday. Year of the World 6168. Year 1 of Theodore, bishop of Constantinople. In this year there was a great plague of locusts in Syria and Mesopotamia. Year of the World 6169. In this year the Mardaites entered Lebanon and took control of the country from the Black Mountain to the Holy City, and seized the heights of Lebanon; and many slaves and natives fled to them, so that in a short time they grew to many thousands. When Mu'awiya and his counsellors learned this they were greatly afraid, reckoning that the empire of the Romans is guarded by God. He sends envoys to the emperor Constantine seeking peace, and promising also to pay the emperor a yearly tribute. The emperor received the envoys and heard their request, and sent with them to Syria John the patrician, surnamed Pitzigaudes, as a man of long standing in the state, highly experienced and possessed of great prudence, to negotiate fittingly with the Arabs and agree the terms of peace. When he reached Syria, Mu'awiya assembled the emirs and the Qurashites and received him with great honor. When many peaceful words had been exchanged

between them, it was agreed by both sides that a written peace should be made under oath, on the terms of a yearly tribute to be paid by the Hagarenes to the Roman state: three thousand [pieces] of gold, eight thousand captive men, and fifty thoroughbred horses. When these terms had been agreed between the two parties, that a general peace should be kept between Romans and Arabs for thirty years, and two such general written instruments had been drawn up with oaths and handed over to each other, the oft-mentioned most [?] man returned to the emperor, bringing many gifts as well. When those who dwelt in the western parts learned this, the Chagan of the Avars and the kings beyond, the exarchs too and [?], and the most eminent of the nations of the West, [?] through envoys [?] of the Saracens, first [?] in the first indiction. He was general for [?] years

on the far shores of the Euxine Sea, at the so-called Maeotic Lake, into which flows a very great river called the Atel, coming down from the ocean through the land of the Sarmatians; into the Atel flows the river called the Tanais, which itself issues from the Iberian Gates in the Caucasus mountains. From the confluence of the Tanais and the Atel (the Atel dividing above the aforementioned Maeotic Lake) comes the river called the Kouphis, which discharges at the end of the Pontic Sea near Nekropyla, at the headland called Ram's Face. From the aforesaid lake a sea like a river flows into the sea of the Euxine Pontus through the land of the Cimmerian Bosporus; in this river is caught the fish called mourzoulin and others like it. Along the eastern parts of the said lake, toward Phanagouria and the Hebrews who live there, lie very many nations; and from the same lake toward the river called Kouphis, where the Bulgarian fish called xyston is caught, lies the old Great Bulgaria, and the so-called Kotragoi, who are of the same race as they. In the times of Constantine who [died] in the West, Krobatos, lord of the said Bulgaria and of the Kotragoi, departed this life and left five sons, having charged them never to separate from their common life, so that they might be masters everywhere and never be enslaved to another nation. But a short time after his death his five sons fell into division and separated from one another, each with the people subject to his authority. The first son, called Batbaian, kept his father's command and has remained in his ancestral land to this day. His second brother, called Kotragos, crossed the river Tanais and settled opposite his first brother. The fourth

and the fifth crossed the river called the Istros, that is, the Danube: the one, in Pannonia of Avaria, submitted to the Chagan of the Avars and remained there with his forces; the other reached the Pentapolis near Ravenna and came under the rule of the Christians. Then the third of them, called Asparuch, crossed the Danapris and the Danastris and reached the Onglos, rivers to the north of the Danube, and settled between these and that river, judging the place to be secure and hard to assail on every side: for it was marshy in front and ringed by rivers elsewhere, and it gave the nation, weakened by the division, much respite from its enemies. When they had thus been divided into five parts and reduced to small numbers, the great nation of the Khazars came out from the inner depths of Berzilia in First Sarmatia and became master of all the land beyond as far as the Pontic Sea; and having made the first brother, Batbaian, ruler of First Bulgaria, its tributary, it receives tribute from him to this day. When the emperor Constantine learned that a filthy and unclean nation had suddenly encamped beyond the Danube in the Onglos and was raiding and ravaging the lands near the Danube, that is, the country now held by them but then held by Christians, he was greatly vexed, and he orders all the themes to cross into Thrace. Having equipped a fleet, he moved against them by land and sea, trying to drive them out by war, drawing up the infantry on the land by the so-called Onglos and the Danube and anchoring the ships along the adjacent shore. When the Bulgars saw this sudden and enormous array, they despaired of their safety, fled to the aforementioned stronghold and made themselves secure. For three or four days they did not dare to come out of this stronghold, and the Romans did not join battle because of the marshes in front of it; and the foul nation, perceiving the slackness of the Romans, took heart and grew bolder.

The emperor was seized with gout and was forced to return to Mesembria for his customary bath, with five dromons and his own men; he left the generals and the army behind, ordering them to skirmish and draw the enemy out of the stronghold, and to give battle if they happened to come out, and if not, to besiege them and keep them shut in their fortifications. But the cavalry spread the rumor that the emperor was fleeing, and, seized with fear, took to the same flight, though no one was pursuing. When the Bulgars saw this they went after them, killed most of them with the sword and wounded many, and chased them as far as the Danube. They crossed it and came to the so-called Varna, near Odyssos and the inland country there, and saw that the place was very secure, protected at the back by the river Danube, and in front and on the flanks by passes and by the Pontic Sea. Having also made themselves masters of the neighboring Slavic nations, the so-called Seven Clans, they settled the Severeis from the front pass of Beregaba toward the eastern parts, and the remaining seven clans toward the south and west as far as Avaria, these being under tribute. Having thus spread out, they grew arrogant and began to attack and plunder the forts and villages under Roman rule. So the emperor was compelled to make peace with them, agreeing to pay them a yearly tribute, to the shame of the Romans because of their many failures; for it was astonishing for those far and near to hear that he who had made everyone subject to him, those in east and west, north and south, had been defeated by this loathsome and newly appeared nation. But he, believing as a Christian that this had come about by the providence of God, made peace in the spirit of the Gospel; and until his death he remained at rest from all wars, with an especial zeal to unite the holy Churches of God, which had been divided everywhere since the times of the emperor Heraclius, his great-grandfather, and of the evil-minded Sergius and Pyrrhus, who unworthily presided over the throne of Constantinople and laid down the doctrine of one will and one operation in our Lord and God and Saviour Jesus Christ. Eager to overturn their false teachings, the most Christian emperor

[?] assembled an ecumenical synod of 289 bishops in Constantinople, confirmed the doctrines previously ratified at the five preceding holy ecumenical synods, and voted for the pious doctrine of the two wills and operations to be decreed at this same holy and most exact sixth ecumenical synod, over which the same most pious emperor Constantine and the pious hierarchs presided. Year of the World 6177. In this year the pious emperor Constantine went to his rest, having reigned seventeen years, and his son Justinian [became emperor]. It should be known that some people idly and foolishly babble that the canonical decrees reputed to be of the sixth synod were issued four years afterwards. For as they are proved to lie in everything, so they are shown in this too to say nothing true. The exact chronological record states that the holy ecumenical sixth synod against the Monothelites took place in the twelfth year of the reign of Constantine, the descendant of Heraclius, in the year from the creation of the world 6172 [?]. And that

after this the same Constantine reigned five years; and when he died, his son Justinian reigned alone for ten years. When Justinian was expelled, Leontius ruled three years, and after Leontius, Tiberius, also called Apsimar, seven years; and then again Justinian, who had been expelled, six years. So it is found from the issued decrees themselves that they were published in the second year of the last reign of this same slit-nosed Justinian, since the third decree contains these words: "We determine that those who have been entangled in two marriages, and who up to the fifteenth of the past month of January of the past fourth indiction, of the year 6199 [?], were enslaved to sin and did not come to their senses, we have chosen to subject to canonical deposition." And after other things: "Those who after ordination unlawfully entered into one marriage, that is, presbyters, deacons and subdeacons, who have already been kept from the sacred liturgy for some short time and been penanced, are to be restored to their own ranks, but in no way to advance to any higher rank, their unlawful union having been manifestly dissolved." So from the chronological record itself it is plainly seen that twenty-seven years are reckoned from the holy ecumenical sixth synod to the issued decrees. George was patriarch of Constantinople at the holy ecumenical synod, in the third year of his patriarchate, and after the synod he was patriarch another three years; after him Theodore three years, Paul seven years, Kallinikos twelve years, and Kyros two years, so that from the patriarchs themselves too twenty-seven years are reckoned. From the issued decrees to the fourth year of Philippikos there were five years; and in that same first year of the reign of Philippikos a mad synod took place against the holy ecumenical sixth synod. Kyros was driven out in the sixth year of his patriarchate, and John became patriarch of Constantinople, Andrew metropolitan of Crete, and Germanus metropolitan of Cyzicus, who manifestly signed and anathematized, with all those of the same time, the aforementioned holy ecumenical sixth synod against the Monothelites. After three years, when John died, Germanus was transferred from

Year of the World 6178. Year 1 of Justinian, emperor of the Romans. In this year Abd al-Malik sends to Justinian to confirm the peace, and the peace was agreed on these terms: that the emperor should remove the corps of the Mardaites from Lebanon and prevent their raids; that Abd al-Malik should give the Romans every day a thousand coins, a horse and a slave; and that they should share in common and equally the tributes of Cyprus, Armenia and Iberia. The emperor sent Paul the magistrianos to Abd al-Malik to secure the agreed terms, and a written guarantee was drawn up with witnesses. The magistrianos was honored with gifts and returned. On hearing this Abd al-Malik comes to Mesopotamia, and Sa'id rises against him as usurper; but Abd al-Malik returned and by negotiation persuaded him to open Damascus, which he had seized beforehand, and afterwards he murders him by treachery. …and Albania, Boukania and Media, and after making these lands pay tribute he sent a great deal of money to the emperor. He ordered the cavalry themes to cross over into Thrace, meaning to take both the Bulgars and the Sklavinias captive. AM 6180. In this year Justinian campaigned against Sklavinia and Bulgaria. For the moment he drove back the Bulgars who came out to meet him. He pushed on as far as Thessalonica and took great numbers of Slavs, some by war and others who came over to him of their own accord. to the Arabs that he would not abide by the peace agreed in writing. Taking the special people and all the cavalry themes, he marched to Sebastopolis by the sea. So they unfastened the written text of the peace, hung it on a tall spear in place of a banner, and carried it before them as they charged the Romans. Justinian busied himself with buildings for the palace. He built the hall called the Triklinos of Justinian, and the walls around the palace. As overseer he appointed Stephen the Persian, his sakellarios and chief eunuch, a lord and master who was extremely bloodthirsty and cruel. Stephen was not content to abuse the workmen without mercy. He even had them stoned, along with their foremen. While the emperor was away, that savage beast even dared to whip the emperor's mother, the Augusta Anastasia, with a strap, as though she were a child. All the while he did many wicked things to the whole population of the city, and he made the emperor hated. In the same way Justinian put in charge of the affairs of the general logothesion an abbot named Theodotos, who had formerly been a recluse in the Thracian parts of the Strait. He too was a most dreadful and savage man. He subjected a great many officials of the state and prominent men, not only from among the administrators but also from among the inhabitants of the city, recklessly and in vain

and without any pretext, to demands for money, confiscations [?] and [?]. He hung them up by ropes and smoked them from below with burning straw. In addition the prefect, on the emperor's orders, shut a great many men up in prisons and kept them there for years. All this increased the people's hatred of the emperor. The emperor demanded that the patriarch Kallinikos say a prayer so that he could pull down the church of the holy Theotokos of the Metropolitan, near the palace. He wanted to set up a fountain on the site and build tiers of seats for the Blue faction, where they could receive the emperor. The patriarch said, "We have a prayer for the founding of a church, but we have received none for the pulling down of a church." The emperor forced him and insisted on having the prayer, so the patriarch said, "Glory to God, who is always patient, now and ever and to the ages of ages. Amen." When they heard this they pulled down the church and made the fountain. They built the church of the Metropolitan again at the Petrion. AM [?]. In this year Muhammad campaigned against Fourth Armenia, took many captives and went back. In the same year Justinian was driven from the throne in the following way. He ordered Stephen, the patrikios and general surnamed Rousios, to massacre the people of Constantinople by night, beginning with the patriarch. Now Leontios the patrikios had been general of the Anatolikoi and had distinguished himself in war. After being accused, he had spent three years in custody. He was suddenly recalled and appointed general of Hellas, and he was ordered to board three dromons and leave the city that same day. That same night, in the Julian harbour of Sophia near the quarter of Mauros,

CHRONOGRAPHY. …he lived with Theodora. When Apsimar heard this, he sent to the Khagan and promised to give him many gifts if he would send Justinian to him alive, or failing that, at least his head. The Khagan gave way to this request and sent Justinian a guard, supposedly to protect him from plots by his own countrymen. He instructed Papatzys, his representative there, and Balgitzin, the governor of Bosporos, to kill Justinian as soon as they were given the signal. Theodora learned of this from a servant of the Khagan, and Justinian came to know of it. He summoned Papatzys to talk with him in private and strangled him with a cord, and he did the same to Balgitzin, the governor of Bosporos. He at once sent Theodora off to Khazaria. He himself slipped away secretly from Phanagouria and went down to the river mouth [?]. Finding a fishing boat ready, he went on board. Sailing past [?], he came as far as Symbolon near Cherson. He sent secretly into Cherson and took on board Barasbakourios and his brother, Salibas and Stephen, and Moropaulos together with Theophilos. Sailing off with them, he passed the lighthouse of Cherson. Then, as they sailed past Nekropyla at the mouth of the Dnieper and the Dniester, a storm arose, and they all gave up hope of survival. Myakes, a servant of his household, said to him, "Look, we are going to die, master. Make a vow to God for your safety, that if God gives you back your throne you will take revenge on none of your enemies." Justinian answered him angrily, "If I spare a single one of them, may God drown me here." He came out of that storm unharmed and entered the river Danube. He sent Stephen to Tervel, the lord of Bulgaria, to ask for his help in regaining the throne of his forefathers. He promised to give Tervel a great many gifts and his own daughter as his wife. Tervel promised on oath to do everything he asked and to join forces with him, and he received Justinian with honour. Then he set in motion the whole people of Bulgars and Slavs under his rule, and the following year they came, armed, to the imperial city.

Year of the World 6197. In this year Abimelech (Abd al-Malik), the leader of the Arabs, died, and his son Walid took power. In the same year Justinian reached the imperial city together with Tervel and the Bulgars who were with him, and pitched camp from the Gate of Charisios as far as Blachernai. For three days they parleyed with the people in the city, but were insulted by them, and the citizens would not accept a word. Then Justinian, with a few men of his own people, got in through the aqueduct without a fight. He raised a sudden uproar [?], took the city, and stayed for a short time in the palace of Blachernai. Year of the World 6198. Year 1 of Justinian, emperor of the Romans for the second time. Year 1 of Walid, leader of the Arabs. Year 1 of Kyros, bishop of Constantinople. Year 1 of John, bishop of Jerusalem. In this year Justinian took back the empire. He gave Tervel many gifts and imperial vessels and sent him away in peace. Apsimar left the city and fled to Apollonias, but he was pursued, captured and brought to Justinian. Heraclius too was brought in chains from Thrace, together with all the officers who had fought alongside him, and Justinian hanged them all on the wall. He sent men throughout the interior, and killed all of their party that he found, whether they held office or not. He had Apsimar and Leontios bound in chains and paraded through the whole city. During the horse races, while he sat on the throne, they were dragged in public and thrown down at his feet, and he trod on their necks until the end of the first race, while the people shouted: "You have trodden on the asp and the basilisk, and trampled the lion and the dragon." Then he sent them to the Kynegion and had them beheaded. He blinded the patriarch Kallinikos and exiled him to Rome. In his place he appointed Kyros, who had been a recluse on the island of Amastris, because Kyros had foretold that he would be restored to a second reign. He destroyed a countless number of men on the civil and military rolls. Many others he threw into the sea in sacks [?]

and so put them to death. Others he invited to lunch or dinner, and as soon as they rose from the table he hanged some and beheaded others. As a result great fear gripped everyone. He sent a fleet to bring his wife back from Khazaria, and many of the ships sank with all hands. When the Khagan heard this he sent him word: "You fool, should you not have fetched your wife with two or three ships, instead of killing so many people? Or do you think you will take her too by war? See, a son has also been born to you. Send and take them both." So he sent Theophylaktos the koubikoularios, who took Theodora and Tiberios her son. Justinian crowned them, and they reigned with him. Year of the World 6199. In this year Walid, the wretch, seized the most holy catholic church of Damascus, out of envy towards the Christians at the surpassing beauty of that church. He also forbade the public account books to be written in Greek, and ordered them to be recorded in Arabic, except for the numerals, since in their language one cannot write a one, a two, a three, eight and a half, or three. That is why the notaries among them are still Christians to this day. Year of the World 6200. In this year Justinian broke off the peace between the Romans and the Bulgars. He moved the cavalry themes across to Thrace, fitted out a fleet, and set out against the Bulgars and Tervel. When he reached Anchialos he anchored the fleet in front of the fortress, and ordered the cavalry to camp on the plains above without setting a guard and with no thought of danger [?]. While the men were scattered like sheep over the plains gathering fodder, the Bulgar scouts in the mountains saw how foolishly the Romans had disposed themselves. They massed together like wild beasts, fell on them suddenly and destroyed the Roman flock completely, taking many captives, horses and weapons, besides those

they killed. Justinian fled into the fortress with the survivors and kept the gates shut for three days. When he saw that the Bulgars were staying put, he was the first to hamstring his own horse, and he urged everyone to do the same. He set up standards on the walls, boarded the ships secretly by night and sailed away, and returned to the city in disgrace. Year of the World 6201. In this year Maslama and Abbas marched against Tyana, enraged at the army that had been killed along with Maimun by Marianos. They besieged it and wintered there. The emperor sent against them two generals, Theodore Karteroukas and Theophylaktos Salibas, with soldiers and a levy of peasants to help, in order to fight them and drive them away. But the generals quarrelled with each other and engaged the enemy in disorder. They were routed: many thousands perished and many were taken prisoner. The Arabs took their camp and their provisions and kept up the siege until they took the city, for they had run out of food and had been about to withdraw. When the people of Tyana saw this they lost hope. They accepted a promise of safety and went out to them, leaving the city empty, as it is to this day. But the Arabs did not keep their promise: they exiled them to the desert and kept many as slaves. [?] Maslama [?] Romania, took many captives and returned. And he began to build Garis in the territory of Heliopolis. Year of the World 6205 [?]. In this year Uthman invaded Cilicia and took many fortresses on terms. Kamachon and the places around it were also betrayed to them. Justinian, nursing a grudge, sent Mauros the patrician to Cherson together with Stephen the patrician, surnamed Asmiktos, fitting out a large fleet, for he remembered the plot against him by the people of Cherson and of Bosporos [?] and of the other districts. He gathered every kind of ship, dromons and triremes and cargo vessels [?] and fishing boats, down to chelandia, by a levy on the inhabitants of the city: senators, artisans,

[?] commoners and every office. When he sent them off, he ordered them to put all the inhabitants of those fortresses to the sword and to leave no one alive. He handed over to them Elias the spatharios, who was to be installed as governor of Cherson. They reached Cherson, took the fortresses without anyone resisting them, and put everyone to the sword except the boys, whom they spared as being children and kept for slavery. Tudun, the governor of Cherson, who acted as the Khagan's representative, and Zoilos, the first citizen by descent and family, and forty other notable leading men of Cherson they fixed to wooden spits and roasted over a fire. Others [?] they tied up and bound to boats [?], filled these with stones and sank them in the deep. When Justinian learned of this, he was furious that the boys had been spared, and ordered the men to return to him at once. The fleet set out in the month of October, and out at sea it was overtaken at the rising of the star called Taurouras [?]. Almost the whole fleet was sunk, and the dead in the shipwreck were counted at 73,000. When Justinian learned of this he was not grieved; rather, he was filled with joy. Still in the grip of the same madness and threatening loudly [?], he sent out another fleet [?], to plough everything up and raze it to the ground, down to every last one that pisses against a wall. The people of those fortresses heard of this and secured themselves [?]. Forced to turn against the emperor, they sent to the Khagan in Khazaria and asked for troops to guard them. At this Elias the spatharios rose in revolt, together with Bardanes the exile, who had then been recalled from Kephalenia and was going to Cherson with the fleet. When Justinian learned this, [?]

he sent off, with a few dromons, George the patrician, surnamed Syros, the general logothete, and John the prefect, and Christopher, the tourmarch of the Thrakesians, with three hundred armed men. He handed over to them Tudun and Zoilos, who were to be restored to their former positions in Cherson. They were to apologise to the Khagan through an envoy, and to bring Elias and Bardanes back to him. When they had crossed over to Cherson, the people of the city paid them no attention [?]. The next day the citizens invited only these men to come in, and then shut the gates. They put the general logothete and the prefect to the sword. Tudun and Zoilos, and the tourmarch already mentioned with his three hundred soldiers, they handed over to the Khazars and sent to the Khagan. Tudun died on the way, and the Khazars killed the tourmarch and his three hundred soldiers as a funeral offering [?] for him. Then the people of Cherson and the other fortresses repudiated Justinian and acclaimed as emperor Bardanes, the exile there, under the name Philippikos. When Justinian learned this he went still madder. He slaughtered the children of Elias the spatharios in their mother's lap, and forced her to marry her own cook, an Indian. Then he equipped another fleet and sent Mauros the patrician, surnamed Bessos [?], giving him a ram, siege engines and every kind of machine for storming fortresses. He ordered him to raze the walls of Cherson and the whole city to the ground, to leave not one soul in it alive, and to report what he had done in frequent dispatches. Mauros crossed over and with the ram brought down the tower called Kentenaresion, and also the one next to it, called Syagros. But the Khazars arrived, and there was a truce in the fighting. Bardanes escaped and went off to the Khagan. Since the fleet had achieved nothing and did not dare return to the emperor, they too repudiated Justinian and acclaimed Bardanes emperor. They asked the Khagan to hand Philippikos over to them. The Khagan demanded a pledge from them that he would not be betrayed by them, and a payment of one nomisma a man to recover him. At once they

gave him these and received Philippikos as emperor. As the fleet was taking so long and no report had come, Justinian guessed the reason. He took with him the men of the Opsikion and part of the Thrakesians and went as far as Sinope to find out what was happening at Cherson. While he was watching the far shore, he saw the fleet sailing towards the city. Roaring like a lion, he too hurried towards the city. But Philippikos got there first and took control of the city, and Justinian came to Damatrys and camped there with his men. Philippikos at once sent Mauros the patrician with John the spatharios, surnamed Strouthos, against Tiberios, and Elias likewise with a strike force against Justinian at Damatrys, and another against Barsakourios, who had fled. Mauros went to Blachernai with the said Strouthos and found Tiberios holding with one hand the column of the holy table in the sanctuary of the holy Mother of God, and in the other pieces of the precious wood of the Cross, with amulets around his neck. Outside the sanctuary sat Anastasia, his father's mother. She threw herself at Mauros' feet and begged that her grandson Tiberios should not be killed, since he had done nothing wrong. While she was clinging to his feet and pleading with tears, Strouthos went into the sanctuary and dragged the boy away by force. He took the precious wood from him and laid it on the holy table, and hung the amulets around his own neck. Then they took the boy to the upper postern of Kallinike, stripped him, laid him out on the threshold and cut his throat like a sheep. They ordered him to be buried in the church of the Holy Anargyroi called the church of Paulina. Barsakourios, the protopatrikios and count of the Opsikion, was also captured and killed. Elias went up to Damatrys with the troops under him and, coming to terms with

the army that was there, gave Justinian's men a promise of immunity [?]. At this they all dispersed and deserted Justinian, leaving him alone, and went over to Philippikos' side. Then Elias the spatharios already mentioned rushed at him in a rage, seized him by the neck, cut off his head with the sword he wore at his side, and sent it to Philippikos by Romanos the spatharios. Philippikos sent it by his own spatharios to the western regions, as far as Rome. Before he became emperor, there was a recluse in the monastery of Kallistratos who had the gift of foresight and was a heretic. When Philippikos visited him he said to him, "The empire is waiting for you." Philippikos was alarmed, and the recluse said: "If God commands it, why do you object? But I tell you this: the sixth council was wrongly held. So if you become emperor, reject it, and your reign will be strong and long." Philippikos agreed with him under oath to do this. When Leontios succeeded Justinian, Philippikos went up to the recluse, who said to him, "Do not hurry; you are going to become emperor." When Apsimar too became emperor, he went up to him again, and again he told him, "Do not hurry; it is waiting for you." Philippikos confided in one of his friends, who reported it to Apsimar. Apsimar had him flogged, tonsured and put in irons, and exiled him to Kephalenia. When Justinian became emperor again, he recalled him. Once Philippikos was emperor, he held a false synod of bishops, as the false abbot and recluse had told him, and rejected the holy and ecumenical sixth council. And in the same year the vain man [?]. He lived in the palace without a care in the world. He found there masses of money and very rich properties that previous emperors had amassed over many years from confiscations and on various pretexts, above all the said Justinian, and he squandered them aimlessly and to no purpose, without any effort. In conversation he was considered learned and sensible, but in his actions he lived unseemly and incompetently, and he proved unfit in every respect. He was also a heretic and an adulterer. He drove out the patriarch Kyros

In this year Philippikos drove the Armenians out of his territory and forced them to settle in Melitene and Fourth Armenia. Maslama took Amaseia along with other fortresses and many captives; and George, the bishop of Amaseia [?], was moved to Martyropolis [?]. Philippikos was not ashamed to move madly against the holy and ecumenical sixth council, eager to overturn the divine doctrines it had confirmed. He found men of his own mind: John, bishop [?] of Constantinople, whom he had appointed after deposing Kyros, its president, whom he confined in the monastery of Chora; Germanos, who afterwards held the throne of Constantinople and was then bishop of Cyzicus; Andrew, himself bishop of Crete; and Nicholas, one of the kauchodiakonoi [?],

who had been a professor of medical science and was then quaestor; Elpidios, a deacon of the Great Church; Antiochos the chartophylax; and others of the same sort, who even anathematized the holy sixth council in writing. The Bulgars came down secretly on the Stenon by way of Philea, carried out a great slaughter and overran the country up to the city. They found many people crossing over [?], local weddings and very lavish banquets with all kinds of silver and other belongings, and they raided as far as the Golden Gate. After taking captives throughout Thrace, they went back home unharmed with countless animals. Likewise the Arabs took Misthia and other fortresses, carrying off a great many households and countless animals. Year of the World 6205. In this year Abbas invaded Romania, took Antioch in Pisidia with many captives, and went home. On 28 Peritios there was a great earthquake in Syria. When two years of Philippikos' reign had passed in this way, the birthday horse races were held, and the Greens won. On the Saturday of Pentecost the emperor decided to make his entry on horseback with a procession and musical instruments, to bathe in the public bath of Zeuxippos, and to have lunch with citizens of old families. While he was taking his midday rest, Rouphos, the protostrator of the Opsikion, suddenly came in through the Golden Gate. He was acting on the plot of George, patrician and count of the Opsikion, surnamed Bouraphos, and of Theodore Myakios the patrician, and had with him the taxatoi of his theme that George had in Thrace. He rushed into the palace, found Philippikos resting, seized him and carried him

off to the dressing room of the [?], and there he blinded him without anyone knowing. The next day, Pentecost, the people gathered in the Great Church, and Artemios the protoasekretis was crowned and renamed Anastasios. On the Saturday George and Theodore Myakios were blinded, and on the second Saturday George Bouraphos was blinded, and they were exiled to Thessalonica. Year of the World 6206. Artemios, emperor of the Romans,

In this year Maslama raided Romania, plundered Galatia and went home with many captives and much booty. Artemios appointed very able generals to the cavalry themes and very learned men to the civil posts, and lived in security. As the Arabs were arming against Romania by land and sea, the emperor sent officials to [Walid] in Syria, supposedly to discuss peace. Among them was Daniel of Sinope, patrician and prefect of the city, whom he ordered to find out exactly how far the Arabs were moving against Romania and in what strength. When Daniel had gone and come back, he told the emperor of their great armament against the imperial city by land and sea. The emperor ordered that each person should provide for his own needs for three years, and that anyone who could not do so should leave the city. He appointed overseers and began building dromons and biremes [?]. He also renewed the sea walls, and likewise the land walls, setting up bow-ballistas, tetrareai [?] and engines on the towers. When he had fortified the city as well as he could, he stored a great deal of grain in the imperial granaries and secured his own position. Year of the World 6207. Year 1 of Suleiman, leader of the Arabs. Germanos, bishop of Constantinople,
In this year Walid [?] died, and Suleiman succeeded to his rule. In that same second year of the reign of Artemios, also called Anastasios,

In the thirteenth indiction, on 11 August, Germanus was translated from the metropolis of Cyzicus to Constantinople [?], and the following decree of translation was proclaimed: "By the vote and approval of the most God-fearing priests and deacons, of all the holy clergy, of the sacred senate, and of the Christ-loving [people] of this God-guarded imperial city, divine grace, which always heals what is weak and supplies what is lacking, translates Germanus, the most holy metropolitan and president of the metropolis of Cyzicus, to be bishop of this God-guarded imperial city." [?] This translation took place in the presence of Michael, the most holy priest and apocrisiarius of the apostolic see, and of other priests and bishops, under the emperor Artemius. Artemius learned that the fleet of the Saracens had sailed from Alexandria to Phoenix to cut cypress timber. He picked out the swift ships from his own fleet, put troops of the Opsikion theme on board, and ordered them all to assemble at Rhodes. As their general and commander he appointed John, deacon of the Great Church, who was at that time general logothete. When John had come down to Rhodes and the naval forces had gathered, he spoke to the commanders about setting out and going to Phoenix to burn the timber and whatever equipment of the Hagarenes was found there. Although all

obeyed willingly, the men of the Opsikion would not accept. They reviled the emperor and cut down the deacon John with swords. After this the fleets split up and sailed off to their own home stations, and the villains set out against the imperial city. When they reached Adramyttium, having no leader, they found there a local man named Theodosius. He was a collector of public taxes, a quiet man and a private citizen, and they urged him to become emperor. He fled and hid in the mountains, but they found him, forced him to accept, and acclaimed him as emperor. When Artemius learned this, he put men of his own household in command of the city, together with the fleet he had fitted out. After arming them, he himself went out to the city of Nicaea and made himself secure there. The rebels set out and stirred up the whole Opsikion theme and the Gothograeci. They seized a great many merchant ships, small and large, and hurried to Chrysopolis by land and sea. The city's fleet lay at anchor in the harbour of St Mamas, and the two sides fought each other every day for six months. When the city's fleet moved to the city's harbour of the Neorion, Theodosius crossed over and took control of the Thracian districts. Through treachery at the gate of the single wall of Blachernae they took the city. The lawless troops of the Opsikion, together with the Gothograeci, ran through the citizens' houses by night and plundered on a vast scale, sparing no one. They seized the officials of Artemius who were in the city, together with Germanus the patriarch of Constantinople, and took them to Nicaea to give assurance to Artemius and those with him. When Artemius saw them, he gave up hope for himself and surrendered. He asked for a pledge of safety and put on the monastic habit. Theodosius kept him unharmed and exiled him to Thessalonica. Philippicus had reigned for two years, Artemius for one year and three months. Leo, who was general of the Anatolikon, took Artemius' side and did not submit to Theodosius. He had as his partner and ally Artabasdus the Armenian, general of the Armeniakon. Leo agreed to give him his daughter as wife, and he did so.

In this year Maslama campaigned against Constantinople. He sent Suleiman ahead with an army by land and Umar by sea, while he himself followed them with a large military baggage train. Suleiman and Bakchar reached Amorium and wrote to Leo, the general of the Anatolikon: "We know that the empire of the Romans is rightly yours. So come to us, and let us discuss terms of peace." Suleiman saw that Amorium had no army and that the general was in disfavour because he had sided with Artemius. So he laid siege to the city, intending to wait there for Maslama. As soon as he approached the city, the Saracens began to acclaim the general Leo as emperor, and they urged those inside to do the same. When the people of Amorium saw how eagerly the Saracens acclaimed him, they acclaimed him too. The general realized that Amorium was about to be lost, since it had no troops or officers. So he sent word to Suleiman: "If you want me to come to you and discuss peace, why are you besieging the city?" Suleiman answered him: "Come, and I will withdraw." The general received a pledge from him and came to him with four hundred horsemen [?]. When the Hagarenes saw him, they put on their mail coats and armour and came out to meet him, and he camped half a mile from their camp. For three days he went over to them, and they discussed peace and their withdrawal from the city. They kept saying: "Agree to [?], and then we will withdraw." The general realized that they meant to seize him. He invited a great many of the leading Saracens to dinner, and while they were eating, Suleiman sent three thousand Saracens in mail coats to surround him and guard him so that he could not [? escape]. The scouts found out and reported to him: "A multitude of Saracens is standing around us, horsemen [?]." Then one of their horsemen, named Zubair, came and stood before him and said: "A slave has run away after stealing a great deal of money, and we have ridden out because of him." The general saw through their trick and said to them: "Do not trouble yourselves." [Critical apparatus:] Μαλσαμᾶς, Μετελμές [?]. For look, Maslama too is drawing near." The bishop came out to him, and Leo told him the same things. When Suleiman learned that the bishop had come out to him, they sent to the general, saying: "Hand the bishop over to us." The general, hard pressed [?], hid him. He told one of his men: "While we are talking, dress him in different clothes and send him off to the mountains, as if he were going for wood or water." When the Saracens pressed him about the bishop, the general said: "He is not here. But go to the emir, and I will come too, and we will talk about everything." They reckoned that if he came with them to the emir they could seize him in their midst, so they let him go. He mounted his horse with two hundred of his men as if he were going hunting, and turned off to the left. The Saracens who were with him said to him: "Where are you going?" He said: "I want to make camp at [?]." They said: "Your plan is not a good one, and we are not coming with you." Then the general said to his own men: "They gave us a pledge and then tried to seize us, and through us to destroy the Christians. But they hold none of our men or of the horses left behind." He went ten miles and made camp. The next day he sent the domestic of his stratores to inform them: "You gave me a pledge and then tried to seize me by guile. That is why I withdrew." Maslama had crossed the passes, but Suleiman did not know it. The emirs and the troops rose up against Suleiman, saying: "Why are we besieging these walls instead of raiding?" They struck their tents and withdrew. The general sent Nicaeas the tourmarch with soldiers into Amorium, after removing most of the women and children, and he himself went off to Pisidia. When Maslama came into Cappadocia, the Cappadocians gave up hope for themselves and came out to him, begging him to take them under his protection. Hearing of the enmity that the emperor Theodosius held toward the general, [? Maslama],
