to him with a gift of five hundred sheep. Justinian was pleased and at once made him a spatharius, and he treated him as a true friend. But some, moved by envy [?], went to the emperor and slandered Leo, saying that he was aiming at the throne. An inquiry was made, and they were shamed as false accusers. Yet from then on many people began to repeat the story. So although Justinian did not wish to harm him openly, he did come to bear him a grudge. He sent him to Alania with money, to stir up the Alans against Abasgia, Lazica and Iberia. Leo went to Lazica and left the money at Phasis. Taking a few of the local people, he went to Apsilia, crossed the Caucasus mountains and came to Alania. Justinian, wanting to destroy him, sent men to take the money away from Phasis. But the Alans received the spatharius with every honour and did as he told them: they invaded Abasgia and carried off captives. The ruler of the Abasgians sent word to the Alans: "As far as I can see, Justinian had no other liar like this one to send and stir you up against us, your neighbours, except this man. For he has deceived you about the promised money too: Justinian sent and took it away. So hand him over to us, and we will give you three thousand nomismata, so that the friendship we have had from the beginning may not be broken." The Alans said: "We did not obey him for the sake of money, but out of love for the emperor." The Abasgians sent to them again, saying: "Hand him over to us, and we will give you six thousand nomismata." The Alans wanted to get to know the land of the Abasgians, so they agreed to take the six thousand nomismata and hand over the spatharius. But they confided everything to the spatharius and said to him: "As you see, the road leading to Romania is closed, and you have no way of getting through. Instead, let us turn the tables on them [?]. We will agree with them to hand you over, and we will send you off together with our own men. That way we will learn their passes [?], and we will raid and lay waste their land, and so we will do you a service." The envoys of the Alans went to Abasgia and agreed to hand over the spatharius. They received a great many gifts from the Abasgians, and more

envoys were sent back again with the sum of gold to take charge of the spatharius. The Alans said to the spatharius: "These men have come to take you, as we told you beforehand, and Abasgia is expecting you. And since we are near them, merchants are constantly going back and forth to them. So that our plan is not betrayed, we will hand you over openly. When they set off, we will secretly send men after them. We will kill them and hide you until our army has gathered, and then we will invade their land without warning." And so it happened. The Abasgian envoys took the spatharius and his men, bound them and set off. But the Alans overtook them from behind with Itaxes their lord and killed the Abasgians. They hid the spatharius, and he raised troops and marched against Abasgia. He went through the passes unexpectedly and inflicted great devastation on the Abasgians, taking many captives. When Justinian heard that his commission had been carried out even without the money, he sent a letter to the Abasgians: "If you keep our spatharius safe and let him pass through your territory unharmed, we will forgive you all your offences." They received this with joy and sent again to Alania, saying: "We will give you our children as hostages. Hand the spatharius over to us, so that we may send him to Justinian." But the spatharius would not accept this. He said: "God can open a door for me to get out, for I will not go out through Abasgia." Some time later an army of Romans and Armenians entered Lazica and besieged Archaeopolis, but when they heard that the Saracens were coming, they withdrew. Some of them, about two hundred, broke away and went up into the districts of Apsilia and the Caucasus, plundering. When the Saracens reached Lazica, the army of the Romans and Armenians fled and went back to Phasis. But the two hundred stayed in the Caucasus mountains and kept to brigandage, having given up hope for themselves. When the Alans learned of this, they supposed that a large force of Romans was in the Caucasus. They rejoiced and said to the spatharius: "The Romans have come near. Go to them." The spatharius took fifty Alans and crossed the snows of the Caucasus on snowshoes in the month of May. He found the men and was overjoyed,

and he asked: "Where is the army?" They said: "When the Saracens attacked, they went back to Romania. Since we could not get back to Romania, we were making for Alania." He said to them: "What are we to do now?" They said: "It is impossible for us to go through this country." The spatharius said: "Is there no way to get out by another route?" Now there was a fort there called Sideron, held at that time by a commander named Pharasmanius, who was subject to the Saracens but at peace with the Armenians. The spatharius sent him a message: "Since you are at peace with the Armenians, make peace with me as well. Come under the empire of the Romans, and help us to go down to the sea and cross to Trebizond." Pharasmanius chose not to do this. So the spatharius sent some of his men, together with Armenians, ordering them to lay an ambush: "When the people come out of the fort to work, seize as many of them as you can, and hold the gates from outside until we arrive too." They went and laid the ambush. When the people came out to work, they fell on them suddenly, seized the gate and took many prisoners. Pharasmanius was left in the fort with a few men. The spatharius arrived as well and called on Pharasmanius to open the gates peacefully, but he refused and fought on. The fort was strong, and the spatharius could not take it. Marinus, the chief of the Apsilians, learned that the fort was under siege and was seized with fear, thinking that the spatharius had a large army with him. He took three hundred men with him and went to the spatharius, saying: "I will see you safely as far as the coast." When Pharasmanius saw how things stood, he said to the spatharius: "Take my son as a hostage, and I promise to serve the empire." The spatharius took his son and said to him: "What kind of servant of the empire do you call yourself, when you speak to us shut up behind your walls? We cannot withdraw until we take the fort." Then Pharasmanius said: "Give me a pledge." The spatharius gave him a pledge to do him no harm, on condition that he himself would enter the fort with only thirty men. But he did not keep this pledge. He ordered the thirty who were going in with him: "When we go in, hold the gates, and let everyone come in [?]." When this had been done, he ordered fire to be thrown into the fort. A great blaze broke out, and the households came out, snatching up whatever of their belongings they could carry.

Chronography [?]. After spending another three days, he pulled down the walls [?] of the land. Then he set out and went down into Apsilia together with Marinus, their chief, and was received by the Apsilians with great honor. From there he went down to the coast, crossed over and came to Justinian. When Justinian had been killed and Philippicus blinded, Artemius became emperor and appointed him general of the Anatolics. When Theodosius became emperor and Artemius was driven out, the Roman state was in confusion, both from the barbarian invasion and from Justinian's bloodshed and Philippicus's impieties. This Leo we have been speaking of then fought on Artemius's side against Theodosius. He had Artabasdus, the general of the Armeniacs, in agreement with him and acting with him. After he became emperor, Leo made Artabasdus his son-in-law by giving him his daughter Anna, and also appointed him curopalates. Maslama, having wintered in Asia, was waiting for Leo's promises to be kept. But he received nothing from Leo and realized that he had been tricked by him. So he came to Abydos, ferried a sizable army across into Thrace, and set out against the imperial city. He also wrote to Suleiman the protosymboulos to come with the fleet that had been made ready. On the 15th of August Maslama laid siege to the city, after ravaging the Thracian forts as well. They put a palisade around the land wall, dug a great ditch, and above it built a breastwork of dry stone. On the 1st of September of the first indiction, Suleiman, the enemy of Christ, came up with the fleet and his emirs. He had huge warships, katinai and dromons, 1,800 in number, and anchored from the Magnaura as far as the Kyklobion. Two days later a south wind blew, and setting out from there they sailed past the city. Some crossed over to the area of Eutropius and Anthemius, while others anchored on the Thracian side, from the fort of Galata as far as Kleidion. The large ships were weighed down by their cargo and moved sluggishly, so about twenty katinai stayed behind as a rearguard, each carrying a hundred men in mail to guard them. When a calm

Theophanes [?]. …caught them in the current and a light breeze blew from the Strait, it drove them outward. At once the pious emperor sent fire-ships against them from the Acropolis, and with God's help set them ablaze. Some were driven burning against the sea walls, others sank to the bottom with all hands, and others were carried off in flames as far as the islands of Oxeia and Plateia. After this the people of the city took courage, while the enemy were badly frightened, having learned how powerful the liquid fire was. That same evening they had intended to anchor at the sea walls and lay the booms [?] of their ships on the battlements, but God scattered their plan through the intercessions of the holy Theotokos. That same night the pious emperor secretly lowered the chain at Galata. The enemy thought the emperor had lowered it to lure them in, so they did not dare to enter and anchor inside Galata. Instead they sailed across into the bay of Sosthenion and made their fleet secure there. On the 8th of October their leader Suleiman died, and Umar became emir. The winter in Thrace was very severe, so that for a hundred days the ground could not be seen for the frozen snow, and a great number of the enemy's horses, camels and other animals died. In the spring Sufyan arrived with the fleet that had been built in Egypt. He had four hundred grain-carrying katinai and

[?] day we commemorate the very great and unsurpassed love for mankind shown toward us [?], when God turned back the godless Hagarenes in shame through the mediation of our most holy Lady, the Theotokos and ever-virgin Mary [?]

dromons. Having learned how powerful the Roman fire was, he went past Bithynia, crossed directly over and anchored in the harbor of Kalos Agros. Not long afterward Yazid also arrived with another fleet, built in Africa. He too had three hundred and sixty katinai carrying arms and provisions. He had learned the same things about the liquid fire, so he anchored at Satyros and Bryas and as far as Kartalimen. But the Egyptians in these two fleets took counsel among themselves. At night they took the katinai's skiffs and fled to the city, acclaiming the emperor, so that from Hiereia to the city the whole sea seemed covered with timber [?]. From them the emperor learned about the two fleets hiding in the bay. He had fire-bearing siphons built, put them on board dromons and biremes, and sent them against the two fleets. With God's help, through the intercessions of the all-immaculate Theotokos, the enemy were sunk on the spot. Our men took the spoils and the enemy's provisions and returned with joy and victory. Again, when Merdasan from Pylai was overrunning the country as far as Nicaea and Nicomedia with the Arab army, the imperial officers who were hiding in Libos and Sophon like Mardaites suddenly fell on the infantry, cut them to pieces and forced them to flee from there. After that the [?] coast enjoyed a little freedom. Many chelandia set out from the city and brought in provisions, and the fishing boats too were not prevented from fishing around the islands and the sea walls. A great famine broke out among the Arabs, and they ate all their animals as they died, horses, donkeys and camels. Some say that they even put dead men and their own dung into ovens, kneaded them into dough and ate them. A plague also fell on them, and countless multitudes
(89) The Egyptians sailing with them boarded the small boats attached to the ships and came to Byzantium.

of them it destroyed. The Bulgar nation also made war on them and, according to those who know the facts precisely, slaughtered twenty-two thousand of them. Many terrible things happened to them at that time, so that they learned by experience that God and the all-holy Virgin, the Mother of God, guard this city and the empire of the Christians, and that God never wholly abandons those who call on him in truth, even if we are chastised for a little while because of our sins. A.M. 6210. Leader of the Arabs: Umar [?].

In this year Sergius, protospatharius and general of Sicily, heard that the Saracens were besieging the imperial city. So he crowned an emperor of his own there, one of his men named Basil, a Constantinopolitan, son of Gregory Onomagoulos, and renamed him Tiberius. Basil made appointments and named his own officials on the advice of this Sergius. When the emperor heard of this, he sent his own chartularius Paul, whom he appointed patrician and general of Sicily. For his support he gave him written orders to the officials of the western regions and a sacra addressed to the people. They boarded a fast dromon by night and went out toward the region of Cyzicus. Travelling from place to place by land and sea, they suddenly reached Sicily. When they entered Syracuse, Sergius heard of it and was dismayed. Aware of his own guilt, he fled to the Lombards who lived near Calabria. The people were gathered and the sacra was read, and from it they learned that the empire was standing firm and the city was in good heart about the enemy. And the general

told them about the two fleets. At once they acclaimed Leo as emperor and handed Basil Onomagoulos and the officials he had appointed over to the general in chains. The general beheaded Basil together with his commander-in-chief, wrapped [?] their heads and sent them to the emperor by the spatharii. The rest he flogged and tonsured, slit the noses of some, and exiled them. From then on there was great stability in the West. The Sergius mentioned above asked the general for a guarantee of immunity, received it and came out to him, and all the western regions were at peace. Umar, having taken power over the Arabs, ordered Maslama to return. The Saracens set out on the 15th of August in great shame. As their fleet was making its way out, a storm from God, sent through the intercessions of the Mother of God, burst on them and scattered them. Some it sank at Proconnesus and the other islands, others in the bays and along the other headlands. The survivors were passing through the Aegean Sea when suddenly a fearful divine wrath came upon them: fiery hail fell on them and made the sea water boil, and as the pitch melted, the ships went down to the bottom with all hands. Only ten of them were saved by God's providence, so that they could announce to us and to the Arabs the mighty works God had done against them. Our men came upon them and were able to capture five, while the other five escaped to Syria, proclaiming the power of God. In the same year, after a great earthquake in Syria, Umar banned wine from the cities and began forcing the Christians to convert to Islam. Those who converted he exempted from taxes, while those who
78: 'en gar tō' A; 'en tō gar' vulg. 'autōn' A [?]. 'phobera' added from A. 'hautai' A; 'autai' vulg. [?]

would not accept it he put to death, and so he made many martyrs. He also decreed that a Christian's testimony against a Saracen should not be accepted. He also wrote a dogmatic letter to the emperor Leo, thinking he would persuade him to convert to Islam. A.M. 6211. In this year the impious emperor Leo had a son born to him, Constantine, more impious still than his father and a forerunner of the Antichrist. On the 26th of October his wife Maria was crowned in the Triclinium of the Augusteus. She went in state procession, alone and without her husband, to the Great Church. After praying before the entrance of the great sanctuary, she went on to the great baptistery, where her husband had gone ahead of her with a few men of his household. There Germanus the high priest baptized Constantine, who would succeed them in their wickedness and in their empire. And from his infancy a terrible and foul-smelling sign was shown about him: he defecated in the holy font, as those who were present report precisely. So the most holy patriarch Germanus said prophetically that this sign meant that a great evil would come upon the Christians and the Church through him. The leading men of the themes and of the senate received him from the font after his baptism. After the divine liturgy the Augusta Maria returned in state with her baptized son, distributing largesse all the way from the church to the Chalke Gate of the palace. In the same year Niketas Xylinites wrote to Artemius in Thessalonica, urging him to go to Tervel so that he might come against Leo with Bulgar help. Artemius did as he was told and went, and Tervel gave him an army and fifty centenaria of gold. With these he came against Constantinople. When the city would not receive him, the Bulgars handed him over to Leo, were treated generously by him, and returned home. The emperor

put him to death together with Xylinites, and confiscated the property of Xylinites, who was a magistros and possessed a great deal. Likewise the Bulgars beheaded Sisinnius the patrician, surnamed Rendakes, and Theognostus the protoasekretis, and Niketas Anthrax, who was also commander of the walls, because they had been with Artemius. Likewise the emperor put to death Isoes, patrician and count of the Opsikion, as accomplices and friends of Artemius. The rest he had their noses cut off, confiscated their property and exiled them. A.M. 6212. Leader of the Arabs: Yazid, year 1. In this year, in the third indiction, on Easter day, Constantine was crowned by his father Leo in the tribunal of the Nineteen Couches, the blessed patriarch Germanus saying the customary prayers. In the same year Umar, ruler of the Arabs, died, having been emir for two years and four months, and Yazid became emir. In his reign a usurper arose in Persia named [?], son of Muhallab [?], and many from Persia went off with him. Yazid sent Maslama, who killed him and brought Persia back under control. A.M. 6213. In this year a Syrian false messiah appeared and led the Hebrews astray, saying that he was the Christ, the Son of God. A.M. 6214. In this year the emperor forced the Hebrews and the Montanists to be baptized. The Jews, baptized against their will, washed the baptism off, and they took the holy gift after eating, and so defiled the
Theophanes [?]. faith. The Montanists, having consulted oracles [?] among themselves, fixed a day, went into the houses appointed for their error, and burned themselves to death.

A.M. 6215. In this year a certain Jew, a sorcerer, from Laodicea in coastal Phoenicia, came to Yazid and promised him that he would rule the Arab realm for forty years if he took down the icons honored in the churches of the Christians throughout his realm. The foolish Yazid was persuaded by him and issued a general decree against the holy and venerable icons. But by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ and the intercessions of his incorrupt Mother and of all the saints, Yazid died that same year, before his satanic decree had become known to most people. The emperor Leo took up this lawless and bitter heresy and became the cause of many evils for us. He found someone who shared his ignorance, a man named Beser. Beser had been born of Christian parents in Syria but had abandoned faith in Christ and been steeped in the doctrines of the Arabs. Not long before, he had been freed from slavery to them and had come to the Roman state. Leo honored him for his bodily strength and for sharing his heresy, and he became the emperor's comrade-in-arms in this great evil. Also of one wicked mind with him was the bishop of Nakoleia, a man full of every kind of uncleanness who lived in the ignorance he was raised in. A.M. 6216. Leader of the Arabs: Hisham, year 1 [?]. I now come to tell the story of the blessed Stephen, pope of Rome, how he fled to Francia and was saved. This celebrated Stephen suffered many wrongs at the hands of Aistulf, king of the Lombards.

He fled to the Franks in the time of Pippin, the majordomo, who was in charge of the administration of all affairs and of the Frankish nation. For it was their custom that their lord, that is, the king, ruled by right of birth, but did nothing and administered nothing. All he did was eat and drink without thought and stay at home. On the first of May each year he presided before the whole nation: he greeted them and was greeted by them, received the customary gifts and gave gifts in return, and then lived by himself until the next May. He has a so-called majordomo who manages all affairs according to his own judgment and that of the nation. Those descended from that family were called Cristatai, which means 'hairy-backed', for they had hair growing down their spines like pigs. So Stephen, under pressure from Aistulf's cruelty and folly, and also given leave by him to go to Francia and do whatever he could, came and ordained Pippin. Pippin was at that time a very highly esteemed man. He presided over affairs in the king's place, and he had fought against the Arabs who had crossed from Africa into Spain, who hold Spain to this day and had tried to fight the Franks as well. Pippin went out against them with his host, killed their leader Abd al-Rahman himself, and destroyed with him a countless multitude by the river Eridanus. He was admired and loved by the nation, not only for this but for his other merits as well, and he became the first leader of the nation who did not rule by right of birth. This same Stephen released him from the sin of breaking his oath to the king, tonsured the king who had reigned before him, and confined him in a monastery with honor and in comfort. This Pippin had two sons, Charles and his brother Carloman. In the same year Yazid, ruler of the Arabs, died, having been emir for four years. And Hisham became emir, his. Note: 'tēs dioikēseōs' added from A; vulg. [?]. 'katagomenoi' A, 'legomenoi' vulg. 'elthōn cheir.' A, 'elthōn de cheir.' vulg. [?] A, 'alla' vulg. 'Karoulon kai Karoulom.' A, 'Karoullon kai Karoullom.' vulg.

brother. He began to build palaces in the country and in the cities, to lay out plantations and gardens, and to bring water to the surface. He campaigned [?] against Romania and lost many of his men [?]

In this year the impious emperor Leo began to raise the question of destroying the holy and venerable icons. When Gregory, pope of Rome, learned this, he withheld the taxes of Italy and Rome. He wrote Leo a dogmatic letter, saying that an emperor should not make pronouncements about the faith or make innovations in the ancient doctrines of the Church laid down by the holy Fathers. In the same year the torrent flooded and entered the city of Edessa, and many

A.M. 6218. In this year Maslama campaigned against Caesarea in Cappadocia and took it. There was plague in Syria, and the camels of the protosymboulos were burned at Saint Elias. Muawiya, son of Hisham, campaigned against Romania, marched about in it and returned. In this same year, in the ninth indiction, in summer, a vapor like that from a fiery furnace boiled up for some days from the depths of the sea between the islands of Thera and Therasia. Little by little it thickened and turned to stone in the heat of the fiery burning, and the whole column of smoke looked like fire. Because the earthy substance was so dense, it threw up great pumice stones the size of rocks over all of Asia Minor, Lesbos, Abydos and coastal Macedonia, so that the whole surface of that sea was covered with floating pumice. In the midst of this great fire an island of earth was formed and joined [?] to the so-called Sacred Island. It had not existed before, but just as the islands mentioned earlier, Thera and Therasia, were once thrown up, so this one was too, now in the time of Leo the enemy of God. He took the divine wrath against him as something in his favor, and more shamelessly

…he stirred up war against the holy and venerable icons. His ally was Beser, the denier of God, who matched him in senselessness, for both were full of every kind of boorishness and ignorance, the source of most evils. The people of the imperial city were deeply grieved at these novel teachings and planned to attack him. They killed some of the emperor's men who had taken down the image of the Lord over the great Bronze Gate. As a result many of them were punished for their piety with mutilation, floggings, exiles and fines, especially those distinguished by birth and learning. Even the schools were extinguished, along with the pious education that had prevailed from Constantine the Great, who is among the saints, until now. This Saracen-minded Leo destroyed it, as he destroyed many other good things. Amid all this the men of Hellas and of the Cyclades islands, moved by divine zeal, made common cause and rose against him with a great naval force. They had with them a certain Cosmas, whom they intended to crown [?]. Agallianus, turmarch of the Helladics, led the force, together with Stephen. They approached the imperial city on 18 April of the tenth indiction, engaged the Byzantines and were defeated, for their ships were burned with liquid fire. Some drowned around the Pit [?], and among them Agallianus threw himself into the sea in full armour. The survivors fled to the ruler for refuge, and Cosmas and Stephen were beheaded. The impious Leo and those who shared his views grew in wickedness and intensified the persecution of piety. At the summer solstice of this tenth indiction, after his wicked victory over his own countrymen, a host under two Saracen emirs was arrayed against Nicaea in Bithynia. Amer ran ahead with fifteen thousand light-armed men and encircled the unprepared city, and Muawiya followed with another eighty-five thousand. After a long siege and the partial destruction of the walls, they…

…did not take the city, thanks to the prayers, acceptable to God, offered in the church of the holy Fathers who are honoured there, where their venerable images had been set up and are honoured to this day by those who share their faith. But a certain Constantine, groom of Artabasdus, saw an image of the Theotokos standing there. He took a stone and threw it at the image, shattered it, and trampled on it when it fell. Then he saw in a vision the Lady standing beside him, and she said: "Do you see what a fine deed you have done against me? Truly you have done this against your own head." The next day the Saracens attacked the wall and battle was joined. The wretched man ran to the wall like a brave soldier and was struck by a stone shot from a siege engine. It shattered his head and face, and he received a recompense worthy of his impiety. The Saracens gathered a great many captives and much booty and withdrew. In this, too, God showed the impious emperor that he had not prevailed over his countrymen because of his piety, as he boasted, but for some divine reason and ineffable judgement [?]. The city of the holy Fathers had repelled that great Arab force through their intercessions, by means of their most faithful images honoured in it. This served to refute the tyrant and condemn him beyond excuse, and to confirm the pious. For the impious man erred not only about the relative veneration of the holy icons but also about the intercessions of the all-pure Theotokos and of all the saints, and the utterly abominable man loathed their relics, as did his teachers the Arabs. From that time on he shamelessly harassed the blessed Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople. He blamed all the emperors, bishops and Christian peoples before him for having practised idolatry by venerating
…as the foundation of his power, putting forward violence rather than law. He took down, even before his own entry, the [image] set up in the forecourts of the pa[lace]…

…the holy and venerable icons, since his unbelief and great ignorance kept him from grasping the doctrine of relative veneration. AM 6219. In this year Maslama took the fortress of Ateous [?] and went back. AM 6220. In this year the son of the Khagan, ruler of Khazaria, invaded Media and Armenia. He found Garach, the general of the Arabs, in Armenia and killed him with the multitude that was with him. Then he plundered the land of the Armenians and the Medes and went back, having struck great fear into the Arabs. AM 6221. In this year Maslama campaigned against the land of the Turks. They met in battle, and men fell on both sides. Maslama lost his nerve, took to flight and returned through the mountains of Khazaria. In the same year Leo, the lawless emperor, raging against the right faith, summoned the holy Germanus and began to entice him with flattering words. The blessed high priest said to him: "We hear that the holy and venerable icons will be destroyed, but not in your reign." When the emperor pressed him to say in whose reign, he said: "In the reign of Conon." The emperor said: "My baptismal name is in truth Conon." The patriarch said: "God forbid, master, that this evil should be accomplished in your reign, for whoever carries it out is a forerunner of Antichrist and overturns the divine dispensation of the incarnation." At this the tyrant grew angry and pressed hard on the blessed man, as Herod once did on the Forerunner. The patriarch reminded him of the agreements made before his accession, how he had given him God as guarantor that he would in no way shake the Church of God from its apostolic and God-given ordinances. But not even this made the wretch ashamed. He kept watching him and planting certain people [?], and strove to find words by which he might catch him acting against his reign, so that he could depose him from the throne as a conspirator and not as a confessor,

[Theophanes]. In this he had as ally and accomplice Anastasius, the patriarch's disciple and synkellos. He had made a pact with him, since Anastasius shared his impiety, that he would become the adulterous usurper of the throne and its successor. The blessed man was well aware that Anastasius was so crookedly disposed. Imitating his own Master, as with another Iscariot, he wisely and gently reminded him of what betrayal means. When he saw that Anastasius persisted in error without turning back, he turned to him once, when Anastasius had stepped on the back of his robe as they were going in to the emperor, and said: "Do not hurry, for you will soon enough enter the Diippion." Anastasius and the others who heard were disturbed by the remark, but did not understand the prediction. It was fulfilled fifteen years later, in the third year of Constantine the persecutor, in the twelfth indiction, and it persuaded everyone that it had been prophesied by divine grace. For Constantine, after overcoming the usurpation of the throne by his brother-in-law Artabasdus, had this Anastasius flogged in the Hippodrome along with his other enemies. Then he paraded him naked through the Diippion, seated backwards on a donkey, because he had joined the enemies in condemning [?] him and had crowned Artabasdus, as will be shown in its proper place. In Byzantium this holy and inspired Germanus was then at his height as champion of the doctrines of piety, fighting like a man thrown to the beasts against Leo, true to his name, the Lion, and against his comrades-in-arms. In elder Rome there was Gregory, the all-holy apostolic man, who shared the throne of Peter, chief of the apostles. He shone in word and deed, and he detached Rome, Italy and the whole West from political and ecclesiastical obedience to Leo and his empire. In Damascus in Syria, John Chrysorrhoas, priest and monk, son of Mansur, an excellent teacher, was outstanding in life and word. But Leo expelled Germanus from his throne, since Germanus was under his authority. Gregory openly refuted him by letters on matters known to many. And John, together with the bishops of the East, subjected the impious man to anathemas. On the [?] of January of the thirteenth indiction, the third day of the week, Leo the impious held a silention against the holy

and venerable icons in the tribunal of the Nineteen Couches. He also summoned the most holy patriarch Germanus, thinking he could persuade him to sign against the holy icons. But Christ's noble servant was not in the least swayed by his loathsome evil counsel. Rightly dividing the word of truth, he renounced the high priesthood and handed over his omophorion. After many words of teaching he said: "If I am Jonah, throw me into the sea. For without an ecumenical council I cannot make innovations in the faith, O emperor." He went away to the place called Platanion, to his family house, and lived there in quiet. He had been bishop for fourteen years, five months and seven days. On 22 January of the same year they ordained Anastasius, the so-called disciple and synkellos of the same blessed Germanus, who had sided with Leo's impiety. Out of worldly ambition he was appointed false bishop of Constantinople. But Gregory, the holy president of Rome, as I said before, repudiated Anastasius together with his libelli. He refuted Leo by letters as impious and detached Rome, with all Italy, from his empire. The tyrant, in a rage, intensified the persecution of the holy icons. Many clergy, monks and devout laymen faced danger for the right doctrine of the faith and won the crown of martyrdom. AM 6222. Year 1 of Anastasius, bishop of Constantinople. In this year Maslama campaigned against Romania. He came into Cappadocia and took the fortress of Charsianon by trickery. AM 6223. In this year Maslama campaigned against Turkey. He reached the Caspian Gates, took fright and turned back. AM 6224. In this year the emperor Leo married his son Constantine to the daughter of the Khagan, ruler of the Scythians. He made her a Christian and named her Irene. She learned the sacred Scriptures and became distinguished for her piety, rebuking the impiety of these men. Muawiya,

the son of Hisham, campaigned against Romania. He came as far as Paphlagonia and went back with many captives. The emperor was raging against the pope and the defection of Rome and Italy. He fitted out a great fleet and sent it against them, putting Manes, general of the Kibyrrhaiots, in command. But the vain man was put to shame, for the fleet was wrecked in the Adriatic Sea. Then the enemy of God raged still more, and, strengthened in his Arab way of thinking, he imposed poll taxes on a third of the people of Calabria and Sicily. The so-called patrimonies of the holy chief apostles honoured in elder Rome, which had been paid to the churches from of old and amounted to three and a half talents of gold, he ordered to be paid to the public treasury. He also commanded that male infants be watched and registered at birth, as Pharaoh once did with those of the Hebrews. Not even his teachers the Arabs ever did this to the Christians in the East.

In this year Theodore, son of Mansur, was exiled to the regions of the desert. A fiery sign appeared in the sky, shining brightly, and Muawiya plundered Asia. AM 6227. In this year Suleiman, son of Hisham, campaigned against the country of the Armenians and achieved nothing. AM 6228. In this year Muawiya campaigned against Romania. Not many days after his return he fell from his horse and died. AM 6229. In this year Suleiman, son of Hisham, took many captives from Asia. Among them he captured a man from Pergamum who claimed to be Tiberius, son of Justinian. To honour his own son and the emperors, Hisham sent this man out with fitting imperial honours, with troops, sceptres and [?]

to Jerusalem. He ordered him to be paraded with great honour throughout Syria, for all to see and marvel at. AM 6230. In this year Suleiman, son of Hisham, campaigned against Romania. He sacked the so-called Iron Fortress and took captive Eustathius, son of the patrician Marinus. AM 6231. In this year, in the month of May of the eighth indiction, Suleiman campaigned against Romania with ninety thousand men under four generals. Gamer led the first, lying in ambush in parts of the Asian land with ten thousand light-armed men. After him came Melich and Battal with twenty thousand horsemen around Akroinon, and after them Suleiman with sixty thousand around Tyana in Cappadocia. Those in Asia and Cappadocia took much booty in men, women and livestock and returned unharmed. But those with Melich and Battal at Akroinon were attacked by Leo and Constantine and defeated. Most of them perished by the sword together with the two commanders. About eight hundred of their fighters held out against six thousand and fled to Synada. They escaped, joined Suleiman and returned to Syria. In the same year many of them also perished in Africa, together with their general, named Damascenus. AM 6232. In this year, the twenty-fourth of the reign of Leo, the tyrant and most lawless Syrian, markets in Damascus were burned by men from Jerusalem, and they were hanged. A torrent

flooded Edessa on 28 Peritios. In the same year a great and terrible earthquake struck Constantinople on 26 October of the ninth indiction, the fourth day of the week, at the eighth hour. Churches and monasteries collapsed and many people died. The statue of Constantine the Great standing over the Gate of Atalus fell, together with Atalus himself, as did the statue of Arcadius standing on the column of the Xerolophos, the statue of Theodosius the Great over the Golden Gate, and the land walls of the city. Cities and villages in Thrace also fell, and Nicomedia in Bithynia, and Prainetos, and Nicaea, where only one church was saved. In some places the sea withdrew from its own bounds, and the earthquake went on for twelve months. When the emperor saw that the walls of the city had fallen, he proclaimed to the people: "You are not able to build the walls, but we have given orders to the tax administrators." They demanded in the assessment one miliaresion for every nomisma, and the government took the money and built the walls. From then on the custom prevailed of paying the "two keratia" to the administrators. It was the year 6243 from the creation of the world, from Adam, according to the Romans, 6232 [?] according to the Egyptians, that is, the Alexandrians, and [?] from Philip of the Macedonians. Leo reigned from 25 March of the fifteenth indiction until 18 June of the ninth indiction, for twenty-four years, two months and twenty-five days. Likewise Constantine, his son and the successor of his impiety and his reign, reigned from the same 18 June

of the [ninth] indiction until 14 September of the fourteenth indiction. By God's permission he too reigned, for thirty-four years, three months and two days. So, as we said before, Leo died in the same year of the ninth indiction, on 18 June, suffering bodily death along with spiritual death, and Constantine his son became sole ruler. Under the impious Leo many evils befell the Christians: in matters of the orthodox faith, and in civil administration through schemes for shameful gain and greed, in Syria, Calabria and Crete; there was the defection of Italy because of his heresy, and there were earthquakes, famines, plagues and uprisings of nations. To pass over the details, these have been set out in the preceding chapters [?]. It is now fitting to go on and recount the unlawful deeds of his most impious and utterly wretched son, which were more unholy and hateful to God. I shall do so truthfully, since the all-seeing God watches and beholds, and without exaggeration, for the benefit of those who come after, and of the wretched and reckless little men now led astray into the loathsome heresy of that most lawless man, beginning from the tenth indiction, the first year of his reign. This utterly pernicious, crazed, bloodthirsty and most savage beast used power tyrannically and unlawfully. First he cut himself off from our God and Saviour Jesus Christ, from his immaculate and all-holy Mother, and from all the saints. He was led astray by sorceries, debaucheries and bloody sacrifices, and by horse dung and urine. He delighted in effeminate vices and in invoking demons, and from his early youth he had lived amid every soul-destroying practice. When he took over his father's rule along with his wickedness, what need is there to say how much wickedness the utterly foul man stirred up from the start? Indeed he fanned it into a higher, soaring flame. No small dismay seized the Christians as they watched this, so that from the very beginning they all hated him for his recklessness

him. They were inclined to go over to Artabasdus, curopalates and count of the Opsikion, who was his brother-in-law, being married to his sister Anna, and to hand the empire over to him as an orthodox man. In the same year Hisham, leader of the Arabs, killed the Christian captives in every city of his dominion. Among them was the blessed Eustathius, son of the renowned patrician Marinus. He was put under great pressure but did not deny his sincere faith, and he was shown to be a true martyr at Harran, a notable city of Mesopotamia. There his precious relics work all kinds of healings by divine grace. Many others too were perfected in Christ through martyrdom and blood. AM 6233. Year 1 of Constantine, emperor of the Romans. In this year Constantine, the persecutor of the ordinances handed down by the fathers, became emperor through God's judgements and the multitude of our sins. On 27 June of the following tenth indiction he set out against the Arabs into the regions of the Opsikion and came to the place called Crasus. Artabasdus was at Dorylaeum with the army of the Opsikion, and the two regarded each other with suspicion. Constantine sent to him and asked that his sons be sent to him, since they were his nephews and he longed to see them. His aim was to detain them and keep them under guard. Artabasdus saw through the deceit. He was conscious of his own intentions and knew Constantine's boundless wickedness. So he spoke to the army, won it over, and set out against him with his whole host. He killed with the sword the patrician Beser, the Saracen-minded, who came out to meet him first. Constantine found a horse [?] ready saddled, mounted it, and fled to Amorion. He hurried to the theme of the Anatolics, then commanded by Longinus, and was saved by them. He won them over with great promises. He also sent at once to Sisinnakios, then general of the theme of the Thrakesians, and persuaded them to fight on his side. From then on the subjects fought the most terrible battles and armed clashes against one another, since each of the two was proclaimed emperor. Artabasdus [?]

…to Theophanes Monoutes, the patrician and magistros, who was acting as regent in the City, by way of Thalassios the silentiary, [reporting] what had happened. Theophanes, an adherent of Artabasdos, gathered the people in the galleries of the Great Church, and through the letters and the aforementioned Thalassios persuaded everyone that the emperor was dead and that Artabasdos had been proclaimed emperor by the themes. Then all the people, together with Anastasios, the falsely so-called patriarch, condemned him with anathema and execration as an accursed and godless man. They gladly welcomed the news of his slaughter, as if delivered from a very great evil, and proclaimed Artabasdos emperor as orthodox and a champion of the divine doctrines. Monoutes at once sent to the Thracian regions, to his own son Nikephoros, who was strategos of Thrace, to gather the [?] army to guard the City. So he closed the gates of the walls and posted watches, and he seized the friends of Constantine, beat them, tonsured them and put them in prison. When Artabasdos had entered the City with the people of the Opsikion, Constantine too arrived at Chrysopolis with the two themes, I mean the Thrakesians and the Anatolikoi. Achieving nothing, he turned back and wintered at Amorion. Artabasdos restored the holy icons throughout the whole City. The Arabs, seeing them fighting one another, took many captives in Romania, with Suleiman as their commander. Anastasios, the falsely so-called patriarch, holding the precious and life-giving wood, swore to the people: "By him who was nailed to it, this is what the emperor Constantine said to me: ‘Do not [think] that the one whom Mary bore, the so-called Christ, is the Son of God, but a mere man. For Mary bore him just as my mother Mary bore me.’" When the people heard this they denounced him. A.M. 6234. Year 1 of Stephen, bishop of Antioch. In this year Hisham, the leader of the Arabs, died. The most holy Church of Antioch had been widowed for forty years, because the Arabs prevented a patriarch from being made there. Hisham had a certain Syrian monk dear to him, named Stephen,

a rather rustic man but pious, and he [told] the Christians of the East that if they wished to be allowed a patriarch, they should elect this Stephen. Thinking that this had come about from God, they ordained him to the throne of Theoupolis, and from that time until now the freedom [to do so] has continued unhindered. In this year Walid [?] Hisham took power over the Arabs. Constantine sent Andrew the spatharios to him, and Artabasdos sent Gregory the logothete, both seeking an alliance. There was a great drought, and earthquakes in various places, so that in the desert of Saba mountains were joined to one another and villages sank under the earth. In the same year Cosmas, patriarch of Alexandria, together with the city [?], turned to orthodoxy from the heresy of the Monothelites, which had prevailed since Cyrus, bishop of Alexandria under Heraclius. Ghamr campaigned against Romania with a multitude of Arabs, took many captives and returned. A sign appeared in the sky in the north in the month of June. Walid ordered that the tongue of Peter, the most holy metropolitan of Damascus, be cut out, because he openly refuted the impiety of the Arabs and the Manichaeans. He exiled him to Arabia Felix, and there Peter died a martyr for Christ, having clearly pronounced the divine liturgy, as those who tell the story say they were assured of this with [their own] ears [?]. His emulator and namesake Peter, the one at Maiouma, was shown in the same period to be a voluntary martyr for Christ. Confined by illness, he summoned the Arab officials, who were acquainted with him because he served as chartoularios of the public taxes, and said to them: "May you receive from God the reward for your visit, even though you are unbelieving friends. But I want you to be witnesses of my testament, which is this: everyone who does not believe in the Father and [the Son and the] Holy Spirit, the consubstantial and life-originating Trinity in unity, [is blind] [?] in soul and deserves eternal punishment. Such a one is Muhammad, your false prophet and the forerunner of the Antichrist. So turn away, if [you] [obey] me,
So that nature itself forgets itself and stands against itself [Latin:] so far forgetful of itself, war [?]

[if you] obey me, who today call heaven and earth to witness before you, from his fables. For I wish you well today, so that you will not be punished together with him." When they heard him speaking about God in these and many other words, they were seized with astonishment and rage, yet decided to be patient, thinking that he was out of his mind from the illness. But after he had recovered from the illness, he began to cry out still more loudly: "Anathema to Muhammad and to his mythmaking, and to all who believe in it!" Then he underwent punishment by the sword and was proclaimed a martyr. Our [holy] father John, rightly surnamed Chrysorrhoas ("golden-flowing") for the golden-gleaming grace of the Spirit that flourished in him in both word and life, honoured him with encomia. The impious emperor Constantine [?] subjected John to anathema because of the surpassing orthodoxy in him, and in place of his ancestral name Mansur, which means "redeemed", renamed the new teacher of the Church "Manzeros", in a Jewish frame of mind. In the same year, in the month of May, Artabasdos went out to the region of the Opsikion, levied troops and reached Asia, ravaging it. When Constantine learned of this he moved against him. He caught him in the region of Sardis as he was coming up from Kelbianon, joined battle with him, routed him and pursued him as far as Kyzikos. Artabasdos reached Kyzikos, boarded a dromon and got safely to the City. In August of the same eleventh indiction, Niketas the monostrategos, the son of Artabasdos, joined battle with Constantine at Modrine, was routed and fled; and [Constantine] killed the patrician Tiridates the Armenian, a brave soldier and cousin of Artabasdos, together with other select officers. There were no small losses on both sides, as the Armenians and the Armeniakoi fought against the Anatolikoi and Thrakesians, the champions of Constantine. In these times the devil, the author of evil, stirred up such madness and mutual slaughter among the Christians that children were roused against parents and brothers against brothers to slaughter without restraint, and they mercilessly burned one another's homesteads and houses.

A.M. 6235 [?]. [Year … ] of Walid, leader of the Arabs [?]. In this year a sign appeared in the north, and dust came down in some places. There was also an earthquake at the Caspian Gates. And Walid was killed by the Arabs on 16 April, a Thursday, having ruled one year, and Yazid the Deficient took power. By scattering a great deal of money he seized Damascus, and received pledges that he should rule from the Arabs in Damascus, Persia and Egypt. Marwan son of Muhammad, who was governing Armenia, heard this and occupied Mesopotamia, ostensibly as champion of Walid's children and in opposition to Yazid. Five months later Yazid died, leaving his brother Ibrahim as his successor at Damascus. Marwan, taking the field against him with the Mesopotamians, came to Edessa, and from there to the region of Damascus and Antilebanon, to a plain called Garis [?]. There he engaged Suleiman, [?] at the [?] Lita, that is, "the Evil", routed him and killed twenty thousand, and only Suleiman with a few others escaped as a fugitive to Damascus. Entering the city, Suleiman killed the sons of Walid, whose champion Marwan claimed to be, and left Damascus after appropriating a considerable amount of money. Marwan in turn took Damascus and killed many of the leading men and those who had had a hand in the murder of Walid and his children, and mutilated others. He transferred the money and all the treasures to Harran, the city of Mesopotamia. In the month of September of the twelfth indiction, Constantine came down to the region of Chalcedon and crossed over to the Thracian side, while Sisinnios, the strategos of the Thrakesians, crossed by way of Abydos and encamped before the land wall. And coming to the [gate] of Charsios

he rode along as far as the Golden Gate, showing himself to the crowds, then turned back again and encamped at St Mamas. Those in the City began to be hard pressed for provisions, and [Artabasdos] sent Athanasios the asekretis and Artabasdos his domestic to bring provisions by ship. But the fleet of the Kibyrrhaiots [?] found them outside Abydos, seized them and brought them to the emperor, who gave the grain to his own people and at once blinded Athanasios and Artabasdos. After this Artabasdos attempted to open the gates of the land wall and join battle with Constantine. When the clash came, Artabasdos's men were routed and many died, among them Monoutes. Artabasdos fitted out vessels carrying fire-pots and sent them to St Mamas against the fleet of the Kibyrrhaiots, and drove them off. A severe famine arose in the City, so that a modios of barley sold for twelve nomismata, of pulses for nineteen, of millet and lupins for eight nomismata, oil at five litrai to the nomisma, and a xestes of wine for a semissis. As the people were dying, Artabasdos was forced to let them go, so that they could leave the City. But he watched their faces and stopped some of them. So some covered their faces and put on women's clothing, and others the monastic habit, and in this way they were able to escape notice and get out. Niketas the monostrategos gathered his own people who had been scattered after Modrine and came as far as Chrysopolis. As he was turning back, the emperor crossed over and pursued him, caught him at Nikomedeia and seized him, together with Markellinos, the former bishop and curator [?], whom he ordered to be beheaded on the spot. The monostrategos he put in fetters and displayed to his father from below the wall. On the second of November he suddenly drew up his forces in the evening and took the City by way of the land wall. Artabasdos, together with the patrician Baktangios, boarded a chelandion and for the moment escaped to the Opsikion, and going to the

fortress of Pouzane, shut himself in. The emperor captured them, blinded Artabasdos along with his two sons, beheaded Baktangios at the Kynegion and hung his head at the Milion for three days. Thirty years later the vindictive and heartless emperor ordered Baktangios's wife to go to the monastery of Chora (for he was [buried] there), dig up his bones, carry them in her own cloak and throw them into the so-called tombs of Pelagios, among those who had died violent deaths. O what inhumanity! He also killed many other leading men who had fought on Artabasdos's side; some he blinded, and others he had their hands and feet cut off. He allowed the officers who had entered with him to go into the houses and plunder the property of the citizens, and he inflicted many other countless horrors on the City. Holding a horse race, he brought Artabasdos with his sons and friends, bound, through the diippion, together with Anastasios, the falsely so-called patriarch, who had been publicly blinded and was seated backwards on an ass; him he brought into the hippodrome and paraded. Then, having terrified and enslaved him as one who now shared his views, he seated him again on the throne of the priesthood. Sisinnios the patrician, strategos of the Thrakesians, who had given him much help and fought at his side and was his cousin, he blinded forty days later, by the just judgment of God. For he who helps the impious will fall into his hands, as it is written.

And Thebit rebelled against Marwan, as did Dahhak of the Harurites [?]; Marwan captured them and killed them in the territory of Emesa, together with a multitude of twelve thousand warriors. In the same year, at the request of the Christians of the East

In this year there was a great earthquake in Palestine, along the Jordan and throughout Syria, on 18 January at the fourth hour, and many countless myriads died, and churches and monasteries collapsed, especially in the desert of the Holy City. The same plague of the bubo spread in the fifteenth indiction to the imperial City. Suddenly, invisibly, a great many small oily crosses began to appear on people's clothes and on the sacred vestments of the churches. This brought people much grief and despondency, at a loss as they were to understand such a sign. And there also came

the wrath of God, destroying without restraint not only those in the City but also those in all the surrounding country. Many people also had hallucinations: falling into a trance, they thought they were travelling with certain strangers, as it seemed to them, of grim appearance, and that those who met them greeted them as friends and talked with them. They took note of what these said and related it afterwards. They also saw the same figures entering houses, killing some of the household and wounding others with the sword. And most of what they told happened just as they had seen it. In the spring of the first indiction the plague grew more severe, and in the summer it blazed up all at once, so that whole households were shut up completely and there was no one left to bury the dead. In this great extremity it was devised to lay boards on saddled pack animals with [?], and so carry out the dead; likewise to pile them on carts one on top of another. suddenly in the harbour of Keramaia, and seized the mouth of the harbour; of a thousand dromons, they say, only three escaped. [?] leader of the Arabs, as I said before [?]. A.M. 6240. In this year peoples called Khorasanites and Black-robed set out from the more easterly regions of Persia against Marwan and against all the kin of those who had ruled before, from Muhammad the false prophet down to this Marwan, that is, against the so-called children of Umayya. For while these, after the killing of Walid, were fighting one another and were preoccupied, the so-called sons of Hashim and of Ali, who were themselves relatives of the false prophet but were in hiding as fugitives in Lesser Arabia, gathered together under the leadership of Ibrahim. These men, having joined with a certain Kahtaba, took counsel and roused the slaves against their own masters, and they killed many in a single night. Armed with their masters' chariots, horses and money, they became powerful. They divided into two tribes, the Kaisites and the Yemenites. Abu Muslim, judging the Yemenites to be the stronger, roused them against the Kaisites, and having destroyed these he arrived in Persia with Kahtaba. He fought Bindaras and with his victory took over all his men, about a hundred thousand. Then he came against [?], who was encamped with two hundred thousand, and broke him too; and catching Marwan at the river Zab [?] with three hundred thousand, he fought him and killed a countless multitude of them. AM 6241. In this year Marwan was pursued by the Black-robed. They caught up with him and he was killed after a very fierce battle. Their leader was Salih son of Ali, one of the fugitives mentioned earlier, who had also sent out Abu Muslim. The rest gathered in Samaria and the region of Trachonitis and assigned the rule by lot to Aboulabbas, after him to his brother Abdallah, and after him to Isa son of Musa. They appointed Abdallah, the brother of Salim [?] and son of Ali, to command Syria, and the same Salim [?] to govern Egypt. Abdallah, the brother of Aboulabbas, who held the succession to the rule by lot after him, they appointed over Mesopotamia. Aboulabbas himself, the leader of them all, took his seat in Persia, since he and the Persians who had fought alongside him had moved the seat of government from Damascus. They also moved all the captured treasure that Marwan had been carrying with him. The sons and kinsmen of Marwan who survived went from Egypt to Africa. From there they crossed the narrow sea by the Ocean that divides Libya from Europe, at the place called Septai, and they have lived in Spain in Europe down to the present time. There they found some who had settled there before them, men cast up there by sea since the time of Mauias [?], who were their kinsmen and of the same religion. The conquest under Marwan lasted six years. During it all the famous cities of Syria had their walls torn down, except Antioch, because he intended to keep it as a refuge, and countless Arabs perished at his hands, for he was very skilled in matters of war. He belonged to the heresy of the Epicureans, or Automatists, having picked up this impiety from the pagans who lived in Harran. On the 25th of January of the third indiction a son was born to the emperor Constantine by the daughter of the Chagan of Khazaria, and he named him Leo. At the same time there was an earthquake in Syria, a great and terrible collapse, so that some of the cities were entirely

wiped out, others partly, while others slid down intact from the mountains to the plains below, walls and houses and all, a distance of six miles or a little more. Eyewitnesses said that the ground in Mesopotamia split lengthwise for two miles, and that another kind of earth, very white and sandy, was thrown up from its depths. From the middle of it, they say, a creature like a mule came up, spotless and speaking with a human voice. It foretold that a people from the desert would invade against the Arabs, and this did happen. In the following year, the fourth indiction, at the feast of holy Pentecost, Constantine the impious emperor crowned his son Leo emperor. He did it through Anastasius, the falsely named patriarch, who shared his views. AM 6242 [?]. Muhammad, leader of the Arabs [?]

In this year the people of Chalcis rose up against the Black-robed Persians, and four thousand of them were killed by those Persians in the territory of Emesa. The same Persians did the same to the Kaisites in Arabia. When Marwan's head arrived, embalmed with myrrh, most of the uprisings ceased. In the same year the most holy [?] patriarch of Antioch, Theophylact, fell asleep, in the month of

AM 6243 [?]. Theodore, bishop of Antioch, year 1. In this year those who had recently come to power killed most of the Christians as kinsmen of the former rulers, having caught them by a trick at Antipatris in Palestine. At the same time Constantine took Theodosiopolis together with Melitene and carried the Armenians off as captives. Theodore, the son of Vicarius, who came from Lesser Armenia, was ordained patriarch of Antioch. AM 6244. In this year Constantine the impious, puffed up with arrogance, held many silentia against the Church
