and the orthodox faith. In every city he used these silentia to persuade the people, by deceit, to follow his own way of thinking, preparing the way for the complete impiety that was to come. AM 6245. In this year Anastasius, the unholy occupant of the throne of Constantinople, died in soul and body of a most pitiable disease called chordapsus. He vomited dung through his mouth and so paid a fitting penalty for his audacity against God and against his teacher. In the same year Constantine the impious assembled an unlawful council of three hundred and thirty-eight bishops against the holy and venerable icons in the palace of Hieria. It was led by Theodosius of Ephesus, the son of Apsimar, and by Pastillas of Perge. They decreed among themselves whatever they saw fit, though none of the catholic thrones was present, that is, Rome, Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem. They began on the 10th of February and continued until the 8th of August of the same seventh indiction. On that day these enemies of the Theotokos came to Blachernae. Constantine went up into the ambo [?], holding by the hand Constantine, a monk who had become bishop of Sylaion. After saying a prayer, he cried out in a loud voice: "Many years to Constantine, ecumenical patriarch!" On the 27th of the same month the emperor went up to the Forum with Constantine, the unholy prelate, and the other bishops. There they proclaimed their heresy and false teaching before all the people, and they anathematized the most holy Germanus, George of Cyprus, and John Chrysorrhoas of Damascus, son of Mansur, holy men and venerable teachers.

What patriarch was found at it? The bishop of Rome refused to come. The bishop of Alexandria did not come at all, the bishop of Antioch not in the least, and the bishop of Jerusalem not even once. What sort of synod is this, then, that has no patriarch? [Latin:] What patriarch was found at it

AM 6246. Constantine, bishop of Constantinople, year 1. In this year Muhammad, also called Aboulabbas, died after ruling for five years. His brother Abdallah was at Mecca, the place of their blasphemy. So he wrote to Abu Muslim, who was in Persia, asking him to hold the seat of government for him, since it had been allotted to him. But Abdallah son of Ali, brother of Salim, sole commander of Syria, was trying to secure the rule for himself. He was coming to take Persia, and he was hostile to the Persians and attached to the Syrians, who were fighting on his side. When Abu Muslim learned this, he roused the armies of Syria [?] and engaged him at [Nisibis?] [?]. Abu Muslim defeated him and killed many, for most of his men were Slavs and Antiochenes. Abdallah alone escaped. A few days later he asked to speak with the other Abdallah, the brother of Muhammad, who had hurried from Mecca to Persia with great zeal. This Abdallah kept him under guard in a rotten little house, secretly had its foundations dug out, and so killed him. Abu Muslim was angry with the Arabs of Syria for rising up against the Black-robed and killing many of them in Palestine, Emesa and the coastland, and he intended to march against them with his armies. But Abdallah stopped him. Abu Muslim was enraged with Abdallah and set off for inner Persia with his host. Abdallah, greatly afraid of him, called him back with persuasive words and entreaties, and even with the loathsome emblems of their rule, I mean the staff and sandals of the false prophet Muhammad. He begged him to turn aside to him for a single day, so that he could give him the thanks owed to a father. Abu Muslim was deceived and came with one hundred thousand horsemen. Once he was alone with Abdallah [?], Abdallah killed him with his own hands. The troops scattered and left that very day, loaded with gifts beyond counting. In this way Abdallah's rule was put in order. AM 6247. Leader of the Arabs [?]

In this year Niketas of Heliopolis was anathematized by the whole Church. The emperor Constantine moved the Syrians and Armenians whom he had brought from Theodosiopolis and Melitene to Thrace, and through them the heresy of the Paulicians spread. The City too had lost many of its inhabitants to the plague, so he brought families from the islands, from Hellas and from the southern regions, settled them in the City and filled it up again. At the same time the Bulgars demanded payment because of the forts that had been built. When the emperor insulted their envoy, they came out in full force and advanced as far as the Long Wall, launching their attack against the imperial city. After much plundering and taking many captives, they returned home unharmed. AM 6248. In this year there was a considerable earthquake in Palestine and Syria on the 9th of March. Theodore, patriarch of Antioch, was exiled through the envy of the Arabs. He was slandered with the charge that he often informed the emperor Constantine of Arab affairs by letter, and so Salim himself banished him to the land of Moab, his own homeland. Salim also ordered that no new churches be built, that no cross be displayed, and that Christians not debate the faith with Arabs. He marched against Romania with eighty thousand men, but when he reached Cappadocia he heard that Constantine was arming against him. He took fright and turned back without achieving anything or doing any damage. He only took a few Armenians who had deserted to him, and [?]
AM 6249. In this year Abdallah raised the taxes on Christians, so that he taxed all the monks, recluses and stylites who were pleasing to God. He also sealed the

[?] Nicephorus [?]: When Constantine had accomplished these things, he began [?] to build towns in Thrace. In them he settled the Syrians and Armenians whom he had uprooted from the cities of Melitene and Theodosiopolis, [providing] what they needed

treasuries of the churches. He brought in Jews to sell their contents, and the freedmen [?] bought them. AM 6250. In this year Constantine took the Sklavinias in Macedonia captive and made the rest subject to him. At the same time some of the Black-robed Persians who held the magian religion were taken in by the devil's deceit. They sold their property, climbed naked onto the walls and threw themselves off, thinking they would fly up to heaven. Instead of any inheritance worth mentioning up there, they fell back to the ground with their limbs shattered. Abdallah had the ringleaders of this error, six in number, put to death through Salim at Beroea and Chalcis. AM 6251. In this year the Arabs, out of envy, barred the Christians from the public record offices for a short time. But they were forced to entrust the same posts to them again, because they themselves could not write the accounts. He also marched against Romania, and they took many captives. They fought Paul, the general of the Armenians, at the Melas and killed him together with a mass of his troops, and they brought back forty-two distinguished men as prisoners, along with many heads. The emperor marched against Bulgaria. When he reached the pass of Beregaba, the Bulgars met him and killed many of his men, among them Leo, patrician and general of the Thrakesians, another Leo, logothete of the Drome, and many common soldiers, and they took their arms. And so they returned without glory. AM 6252. In this year there was a mistake over Easter. The orthodox in the East celebrated Easter on the 6th of April, while the misguided heretics celebrated it on the 13th. In the same year the head of Saint John the Forerunner and Baptist was moved from the monastery

of the Cave to his church in the city of Emesa, which is a famous one. The crypt was built where, to this day, it is venerated by the faithful and honoured with fragrance both bodily and spiritual, pouring out healings on all who run to it in faith. In the same year a very bright beam-shaped comet appeared in the East for ten days, and then in the West for twenty-one days. A certain Theodore, called Libanites, a Syrian, rose against the Arabs in the region of Heliopolis near Lebanon. He fought them and many fell on both sides [?]. In the end he was routed and fled, and the Lebanese who were with him were all killed. There were also disturbances and wars in Africa, and there was a solar eclipse on the 15th of August, the sixth day of the week, at the tenth hour. Some of the Black-robed rose up at Dabekos, declaring that the son of the chief counsellor was God, as their sustainer, and they put forward such a doctrine. The Black-robed went into the house of their error and killed the key-keepers, five persons. Some also went out against Basrasos [?], took many captives and seized much money. AM 6253. In this year the Kasiotes rose up against the Black-robed over women. Some of the Black-robed had lodged in a house where three brothers lived

THEOPHANES. and they tried to violate [?] their wives. The three brothers rose up, killed them and buried them. Then the others gathered and killed the rest as well. Salim sent troops against them by a trick, and they came down on them from above. They seized them, hanged the three brothers on forked gallows, and killed many. At the feast of Easter he came into the holy service in the catholic church. The metropolitan was standing at the altar and had just proclaimed, "For your people beseech you and entreat you," when they carried him out and shut him up in prison, and someone else finished the holy service. There was great fear, and if the metropolitan had not calmed him with good manners and humble words, a great evil would have been done at that hour. The metropolitan was the blessed Anastasius. In the same year Constantine the persecutor had the celebrated monk Andrew, called Kalybites, flogged to death at Blachernae, in the hippodrome of Saint Mamas, because Andrew rebuked his impiety and called him a new Valens and a new Julian. He also ordered his body thrown into the stream, but his sisters snatched it away and buried it in the market of Leukadios. AM 6254. Constantine, bishop of Rome, year [?]. In this year a beam-shaped comet appeared in the East, and the son of Fatima was killed. The Bulgars rose up and murdered their lords, who were descended from the ruling line. They set up an evil-minded man named Teletz, thirty years old. Many Slavs fled and took refuge with the emperor, and he settled them on the Artanas. On the 17th of June the emperor set out for Thrace. He also sent a fleet into the Black Sea of up to two thousand chelandia, each carrying twelve horses. When Teletz heard of the advance against him by land and sea, he took as allies from the neighbouring

peoples twenty thousand men, posted them in the strongholds and so made himself secure. The emperor arrived and pitched camp in the plain of Anchialus. On the 30th of June of the first indiction, the fifth day of the week, Teletz appeared, coming on with a host of peoples. They joined battle and cut each other down for a long time, until Teletz was routed and fled. The battle lasted from the fifth hour until late in the evening. Great numbers of Bulgars were killed, many were captured, and others deserted. The emperor, elated at such a victory, celebrated a triumph for it in the City. He entered in arms with his army, acclaimed by the factions, and dragged the captured Bulgars along in wooden stocks. He ordered the citizens to behead them outside the Golden Gate. The Bulgars rebelled against Teletz and killed him together with his officials, and they set up Sabinus, the son-in-law of Kormesios, their former lord. Sabinus at once sent to the emperor seeking to make peace. The Bulgars held a council and stoutly opposed Sabinus, saying, "Through you Bulgaria is going to be enslaved to the Romans." A revolt broke out, and Sabinus fled to the fort of Mesembria and took refuge with the emperor. The Bulgars then set up another lord named Paganos. AM 6255. In this year two brothers from the desert and from Barathon [?] rose against Abdallah. He sent eighty thousand troops against them and killed them. In the same year Turks came out through the Caspian Gates. They killed many in Armenia, took many captives and went back. A certain Cosmas, bishop of Epiphaneia near Apamea in Syria, surnamed Komanites, was accused by the citizens of Epiphaneia before Theodore, patriarch of Antioch, of making away with sacred vessels. Unable to restore them, he abandoned the orthodox faith and took up Constantine's heresy against the holy icons. By common decision Theodore, patriarch of Antioch, Theodore of Jerusalem and Cosmas of Alexandria, together with the bishops under them, anathematized him with one mind on the day of holy Pentecost, after the reading of the holy Gospel, each in his own city. In the same year, from the beginning of October, there was a great and most bitter cold, not only in our own land but also in the East,

the North and the West. Along the northern coast of the Pontus the sea turned to stone with the cold for a hundred miles out, to a depth of thirty cubits. The same thing happened from Zichia to the Danube, the river Kouphis, the Dniester and the Dnieper, Nekropyla and the rest of the coast as far as Mesembria and Medeia. Snow then fell on this ice and it grew by twenty cubits, so that the sea became like dry land. People walked across the ice from Khazaria, Bulgaria and the other neighbouring nations, and so did animals, wild and tame alike. In February of the fourth indiction, by God's command, this ice broke into a great many separate pieces like mountains. The force of the winds carried them down to Daphnousia and Hieron, and so through the Strait they reached the City. They filled the whole coast as far as the Propontis, the islands and Abydos. We ourselves saw this with our own eyes, for we climbed onto one of them with some thirty companions of our own age and played on it. They also held dead animals, both wild and tame. Anyone who wished could walk unhindered, as on dry land, from Sophianai to the City, and from Chrysopolis to Saint Mamas and to Galatou. One of them struck the landing stage of the Acropolis and smashed it. Another, enormous one struck the wall and shook it violently, so that the houses inside felt the shock too. It broke into three pieces and girdled the City from the Mangana to the Bosporion [?], and it rose higher than the City walls. All the people of the City, men, women and children, kept watching these sights without stopping, and went back home lamenting and weeping, not knowing what to say about it. In March of the same year stars were seen falling from the sky in great numbers, so that everyone who saw it supposed that the end of the present age had come. There was also a great drought, so that even the springs dried up. The emperor sent for the patriarch and said to him, "Now what harm would it do us if we called the Theotokos 'Christotokos'?" The patriarch embraced him and said, "Have mercy, master, do not let this word even enter your mind. Do you not see how [?]" [?] [Variant readings:] κατενεχθέντος A, διενεχθέντος common text; πόλεως omitted [?] in A; "and children" added from A; ἀθρόως [?]; λέγωμεν; οὗτος A.

…all the things for which Nestorius is publicly denounced and anathematized by the whole Church." And the emperor answered and said: "I asked because I wanted to learn; let the matter rest with you." Year of the World 6156. In this year the Turks again came against the Caspian cities and into Iberia, and fought with the Arabs, and many perished on both sides. Abdallah removed Isa from power by the following trick. Isa was the one on whom, as was said above, the third lot to rule after him had fallen. Seeing him suffering from a migraine and overcome with dizziness, Abdallah persuaded him that he would be cured if a sneezing powder, prepared by Abdallah's own physician, were blown into his nostrils. This physician was a certain Moses, a deacon of the church of Antioch, whom Abdallah had already won over with gifts to prepare a very sharp drug that was also strongly narcotic. Isa was persuaded by Abdallah's Moses. Although he had been guarding himself against eating with him for fear of a plot, he accepted the snuff. His head was filled with it, and he lay there speechless, deprived of all his senses together with the governing faculties of the mind. Then the brother called together the governors and the leading men of the nation and said: "What is your view about the heir to the throne? [?]" They rejected Isa with one mind and gave their pledges to Abdallah's son Muhammad, called Mahdi [?]. They carried Isa home [?] senseless. Three days later, when he recovered, Abdallah consoled him with a great many excuses and made up for the outrage with a hundred talents of gold. In the same year Paganus, the lord of Bulgaria, wrote to the emperor asking to meet him face to face. Once he had received a safe-conduct, he came out to him with his [?] nobles. The emperor sat with Sabinus seated beside him, and he received them. He reproached them for their disorder and their hatred of Sabinus, and they made a pretense of peace. Then the emperor sent secretly into Bulgaria and seized Severus, the ruler of the Slavs, who had done much harm in Thrace. Christinus was also captured, an apostate from the Christians and chief of the Skamaroi. Him, in the

harbour of Saint Thomas, they mutilated, cutting off his hands and feet. Then they brought in the physicians, who dissected him alive from the groin to the chest in order to understand how a human being is made, and after that they gave him to the fire. Suddenly the emperor left the city, and finding the passes unguarded because of the deceptive peace, he entered Bulgaria as far as Tounzas. There he set fire to the settlements he found and turned back in fear, having done nothing brave. Year of the World 6257. In this year, on the 20th of November, in the fourth indiction, the impious and unholy emperor raged against everyone who feared God. He ordered Stephen, the new protomartyr, to be dragged off. Stephen was a recluse at Saint Auxentius, on the mountain near Damatrys. He was seized by the emperor's enemies of the faith, who shared his ignorance and had come to think as he did: scholarii and men of the other tagmata. They tied his foot with a rope and dragged him from the praetorium to the Pelagiou, where they tore him apart. They threw his precious remains into the pit of those who die by violence, because he had been urging many toward the monastic life and persuading them to despise imperial dignities and riches. For he was a man respected by all, since he had spent about sixty years in his enclosure and shone with many virtues. Many officials and soldiers were accused of venerating icons, and the emperor handed them over to [?] punishments and the bitterest tortures. He demanded a general oath from everyone under his rule that no one would venerate an icon. After this he made Constantine, the falsely named patriarch, go up onto the ambo, lift up the precious and life-giving wood, and swear that he was not one of those who venerate icons. He immediately made him a man who wears garlands instead of a monk [?]… [Apparatus:] [?] … "to the physicians" … "to all" [?] … added from A. "to the icon" A, "by the icon" f. "to raise" A L. …[?], and to endure lyre-songs at the imperial table. But before long justice handed him over into the hands of [?]. On the 21st of January of the fourth indiction he marched against Bulgaria. He sent two thousand six hundred chelandia to Anchialus, having equipped them from all the themes. These were anchored off the shore when the north wind blew, and almost all of them were smashed. Many people drowned, so that the emperor had to spread out nets and gather up the dead and bury them. On the 17th of July he entered the city without glory. On the 21st of August of the same fourth indiction he publicly denounced and dishonoured the monastic habit in the hippodrome. He ordered each of the monks to hold a woman by the hand and in that way to pass through the hippodrome, while all the people spat on them and insulted them. Likewise, on the 25th of the same month, nineteen distinguished officials were brought into the hippodrome and paraded. They were charged with having plotted evil against the emperor, but the charge was false and not in truth. He simply envied them because they were handsome and strong and praised by everyone. and] he killed them. The foremost of them were these. First, Constantine, patrician and former logothete of the drome, whom he nicknamed Podopagouros. Second, his brother Strategius, patrician and domestic of the excubitors. Third, Antiochus, former logothete of the drome and strategos of Sicily. Fourth, David, spatharios of Beser and count of the Opsikion. Fifth, Theophylact of Iconium, protospatharios and strategos of Thrace. Sixth, Christopher, spatharios of the patrician Himerius. Seventh, Constantine, spatharios and imperial protostrator, the son of the patrician Bardanes. Eighth, Theophylact, candidatus of Marinakes. There were others besides. He publicly exposed these men in the hippodrome and had them spat upon and jeered by all the people, and then he pronounced sentence. The two brothers, Constantine and Strategius, he beheaded at the Kynegion, and all the people lamented greatly over them. When the emperor learned of this he was angry, and he flogged the eparch Procopius and replaced him for having allowed it. All the rest he blinded and exiled. Every year, full of madness, he sent men to the places where they were and ordered each of them to be beaten with a hundred lashes of the ox-hide whip. On the 30th of the same month of August, in the same indiction, the man of ill name raged against his own like-minded patriarch, who had shared his counsels. He prepared some monks, clergy and laymen, his initiates and friends, to say: "We heard the patriarch talking with Podopagouros against the emperor." He sent them to the patriarch in the patriarchate to convict him. When the patriarch denied it, he made them swear on the precious wood: "We heard these slanders from the patriarch." Thereupon he sent men and sealed the patriarchate, and he exiled him to Hieria, and later to Prinkipo.

[?] Of these, Antiochus was the one who served him with the reports on public affairs [?]… those around the palace call the dignity "logothete of the drome" [?]… those around the palace call the dignity "logothete of the drome"… Of these, Antiochus the magister [?]

Year of Nicetas [?]. In this year Abdallah ibn Ali died when the tower in which he was being held collapsed on him [?]. Abdallah, while he was emir, did many evils to the Christians under his rule. He removed the crosses from the churches and forbade all-night vigils and the learning of their own letters. Meanwhile those whom the Arabs call Harurites, which means "zealots," rose in revolt in the Palmyrene desert. But the wickedness of those men toward the churches of God is plain enough, since they were unbelievers. He who reigned over the Christians, however, perhaps by the unspeakable judgments of God, behaved like the raving Ahab of Israel. He showed far worse than the madness of the Arabs toward the Orthodox under his rule: bishops, monks and laypeople, rulers and ruled alike. Everywhere, in writing and by word of mouth, he denounced as useless the intercessions of the holy Virgin and Mother of God and of all the saints, through whom every help flows to us. He buried their holy relics and made them disappear. Wherever a notable relic was heard of, dedicated to the healing of souls and bodies and honoured by the devout according to custom, death was at once threatened against such people as impious, along with confiscations, exiles and tortures. The relic, so full of God's grace, was taken away like a treasure from its owners and vanished from then on. The unholy emperor did something of this kind to the most precious relic of the all-praised martyr Euphemia. He sank it in the sea with its coffin, because he could not bear to see it pouring out myrrh before all the people and exposing his drivel against the intercessions. But God, who guards the bones of those who please him, as the Scriptures say, kept it unharmed and brought it to light again on the island of Lemnos. Moved by a vision at night, he commanded it to be taken up and kept safe. Under Constantine and Irene, the pious emperors, in the fourth indiction, it returned with fitting honour to its shrine. The enemy of the churches himself

had profaned that shrine and made it into an armoury and a dung-heap. But they cleansed it and consecrated it again, to expose his godlessness and to display their own piety. Twelve years after the death of the lawless one, we saw this marvellous miracle, worthy to be recorded, together with the most fragrant emperors and Tarasius, the most holy patriarch. With them we kissed the relic, unworthy as we are, and were counted worthy of great grace. On the 16th of November of the same fifth indiction, by the emperor's decree, Nicetas the eunuch, of Slavic origin, was unlawfully ordained patriarch of Constantinople. There was a drought, so that not even dew fell from the sky, and water failed entirely in the city. The cisterns and the baths fell idle, and so did the springs that had formerly flowed without ceasing. Seeing this, the emperor began to restore the aqueduct of Valentinian, which had been in service until the time of Heraclius and had been destroyed by the Arabs. He chose craftsmen from various places. From Asia and Pontus he brought a thousand builders and two hundred plasterers. From Hellas and the islands he brought five hundred clay-workers. From Thrace itself he brought five thousand labourers and two hundred brickmakers. He set officials over them as taskmasters, with one of the patricians in charge. So the work was completed, and water entered the city. In the same fifth indiction he appointed generals who shared his views, workers well suited to his wickedness. He put Michael Melissenus in the theme of the Anatolics and Michael Lachanodrakon over the Thracesians, and over the Bucellarians Manes, who took his name from wickedness. Who is able to recount their unholy deeds? We shall record some of them in their proper places. To use the Gospel's words, which suit the case better: if all their deeds, done to flatter the ruler, were written down one by one, I think not even the world itself could contain the books that would be written.

In this year, on the 6th of October, in the sixth indiction, Constantine, the falsely named patriarch, was brought from the island of Prinkipo. The tyrant Constantine had him beaten so badly that he could not walk. He ordered him to be carried in a litter and, once he arrived, to be seated on the solea of the Great Church. An asekretis was with him, carrying a paper roll on which the charges against him were written. All the people of the city were gathered there by imperial order and looked on while the document was read aloud in the hearing of all. At each charge the asekretis struck him in the face, while the patriarch Nicetas sat on the synthronon and watched. After this they brought him up onto the ambo and stood him upright. Nicetas took the document, sent bishops [?], took away his omophorion and anathematized him. They named him Skotiopsis, "Dark-face," and drove him out of the church backwards. The next day, when there were races, they plucked his face, stripping off his beard, the hair of his head and his eyebrows. They dressed him in a short, sleeveless silk tunic and set him backwards on a saddled donkey, holding its tail. They brought him through the Diippion into the hippodrome while all the people and the demes jeered and spat at him. His nephew Constantine, whose nose had been cut off, led the donkey. When he came to the demes, they came down, spat on him and threw dust over him. They brought him to the Stama, threw him off the donkey and trampled on

his neck. They seated him opposite the demes, and he heard mocking words from them until the races were dismissed. On the 15th of August the emperor sent the patricians to him, and said to him through them: "What do you say about our faith and about the synod we held?" His mind had been made foolish, and he answered: "You believe rightly, and you were right to hold the synod," thinking that he could win the emperor's favour again in this way. They answered at once: "This is what we wanted to hear from your foul mouth. From now on, go into darkness and under the anathema." So he received his sentence and was beheaded at the Kynegion. They tied his head by the ears and hung it at the Milion for three days, for the people to see. His body they tied by the foot with a rope and threw it among [?] the bodies of those who die by violence. Likewise they took his head away after three days and threw it there as well. O the senselessness, the cruelty and the heartlessness of the savage beast! Did the wretch feel no reverence for the holy font? [?] … one who had opposed his doctrines he tied alive [?] at the Pelagia, and ordered him to be dragged through the Mese and cast away. Others he bound in sacks, tied stones to them, and ordered them thrown into the sea. He blinded people, cut off their noses, tore them with whips, and devised every kind of punishment against the devout. In the city he did these things himself and through the men who shared his views: Antony, patrician and domestic of the scholae, Peter the magister, and the men of the tagmata whom he had trained. In the themes outside the city he did them through the generals mentioned above. He himself delighted in lyre-songs and drinking parties, and trained those around him in obscene talk and dancing. Suppose anyone, falling or in pain, let out the cry customary among Christians, "Mother of God, help!" Or suppose he was caught keeping vigil, attending church, living devoutly, or refraining from swearing oaths freely. Such a man was punished as an enemy of the emperor and called "unmentionable." Monasteries, built for the glory of God and as refuges for those being saved, he turned into common lodgings for the soldiers who shared his views. Thus the

monastery of Dalmatus, the foremost of the coenobia of Byzantium, he gave to the soldiers to live in. He also razed to their foundations the so-called monastery of Callistratus, the monastery of Dius and that of Maximinus, along with other holy houses of monks and [?]. Some distinguished men, in the army or in office, set out to take up the monastic life. He put them to death, especially those close to him who had become initiates of his debaucheries and unspeakable deeds, because he suspected the shame their confessions would bring on him. For this reason he also killed Strategius, the brother of Podopagouros, who was handsome in appearance. He had attached Strategius to himself, for in his licentiousness he loved to keep such men close. But he perceived that Strategius was disgusted by his unlawful lust for men, and that he was confessing these things to Macarius, the recluse of Saint Auxentius, and receiving the remedies of salvation. So he spread it about that Strategius was plotting against him, and killed him together with the recluse, as has already been told. At this time he brought it about that goods became cheap in the city. For he became a new Midas: he hoarded the gold and stripped the farmers bare, and because of the demands of taxation people were forced to sell God's gifts cheaply. In the same year Nicetas, the falsely named patriarch, [removed] the images in the small secreton of the patriarchate, which were in mosaic,

Constantine, the impious [?], the [?] of wickedness, the many-headed dragon, the champion of the iconoclast heresy, the persecutor of the monastic order: which of our [?] did he not wipe out? Who was in hiding that he did not drag into the open? Who resisted him that he did not pull down into the pit of impiety? So that if any [?] of the notable ones was left, like a spark lying in a hidden place, he was counted among the dead…

[?] and he took down the images in the great secreton, which were painted on wood [?], and smeared over the faces of the other icons. He did the same in the Abramiaion. Year of the World 6260. In this year the thrice-married emperor crowned his wife Eudocia, his third Augusta, in the tribunal of the Nineteen Couches. This was on the 1st of April, in the sixth indiction, a Saturday. The next day, the 2nd of April, which was the Sunday of holy Easter, he made Caesars of his two sons by her, Christopher and Nicephorus, in the same tribunal. The patriarch said the prayer, and the emperor placed the cloaks and the Caesar's headdresses on them. Likewise he made Nicetas, their youngest brother, nobilissimus and put a golden cloak and the crown on him. Then the emperors went in procession as far as the Great Church, scattering the consular largesse: tremisses, semisses and newly minted coins. Year of the World 6261. In this year there was a registration [?] in Syria, man by man, woman by woman, and likewise child by child. Abdallah ordered their beards to be shaved [?] and caps a cubit and a half high to be made. Abdallah besieged Kamachon with eighty thousand men the whole summer, and returned in disgrace, having accomplished nothing. On the 1st of [?]…

…in the month […] of the 8th indiction [?], Irene came from Athens, from Hiereia, to the imperial city, with a great many dromons and chelandia decked out with silk cloths, while the leading men of the city went out with their wives to meet her and escort her. On the 3rd of the same month of September the patriarch came to the palace, and in the church of the Pharos the betrothal of the emperor Leo to this Irene took place. On the 17th of December the empress Irene was crowned in the triclinium of the Augusteus, and she then went to the oratory of Saint Stephen in the Daphne and received the wedding crowns with Constantine's son, the emperor Leo. Year of the World 6262. — Bishop of Rome: Hadrian.

In this year Banakas campaigned against Romania and took many captives, and the Romans entered Fourth Armenia and plundered it. Salih died, and Germanikeia was reassigned to Palestine. In the same year Lachanodrakon, imitating his teacher, gathered at Ephesus all the monks and nuns of the theme of the Thrakesians. He led them out to a plain called the Tzoukanisterion and said to them: "Whoever wishes to obey the emperor and us, let him put on white clothing and take a wife this very hour. Those who do not do this will be blinded and exiled to Cyprus." And the deed followed at once upon the word. Many showed themselves martyrs that day, but many also deserted their post and were lost, and the Dragon made them his own. In the same 9th indiction, on the 14th of January, a son was born to the emperor Leo and to Irene, and he was named Constantine, while his grandfather Constantine was still living.

-kellarion, and to Bardanes, the strategos of the Armeniakon. They came and seized the way out, which was a pass and very hard to cross. He killed many, took captives from all that surrounding country, and returned with much spoil. In the same year the strategos of the Thrakesians, Michael Lachanodrakon, sent out his bastard Leo, surnamed Koulloukes, and Leo Koutzodaktylos, a former abbot. He sold all the monasteries, both of men and of women, together with all their sacred vessels, books and livestock, and everything that belonged to their property, and he brought the proceeds to the emperor. All the monastic and patristic books he found he burned. Wherever anyone was found with a holy relic in an amulet, he gave that to the fire too, and he punished its owner as an impious man. He killed many of the monks with the lash and some with the sword, and he blinded countless others. He smeared the beards of some with wax and oil and set them alight, so burning their faces and heads. Others he sent into exile after many tortures. In the end he did not leave a single person wearing the monastic habit in the whole theme under his command. When the hater of good, the emperor, learned of this, he wrote to thank him, saying, "I have found in you a man after my own heart, who does all my will." The others imitated him and did the same things. Year of the World 6264. — In this year Abdallah sent Mouslabitos [?] to Africa with a large army. Alphadal Barinar entered Romania and took five hundred captives. The people of Mopsuestia went out against him, fought him, and killed a thou- [?] of the Arabs. [Apparatus:] "strategos" added from A. -sand [?]. Abdallah went to Jerusalem and fasted there [?], and he ordered the Christians and the Jews to be branded on their hands. Many of the Christians fled by sea to Romania. Sergios of Korykos was captured outside Syke, and Sergios Lachernaios [?] was captured in Cyprus, where he was the representative of the people there. Year of the World 6265. — In this year, in May of the 12th indiction, Constantine sent out a fleet of two thousand chelandia against Bulgaria. He himself boarded the red chelandia and set out to sail to the river Danube. He left the strategoi of the cavalry themes outside the passes, in case they could enter Bulgaria while the Bulgarians were busy with him. But when he had come as far as Varna, he lost his nerve and began to think of turning back. The Bulgarians saw this, and they too were afraid. They sent Boilas and Tzigatos to ask for peace. The emperor was overjoyed to see them and made peace. Each side swore to the other that the Bulgarians would not invade Romania and that the emperor would not try to invade Bulgaria, and they exchanged written agreements to this effect. The emperor then returned and entered the city, leaving taxatoi from all the themes in the fortresses he had built. In October of the same 12th indiction the emperor received a message from his secret friends in Bulgaria: the lord of Bulgaria was sending 12,000 men and a boilas to carry off Berzitia into captivity and resettle its people in Bulgaria. Envoys of the lord of Bulgaria had come to him and were still in the city, and so that it would not become known that he was moving against the Bulgarians, he pretended to be moving against the Arabs. He sent the standards and the baggage train across. Then he dismissed the envoys, learned through spies that they had left, and set out in haste with the army. He gathered together the taxatoi of the themes and the Thrakesians [?] and joined the optimatoi to the tagmata, bringing their number to 80,000. And entering

a place called Lithosoria, he fell upon them without sounding the trumpets, routed them and won a great victory. He returned with much booty and many captives and held a triumph in the city. He entered in state [?] and named this war "the noble war", since no one had resisted him and there had been no slaughter or shedding of Christian blood. Year of the World 6266. — In this year [?] heads were brought from Africa and paraded in Syria. The emperor, now that he had broken the peace with the Bulgarians, again fitted out a large fleet. He put 12,000 cavalry on board and sent all the strategoi of the naval forces off with it. He himself was afraid and stayed with the cavalry. When they had come as far as Mesembria, a violent north wind blew, nearly all the ships were wrecked, and many men perished. He returned without having done anything. Tzerigos, the lord of Bulgaria, learned that the emperor was finding out his plans from members of his own household. So he wrote to him: "I intend to flee and come to you. But send me a pledge of my safety, and tell me who your friends here are, so that I may confide in them and they may join me." The emperor foolishly wrote back to him, and once Tzerigos had learned their names, he cut them all down. When Constantine heard of it, he tore out much of his grey hair. Year of the World 6267. — In this year, the 13th indiction, in August, the emperor Constantine set out against the Bulgarians. His legs were terribly afflicted with carbuncles by a wrath sent from God, and he was then seized by a very violent fever that the physicians could not identify, so extreme was its burning. He turned back at Arkadioupolis, carried in a litter on the shoulders of his subjects. He came to Selymbria and sailed from there on the 13th of September of the

905 CHRONOGRAPHY 906. 14th indiction. On reaching the fortress of Strongylon he died miserably in the chelandion, crying aloud, "I have been handed over, while still alive, to the unquenchable fire!" He, her implacable enemy, begged that hymns be sung to the holy Virgin and Theotokos. He had reigned as sole emperor for 34 years, 2 months and 26 days after his father's death. So he ended his life stained with much Christian blood, with invocations of demons and with sacrifices, with persecutions of the holy churches and of the right and blameless faith, and also with the killing of monks and the confiscation of monasteries. He had excelled in every kind of evil no less than Diocletian and the tyrants of old. In the same month Abdallah, the leader of the Arabs, died. So these two most terrible beasts, who together had long been devouring the human race, died by the providence of God. Their sons Leo and Mahdi took power. In the same year Theodotos, king of the Lombards, came to the imperial city and took refuge with the emperor. Year of the World 6268. — Emperor of the Romans: Leo,

leader of the Arabs: Mahdi, year 1. In this year Mahdi sent Abbas against Romania with a large force. He opened the cave called Kasin by means of smoke, took the people inside it captive and returned. The emperor Leo began to spend freely the money his father had left him. He won over the people and those in the city, and for a short time he seemed pious and a friend of the Theotokos and of the monks. So he appointed metropolitans from among the abbots to the foremost sees. He also raised many military units in the themes and enlarged the tagmata. Then the officers of the themes were stirred to action, and they all came with a great crowd of people, asking that his son Constantine be made emperor. He, as is the custom of emperors, answered them: "My son is my only child, and I am afraid to do this. If the lot of all men befalls me while he is still a child, you may put him to death and set up another." They promised on oath, as an assurance to him, that they would accept no emperor except his son, even if God willed that Leo should die. The people kept pressing him from Palm Sunday until Holy Thursday, crowding into the hippodrome and making their demand. On Holy Friday he ordered them to swear. All the people swore on the precious and life-giving wood: the men of the themes and of the senate, those of the inner tagmata, all the citizens, and the men of the workshops. They swore to accept no emperor other than Leo and Constantine and their offspring, and they made written undertakings in their own hand, just as they had sworn. On the next day, Holy Saturday, the emperor went out to the tribunal of the Nineteen Couches and appointed his brother Eudokimos nobelissimos, for their father had appointed Anthimos in his lifetime. Then the emperor went in procession to the Great Church with the two Caesars, the nobelissimoi and the young Constantine. He changed his robe, as is the custom for emperors, and went up onto the ambo with his son and the patriarch. All the people came in and laid their written undertakings on the holy altar. The emperor proclaimed: "See, brothers, I am granting your request and giving you my son as emperor. See, you are receiving him from the Church and from the hand of Christ." They cried out with a loud voice: "Be our witness, Son of God, that we receive from your hand the lord Constantine as emperor, to guard him and to die for him." The next day was Easter Sunday of the 14th indiction. At dawn the emperor went out with the patriarch to the hippodrome, and a portable altar was brought. With all the people looking on, the patriarch said the prayer, and the emperor crowned

his son. Then the two emperors went in procession to the Great Church with the two Caesars and the three nobelissimoi. After the emperors had gone ahead, the empress Irene followed in procession, escorted by the men of the scholae with their sceptres. She went up the staircase of the Chalke to the galleries of the church, without going out into the middle of the portico. In May of the same indiction Nikephoros, the Caesar and the emperor's brother, was denounced to the emperor for plotting against him with some spatharioi, stratores and other imperial men. The emperor held a silentium in the Magnaura and read out to the people what had been said about him. They cried out with one voice that both should be put out of the way. Those perpetual perjurers did not remember what they had sworn to his father: that they would not allow his children to be wronged after his death. The emperor had the rebels flogged and tonsured, and he exiled them under guard and close watch to the region of Cherson. Year of the World 6269. — In this year Thumama, son of Kaka [?], entered Romania, took captives and returned. Telerig, the lord of the Bulgarians, fled to the emperor, who made him a patrician and gave him in marriage a cousin of his wife Irene. The emperor received him from the holy font at his baptism and greatly honoured and loved him. Year of the World 6270. — In this year Thumama established himself at Dabekon and rebelled. The emperor Leo sent out the armies of the Romans, and 100,000 men entered Syria. They were led by Michael Lachanodrakon of the Thrakesians, Artabasdos the Armenian of the Anatolikon, Tatzates of the Boukellarion, Karisterotzes of the Armeniakon, and Gregory son of Mousoulakios of the Opsikion. They surrounded Germanikeia, where Isbaali, the uncle of Mahdi, was, and they took all his camels. They would have taken Germanikeia too, had Isbaali not won Lachanodrakon over with gifts. So he withdrew from the fortress and went out to plunder the countryside. He took the heretical Jacobite Syrians captive and then returned to the fortress. Thumama sent an army and emirs from Dabekon, and they fought with the Romans. Five emirs and two thousand Arabs fell, so they say, and on the Friday the Romans returned. For they had

entered on the Sunday. The emperor held a Maioumas at the Sophianai and sat on a throne with his son, and so the strategoi celebrated [?] the victory festival. He also moved the heretical Syrians to Thrace and settled them there. Year of the World 6271. — In this year Mahdi, the leader of the Arabs, in his anger sent Hasan with a great force of Black-robes and of men from Syria and Mesopotamia, and Hasan came down as far as Dorylaion. The emperor ordered the strategoi not to fight them in open battle. They were to secure the fortresses and bring in men to guard them, and he sent senior officers to each fortress as well. The strategoi themselves were each to take three thousand picked soldiers and follow the enemy, so that the Arabs could not send out their raiding parties. They were also to burn in advance the pasture for the horses and any provisions to be found. The Arabs stayed at Dorylaion for seventeen days. When their supplies ran out, their horses grew weak and many of them were lost. On their way back they besieged Amorion for one day, but seeing that it was well fortified and well equipped, they went home. Year of the World 6272. — Patriarch of Constantinople: Paul, year 1. In this year Mahdi, the leader of the Arabs, came to Dabekon with a great force and much equipment. He sent his son Aaron against Romania, while he himself went back to the Holy City. He also sent Mouhesias [?], called the Zealot, and gave him authority to make the slaves of Christians apostatize and to lay waste the churches. Mouhesias came as far as Emesa and promised to force no one to become Muslims except those who [?], until the Jews and Christians had been brought into the open [?]. At once he began to torture people in a godless way, as not even Lysias and Agricolaus had ever done, and he destroyed many. But women overcame his madness by the grace of Christ our God: the wives [?] of the archdeacon of Emesa and of his son Estios [?]. They were tortured severely so that they would not yield to the impiety. For from a thousand

lashes with ox-sinew [?] and many other punishments that they endured, they received the crown of victory from Christ. Mouhesias went as far as Damascus too and laid waste many churches, paying no heed to the word the Arabs had given to the Christians. On the 6th of February of the 3rd indiction, on Cheesefare Sunday, Niketas, the eunuch of Slavic descent and patriarch of Constantinople, died. On the second Sunday of Lent Paul was ordained patriarch of Constantinople. He was an honourable reader, a Cypriot by birth, distinguished in word and deed, and he was ordained by main force after he had refused for a long time because of the prevailing heresy. In the middle week of Lent several men were arrested for venerating the holy and august icons: Jacob the protospatharios, Papias, Strategios, Theophanes the koubikoularios and parakoimomenos, and Leo and Thomas, who were also koubikoularioi, together with other devout men. Then Leo, the son of the persecutor, laid bare the wickedness he had kept hidden. He had them flogged mercilessly and tonsured, paraded them in bonds along the Mese, and shut them up in the praetorium. There the Theophanes mentioned above died, having become a confessor and received the crown of martyrdom. All the others, after his death, proved themselves worthy monks. Aaron entered the theme of the Armeniakon and besieged the fortress of Semaluos the whole summer, and in September it surrendered to him on terms. He had sent Thu-

…Thumman into Asia with [?] thousand men. Michael Lachanodrakon met him with a small [?] of his own men, fought him, and killed Thumman's brother. On the eighth of September, in the fourth indiction, Leo the son of Constantine died, in this way. He was mad about precious stones, and he fell passionately in love with the crown of the Great Church, so he took it and wore it. Carbuncles broke out on his head, and he was seized by a violent fever and died, having reigned five years less [?] months (53). A.M. 6273. Constantine, emperor of the Romans, year 1. In this year the most pious Irene, together with her son Constantine, was unexpectedly entrusted by God with the empire, in the month of September of the fourth indiction. God meant to show his wonders in this also: through a widowed woman and an orphaned child he was about to bring down the boundless impiety of the God-fighting Constantine against him and his servants, and his tyranny over all the churches [?], just as of old he brought down the devil through the weakness of fishermen and unlettered men. Forty days after she took power, when her son was ten years old, some of the men in high office formed a plot. They wanted to raise up Nicephorus, one of the Caesars, and [make him emperor?]. When the plot became known [?], those arrested were [Gregory?], the [logothete] of the Drome; Bardas, formerly general of the Armeniakoi; Constantine, son of Bilarios, spatharios and domestic of the Excubitors; Theophylact, son of Rhangabe, drungarios of the Dodecanese (54); and many others. She seized them, had them tonsured and exiled them to various places. Her brothers-in-law, the Caesars and nobelissimi, she had tonsured, and on the feast of Christ's Nativity she made them serve as priests and give communion to the people (55), so that [all might know of it?]. She herself went out in imperial state, in public, with her son, and offered to [the church] the crown that her husband had taken, [adorning it?] with pearls. She also appointed Elpidius the patrician as general in Sicily, since he had earlier [?]

commanded the forces there as general, and she sent him off in the month of February. In April, on the 15th [?], this same Elpidius was denounced as a supporter of the Caesars' cause. She sent the spatharios Theophilus with orders to seize him at once and bring him back. When he arrived, however, the Sicilians would not hand Elpidius over. So she had his wife flogged and tonsured and sent her, together with her sons, to the praetorium to be held under guard. In the month of June she sent all the themes across the straits to the passes, to guard them and watch for the Arabs' advance. She set over them as commander John the sakellarios, a eunuch and a member of her household. Mahdi sent Kebir with a large force, and they met at a place called Melon. Battle was joined, the Arabs were defeated, many of them were killed, and they went back in disgrace. The pious began to speak freely, the word of God began to spread, those who wished to be saved began to renounce the world, the glorification of God was exalted, the monasteries were restored, and every good thing came to light (56). At this time a man digging in the Long Walls of Thrace found a coffin. When he had cleaned it and taken off its cover, he found a man [lying in it?], and letters were carved on the coffin which read: "Christ is to be born of Mary the Virgin, and I believe in him. Under the emperors Constantine and Irene, O Sun, you will see me again." A.M. 6274. In this year Irene sent Constantine the sakellarios and Mamalos the primikerios to Charles, king of the Franks, so that his daughter, who was called Erythro (57), might be betrothed

to the emperor Constantine, her son. An agreement was reached and oaths exchanged between them, and Constantine left behind Elissaios, the eunuch and notary, to teach her Greek letters and the Greek language and to instruct her in the customs of the Roman empire. Irene then fitted out a large fleet and picked troops from the themes, with capable commanders. At their head she put Theodore, patrician and eunuch, a man of action, and sent him to Sicily against Elpidius. Many battles were fought, and Theodore's forces won. When Elpidius saw this he was afraid. Taking all the money he had, and Nicephorus the Doux, he crossed over to Africa, and after receiving a promise of safety he went over to the Arabs. They welcomed him and treated him as emperor of the Romans, crowning him to no purpose and dressing him in the imperial boots and a crown (58). While the Roman people were busy with these matters, Aaron the son of Mahdi came out with a force and equipment beyond measure, drawn from the Black-robed and from all Syria, Mesopotamia and the desert. He came as far as Chrysopolis, leaving Bounousos behind to besiege Nakoleia and guard his rear. He also sent Bournichos into Asia with thirty thousand men. Bournichos fought Lachanodrakon and the Thrakesian theme at a place called Darenos, and of their thirty thousand men he killed fifteen thousand (59). The empress sent Antony the domestic with the tagmata, and he seized the Banes and shut the Arabs in. But Tatzates, the general of the Boukellarioi, defected to them, out of hatred for the patrician Staurakios, logothete of the Drome and a eunuch, who was then first among all men and managed everything. On his advice the Arabs asked for peace. Staurakios, Peter the magistros and Antony the domestic went out for this purpose. They did not secure the terms carefully [by taking the children of the leading men as hostages]. Instead they went out heedlessly, and the Arabs seized them and put them in chains. Both sides were then compelled to make peace. The Augusta and Aaron gave each other many gifts, and the Romans agreed to pay them [tribute?] at fixed times. When peace had been made the Arabs withdrew, releasing also the fortress [?]. Tatzates took his wife with him, and all his property.

A.M. 6275. In this year Irene, having made peace with the Arabs and finding herself free to act, sent the patrician Staurakios, logothete of the Drome, with a large force against the Slavic nations. He went down to Thessalonica and Hellas, subdued them all and made them tributaries of the empire. He also entered the Peloponnese and brought back many captives and much booty for the empire of the Romans. A.M. 6276. In this year, in the month of January of the seventh indiction, the aforesaid Staurakios returned from the Slavs and celebrated his triumph at the hippodrome races. In the month of May of the same seventh indiction the empress Irene set out with her son and a large force for Thrace, taking organs and musical instruments with her. She went as far as Beroea and ordered it to be rebuilt, naming it Irenopolis. She went on as far as Philippopolis in complete safety (60), and returned in peace, after also building Anchialos. In the same year the leader of the Arabs, Mahdi, also called Muhammad, died, and his son Moses (61) took power in his place. On the thirty-first of August of the same seventh indiction, Paul, the holy and most saintly patriarch, fell ill. He left the throne, went down to the monastery of Florus and took the monastic habit, without the empress knowing. When the empress learned of this she came to him with her son, grieving and crying out against him: "Why have you done this?" With many lamentations he said to her: "Would that I had never sat on the throne of the priesthood while the Church of God was under tyranny, cut off from the other catholic thrones and anathematized!" She summoned the patricians and the leading men of the senate and sent them to him to hear what he had to say. He told them: "Unless an ecumenical council is held and the error in your midst is corrected, you have no salvation." They said to him: "Then why did you sign, when you were ordained, that you would not venerate icons?" He answered: "That is why I lament and have fled to repentance. I am begging God not to punish me as a priest who kept silent until now and did not proclaim the truth, for fear of your madness." With these words he fell asleep in peace, leaving great mourning to the empire and to the pious people of the city. For he was a venerable man, merciful beyond measure and worthy of all respect, and both the city and the empire had great trust

in him. From that time on the question of the holy and venerable icons began to be discussed and debated openly by everyone. [?] Leader of the Arabs, Moses [?]. A.M. 6277. Leader of the Arabs, Moses, year 1. Bishop of Constantinople, Tarasius

In this year the empress Irene gathered all the people in the Magnaura and said to them: "You know, brothers, what Paul the patriarch has done. If he were still alive we would not have allowed him to step down from the throne of the high priesthood, even though he had put on the monastic habit. But since, as was pleasing to God, he has departed this life, let us look for a man who can shepherd us and strengthen the Church of God with words of teaching." All said with one voice that there was no one but Tarasius the asekretis. She said to them: "We too vote for him, but he refuses. Let him tell us why he does not accept the vote of the empire and of all the people." He made his defense to the people, saying: "Our faithful emperors are guardians of our blameless Christian faith and zealous for all that is done to the glory of God. They take thought for everything that pleases him and benefits us, and above all for the affairs of the Church. Now they have carefully considered and deliberated about appointing a high priest in this their imperial city, and they have brought me into their pious counsel and commanded me to declare openly what they have resolved. I declared myself unworthy of this and gave no consent to bearing the yoke of a burden I cannot carry or endure, so they [ordered] me to be brought before you, since you too have joined in voting for this decision. And now, you men who fear God and always keep him in your hearts, you who are named by the calling of Christ our [true] God — Christians, I mean — hear a brief word of defense from my lowliness and nothingness. I have already made my defense to our pious and wholly orthodox emperors, and I now make it again before you. I am gripped by fear of consenting to this vote. I dread rushing forward in this way before the face of God, heedlessly and as chance may have it, lest I fall under a fearful condemnation. For if he who heard divine voices, who had heaven for his school, who beheld paradise and heard unspeakable words, and who carried the name of God before nations and kings — Paul the divine

apostle, writing to the Corinthians, said, 'Lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified,' then how can I, who live in the world, am counted among the laity and serve in the imperial service, leap like this into the greatness of the priesthood without examination and reflection? For someone as small as I am the undertaking is fearful, and the venture reckless. The cause of my fear and my refusal is this. I see and observe that the Church which Christ our God founded on the rock is now torn and divided. We say one thing at one time and another at another. The Christians of the East who share our faith, and the Christians of the West together with them, are estranged from us, and we from all of them, and every day they anathematize us. Anathema is a terrible thing: it drives a man far from God and casts him out of the kingdom of heaven, leading him into outer darkness. The rule and law of the Church knows nothing of strife and contention. Just as it knows one baptism and one faith, so too it knows one accord in every matter of the Church. For nothing is so worthy and pleasing before God as that we should be united and become one catholic Church, as we confess in the creed of our sincere faith. And I ask, brothers — and I think you ask it too, since I know you have the fear of God — that an ecumenical council be gathered by our most pious and orthodox emperors. Then we who belong to the one God may be one; we who belong to the Trinity may be united, of one soul and of equal honor; we who belong to Christ our head may be one body, fitted and knit together; we who belong to the Holy Spirit may be not against one another but with one another; we who belong to the truth may think and say the same thing, with no strife or dissension among us; and so the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, may guard us all. If our emperors, heroic champions of orthodoxy, will consent to grant my request, then I too consent: I will carry out their command and embrace your vote. If not, I cannot do this, lest I fall under the anathema and be found condemned on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ, the judge of righteousness, where neither emperor nor priest nor ruler nor any multitude of men can rescue me. And now, brothers, give whatever answer pleases you to my defense — or rather, to my request." Everyone gladly heard what had been said and agreed that a council should be held. Tarasius, speaking to the people again, said: "Leo the emperor destroyed the icons,

and when the council was held it found them already destroyed. Since they were destroyed by an imperial hand, the matter calls for fresh inquiry, because those men dared, as they saw fit, to abolish an ancient custom handed down in the Church. But the truth of God is not bound, to speak as the Apostle does." On the twenty-fifth of December of the same eighth indiction our holy father Tarasius was ordained patriarch of Constantinople. He sent his synodical letters and the statement of his faith to Rome, and was accepted by Pope Hadrian. The empress too sent to the same pope, asking him to send letters and men to be present at the council. He sent Peter, the steward of his church, and the abbot (62) of St Sabas, honorable men adorned with every virtue. The empress and the patriarch also sent to Alexandria and Antioch, for peace with the Arabs had not yet [been broken?]. From Antioch they brought John, a great man renowned in deed and word, who shared in holiness and had been synkellos of the patriarch of Antioch, and from Alexandria Thomas, a zealous and most devout man, who also became archbishop of Thessalonica, the great city of Illyricum

A.M. 6278. Leader of the Arabs, Aaron, year 1. In this year Moses, the leader of the Arabs, died, and his brother Aaron took power in his place; he did much harm to the Christians. In the same year the emperors sent out and summoned all the bishops under their authority. The letters and men sent from Rome by Pope Hadrian arrived, as did [the representatives?] of Antioch and Alexandria. On the [?] of August of the ninth indiction they took their seats in the church of the Holy Apostles in the imperial city and began to read the holy Scriptures and to compare them with one another, while the emperors were in the galleries (63). But the soldiers of the Scholae (64) and the Excubitors and the other

tagmata, [stirred up?] by their own officers and holding to the teaching of their wicked teacher, drew their swords and came at them, threatening to kill the archbishop and the orthodox bishops and abbots. The empress tried to restrain them through the members of her household standing beside her, but they would not obey, and instead added insults. The patriarch [rose?] and entered the sanctuary with the orthodox bishops and monks, and the bishops who shared the soldiers' wicked views went out to them shouting, "We have won!" By the grace of God those mad and inhuman men harmed no one. So the council broke up, and each man went back to his own home. A.M. 6279. In this year, in the month of September at the beginning of the tenth indiction, the empress sent the patrician Staurakios, logothete of the Drome, to Thrace, to the themes from across the straits that were there at the time. He persuaded them to cooperate with her and drive out of the city the impious soldiery whom the accursed Constantine had enlisted and trained. The empress pretended that she was about to campaign in the eastern regions, as if the Arabs had come out, and the whole imperial service and the court (65) went out as far as Malagina. Then the men of the outer themes (66) came in and took control of the city. She sent word to the soldiers: "Send me your arms; I have no need of you." They, made foolish by God, handed them over. Then she put their families (67) on ships and banished them from the city, ordering each man to go off to his own region, where he had been born. She formed an army of her own, with commanders obedient to her. In the month of May she again sent to every place and summoned the bishops to come to the city of Nicaea in Bithynia, so that the council might be held there. Throughout the summer they all gathered at Nicaea. She had not dismissed the representatives of Rome and of the East, but had kept them with her. On the ninth of the

A.M. 6281. In this year, in the month of September, an Arab raiding force came out against Romania and entered the Anatolikon theme, at a place called Kopidnadon. The Roman generals gathered and fought them, but were [defeated?], and many died, among them not a few of the exiles. Diogenes, the capable tourmarch of the Anatolikoi, also fell, and so did officers of the Opsikion. The empress Irene broke off the arrangement with the Franks and sent Theophanes the protospatharios. He brought back a girl from the Armeniakon named Maria, from Amnia, and Irene married her to the emperor Constantine, her son. He was deeply grieved and unwilling, because of his attachment to the daughter of Charles, king of the Franks, to whom he had been betrothed. They celebrated his wedding in the month of November of the twelfth indiction. Philetos [?], the general of Thrace, went to the Strymon, and carelessly [?]

(68) The acts of the council itself: "In the name of the Lord and Master Jesus Christ our God, in the reign of our most pious and Christ-loving sovereigns Constantine and Irene his mother, in the eighth year of their consulship, eight days before the Kalends of October, in the eleventh indiction [?]

[?] …when the Bulgarians suddenly fell upon him, he was killed by them along with many others. Irene sent John, the sakellarios and logothete of the military, to Lombardy, together with Theodotus, son of the former king of Great Lombardy, to see whether they could hold off Charles and win some people away from him. They went down with Theodore, patrician and strategos of Sicily; and when battle was joined, John himself was captured by the Franks and cruelly put to death. AM 6282. In this year wicked men, moved by envy of the emperors' piety, set the mother against the son and the son against the mother. They persuaded her, claiming to have been informed by prophetic foreknowledge, that "it is not ordained by God for your son to hold the empire. It is yours, given to you by God." Being a woman she was deceived, and since she also loved power she was convinced that it was so. She did not stop to think that they had put this forward as a pretext because they wanted to manage affairs themselves. Now the emperor had reached twenty years of age, and he was robust and very capable. He saw that he exercised no authority. He saw Staurakios, the patrician and logothete, controlling everything, with everyone going to him and nobody daring to visit the emperor. He took counsel with his own people, who were very few, and with Peter the magistros, Theodore Kamoulianos the patrician and Damian the patrician, and he resolved to seize her, exile her to Sicily and hold the empire himself. On 9 February of the 13th indiction a most terrible earthquake occurred, so that no one dared to sleep in a house, and everyone made tents in the gardens [?] and open spaces and lived there. The empress went out with her son to St Mamas. When this plot was reported to Staurakios, he stirred up the Augusta against the emperor. She seized [?] all the emperor's men, flogged [?] them, tonsured them, and with John the proto- [Apparatus:] "with others" A; "with also others" vulg. — "might be able" A; "might be able" (singular) vulg. — "were moved… wicked men" [?]: "[?] moved wicked men"; "moved wicked men" vulg. — "your son" A. — "the" added in A. — "is yours" A. — "the empire together with his own mother" A. — "of the 3rd indiction" A. — "to dare" [?]. — "having bound" A. [Latin:] "ordered to be laid waste," etc. — "With also Theodotus the former")

-spatharios and his tutor, called Pikrides, she exiled to the lower regions as far as Sicily. Peter the magistros she covered with disgrace and confined to his own house, and likewise Theodore Kamoulianos the patrician. Damian the patrician she had flogged and tonsured, and exiled him to the fortress of Apollonias. She also beat her son and heaped abuse on him, and kept him from appearing in public for many days. Then she began to make the army swear an oath: "As long as you live, we will not accept your son as ruler." And they all swore it, for no one dared to speak against it at all. An Arab fleet set out against Cyprus. Learning of this in advance, the empress gathered all the Roman ships and sent them against it. Both strategoi came as far as Myra, rounded the cape of the Chelidonia and entered the gulf of Attaleia. The Arabs set out from Cyprus, but were caught by calm weather and drifted about on the open sea. When they came into view of land, the strategoi saw them, drew up their line and prepared to fight. Theophilus, strategos of the Kibyrrhaiots, a robust and most capable man, took heart, advanced ahead of all the rest and engaged them, but he was captured. They brought him to Aaron, who looked him over and urged him to turn traitor and receive gifts for this present life. He would not accept. They pressed him further, but he did not yield, and he endured punishment by the sword and was shown to be a most excellent martyr. AM 6285 [?]. Year 1 of Constantine [?], emperor of the Romans. In this year, in September of the 14th indiction, the men administering the oath reached the Armeniac theme. But the Armeniacs refused to swear, saying: "We will not be ruled by your son during your lifetime. Nor will we put the name of Irene before Constantine. It will be Constantine and Irene, as we received it from the beginning." She sent Alexios, spatharios and droungarios of the Watch, surnamed Mousele, to seize them, but they held on to him and put him forward to rule over them. They placed their strategos Nikephoros the patrician under guard and acclaimed Constantine alone as emperor. When the people of the other themes learned this, they drove out their own strategoi and they too proclaimed Constantine sole emperor. Oh,

the cunning of the wicked devil! By how many wiles he hastens to destroy the human race! Fifteen years earlier these men had sworn that fearful oath, put it in writing and laid it on the holy sanctuary. Then they swore again to Irene that they would not be ruled by her son during her lifetime. And then they forgot this too and acclaimed Constantine autokrator. The wretches did not realize that they should never have sworn a counter-oath, because perjury must follow a counter-oath, and perjury is a denial of God. In October of the fourteenth indiction the men of the themes assembled at Atroa, and by common consent they all demanded Constantine as emperor. He was then in his twentieth year. Fearing the people's onrush, Irene released him. They confirmed him as autokrator and repudiated his mother. The emperor at once sent Michael Lachanodrakon and John, his tutor and protospatharios, and they made the Armeniacs swear not to accept his mother Irene as empress. He also confirmed Alexios as their strategos. The emperor returned to the City in December. He had Staurakios flogged and tonsured and exiled him to the Armeniac theme, to satisfy the Armeniacs. He also exiled Aetios the eunuch, her protospatharios and personal attendant, along with all her household eunuchs. Irene herself he settled in comfort [?] in the palace of Eleutherios, which she had built and in which she had hidden most of her money. In the same month there was a fire, and the triklinos of the patriarchate called the Thomaites burned down, along with the quaestor's office and many other houses as far as the Milion. In April Constantine campaigned against the Bulgarians and came to the fortress called Probatou, at the stream of St George. There he met Kardam, lord of Bulgaria. A small battle was fought toward evening, and then the Romans lost their nerve, fled during the night and returned ingloriously. The Bulgarians also took fright and turned back.

AM 6284. In this year, in September, the emperor campaigned against the Arabs. He set out from Amorion and marched toward Tarsus in Cilicia. But when he reached Anydroi Pyrgoi, he turned back again empty-handed in October of the 15th indiction. On 15 January, at the request of his own mother and many officials, the emperor proclaimed her again, and she was acclaimed together with him as "Constantine and Irene," as at the beginning. Everyone else obeyed, but the Armeniac theme rose in revolt over it. They demanded Alexios, who had shortly before been their strategos. At the time the emperor had summoned him with a sworn assurance, honoured him with the rank of patrician and kept him at his side. Because of this demand, and because of rumours spreading about him that he was going to become emperor, the emperor had him flogged and tonsured and confined him in the praetorium. In July he campaigned against the Bulgarians and built the fortress of Marcellae. On 20 July Kardam, lord of Bulgaria, came out with all his forces and took up position in the fortifications. The emperor grew hotheaded, and false prophets persuaded him that the victory would be his. He joined battle rashly and in disorder, and he was soundly defeated. He came back to the City a fugitive, having lost many men, not only from the common people but also from the officials. Among them were Michael Lachanodrakon the magistros, Bardas the patrician, Stephen Chameas the protospatharios, Niketas and Theognostos, who had served as strategoi, and not a few imperial officers. Pankratios the false prophet and astronomer, who had foretold that he would win, was also lost. The Bulgarians also took the baggage train, the money, the horses and the imperial tent with all the imperial service. When the tagmata had gathered in the City, they plotted to bring out Nikephoros, the former Caesar, and set him up as emperor. When Constantine learned of this, he sent men to bring out all the sons of his grandfather Constantine to St Mamas. He blinded Nikephoros and had the tongues of Christopher, Niketas, Anthimos and Eudokimos cut out. Along with them he also blinded Alexios, the patrician mentioned above. He did this persuaded by his mother's suggestions and by those of Staurakios, the patrician mentioned earlier, who claimed that unless he blinded Alexios the men would vote him emperor. Their punishment was carried out in August, on a Saturday, in the 15th indiction, at the ninth hour. But divine justice did not leave this unjust deed unavenged. Five years later, in the same month

and on the same day, a Saturday, this same Constantine was blinded by his own mother. AM 6285. In this year the Armeniacs heard that Alexios the patrician had been blinded, and they imprisoned their strategos, Theodore Kamoulianos the patrician. When the emperor learned of this, he sent the protospatharios Constantine Artaser and Chrysocheres, strategos of the Boukellarioi, with the forces of the other themes to win them over. But the Armeniacs fought a battle against them, captured them both and blinded them, and many were slain on both sides. This was in November of the 1st indiction. On 25 December, at the second hour of the night, there was thunder and lightning, and part of the imperial workshop of the gold-embroiderers at the Chrysion caught fire. After holy Easter the emperor campaigned against the Armeniacs with all the other themes. On 27 May of the first indiction, Pentecost Sunday, he fought them, and because the Armenians who were with them treacherously betrayed them, he was victorious and captured them. He put to death Andronikos, spatharios and their tourmarches, Theophilos the tourmarches and Gregory, bishop of Sinope, and he subjected the rest to fines and confiscations. A thousand men from their fortress he had bound and led into the City through the Blachernae gate on Monday, 24 July. He had "Armeniac plotter" tattooed on their faces in ink and scattered them in Sicily and the other islands. As for the Armenians who had betrayed them, they received no reward from the emperor, and they handed the fortress of Kamachon over to the Arabs. AM 6286. In this year, in October of the second indiction, the Arabs took the fortress

[?] came to terms, and so they also released its commanders to go to their own homes. AM 6287. In this year the emperor came to hate his own wife Maria at the instigation of his mother, who coveted power, so that [he might be] condemned [?]. … [?] to his face, if it is not too bold to say so, like John, the Forerunner of the Lord. [The difference was] only that the one acted of his own accord and the other was moved by another. O manly heart! It did not cower before power, it did not give way to threats, it was not softened by persuasions, and these came from men who were of one mind with Herodias [?]. Instead it spoke out [?] and boldly [?] proclaimed the word of truth. The Forerunner of the Lord said, "It is not lawful for you to have [?]…" … [?] Constantine, the son [?] of Irene. His faith was upright, formed by his mother's piety, but his life was crooked, driven wild by imperial [?] license.
