For he was just in the bloom of youth when he threw off his mother's rein and guardianship and at the same time despised the laws of God. He cast out the wife lawfully joined to him and committed adultery, as Herod had. But why tell this story? Because in it our teacher has been revealed as an emulator [?] of the Forerunner. For when nearly everyone else had gone along with the transgression, he alone, so to speak, remained unshaken together with [?] his own disciples. How many and how great were his struggles on that account through a whole year [?]: … threats upon threats, scourgings, banishments, [?]. When none of what the Caesar was striving for was achieved by these means, he turned to another method. The drama, as the saying goes, was written by others, but the hand that carried it out was [?]. [?] … sent [?] … letters [?]. And finally these too proved [?] futile and unreliable, since the father answered and wrote back what was fitting, and [?] … the unveiling of the imperial form [?] … [?]. … [?] what was done by the generals sent [?], who went, as if against some enemies, against the unarmed monk of Christ, fenced about only by the divine law. The shepherd was taken from their midst, and the sheep of the flock were scattered. Some were beaten, others banished beyond the frontiers, others hunted down. Most pitiable of all, an imperial decree ordered that those persecuted for the Lord's sake were to be received nowhere. The heads of the monasteries obeyed, and rare was the one who dared to receive them. And Christ slept, for reasons known to him, testing what was happening. He tested some in their longing for him, to see whether they would persevere, and he took pity on the inhumanity of others, to bring them to repentance. What then did Christ's athlete do? Of his own will he cut himself off from his own people. He was left utterly alone, laying down his life for the sheep, as the Gospel says, truly a good shepherd. He was brought before the Caesar by the hand [?] of Briareus

[?] to be [?] by all. He forced her to become a nun, and having persuaded her, he had her tonsured in January of the 3rd indiction. In April he campaigned against the Arabs. On 8 May he fought one of their raiding parties at a place called Anousan, defeated and routed it and drove it as far as the river. Then he went down to Ephesus and prayed at the church of the Theologian. There he remitted the trade tax on the fair, which came to a hundred pounds of gold, for the service of the holy apostle and evangelist John. In August the emperor crowned Theodote the koubikoularia as Augusta and was unlawfully betrothed to her. AM 6288. In this year, in September of the 4th indiction, the emperor celebrated his wedding with Theodote in the palace of St Mamas, on Wednesday the 5th [?]. In April of the same 4th indiction, on the seventh day [?], at night, there was a most terrible earthquake on the island of Crete. There was also a very terrible one in Constantinople on 4 May. Kardam, lord of Bulgaria, sent word to the emperor: "Either pay me tribute, or I will come as far as the Golden Gate and lay Thrace waste." The emperor put horse dung in a napkin and sent it to him with this message: "I have sent you the kind of tribute that befits you. You are an old man, and I do not want you to wear yourself out coming all the way here. Instead I will come as far as Marcellae, and you come out to meet me, and let God judge as He will." The emperor sent to the Peratic [?] themes and gathered his army, and he came as far as Versinikia. And Kard-

"He himself," he says, [?] … made a defence on behalf of the man and was called to reunion. This reunion did take place, with the expulsion of the one who had performed the crowning and with care to avoid the division, which the blessed man was especially eager to shun [?].

-am came as far as the forest of Abroleba. There, being wary [?], he stayed in the woods. The emperor encouraged his army and advanced as far as the open ground of Abroleba, where he challenged Kardam to battle for 17 days. Kardam did not dare to fight and fled back to his own land. At the same time the Arabs also came as far as Amorion. They achieved nothing and returned home after taking captives in the surrounding region. In the same year Plato, abbot of Sakkoudion, broke off communion with Tarasios the patriarch. Tarasios had received the emperor into communion. He had also permitted the catechist [?] to tonsure the emperor's wife Maria, and allowed the abbot Joseph, hegumen of the Kathara monastery, to crown the emperor with Theodote. When the emperor learned of this, he sent Bardanes, patrician and domestic of the Schools, and John, count of the Opsikion. He brought Plato into the City and shut him up in a cell in the church of the Archangel in the palace. The rest of the monks, together with Plato's nephews, he had beaten and exiled to Thessalonica. The emperor's mother was supporting them, because they opposed her son and put him to shame. AM 6289. [Year ?] of Leo, bishop of Rome.

In this year, in September, the emperor went with his mother to Prousa to take the hot springs. On 7 October of the 5th indiction a son was born to the emperor, and he named him Leo. When the emperor learned of it, he left his mother at the Baths with the whole imperial retinue and the officials and hurried back to the City. His mother found her opportunity and approached the commanders of the tagmata. With gifts and promises she won them over to depose her son,

flattering some of them in person and others through her men. She drew them all to her side and waited for a suitable day. In Rome, Hadrian died and Leo was ordained, a most honourable man and venerable in every respect. In March the emperor marched out against the Arabs, taking with him Staurakios the patrician and other friends of his mother. He also took a picked force of twenty thousand lightly armed soldiers from both [?] themes. When Staurakios and his associates saw how eager the army and the emperor were, they were afraid that he might fight and win, and that their plot against him would come to nothing. So they bribed the men of the Watch and persuaded them to report falsely that the Saracens had fled. The emperor was much grieved and went back to the City without achieving anything. On 1 May his son Leo died, and he mourned him bitterly. On 17 June of the 5th indiction, the emperor crossed over to St Mamas after a horse race. The men of the tagmata who had been won over crossed over against him to seize him. When he learned of it, he boarded his chelandion and crossed to Pylai, intending to take refuge in the Anatolikon theme. With him were his mother's friends, though he did not know them for what they were. His wife also came out as far as Triton. His mother's friends who were with him took counsel and said to one another: "If an army gathers around him, he will no longer [?] … and we will not escape his notice, and he will destroy us." Meanwhile his mother gathered at the Eleutheriou palace the men of the tagmata whom she had won over and entered the palace. When she learned how the people were flocking to the emperor, she was very much afraid. She considered sending bishops to him, receiving a sworn assurance of safety, and retiring into a corner. But she wrote secretly to her friends who were with him: "Unless you find some way to hand him over, I will reveal to the emperor the dealings you have had with me." They were frightened and seized him while he was at prayer [?]. They put him aboard a chelandion and reached the City on Saturday morning, the 15th [?] of the same month. They shut him up in the Porphyra, where he had been born. And about the ninth hour they blinded him, cruelly and incurably, so that he would die,

[Running head: Theophanes] …by the decision of his mother and her advisers. And the sun was darkened for seventeen days and gave no rays, so that ships lost their way and were driven off course. Everyone said and admitted that the sun had withheld its rays because of the emperor's blinding. And so his mother Irene took power.

In the same year the relatives of the blessed Pope Hadrian in Rome stirred up the people and rose against Pope Leo. They seized him and blinded him, but they could not put out his sight completely, because the men who blinded him were merciful and spared him. He fled to Charles, king of the Franks, who took bitter vengeance on his enemies and restored him to his own throne. From that time Rome came under the authority of the Franks. Leo repaid Charles by crowning him emperor of the Romans in the church of the holy Apostle Peter. He anointed him with oil from head to foot and clothed him in imperial robes and a crown, on 25 December, in the ninth indiction. Year of the world 6290. Irene, empress of the Romans, again: year 1. In this year Irene, having taken power, at once sent Dorotheos, abbot of Chrysopolis, and Constantine, chartophylax of the Great Church, to Abimelech, who was plundering the regions of Cappadocia and Galatia, to negotiate for peace. But no peace came of it. In the month of November some rebels approached the sons of Constantine, the enemy of God, who were held under guard in the palace of Therapeia. They persuaded them to take refuge in the Great Church and, supposedly, to ask for a guarantee of their safety from then on. Their aim was to use this pretext to proclaim one of them emperor. A great crowd ran to the church, but Aetios, the eunuch patrician, went in and brought them out, since no one paid any heed to what they said, and he exiled them to Athens. The two patricians, Staurakios and Aetios,

though both were intimates of the empress, turned against each other, so that they openly displayed their enmity. Each aimed to secure the empire for his own relatives after her death. Year of the world 6291. In this year Abimelech marched out against Romania. He sent a raiding party of light-armed men, which came down as far as Mangana. They seized the horses in the stables of Staurakios and took the imperial saddle-horse [?], and returned unharmed. The rest went down as far as Lydia and took many captives. Another of their raiding parties sallied out and fell upon Paul, patrician and count of the Opsikion, with his whole theme and the Optimatoi, and made a great slaughter of them. They also carried off his baggage train, and they too returned. In March of the seventh indiction Akameros, ruler of the Slavs of Belzetia, wanted to bring out the sons of Constantine and appoint one of them emperor, at the urging of the Helladics. When the empress Irene learned of this, she sent to the patrician Constantine Serantapechos his son Theophylaktos, who was a spatharios and her nephew. He blinded them all and broke up their plot against her. On Easter Monday the empress went in procession from the Holy Apostles. She rode in a golden carriage drawn by four white horses, which was held by four patricians: Bardanes, strategos of the Thrakesians; Sisinnios, strategos of Thrace; Niketas, domestic of the Scholae; and Constantine Boilas. As she went she lavishly scattered largess. In May the empress fell ill and came close to death, and the strife between the eunuchs flared up. Aetios took on as his ally Niketas, patrician and domestic of the Scholae, and fiercely opposed Staurakios. They persuaded the empress that Staurakios was aiming at the throne. She was furiously angry with him and turned on him in the palace of Hieria, telling him

that he was plotting riots and uprisings and bringing swift ruin on himself. He defended himself to her and made himself safe, but he raged against Aetios and Niketas, the patricians already mentioned. Year of the world 6292. In this year, in February, in the eighth indiction, the Staurakios already mentioned was preparing a usurpation and an uprising in the imperial city. He was winning over the Scholarii and Excubitors there, together with their officers, with money and gifts. But the pious Irene held a silentium in the Triclinium of Justinian and forbade every soldier to approach Staurakios. In this way affairs settled into some sort of order. Meanwhile Aetios and Niketas, with some others, kept up the struggle against Staurakios. He was stricken in the heart and brought up frothy blood through his mouth from the region of his chest and lungs. When the doctors saw this, they declared it fatal. But the rest, flatterers and fools, not only doctors but also some monks who were no monks, and sorcerers, kept assuring him with oaths that he would live and reign. They did so right up to the day of his death, which came in June of the same eighth indiction, on the third day. Emboldened by them, he arranged for a revolt against Aetios to take place in Cappadocia, but he was not granted to hear of it while still alive. Two days after he died, the report of it arrived, and the rebels were arrested and sentenced to exile and punishment. Year of the world [?]. In this year, on 25 December, in the ninth indiction, Charles, king of the Franks, was crowned by Pope Leo. He had intended to send a fleet against Sicily, but changed his mind and wished instead to be joined with Irene. For this purpose he sent envoys in the following year, in the tenth indiction. In March of the ninth indiction the pious Irene remitted the civic taxes of the Byzantines and lightened the so-called kommerkia of Abydos and Hieron. For these and many other benefactions she received great thanks.

Year of the world 629[?]. In this year the patrician Aetios, rid of Staurakios and free of worry, hurried to transfer power to his own brother. He appointed him sole strategos of Thrace and Macedonia, while he himself held the themes across the strait, the Anatolikon and the Opsikion. So, full of arrogance, he belittled the officials in authority and counted them as nothing. They were deeply aggrieved with him, and they plotted a revolt against the empress and carried it out. At this point the envoys sent by Charles and Pope Leo also arrived at Irene's court. They asked that she be joined to Charles in marriage and so unite East and West. She would have agreed, had not this Aetios, so often mentioned, prevented it, for he held power behind the throne and was trying to claim the rule for his own brother. Year of the world 6295. Nikephoros, emperor of the Romans.

In this year, on 31 October, in the eleventh indiction, at the fourth hour of the night, as Monday was dawning, Nikephoros, patrician and general logothete, rose up as usurper against the most pious Augusta Irene. God allowed it by his inscrutable judgments because of the multitude of our sins. He had the help of Niketas, patrician and domestic of the Scholae, and Sisinnios, patrician and Niketas's brother, the treacherous and perjured Triphyllioi. [?] Also with them were Leo Serantapechos, patrician and quaestor; Gregory, son of Mousoulakios, the patrician; Theoktistos, patrician and quaestor; and Peter the patrician. They also deceived some of the officers of the tagmata. They seized the so-called Chalke and deceived all the guards at once with lies. They persuaded them that Irene herself had sent them to proclaim this Nikephoros emperor, because the patrician Aetios was forcing her to proclaim his brother Leo emperor. The guards believed this enormous lie and joined in proclaiming the usurper emperor. So these patricians came to the palace and went in. From there they sent some obscure persons and slaves throughout the whole city and made the proclamation before midnight. They also posted guards around the palace of Eleutherios, where she happened to be. At dawn they sent for her and shut her up in the Great Palace. Then they went to the Great Church to crown the wretch. The whole

[?] crowd of the city gathered, and everyone was indignant at what was being done. They cursed the one doing the crowning, the one being crowned, and those who rejoiced with them. Those who lived with piety and good sense marveled at God's judgment. How had he allowed her, who had struggled and borne witness for the orthodox faith, to be thrown out by a swineherd? And her most devoted men had gone over to him out of greed: I mean Leo of Sinope, patrician and sakellarios, the God-hated Triphyllioi, and the patricians mentioned above. She had enriched them with a great many gifts, and they had often dined with her. With flattery and fearful oaths they had persuaded her that they valued their loyalty to her above everything in the world. Others were as if stunned by what was happening. They could not grasp that it was real and thought they were dreaming. Still others, those well able to judge what was coming, called the past prosperity blessed and lamented the misfortune that the tyranny would bring. This was especially true of those who had already had some experience of the usurper's wicked mind. A common gloom and an inconsolable despondency gripped everyone. But I will not lengthen my account by setting down in detail the unlovely words of that pitiable [?]. For on that day the weather, too, changed suddenly and against nature, becoming gloomy and sunless. An unrelenting cold set in, though it was autumn, clearly foretelling his harsh character and unbearable oppression, especially for those who had voted for him. On the next day he took some of the patricians and went up to the empress, who was under guard. He put on the false kindness that was habitual to him, by which he had also deceived the faithful. He apologized to her, saying that he had been raised to power against his will and had no desire for it. He cursed those who had promoted him and plotted against her, as the traitor Judas had betrayed the Lord after dining with him, and declared that they were his imitators in every respect. He even showed her that he liked to wear black shoes, contrary to imperial custom. With guile he urged her to take courage, and he gave oaths about every bodily comfort fitting for a mistress to receive from a slave. He told her to consider her deposition no misfortune. He urged her to hide none of the imperial treasures from him, and so he convicted himself of the passion of avarice, unable to hold it back. For he was gravely sick with it, that all-devourer, who placed his hopes in gold. But the wise and God-loving Irene, although she might well have been overwhelmed by the suffering of so sudden a change,

being a woman, spoke with a noble and sensible mind to the man who yesterday had been a servant and perjurer, and today was a wicked rebel and shameless tyrant: "I believe, sir, that it was God who raised me up when I had been left an orphan, and set me on the imperial throne though I was unworthy. I lay the cause of my deposition on myself and on my sins. In all things and in every way may the name of the Lord be blessed," she cried, "the only King of kings and Lord of lords. The manner of your advancement I ascribe to the Lord, without whom I believe nothing comes to pass. Reports were often brought to me against you concerning the dignity you now wear. They were true, as the outcome has shown, and you are not unaware of them. I was even partly convinced by them, and I was free to do away with you without hindrance. But partly because I trusted your oaths and partly because I wanted to spare you, I disregarded many informers. Instead I entrusted my affairs to God, through whom kings reign and rulers hold the earth. And now I do obeisance to you as emperor, as to a pious man put forward by him. I ask you to spare my weakness and grant me the house of Eleutherios, which I built, as a consolation in my incomparable misfortune." He replied, "If you want this done for you, swear to me by every divine power that you will hide none of the treasures of the empire. Then I will grant your request and provide you with every care and comfort." She swore to him on the precious and life-giving wood [?], saying, "I will not hide from you so much as an obol." And she kept her word. Once he had got what he wanted, he immediately exiled her to the island of Prinkipo, to the monastery she herself had built. Charles's envoys were still in the city and saw what was done. Having seized power, this all-devourer could not conceal his innate wickedness and avarice by hypocrisy for even a short time. Pretending that he meant to root out injustice, he set up the wicked and unjust tribunal in the Magnaura. But the tyrant's aim was not to give the poor their rights, as events showed. He meant to use it to disgrace and plunder all those in authority and to transfer everything to himself. And so he did.

He saw that everyone was aggrieved with him, and he feared that they might remember the pious Irene's benefactions and call her back to rule again. So in November, when the harshest winter was setting in, the heartless man had no pity on her. He exiled her to the island of Lesbos, ordering that she be kept under close guard and be seen by no one at all. On 30 April Niketas Triphyllios died, poisoned by Nikephoros, so they say. On 4 May, a Thursday, Nikephoros went out to a suburb at Chalcedon. He mounted an extremely tame and gentle horse, but by divine providence it threw him and he broke his right foot. On 19 July, a Wednesday, at the first hour, the patrician Bardanes, surnamed the Turk, strategos of the Anatolikon, was proclaimed emperor by the themes across the strait. He refused many times but could not escape them. He came down to Chrysopolis and moved about there for eight days, but the city would not receive him, and he withdrew to Malagina. He feared God and reckoned that Christians might be slaughtered on his account. So he sent to Nikephoros and obtained a pledge written in the emperor's own hand, which the most holy patriarch Tarasios and all the patricians also signed. It promised that he and all those with him would be kept safe and unpunished. On 8 September, at midnight, he slipped away in secret and came down to Kios in Bithynia, to the monastery of Herakleios. There he found the emperor's chelandion, which had been sent for him. He was tonsured on board, put on the monastic habit, and sailed in it to the island called Prote, where he had built a monastery. He thought that Nikephoros would respect the fearful pledge he had given him and would do him no harm of any kind, but Nikephoros was a cheat. First he stripped him of his property. Then he seized on the pretext to despoil all the officials and landowners of the themes, and some from the imperial city as well, while leaving the whole army without pay. Who could worthily recount what he did in those days, by God's permission, because of our sins? On 9 August of the eleventh indiction the empress Irene died in exile on the island of Lesbos, and her body was transferred to the [?] [Apparatus: τοῦ A; τῶν vulg. — η' vulg. — αὐτῷ A; αὐτῇ vulg. — αὐτὸν omitted in A.]

[?] Year of the world 6296. In this year, in December, in the twelfth indiction, Nikephoros had his son Staurakios crowned emperor by Tarasios, the most holy patriarch, at the ambo of the Great Church. Yet the boy was in every way unfit for such a dignity, in looks, strength and judgment. Nikephoros, who never kept faith in anything, sent some Lycaonians, or rather werewolves, who were of one mind and spirit with him, to Prote. He ordered them to land on the island by night and blind the Bardanes already mentioned, as though without his knowledge, and after the deed to take refuge in the church. When this was done, the patriarch and the senate were deeply grieved, as were all who fear God. The most lawless emperor Nikephoros swore oaths and, to all appearances, sought to put the Lycaonians responsible to death, pretending to avenge Bardanes. He always did everything for show and nothing as God would have it. Along with his other iniquities, this was a special trait of his character, and by it he had deceived many even before he became emperor. But to those who knew him well, the act was utterly ridiculous. His most foul face was always darkened with great shamelessness, yet now he stayed shut up in the imperial bedchamber for seven days, whimpering deceitfully. By nature he had womanish tears at his command, as many of the base false christs commonly do. But most people saw through him. In August he marched out against the Arabs and met them at Krasos in Phrygia. He fought and was defeated, and lost many men. He himself came close to being captured, and would have been, had not some of the bravest officers barely rescued him from danger.

Year of the world 6297. In this year an uprising broke out in Persia, and the leader of the Arabs went down to pacify the rebels. Nikephoros, finding himself free to act, rebuilt Ankyra in Galatia, Thebasa and Andrasos. He also sent a raiding party into Syria. It achieved nothing and came back, having instead lost many men. Year of the world 6298. Nikephoros, bishop of Constantinople: year 1. In this year, on 25 February, in the fourteenth indiction, Tarasios, the most holy archbishop of Constantinople, departed this life in glory. His

remains were carried to the Strait of the Pontus and buried in the monastery he had built, on the Wednesday of the first week of Lent. On 12 April, the great Sunday of Easter, the most holy patriarch Nikephoros was ordained. He came from among the asekretis and was chosen by the vote of all the people and the priests, and of the emperors as well. Plato and Theodore, abbot of the monastery of Stoudios, did not consent to Nikephoros's ordination. They opposed it strongly and contemplated a schism. Their supposedly reasonable ground was that a layman ought not to be raised suddenly to a bishopric. The emperor Nikephoros wanted to drive them out of the city, but he was turned from his purpose. Some advised him that the patriarch's ordination would hardly be praiseworthy if it led to the dissolution of so great a monastery, with some seven hundred monks under Theodore's rule. Yet the practice was nothing foreign to the Church or newly invented. Many others had also become bishops straight from the laity and served God as priests worthily of their dignity. In the same year Aaron, leader of the Arabs, campaigned against Romania with a heavy force of three hundred thousand men drawn from the Maurophoroi, Syria, Palestine and Libya. Coming to Tyana, he built
[…of Nikephoros, among the holy patriarchs. That Tarasios and Nikephoros, etc.] This narrative survives

Having recounted the tragedy, Theodore explains its cause as follows: "And all this for what? (For in my astonishment I take pains to go over the drama again.) So that he who crowned the adulterers, contrary to the Gospel and contrary to [?] the Forerunner, may be cleared to celebrate the liturgy, on the grounds that he exercised a saving economy for the Church; and so that those who, following the Gospel, refuse to accept him may be counted lawless and estranged from God. O laws of God despised! O bitter persecutor, who bears the name of Christian and burns to trample on the laws of Christ! Why are you raving so, you hard-hearted and most cruel man, together with your whelp who is just like you? Do you not know that you are drawing up your ranks against the invincible laws of God, which no ruler has ever overcome? Indeed, whoever clashed with them as you do perished in plain sight." [?] But for whose sake [?] again [?]:

[?] …built a house for his blasphemy. After a siege he took the fortress of Herakleia, which was extremely strong, along with Thebasa, Malakopaia, Sideropalos and Andrasos. He also sent out a raiding force of sixty thousand men, which went down as far as Ankyra, looked it over and turned back. The emperor Nikephoros was seized by fear and helplessness. He too went out, in despair, putting on a fine show of his misery, and after setting up many "trophies" he sent to Harun the metropolitan of Synada [?], Peter the abbot of Goulaion and Gregory the steward of Amastris to ask for peace. After much discussion they agreed terms: each year thirty thousand nomismata would be paid to the Arabs, along with a head tax of three nomismata for the emperor himself and three for his son. Harun received this and was delighted. He rejoiced more than if he had received countless talents, as though he had subjected the empire of the Romans. They also agreed that the captured fortresses would not be rebuilt. But as soon as the Arabs had withdrawn, Nikephoros rebuilt those same fortresses and strengthened them. When Harun learned of this, he sent troops again and took Thebasa. He also sent a fleet to Cyprus, which destroyed the churches and deported the Cypriots, and after taking many captives [?] the peace

AM 6299. In this year Nikephoros campaigned against the Bulgarians. When he reached Adrianople, the men of the imperial household and the tagmata were plotting a revolt against him. He became aware of it and turned back without achieving anything, except to punish his own people, putting many to floggings, exile and confiscation of property. He sent Bardanios the spatharios, surnamed Anemas, who rounded up every proselyte and every tenant as if they were captives and moved them across into Thrace. Nikephoros expected to get no small weight of gold out of them from

their yearly taxes, for he did everything for the sake of the gold he loved, and nothing for the sake of Christ. AM 6300. In this year, in the month of September, in the first indiction, Harun, the leader of the Arabs, sent Humayd with a fleet against Rhodes. He sailed in with his whole force, seized Rhodes and took many captives there, though its fortress held out and was not taken. On his way back, however, he was openly defeated by the holy wonderworker Nicholas. He came to Myra and tried to smash the saint's sacred coffin, but broke another one near it instead. Immediately a great turmoil of winds and sea waves, thunder and lightning struck the fleet, so that a good number [?] were wrecked. Humayd, that enemy of God, recognized the power of the saint and escaped the danger against all hope. On 20 December Nikephoros, after a great selection of virgins from all the lands under his rule to find a wife for his son Staurakios, chose Theophano of Athens, a relative of the blessed Irene. She was betrothed to a man and had often slept with him, but he separated her from him and married her to the wretched Staurakios. In this, as in everything, he broke the law shamelessly. He also picked out two other girls more beautiful than she, and openly debauched them along with her during the very days of the wedding, so that everyone laughed at the foul man. In February many of the officials planned a revolt against him and voted for Arsaber the quaestor, a patrikios and a [?] and very learned man. When the wily Nikephoros learned of this, he had Arsaber flogged and tonsured, made him a monk and exiled him to Bithynia. The rest he subjected to floggings, exile and confiscation of property as well. This included not only those who held office in secular life, but also holy bishops and monks, and the clergy of the Great Church: the synkellos, the sakellarios and the chartophylax, all men of distinction who deserved respect. AM 6301. Muhammad, leader of the Arabs.

In this year Harun, the leader of the Arabs, died in the inner [?] country called Khurasan, in the month of March, in the second indiction. His son Muhammad, inept in every respect, succeeded him in power. His brother Abdallah rose against him from his own country of Khurasan with their father's forces, and so caused a civil war among their people. As a result, those in Syria

[?] CHRONOGRAPHY. …in Egypt and in Libya split into separate rulerships and wrecked both public affairs and one another [?], thrown into chaos by slaughter, plunder and every kind of outrage, against one another and against the Christians under their rule. At this time the churches in the holy city of Christ our God were deserted, as were the monasteries of the two great lavras, those of Saint Chariton and Saint Kyriakos and of Saint Sabas, and the other communities of Saints Euthymios and Theodosios. The bloodshed of this anarchy, against one another and against us, went on [?]. Theodore, abbot of the Stoudios, his brother Joseph, archbishop of Thessalonike, the recluse Plato and the rest of their monks broke communion with the most holy patriarch Nikephoros. The reason was Joseph the steward, who had unlawfully performed the wedding of Constantine and Theodote. The emperor Nikephoros seized on this as a pretext. He gathered many bishops and abbots and ordered them to convene a synod against the monks, by which they were expelled from the monastery and from the city and sent into exile, in the month of January, in the second indiction. In the same year, while the army's pay was being handed out on the Strymon, the Bulgarians fell upon it and carried off eleven hundred pounds of gold. They also slaughtered many men, together with the strategos and the officers. Not a few officers from the other themes had been posted there, and all of them perished. The Bulgarians also took the entire baggage train and went home. In the same year, before the feast of Easter, Krum, the leader of the Bulgarians, marched against Serdica and took it by trickery and fair words. He slaughtered six thousand Roman soldiers, not counting a multitude of civilians. Nikephoros set out, supposedly against him, on the Tuesday of Holy Week, but he achieved nothing worth mentioning. The officers who had escaped from the rout asked him for a pledge of safety. He refused to give it and so forced them to flee to the enemy. Among them was Euthymios the spatharios, an expert in siege engines. On top of this great disgrace, Nikephoros tried to convince the imperial city with sworn imperial letters that he had celebrated Easter Day in Krum's palace. He wanted to rebuild the captured Serdica, but he was afraid the troops would oppose it. So he had the strategoi and officers suggest to the men that they petition the emperor about the rebuilding. The troops saw through the charade, recognized that it came from his malice, and rose against him and against

their own officers at the sixth hour. They attacked and tore down the officers' tents. Then they came as far as the imperial tent and pelted him with insults and curses, swearing that they would no longer put up with his boundless greed and his scheming, malicious mind. He was badly frightened by the suddenness of the revolt. He got up from the table and first tried to calm the army with oaths and persuasive talk through the patrikioi Nikephoros and Peter. The soldiers calmed down a little. Then the thrice-wretched men seized a hill and, forgetting the business at hand, cried out "Lord, have mercy", as if for an earthquake or a drought. But he was ready for any villainy. During the night he deceived many of the officers with secret gifts, and the next day he came himself into the middle of the crowd and spoke to them. He promised them every kind of prosperity and the same affection he had for his own children, confirming it with dreadful oaths. Then he went straight back to the capital, leaving behind the patrikios Theodosios, [?] surnamed Salibaras, to identify the mutineers by having them inform on one another. When the troops came back, he pretended he was going to pay them. Instead, at Saint Mamas, he punished most of them with floggings, tonsure and exile, and shipped many across to Chrysopolis, trampling on those terrible oaths of his. Because of this disaster they called the crossing the Fiery River [?]

AM 6302. In this year, after his godless measures, Nikephoros set out to humble the armies in every way. He ordered Christians from every theme to be resettled in the Sklavinias and their property to be sold. The thing was no better than captivity. Many in their folly blasphemed and prayed for enemy invasions, while others lamented at their ancestors' graves and called the dead blessed. Some even hanged themselves to escape their troubles. They could not take their immovable property with them, and they watched the estates built up by their parents' labours being lost. Everyone was in utter helplessness. The poor suffered both in this and in the measures I am about to describe, while

the prominent felt for them but could not help them, and waited for still heavier misfortunes. This began in September and was completed by holy Easter. Along with it he ordered a second evil: poor men were to be enlisted and equipped by the people of their own commune, who also had to pay eighteen and a half nomismata each to the treasury and were jointly liable for the public taxes. The third evil was that everyone was to be reassessed and their taxes raised, with an extra fee of two keratia each for the paperwork. Fourth, he ordered all tax remissions to be revoked. Fifth, the hearth tax was to be exacted from the tenants of the charitable houses, that is, the orphanage, the hostels, the old people's homes, the churches and the [?] monasteries, back to the first year of his tyranny. The best of their estates were to be taken into the imperial domains, while the taxes on them were laid on the lands and tenants left to those same charitable houses. Many people's taxes were thus doubled while their homes and lands were cut back. Sixth, the strategoi were to investigate anyone who had suddenly risen out of poverty and demand money from them as finders of treasure. Seventh, anyone who over the past twenty years, up to the present, had found a jar or any vessel at all was also to pay for it in money. Eighth, poor people who had inherited from grandfathers or fathers and divided the inheritance during those same twenty years were to pay it back to the treasury. He also ordered those who had bought household slaves beyond Abydos to pay two nomismata a head, especially those in the Dodecanese. Ninth, those who lived by the sea, especially the shipowners of Asia Minor, who had never lived by farming, were forced to buy some of the estates he had seized, at whatever price he set. Tenth, he gathered the leading shipowners of Constantinople and lent each of them twelve pounds of gold at an interest of four keratia per nomisma, while they still paid the customary trade duties. I have recorded these few measures out of many, in summary, to show how inventive he was in every kind

of greed. The evils he inflicted in the capital on high officials, the middle ranks and humble people alike are beyond writing down. He tracked how people lived at home. He incited the wicked among the servants to slander their masters, and at first pretended to hesitate over what was said, then upheld the false charges. He did the same with obscure men against prominent ones, and rewarded good slanderers with honours. He ruined many households, from the first generation to the third, in the hope that they would quickly fall and he would inherit from them. One more thing deserves mention, for the reader's amusement or as an example. There was a chandler in the Forum who had become well-off by his own labour. The all-devourer summoned him and said, "Put your hand on my head and swear to me how much gold you have." The man made a show of declining a little, as though he were unworthy, but was forced to do it, and declared that he had a hundred pounds. At once Nikephoros ordered it brought, saying, "What need do you have to drag around [?]? Dine with me, take a hundred nomismata and go on your way content." AM 6303. In this year Nikephoros extended his godless investigations of Christians. He imposed forced purchases of all kinds of animals, livestock and produce. He imposed unjust confiscations and fines on officials, and audits on ships. Though he had passed a law for everyone forbidding lending at interest, he did this and devised countless other evils, whose detailed history would be tedious for those who like to learn things in brief. On the first day of October, a Tuesday, an obscure man in a monk's habit drew the sword of one of the soldiers and ran into the palace, intending to kill Nikephoros. Two of the bystanders ran up and rushed at him, and he wounded them badly. He was seized and tortured at length, but claimed he was possessed by a demon and accused no one. Nikephoros had him locked in the stocks among the possessed. From this many took it as an omen of great evil for both the rulers and their subjects, as had happened in the case of the impious Nestorius. He was an ardent friend of the Manichaeans, now called Paulicians, and of the Athinganoi of Phrygia and

Lycaonia, his near neighbours, and delighted in their oracles and rites. When the patrikios Bardanes rose against him, he summoned these people and overcame Bardanes by their sorcery. He had a bull tied by the horns to an iron ring in a pit, bent down to the ground, and had it killed there, bellowing and writhing. Then he had Bardanes' garment ground in a mill turned backwards, used incantations, and won the victory, God permitting it because of the multitude of our sins. Under his reign these people were given the opportunity to live freely, and many of the more frivolous were corrupted by their unlawful doctrines. At the Hexakionion there was a false hermit named Nicholas, with those who had become his followers. They blasphemed against the true faith and the holy icons. Nikephoros took their side, grieving the patriarch and all who lived according to God. The patriarch often complained about them, and Nikephoros was angry with him for it. He took great delight in people who were at odds with one another, and he was hostile [?] to every Christian who loved his neighbour, as one who overturned the divine commandments. He was eager to bring lawsuits, with or without grounds, against every Christian in the prison of the Magnaura, so that no one would have time to speak out against his impieties. He ordered the military officers to treat bishops and clergy like slaves, to lodge in the bishops' residences and monasteries as if they owned them, and to use up their goods. He found fault with those who from of old had dedicated gold or silver vessels to God, and declared that the sacred things of the churches ought to be put to common use, as Judas said of the Lord's ointment. He criticized all the emperors before him as having no grip on the helm, and denied Providence altogether. He said that no one could become more powerful than the ruler, if the ruler chose to rule skilfully. But this man, struck down by God, "became futile in his reasonings". In February of the same fourth indiction, on the first Saturday of the holy Lenten fast, the Saracens fell upon Leo, the strategos of the Armeniacs, at [?] while he was carrying the theme's pay. They took the pay, along with a great number of men. It amounted to thirteen talents, that is, thirteen hundred pounds. Even so Nikephoros was not chastened or brought to stop his greed. Undeterred by such signs, like a new Ahab, more insatiable than Phalaris and Midas, he marched against the Bulgarians together with his son Staurakios. On the

[?] of the month of May he left the capital. He ordered the patrikios Niketas, the general logothete, to raise the public taxes of the churches and monasteries, and to charge the households of the officials eight years of back taxes. There was great lamentation. One of his genuine servants reproached him. This was Theodosios Salibaras, who was a patrikios, and he said, "Everyone is crying out against us, master, and in a time of trial they will all rejoice at our fall." Nikephoros replied, "If God has hardened my heart like Pharaoh's, what good can come to those under my hand? Theodosios, expect nothing from Nikephoros but what you see." The Lord knows that I heard this myself, from Theodosios' own lips. He gathered the armies not only from Thrace but also from the themes across the straits. He also gathered many poor men, armed at their own expense with slings and staves, who cursed him along with the soldiers, and marched against the Bulgarians. Krum was afraid of their numbers, and when they were at Markellai he asked for peace. But Nikephoros was held back by his own bad judgement and by the advice of his like-minded counsellors. After much wandering through trackless country, the bold coward recklessly entered Bulgaria on 20 July. It was the rising of the Dog Star, which brings utter ruin. He kept repeating, "Who will go and deceive Ahab?" and saying that whether it was God or the Adversary drawing him on, everything [?]. Before he entered, Byzantios, his intimate servant, fled from Markellai to Krum, carrying off imperial clothing and a hundred pounds of gold. Many took his flight as an omen of evil for Nikephoros. For three days after the first engagements he seemed to be succeeding. He did not ascribe the victory to God, who gave the success, but proclaimed only the good fortune and good judgement of Staurakios, and threatened the officers who had opposed the invasion. He ordered animals, infants and people of every age to be slaughtered without mercy. He left the bodies of his own countrymen unburied and cared only about gathering the spoils. He put locks and seals on Krum's treasuries and secured them as if they were already his own. He cut off the ears and other limbs of Christians who touched the spoils, and he burned what was called Krum's palace. Meanwhile Krum humbled himself and declared, "See, you have won. Take whatever you please, and depart in peace." But

he, the enemy of peace, would not accept it. Krum was enraged by this. He sent men to block the entrances and exits of the country with wooden barricades. When Nikephoros learned of this, he was at once as if struck by thunder and went about not knowing what to do. He told his companions they were doomed: "Even if we grew wings, let no one hope to escape destruction." These preparations went on for two days, Thursday and Friday. On the night of Saturday the noise and tumult of armed men could be heard around Nikephoros and his companions, the sound of troops forming for battle, and it unnerved everyone. Before daybreak the barbarians attacked the tent of Nikephoros and those of the magnates with him and killed him miserably. Among those killed were the patrikios Aetios, the patrikios Peter, the patrikios Sisinnios Triphylles and the patrikios Theodosios Salibaras, who had grieved the blessed Irene and done her harm. Others killed were the eparch, a patrikios, and Romanos, a patrikios and strategos of the Anatolics, along with many other protospatharioi and spatharioi and the officers of the tagmata. The domestic of the Excubitors, the droungarios of the imperial Watch, the strategos of Thrace and many officers of the themes also fell, with countless men. The whole flower of the Christians was destroyed. All the arms were lost, and the imperial equipment too. May Christians never again see the hideous events of such a day, for it was all beyond lamenting. This happened on 25 July, in the fourth indiction. Krum cut off Nikephoros' head and hung it on a stake for many days, to display it to the peoples who came to him and to shame him. Afterwards he took it, stripped the skull bare, covered it with silver on the outside and, boasting, made the rulers of the Slavs drink from it. In one day many women were widowed and many children orphaned, and the lamentation could not be restrained. Even so, his death was a consolation to many. None of the survivors gave a precise account of how he was killed. Some say that Christians also wounded him after he fell. His effeminate servants, with whom he also slept,

[?] …the mighty hand of God drove you out to the Scythians and destroyed you there with your whole army. It left later generations a fearful tale and a dreadful report of the inscrutable judgements of his most wise providence.

…some perished by fire, and others died by the sword along with him. Never at any time did the Christians suffer a reign more grievous than his. For he outdid all who had reigned before him in greed, licentiousness and barbaric cruelty. To go through these things one by one would be hard for later generations to believe and laborious for us; but, as the proverb says, the cloth is plain from its hem. His son Staurakios was also mortally wounded in the right side of the spine. He barely came out of the battle alive and reached Adrianople, sorely tormented by the wound. Stephen, patrician and domestic of the Scholae, with Theoktistos the magistros also present, proclaimed Staurakios emperor. He then addressed the surviving army against his own father, and this greatly pleased them. Michael the kouropalates had escaped unharmed, and his friends pressed him hard to be proclaimed emperor, but he refused because of his oaths to Nikephoros and Staurakios. Stephen the domestic opposed this, hoping that Staurakios would live, while Theoktistos the magistros worked for Michael's accession to the throne. Staurakios bled without measure through his urine, and his thighs and legs withered; he came to Byzantium on a litter. The patriarch Nikephoros, who was very devoted to him, advised him to propitiate God and to compensate those whom his father had wronged through his greed. But he, the true heir of his father's mind, said he could not repay more than three talents. That was a small fraction of his father's injustices. Yet even over this he hesitated, expecting to live. Having his father's implacable temper, he frequently heaped insults on Theoktistos the magistros, Stephen the domestic and Michael the kouropalates. He also turned away entirely from his own sister Prokopia, believing that she had plotted against him, and from the schemes of the Augusta Theophano. For the wretched woman, being childless, at once hoped to rule the empire in imitation of the holy Irene. Staurakios, seeing that his condition was incurable, was eager either to secure the empire for his wife or to set up a democracy for the Christians, on top of the evils that had gone before. Alarmed at this, the patriarch Nikephoros, Theoktistos the magistros and Stephen the domestic passed from bitter enmity to friendship with one another and with Michael the kouropalates.

They came to this agreement at the end of September of the fifth indiction. On the evening of the first of October Staurakios summoned Stephen the domestic and asked him how he might bring Michael, his brother-in-law, out of his house in order to blind him. Stephen said that this was impossible at that hour, because of the force around Michael and the security of his house. Staurakios then begged him to let no one know what had been said. Stephen persuaded him with plausible words to be at ease, and then spent the whole night gathering the remaining troops of the tagmata, with their own officers, in the Covered Hippodrome, in order to proclaim this same Michael emperor. When the whole senate came to the palace at dawn, they proclaimed him emperor, as will be told next. The patriarch Nikephoros demanded from Michael a written pledge in his own hand concerning the orthodox faith. In it he was to promise to keep his hands unstained by Christian blood, and not to beat men in holy orders, monks, or anyone on the ecclesiastical register at all.

Anno Mundi 6304. Michael, emperor of the Romans.

In this year, on 2 October, in the fifth indiction, on the fifth day of the week, at the first hour, Michael, the most pious kouropalates, was proclaimed emperor of the Romans in the Hippodrome by the whole senate and the tagmata. When Staurakios heard of his proclamation he immediately cut off his hair and put on monastic garments, through the monk Symeon, a relative of his, and he called urgently for the patriarch. The patriarch came to the palace, and together with the emperor Michael and his sister he earnestly begged Staurakios not to be grieved at what had happened: it had been done not by conspiracy but because his life had been despaired of. But Staurakios, raging with his father's wickedness, would not accept this, and said to him: "You will not find a better friend than him." At the fourth hour of the day Michael was crowned by the patriarch Nikephoros at the ambo of the Great Church, and there was general rejoicing. He gave the patriarch

fifty pounds of gold, and the clergy twenty-five. Being magnanimous and free from love of money, he consoled all who had been wronged by Nikephoros' greed, and won over the senate and the armies with gifts. On the 12th of the same month Prokopia was crowned Augusta in the triclinium of the Augusteus, and she honoured the senate with many gifts. To the wives of the thematic soldiers killed in Bulgaria he gave five talents of gold. He enriched Staurakios' wife Theophano, who had become a nun, and her relatives, who had lived wretchedly under Nikephoros. Among other gifts he gave her a distinguished house called ta Hebraika to serve as a monastery, and Staurakios was buried there. He enriched all the patricians and senators, bishops, priests and monks, soldiers and poor, both in the imperial city and in the themes. As a result, within a few days the boundless avarice of Nikephoros, through which he had come to a bad end, was wiped out. Besides his many excellent ways he was pious and most orthodox, and he grieved over those who had separated from the holy Church on any pretext, reasonable or unreasonable. He never stopped urging the most holy patriarch, and all who were able to work for the common peace. Among those he hastened to reunite with the Church were Theodore, the abbot of Stoudios, Plato, and Joseph, archbishop of Thessalonike and Theodore's brother, who were being held in harsh prisons along with the leading men of their monastery; and he accomplished this. He also sent to Charles, king of the Franks, concerning peace and a marriage alliance for his son Theophylaktos. And Nikephoros, the most holy patriarch, sent synodal letters to Leo, the most holy pope of Rome; for before this

[…concerning] the union, he continues thus: "A certain scandal has been removed from our midst, on account of which there was also a disagreement with the one holding the hierarchy. The rulers entreated, and the most holy [patriarch] answered in defence [?] that everything that had happened was due to pressure [?] — that everything that had happened was due to the pressure of the reigning emperor. Then [?] … and the [?] towards him: that nothing is so dear to God, nothing so good, as peace and concord, when concord [?] …; and that this involves no transgression of God's commandment, nor indeed any violation of a canon, as the present case has been shown to be, in so far as we, for our part, have allowed what stood between us to be removed, since it is of the same kind as things that happened long ago in the time of the God-bearing Fathers and were likewise overlooked by way of economy. Or rather, since the precise examination of these matters is reserved for the impartial Judge in the age to come." Removed from the midst.

for he had been prevented by Nikephoros from doing this. On 25 December of the fifth indiction, Michael, the most serene emperor, had his son Theophylaktos crowned emperor by the patriarch Nikephoros at the ambo of the Great Church, on the fifth day of the week. He offered costly adornments to the holy altar: gold vessels set with precious stones, and curtains of antique workmanship, splendidly woven of gold and purple and decorated with wonderful holy images. He also gave the patriarch 25 pounds of gold and the holy clergy a hundred pounds, adding splendour to the holy feast and to his son's proclamation. Moved by great zeal for God, the most pious emperor decreed the death penalty for the Manichaeans, now called Paulicians, and for the Athinganoi in Phrygia and Lykaonia, at the urging of Nikephoros the most holy patriarch and of other pious men. But he was turned from this by other, wrong-headed counsellors on the pretext of repentance, though it was impossible for those caught in that error to repent. In their ignorance these men taught that it is not lawful for priests to pronounce sentence of death against the impious, and in this they contradicted the divine Scriptures at every point. For Peter, the chief of the apostles, put Ananias and Sapphira to death for a mere lie, and the great Paul cries out that those who do such things are worthy of death, and that concerns bodily sin alone. How, then, are they not opposed to the apostles, when they rescue from the sword people who are full of every uncleanness of soul and body and given to the worship of demons? Yet the pious emperor Michael beheaded not a few of them. Staurakios, his back ulcerated from the mortal wound, so that no one could come near him because of the great stench, died on 11 January of the fifth indiction, having reigned in name for two months and six days. On 14 May, the sixth day of the week, there was a great eclipse of the sun lasting three and a half hours, from the eighth hour to the eleventh. On 17 June Michael marched out against the Bulgarians, and Prokopia went with him as far as Tzouroulos. Krum, the ruler of the Bulgarians, had taken Debeltos by siege and resettled its inhabitants elsewhere together with their bishop. Then, through the great folly of the emperor's misguided counsellors, the troops who had joined the emperor turned to conspiracy and insults, above all the men of the Opsikion and the Thrakesians. Michael calmed them with gifts

and silenced them with exhortations. The Bulgarians learned of the sedition in the armies and that the tagmata were out of order for fear of the war, and they gained a stronger hold over Thrace and Macedonia. Then the Christians abandoned Anchialos and Beroe and fled, though no one was pursuing them. They also abandoned Nicaea, the fort of Probaton and some other strongholds. Likewise the settlers living in Philippopolis, Philippi and the Strymon seized on this pretext and fled back to their own lands. This was God's wrath exposing the madness of Nikephoros, by which his apparent successes, in which he had boasted, quickly collapsed. Yet the many did not blame the false beliefs of the people and the abounding God-hated heresies of the Paulicians, the Athinganoi, the iconoclasts and the Tetradites, to say nothing of adulteries and fornications, licentiousness and perjury, hatred of brethren and greed, and other lawless deeds. Instead they turned their tongues against the divine and venerable icons and the monastic habit. They called blessed the God-abhorred and thrice-wretched Constantine, because he had triumphed over the Bulgarians, and claimed, as those wretches impiously said, that this was because of the piety he had. In the imperial city some armed themselves to overturn the orthodox faith after an ecumenical council, and wished to make blind men reign without God, those whose souls were themselves maimed. They planned to steal away by night the sons of Constantine the God-fighter, who were held under guard on the island of Panormos, and bring them to the army. But the Lord put them to shame by rousing the most pious Michael to vindicate the truth. Having spoken sincerely and fittingly to the people about the faith, he returned to the reigning city. Then, with a wise plan, he struck fear into the many who were plotting innovations by means of a few punishments. He exiled the blind sons of Constantine to Aphousia. One of the wandering hermits, a fellow sorcerer of Nicholas the Hexakionite, had scraped and pierced [?] an icon of the all-holy Mother of God, and Michael had his tongue cut out; he died, tongue and body together. Nicholas, who shared their views, promised to repent, and Michael paraded [?] him before everyone, confessing his own misdeeds. He then handed him over to a monastery so that he could no longer live as he pleased. Michael addressed the people at a silention in the Magnaura and made known the doctrines of his pious and godly

mind. He confiscated the property of the Athinganoi and sent them into exile through Leo, the strategos of the Anatolikon. In August of the fifth indiction Thebith marched against the Christians. Leo, the strategos of the Anatolikon, engaged him and won distinction, killing two thousand men and capturing horses and equipment. Muhammad, the eldest son of Harun, who held the rule of the nation, engaged his brother Abdallah in inner Persia and was defeated, and he fled to Baghdad and held it. Another usurper seized Damascus, two men divided Egypt and Africa between them, and yet another occupied Palestine like a brigand.

Anno Mundi 6305.

In this year Krum, the ruler of the Bulgarians, again sent an embassy to the emperor Michael through Dargamer concerning peace. He asked for the treaty made in the time of Theodosios of Adramyttion and the patriarch Germanos with Kormesios, who was then lord of Bulgaria. That treaty set the frontier from Meleona in Thrace and provided for robes and red-dyed skins up to the value of thirty pounds of gold. It also required that refugees on each side be returned to the other, even if they happened to be plotting against the authorities. Merchants travelling into either country were to be certified by sigillia and seals, and [those without them were to have] their goods [confiscated] and brought into the public treasury [?]. He also wrote threats to the emperor: "If you do not

hasten to make peace, I shall march against Mesembria, and the decision will be on your head." When the emperor received this, he rejected the peace at the urging of his evil counsellors. On the pretext of piety, or rather out of ignorance, and to the common ruin, those misguided counsellors kept saying that refugees must not be handed over. As evidence they cited the Lord's saying in the Gospel: "Whoever comes to me I will never cast out." In the middle of October Krum drew up against Mesembria with siege engines, mangonels and siege towers. He had learned to use them in the time of Nikephoros, the destroyer of the Christians, in this way. An Arab who had come to baptism and was highly skilled in mechanics was enlisted by Nikephoros and stationed at Adrianople. Nikephoros gave him no support or reward worthy of him, but instead even cut his pay, and when he complained he had him severely beaten. Driven to despair by this, the man fled to the Bulgarians and taught them the whole art of siege engines. With these Krum attacked Mesembria, and since no one opposed him because of great negligence [?], he took it within the month. On 1 November the emperor, hard pressed, summoned the patriarch and took counsel about peace. Metropolitans were also present, those of Nicaea and of Cyzicus, together with the misguided counsellors. The patriarch and the metropolitans, along with the emperor, favoured peace, but the evil counsellors, with Theodore the abbot of Stoudios, overturned it. They said: "We must not embrace a peace that overturns the divine commandment, for the Lord declared: Whoever comes to me I will never cast out." They did not know what they were saying or what they were so confidently asserting. First, not one of them had fled to us, yet we betrayed those within the fold when we could have saved them by making peace. Second, even if a rare few had fled to us, we ought rather to have sought the safety of the many, our own people, than to grow rich on uncertain and doubtful gains. For it is dearer to God that many be saved than few, and to suffer great losses for a small gain is the height of folly. Moreover, according to Paul, whoever does not provide for his own household has denied the faith and is judged worse than an unbeliever. And how is one to be "peaceable with those who hate peace," unless perhaps these men are wiser than Paul and David? And who now is wiser than the thrice-blessed Germanos, except, in their own soul-destroying conceit, the evil counsellors who

prevented peace? These things happened on 1 November, as has been said. On the fourth of the same month a comet appeared in the form of two bright moons, which joined together and then separated again into various shapes, so that it took on the form of a headless man. On the next day the pitiful news of the capture of Mesembria reached us, and it terrified everyone with the expectation of still greater evils. The enemy found the city filled with everything needed for human habitation and seized it together with Debeltos. Among the spoils they found 36 bronze siphons, no small quantity of the liquid fire that is shot through them, and a great deal of gold and silver. In the same year many of the Christians of Palestine, both monks and laymen, and others from all Syria, reached Cyprus, fleeing the boundless ill-treatment of the Arabs. Complete anarchy had taken hold of Syria, Egypt, Africa and all their dominions, and murders, robberies, adulteries, licentiousness and every God-hated deed were committed in the villages and cities by that God-accursed nation. In the holy city of Christ our God the venerable places of the holy Resurrection, of Calvary and the rest were profaned. Likewise the famous lavras in the desert, those of Saint Chariton and Saint Sabas, and the other monasteries and churches were laid waste. Some were killed as martyrs, while others reached Cyprus, and from there Byzantium. The pious emperor Michael and the most holy patriarch Nikephoros received them kindly. To those who came to the city they gave a distinguished monastery. To the monks and laymen who remained in Cyprus they sent a talent of gold, and they cared for them in every way. Michael was kind and gentle towards everyone, but he had no grip on the management of affairs, being enslaved to Theoktistos the magistros and the other officials. In February two Christians who had fled from Bulgaria informed the emperor that Krum was hastening to ambush the people in Thrace in a sudden attack. On the 15th of the month the emperor went out of the city, and by God's providence Krum turned back without achieving anything, having lost a good many men. The emperor reached Adrianople, set its affairs in order and returned with joy. And going up to the monastery of Saint Tarasios the patriarch, and celebrating his memorial service together

…with Procopia the Augusta, he [?] his holy tomb with silver plating weighing ninety-five pounds. After the capture of Mesembria, the emperor rejected Krum's peace terms and raised troops from all the themes. He ordered them to cross into Thrace before spring, which angered everyone, especially the Cappadocians and the Armeniacs. When the emperor set out with the tagmata in May, Procopia the Augusta again went out with him, as far as Aqueduct near Heraclea. The troops resented this and turned to abuse and slander against Michael. On the fourth of May there was an eclipse of the sun at about the twelfth degree of Taurus, [?] in the ascendant as the sun was rising, and great fear fell on the crowds. The emperor roamed about Thrace with his generals and armies. He neither marched against Mesembria nor did anything else needed to destroy the enemy, but simply trusted the empty words of his advisers, who knew nothing of war and claimed that the enemy would not dare come against him while he was encamped in his own country. And the mass of their own countrymen was a heavier burden than a barbarian invasion: lacking the necessities of life, they ravaged the local people with plundering and trespass. Around the beginning of June, Krum, the leader of the Bulgars, with his own armies, suspecting that the forces of the Christians were very numerous [?]… When he had encamped at Versinikia, about thirty miles from the imperial camp, Leo, patrician and general of the Anatolics, and John Aplakes, patrician and general of Macedonia, were very eager to fight them, but were prevented by the emperor through his evil advisers. While the City was holding a litany with the patriarch in the church of the Holy Apostles, some impious followers of the foul heresy of the God-hated Constantine prised open the gate of the imperial tombs. No one noticed because of the press of the crowd, and they arranged for it to fly open suddenly with a crash, as though by some divine wonder. Rushing inside, they threw themselves down before the tomb of the deceiver, calling on him and not on God, and saying, 'Arise and help the state that is perishing!' They then spread the rumour that he had risen on horseback and was going out to fight the Bulgars: he who dwells in Tartarus with the demons! The prefect of the city arrested them. At first they falsely claimed that the gates of the tombs had opened of their own accord by God's doing. But when they stood before the prefect's tribunal and [?] in their testimony, they confessed the whole drama of the prising-open before any torture was applied. He punished them as they deserved and sent them off in a public procession, proclaiming the reason for their punishment. [Textual notes: 'with silver plating' A, 'and with silver plating' vulg.; 'Aug.' vulg.; 'at this' A, other readings 'this' and 'of this' vulg.; 'Mesembria' A, 'Mesembria' vulg.; 'evil advisers' A, 'bad advisers' vulg.; 'prefect' A; 'I declare' [?].]

…For this is how the devil, the inventor of wickedness, had trained the soldiers: not to blame their own sins, but the orthodox faith handed down from the fathers, and the holy habit of the monks, the school of godly philosophy. Many of those who uttered these blasphemies were Christians in outward form only. In truth they were Paulicians. Unable to show their foul doctrines openly, they used this pretext to corrupt the ignorant. They called Constantine, that man of Jewish mind, blessed, as a prophet and a victor, and embraced his heresy so as to overturn the incarnate dispensation of our Lord Jesus Christ. On the twenty-second of June the Christians and the Bulgars drew up for battle not far from Adrianople. The Christians failed terribly in the fighting, and the enemy won so completely that most of the Christians fled headlong without even seeing the first clash. Krum was astonished and thought that what was happening must be some kind of ambush, so he held his men back from the pursuit for a little while. But when he saw them fleeing in disorder, he gave chase and killed great numbers, and his men also captured the baggage train and plundered it. The emperor returned to the City in flight, cursing the troops and their commanders, and even swearing that he would abdicate. Meanwhile he also discussed with Leo, patrician and general of the Anatolics, taking over the throne, since Leo was pious and very brave and well suited in every respect. When Leo would not agree at all, [?] him to take command of the themes, and the emperor himself reached the capital on the twenty-fourth of June. He wanted to lay down his power and appoint someone else, but his wife and the powerful men at court would not allow it. Nikephoros, the most holy patriarch, agreed with him in this, on the grounds that both he and the

…[Latin:] …that they took to flight in this way through cowardice and betrayed the cause. Some, however, rather credit Leo with having saved the forces and fought steadfastly, while the imperial troops deliberately played the coward and betrayed their own battle line, but not of the… [?]

…his children would be kept safe if [?] were appointed in this way. When the generals and the troops learned that the emperor had fled, they gave up on being ruled by him. They took counsel among themselves and begged Leo, the general of the Anatolics, to come to the aid of the commonwealth and take charge of the Christian state. For a time Leo wavered greatly. He weighed the hardship of the moment and the unbearable force of the barbarian onslaught, and he kept his integrity and loyalty towards the reigning emperors. But when he saw the enemy pressing on towards the City, he wrote to Nikephoros the patriarch, assuring him of his orthodoxy and asking to take power with his prayer and consent. Then he went to the Tribunal outside the City with the generals and the armies, and was proclaimed the most lawful emperor of the Romans. At midday he entered Constantinople through the Golden Gate and took possession of the palace. When Michael heard of Leo's proclamation, he ran to the chapel of the Forum with Procopia and their children, and they cut their hair and put on monastic garb. On the eleventh of July, in the sixth indiction, a Monday, the next day, Leo was crowned by Nikephoros the patriarch on the ambo of the Great Church. He ordered the walls of the City to be guarded night and day. He made the rounds in person, rousing everyone and urging them to be of good hope, since God would very soon work a wonder through the intercessions of the all-immaculate Theotokos and all the saints, and would not allow us to be utterly put to shame for the multitude of our sins. But Krum, the new Sennacherib, was elated by his victory. He left his own brother with his forces to besiege Adrianople, and six days after Leo's accession he came with his forces against the imperial city. He went round in front of the walls from Blachernae to the Golden Gate, displaying [?]

…the force around him [?]. After performing foul and demonic sacrifices in the meadow by the sea at the Golden Gate, he asked the emperor to let him fix his spear on the Golden Gate itself. When the emperor refused, he went back to his own tent. He marvelled at the walls of the City and at the emperor's well-ordered battle line, and gave up hope of the siege he had planned. So he turned to negotiation, and first made some proposals to test the prospects of peace. The emperor seized the opportunity and tried to have him speared. But because of the multitude of our sins he was prevented from carrying it through by the incompetence [?] of those who carried out the deed: they wounded Krum but did not strike a fatal blow. Enraged at this, the fiend sent a raiding party to Saint Mamas and burned the palace there. He loaded onto wagons the bronze lion of the hippodrome, together with the dragon of the Hydrion and some choice marbles, and went back. Then he laid siege to Adrianople and took it.
